--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This is the title page of the third edition of Girolamo Mercuriale's seminal work on physical education, printed in Venice in 1587.</meta>

<insert><unclear>M. A. H.</unclear></insert>

# GIROLAMO <note>original: "Hieronymi"</note>
## MERCURIALE <note>original: "Mercurialis"</note>

# ON THE ART OF GYMNASTICS
## In Six Books,

->IN WHICH ALL<-
->kinds, locations, methods, and benefits of ancient exercises,<-
->and finally, everything that pertains to the physical<-
->training of the human body, is diligently explained.<-

->*Revised and expanded for this third edition.*<-

->A work very useful not only for physicians, but also for everyone<-
->interested in learning about antiquity and the<-
->preservation of health.<-

## TO MAXIMILIAN II,
### EMPEROR.

<note>A large, ornate woodcut depicts the printer’s mark of the Giunta family: a fleur-de-lis (lily) set within an oval frame and flanked by the letters "L" and "A." The oval is framed by intricate scrollwork and floral designs. To the right, a circular ink stamp from a later Spanish collection identifies the book as belonging to the "Sagasta Library in Seville," featuring a heart pierced by arrows and topped with a cross.</note>

<insert>SAGASTA LIBRARY IN SEVILLE</insert>

->VENICE, 1587.<-
->**At the Giunta Press.**<-

<summary>This title page introduces Girolamo Mercuriale's influential treatise on the history and medical benefits of ancient exercise, dedicated to Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian II. This 1587 edition represents a refined and expanded version of what is considered the first modern text on sports medicine.</summary>
<keywords>Girolamo Mercuriale, physical education, ancient Greece, Roman exercise, sports medicine, Giunta Press, Venice, Maximilian II, health preservation</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This is the beginning of the dedication to Emperor Maximilian II. The catchword "gum" on the following page indicates the continuation of the word "legum" (of laws).</meta>

# TO MAXIMILIAN II.
## TO THE MOST INVINCIBLE EMPEROR.

### GIROLAMO MERCURIALE
->wishes perpetual happiness.<-

<note>A small decorative woodcut ornament (fleuron) features symmetrical floral and scroll motifs, common in 16th-century printing to fill space and add elegance.</note>

<note>A large historiated woodcut initial 'S' is set within a square frame. The letter 'S' is formed amidst a landscape of rolling hills and a building, surrounded by dense, leafy scrollwork. In the Renaissance, "historiated" initials contained scenes or figures relevant to the theme or simply for ornamentation.</note>

**S**hould I ever consider quite carefully with myself, **Most Invincible MAXIMILIAN**, how many and how great are the things that Emperors and the highest Princes have performed for the health and tranquility of mankind—both in war and in peace—I easily arrive at the opinion that almost all peoples and nations acted rightly and with the best justification when they deemed such leaders worthy of being numbered among the immortal Gods. <note>In the classical tradition, great rulers were often "apotheosized" or raised to divine status for their service to humanity.</note> Among those innumerable benefits which they have conferred upon the human race, nearly all the <term>liberal arts</term> <note>The "artes liberales" were the branches of knowledge suited for a free person, including grammar, rhetoric, logic, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note> claim a great share for themselves. For by offering the greatest rewards, rulers did not merely rouse these arts and lift them up when they were at times lying neglected, but they also so amplified their dignity that the rulers themselves almost seem to be their sole authors and restorers. Anyone can easily perceive this, who examines the history of military discipline, of laws...

<summary>In this opening dedication, Girolamo Mercuriale praises Emperor Maximilian II, arguing that great rulers deserve divine honors for their protection of humanity and their vital patronage of the liberal arts.</summary>
<keywords>Maximilian II, Girolamo Mercuriale, dedication, patronage, liberal arts, imperial history, health and tranquility</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Emperor Maximilian II. It picks up from the previous page's discussion on the role of rulers in fostering the arts and sciences, specifically transitioning from the "laws" mentioned at the end of the last page into a defense of the medical and gymnastic arts.</meta>

<meta>catchword: res (refers to "vires," the strength or forces of the enemy, which would begin the next page)</meta>

*...of laws, and the origin and growth of the other praiseworthy arts, without which this life of ours would hardly be worth living, should someone wish to recall them to mind. But, lest I become troublesome to a most wise Emperor by recounting things known everywhere to everyone, I shall propose one example: the medical art, the most useful of all. This art would undoubtedly either not exist at all, or certainly would not possess the splendor and elegance it shows today, had the kindness of Princes—without which all hard work usually fades away—not shone upon the great men who were its creators. Indeed, the writings of many learned men testify to how much help was brought to medicine in its infancy by Cadmus, Solomon, and Alexander, and in later times by Attalus, Ptolemy, Nero, Hadrian, Constantine, Justin, and many others.* <note>Mercuriale lists a mix of legendary and historical figures. In the Renaissance, it was common to attribute medical or scientific discoveries to ancient kings like Solomon or Alexander the Great to emphasize the dignity of the profession.</note> *Nevertheless, to set aside other matters for now, we must consider it a matter of no small importance that they built most magnificent and grand Gymnasia.* <note>The word "Gymnasium" here refers to the ancient Greek institution where citizens engaged in both physical training and intellectual discussion.</note> *By establishing the Gymnastic art within these places, they supported teachers and overseers who prepared men for a good and blessed life through exercises that benefit both the health of the body and the mind. For this is the very art that once allowed the Persian kings, the Spartans, the Athenians, and the Romans to excel so greatly in waging war that often, with a modest force, they [overcame] incredible [numbers] of the enemy...* <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "res" indicates the next page begins with "vires," referring to the "forces" of the enemy.</note>

<summary>Mercuriale argues that the medical and gymnastic arts owe their existence and prestige to the patronage of great rulers throughout history. He specifically highlights how ancient gymnastics was used to cultivate both physical health and military dominance.</summary>
<keywords>medical art, gymnastics, patronage, Maximilian II, ancient history, physical education, health of body and mind</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Emperor Maximilian II, following the author’s discussion on how ancient rulers supported the medical and gymnastic arts. The previous page ended mid-sentence, describing how ancient exercises "bene..." (fitted/benefited) men. The catchword "res" from the previous page begins this page's first word, "vires" (implied) or "res" (matters/powers).</meta>

<sig>* iij</sig>
<meta>catchword: men</meta>

*...broke the power [of enemies], routed countless forces, and finally subjected so many kingdoms and so many nations to their rule that they cannot easily be recounted even by counting. Equipped with this same strength, there was no lack of Princes who dared to compete in physical power against any Athlete. We have received word that such men included Cyrus, Nero, Trajan, Antoninus, and Severus.* <note>Mercuriale lists several Roman Emperors (and the Persian King Cyrus) known for their physical vigor or interest in the games. Trajan and Antoninus were often idealized as "good" emperors, while Nero was infamous for his obsession with public performance.</note> *Beyond the fact that it is handed down in memory that they preserved their health and became exceptionally strong through this art alone, it is likely they also did this so that they might invite others to these same exercises by their own example. Who is unaware that, with the help of this kind of art, the ancient governors of kingdoms and provinces introduced the spectacles of athletes and gladiators—wisely devised to keep their subjects loyal and dutiful?* <note>The author suggests that public games were not just for entertainment, but a clever political tool (social control) used by rulers to maintain order and keep the population disciplined.</note> *I shall not even mention the many other benefits which gymnastics, in the time when it flourished, always most abundantly provided for the perfection of human happiness. But, the more benefits we know have flowed from this art, the more we must grieve that, by some miserable fate, it has perished along with many other studies of the finest arts, and is now utterly extinct. Because of this, there are very few in this time who attain that old military strength and true health. Instead, so many types of diseases infest us daily; it is reasonable to believe the ancients did not experience these, thanks to their habit of exercising their bodies. However, although these things are so, [we must] nevertheless...* <note>original: "tamen" (implied by the catchword "men"). Mercuriale is transitioning from a lament about the loss of ancient knowledge to a reason for hope or his own effort to restore it.</note>

<summary>Mercuriale argues that ancient rulers used gymnastics to maintain their own health and to govern their subjects, lamenting that the disappearance of these physical traditions has led to the decline of modern health and the rise of new diseases.</summary>
<keywords>gymnastics, Roman Emperors, physical health, military strength, history of medicine, social order, ancient vs. modern health</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to Emperor Maximilian II. The previous page ended with a discussion on the benefits of ancient gymnastics, concluding that the more we learn of its advantages, the more we realize it can be restored. The catchword "men" from the previous page completes the word "tamen" (however/yet) at the start of this page.</meta>

*...[yet] there is no doubt, most wise Emperor, that by the benefit of those writers in whose works some crude and shadowed outline of that art remains, it can be rescued from oblivion and brought forth again into the sight and light of men. This is possible if both the favor of Princes is present for this task, and if learned men skilled in antiquity are found who do not refuse to apply themselves to this study and to strain every nerve of their talent.* <note>Mercuriale is arguing that ancient knowledge isn't lost forever; it just requires two things: royal funding ("the favor of Princes") and hard-working scholars.</note> *Furthermore, why no one in our current age has undertaken a province of this kind, I certainly do not dare to declare; I know only this one thing: that just as the matter is of the greatest utility, so it is a task of immense labor.*

*And I, although there were many things that could have deterred me from it, nevertheless eventually began the task. Those things relevant to this subject which I had observed while reading various authors, I collected into one body, as it were, and reduced into a commentary.* <note>original: "commentarium." In the Renaissance, a 'commentary' was a serious scholarly work that gathered and explained fragments of ancient knowledge.</note> *This was done by me with great mental effort and zeal—with an outcome, however, as I have learned from the testimony of many, that I dare say was not unsuccessful.*

*This is the same reason that urged me—even though I produced these books and published them for the public dedicated to the most wise and prudent Cardinal Alessandro Farnese* <note>Alessandro Farnese (1520–1589) was a massive patron of the arts and sciences in Rome. Mercuriale served as his personal physician for seven years, which gave him access to the great libraries of Rome.</note> *at the time I was serving as his physician in Rome—nevertheless, even though I am entangled in the duty of public teaching and frequent visits to the sick, I took them up again in my hands during these last months. I have changed some things and added many others, including illustrations of certain exercises represented from ancient monuments...* <note>Mercuriale is famous for being one of the first to use detailed woodcut illustrations to show how ancient athletes actually moved, based on his study of Roman ruins and coins.</note>

<summary>Girolamo Mercuriale explains that while restoring ancient gymnastics is a massive labor, he has successfully compiled a scholarly "commentary" on the subject. He notes that this new edition has been expanded and updated with illustrations based on ancient archaeological finds, despite his busy schedule as a physician and professor.</summary>
<keywords>Hieronymus Mercurialis (Girolamo Mercuriale), Emperor Maximilian II, Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, De Arte Gymnastica, history of medicine, ancient monuments, classical scholarship, restoration of antiquity</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues Girolamo Mercuriale’s dedication to Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian II. The previous page mentioned that Mercuriale had first published a less refined version of this work under the patronage of Cardinal Alessandro Farnese. The word fragment "tis" at the start of this page completes "commentariis" (commentaries) from the previous page's final sentence.</meta>

...[these commentaries] I have so refined that I do not fear but that they will come forth into the light much more pleasing and delightful (just as second efforts are always better). <note>original: "posteriores curae esse meliores." A Latin proverb suggesting that revision leads to a superior work.</note> From this it has also come to pass that, although I previously did not dare, I have not hesitated now to dedicate them to Your Majesty out of my respect for you. 

Especially since, if any patron is to be sought for the renaissance of Gymnastics, it is certain that no one is better than you. <note>Mercuriale is positioning the Emperor as the modern successor to the Roman Emperors who originally funded and managed public physical training.</note> For just as the Emperors of old established, increased, and brought fame to this art, you likewise—given your supreme authority, power, and ready desire to serve the human race—are both able and willing to restore it to its original splendor and ancient dignity from its currently lost state. 

It also happens that I believed I would do something very pleasing to Cardinal FARNESE—to whom, after God, I confess I owe everything, and whom I have always known to be a most devoted admirer and a tireless herald of your praises—if I were to bring this work to Your Majesty in his name. The work was born under his own roof <note>original: "in ipsius laribus natum." Mercuriale served as the household physician to Cardinal Alessandro Farnese in Rome while researching this book.</note> and was published in his name when it was less polished; now, I offer it to Your Majesty rendered more perfect, richer, and more beautiful. 

Therefore I pray that, with that incomparable greatness of soul for which you are known, you might deign to accept this gift—which, though it is unequal to Your Majesty’s status, is nonetheless the best my humble means can offer—and that you might count me among your subjects, protecting and cherishing me. For although I...

<meta>This page concludes Girolamo Mercuriale’s dedication to Emperor Maximilian II. It follows his explanation that while the first edition of "De Arte Gymnastica" was published under Cardinal Farnese, this new, improved version is being offered to the Emperor as the ultimate patron of the "restoration" of ancient physical culture. The text begins mid-sentence, transitioning from his humble offering to a comparison of himself with other imperial courtiers.</meta>

to those who, excelling in every kind of discipline and art, serve Your Majesty, I am not unaware that I am not to be compared. Nevertheless, if my spirit is considered, I have no doubt that, just as no one’s devotion to Your Majesty is more ardent, nor their respect greater, I might also seem not unworthy of some place in your favor among others. 

May God, Most Good and Great, <note>original: "Deus Optimus Max." This title, originally used for Jupiter in ancient Rome, was frequently used by Renaissance humanists to refer to the Christian God.</note> preserve Your Majesty safe and happy for many years for the sake of the health of the Christian world.

->Padua, August 1st, 1573.<- <note>original: "Patauy, Kal. Sext. CIƆ IƆ LXXIII." Mercuriale was a professor at the University of Padua at this time. The date uses the Roman "Kalends of Sextilis" (the sixth month in the old calendar) and archaic Roman numerals for 1573.</note>

<summary>In this concluding portion of the dedication, Mercuriale humbly asks for the Emperor's favor and offers a blessing for his continued rule. The dedication is dated from Padua in 1573, marking the publication of this definitive second edition of his work on gymnastics.</summary>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page serves as a poetic frontispiece to the work. It follows the formal prose dedication to Emperor Maximilian II, transitioning from the author’s formal address to a celebratory poem by the Neo-Latin poet Lorenzo Gambara. This poem uses mythological metaphors to describe Mercuriale’s achievement in "resurrecting" the lost knowledge of ancient exercise.</meta>

# A POEM BY LORENZO GAMBARA
## OF BRESCIA.

> Just as the son of Coronis <note>Aesculapius, the god of medicine and son of Apollo and Coronis. According to myth, he was so skilled that he could bring the dead back to life.</note>—once most famous in the medical arts—used the help and skill of his father Apollo to gather the limbs of Hippolytus <note>Hippolytus was a mythological figure who was dragged to death by his horses. Aesculapius gathered his scattered remains and restored him to life.</note>, which had been torn apart and scattered across his father’s fields; and just as he painstakingly fitted limb to limb and called the youth back from the shadows of the underworld—though he was already without the light of heaven and held in black Tartarus—back to the world above;
> 
> And just as he restored beauty to those limbs and light to those eyes, so that the body regained its youthful glow:
> 
> So now Girolamo Mercuriale, trusting in his own skill and the favor of his patron, Cardinal Farnese <note>Alessandro Farnese (1520–1589), a powerful prince of the Church and the original patron of this book.</note>, has gathered into one volume the Art of Gymnastics. This is the art in which our ancestors used to train themselves once they had left the starting gates <note>original: "relicto Carcere." In Roman chariot racing, the *carceres* were the stalls where the horses waited for the start of the race.</note>, while the people looked on.
> 
> One part of this work looks toward games; another part commemorates how men display themselves in decorated armor so they might become brave soldiers. A third part describes the things that keep mortals healthy and free from disease for as long as life remains. Furthermore, this section teaches the method by which people can extend their fragile lives for a long time, and lead a slow old age, free from suffering and worry.
> 
> All these things lay scattered and hidden for a long time in Cimmerian darkness <note>The Cimmerians were a mythical people described by Homer as living in a land of perpetual mist and darkness; the phrase became a common metaphor for total obscurity.</note>. But now, through great labor and intense study, they shine like new stars among the works of both Greek and Latin authors.

<image-desc>Six decorative printer's ornaments arranged in two horizontal rows of three, resembling stylized floral rosettes.</image-desc>

<summary>A commendatory poem by Lorenzo Gambara comparing Girolamo Mercuriale to the god of medicine, Aesculapius. Just as the god resurrected Hippolytus, Mercuriale is credited with resurrecting the ancient Greek and Roman "Art of Gymnastics" from historical obscurity.</summary>

<keywords>Lorenzo Gambara, Girolamo Mercuriale, Aesculapius, Hippolytus, Alessandro Farnese, Greek medicine, Roman exercise, Cimmerian darkness, resurrection of antiquity, Neo-Latin poetry</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the series of commendatory poems following the dedication. While the previous page featured Lorenzo Gambara, this page presents contributions from the Greek scholar Matthaios Devaris and the Portuguese humanist Achilles Statius, both of whom were part of the same Roman intellectual circle as Mercuriale.</meta>

# Matthaios Devaris. <note>Matthaios Devaris (c. 1505–1581) was a Greek scholar and scribe who worked in Rome, specifically at the Vatican Library, and was a close associate of Mercuriale’s circle.</note>

Just as in ancient times the son of Paeon <note>original: "Παιήονος υἱὸς." Paeon is a title for the god of healing, and his son refers to Aesculapius. According to myth, Aesculapius was so skilled a physician that he could restore the dead to life.</note> fitted the limbs of Hippolytus <note>Hippolytus was a mythological figure who was dragged to death by his horses. Aesculapius gathered his scattered remains and restored him to life.</note> back into the structure of a living body, so now Girolamo <note>original: "Ἱερώνυμος" (Hieronymus), the Latinized version of Girolamo Mercuriale's name.</note>, who stands at the summit of the healing art, has gathered the beautiful but dim remnants of a lost craft through the exercise of his skill. He has crafted it with his mind so that it is immortal once again and shall never die. He who reveals such beneficial works is equal to the gods; like the gods, he is worthy of immortal honor.

# Achilles Statius the Lusitanian. <note>Achilles Statius (1524–1581) was a celebrated Portuguese humanist and scholar who lived in Rome. "Lusitanian" is a classical term for someone from Portugal.</note>

With immense labor, you have gathered the training-ground <note>original: "Γυμνάσιον" (Gymnasion), referring to both the physical space and the system of ancient exercise.</note>—once so pleasant—which was scattered throughout all sorts of books. Because of this, Girolamo, you will support the souls of the wise; you are not only a pentathlete <note>An athlete who competes in five events.</note>, but you alone are a "pan-athlete" <note>original: "πάνταθλον." A clever play on words suggesting Mercuriale is a master of *all* contests and all knowledge.</note>.

# Achilles Statius the Lusitanian.

> Girolamo begrudges the Underworld <note>original: "Orco." Orcus was a god of the underworld, synonymous with Hades or Pluto.</note> its sick mortals, calling those who are half-dead back to the light of the heavens. 
> 
> Because he does this often, he is often praised, and the fame of his name flies through the three parts of the world. 
> 
> But now a new fame spreads: that he renews the extinct arts and the training-ground of the ancients. 
> 
> Well done, great man! Therefore, while you exercise the limbs of others with your voice <note>original: "Ore." Suggesting his teaching or writing.</note>, your own praise shall be on the lips of men.

<image-desc>Six decorative printer's ornaments arranged in two horizontal rows of three, identical to those on the previous page.</image-desc>

<summary>This page contains three short laudatory poems written by contemporary scholars Matthaios Devaris and Achilles Statius. They use the mythological metaphor of Aesculapius resurrecting the dead to describe Mercuriale’s scholarly "resurrection" of the ancient art of gymnastics.</summary>

<keywords>Matthaios Devaris, Achilles Statius, Aesculapius, Hippolytus, Pan-athlete, gymnasium, Underworld, medical fame</keywords>

# THE ART OF GYMNASTICS
## BOOK ONE

### On the Principles of Medicine.
### Chapter I.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'V' set within a square border. Inside the letter is a circular medallion depicting a classical figure, possibly a philosopher or physician, seated and holding a book or scroll. The surrounding space is filled with ornamental floral motifs.</image-desc>

**AS LONG AS** men were content with very few things and did not know lavish tables or sumptuous banquets, and remained entirely ignorant of the gradually introduced custom of social drinking—as is recorded to have been the case in those first ages—diseases neither appeared, nor were their names even known. For example, Plato recorded that until the time of Socrates, the name for "distillations" (which the Greeks call <term>catarrhs<note>original: "κατάῤῥους". In ancient medicine, this referred to a "down-flow" of excess humors, usually from the brain to the respiratory tract.</note></term>), a term than which nothing is more common today, was unknown. For this reason, it is certain that at that time there were either very few uses for medicine, or none at all, and no established principles; <margin>Book 3 of the *Republic*.</margin> even though Homer, the most ancient author, wrote that Egypt possessed many herbs and many medicines. 

But after the unspeakable plague of intemperance, the refined arts of cooks, the most delicate seasonings of feasts, and foreign blends of wines crept in among men, various kinds of diseases simultaneously and continually cropped up, forcing men to invent medicine. Indeed, they could have surely done without it forever, had not human—or rather, beastly—gluttony, the offspring of all vices, made the use of medicine the most necessary of all things. 

Medicine, however, although in that first origin it was quite crude and uncultivated—when those ancients (as Herodotus and Galen report) used to expose the sick in public <margin>In the book titled *The Physician*.</margin> so that everyone might teach another what they held to be useful and proven by experience—was in later ages wonderfully adorned by Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note>, the physician known as the "Epidaurian" among the Cyrenaeans. He made medicine, as it were, into something urban and elegant rather than rustic. Yet even he was by no means able to bring it to perfection, since he devoted his work only to the diseased and the faint, and always had that one pursuit of curing; he either did not know there was any care for the healthy, or he utterly despised it. His successors later understood this and considered the care of the healthy so worthy of esteem that they believed medicine without this *Gymnastics* to be entire- <meta>catchword: entirely</meta>

<summary>Mercuriale introduces the history of medicine, arguing that disease arose from human luxury and gluttony, and that while early medicine focused only on the sick, the ancients eventually realized that "Gymnastics" (exercise and hygiene) was a necessary part of the field.</summary>

...they realized that [medicine] was entirely incomplete and could in no way be perfect. And these men were the first: Herodicus of Selymbria and his disciple Hippocrates, who were seen to have added the preservative part of health—which is concerned almost exclusively with healthy bodies—to the curative medicine of diseases. They believed it to be no less a noble and skillful work to protect healthy men from diseases than to free those already afflicted by them. Hence medicine, which before had always been as if a virgin, was made pregnant by them, since previously it was only in charge of curing illnesses, but then was also appointed to the preservation of health. 

Whether Hippocrates forged that entire part of medicine which pertains to both the healthy and to the regimen of diet from the small tablets or other votive offerings dedicated in the temple of Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of healing; patients would sleep in his temples (a practice called "incubation") hoping for a miraculous cure or a dream-vision from the god.</note>; or whether he only developed the "clinical" part concerned with treating diseases—as Varro, Strabo, and Pliny <margin>Book 19, chapter 1.</margin> seem to have believed—is not entirely clear to me. However, it was certainly the custom for those freed from disease to write in the temple of that God what had been of help to them. This practice endured from those early times until the age of the Emperor Antoninus, not only in Greece but also in Italy. This can be understood especially from a marble tablet found in Rome in the temple of Aesculapius on the Tiber Island, which is preserved to this day in the Maffei household, and in which the following is read in Greek:

> In those days, an oracle gave a response to a certain blind man named Gaius, telling him to come to the sacred altar and kneel; then he should go from the right side to the left, and place five fingers upon the altar, and raise his hand and place it over his own eyes. And he saw correctly while the people were present and rejoicing that living virtues <note>original: "ζῶσαι ἀρεταὶ" (zosai aretai); here meaning "manifest powers" or "living miracles."</note> were performed under our Emperor Antoninus. *That is:*

> *IN those days, an oracle gave a response to a certain blind man named Gaius, that he should come to the sacred altar and bend his knees, then go from the right side to the left, and place five fingers upon the altar, and raise his hand, and place it over his own eyes: and he saw correctly with the people present and congratulating him that great miracles were being done under our Emperor Antoninus.*

...that knowledge could be extracted from that point by Hippocrates and, being established under certain rules and principles, was advanced to the form of an art. It is certain, however, that the most wise old man <note>A common honorific for Hippocrates.</note> discovered this not by any chance or fortune, but by those most divine powers of intellect and training in which he excelled. Just as with everything else, he found this knowledge, refined it once found, and joined it to the curative part of medicine. In these branches of medicine, his ancient predecessors do not deserve less praise simply because there were many diseases which it is clear they neither recognized nor indicated a way of curing. For it was not the laziness of the ancients or their lack of skill that caused this, but rather the infinite temptations of gluttony, insatiable lust, and immense voracity. As Seneca wisely argued, and after him Plutarch, new types of <margin>Seneca, Letter 95, 18; Plutarch, Symposiacs, Question 9.</margin> diseases were born, and are still born every day, of which some received a cure late, and others never. <margin>A</margin> ...passed a creature with many feet while urinating. In the same way, a youth at Athens expelled, along with much semen, a small, hairy serpent with many feet that began to walk immediately. So too, it is recorded that the grandmother of Timon in Cilicia lay hidden in caves for two months out of every year, known to be alive only by her breathing. Likewise, in the writings of Melonius, a sign of a certain 
<margin>From Book 1 of *On Abstinence from Animal Food*.</margin> liver condition is described, in which those who were afflicted would carefully observe and pursue domestic mice. Similarly, according to Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on various scientific and ethical subjects.</note>, a slave of the physician Craterus was seized by a new kind of disease, such that his flesh fell away from his bones. In our own times, that cursed and almost fatal French plague <note>original: "gallica... lues"; a common 16th-century term for syphilis.</note> began to harass every region. Thus, in no way should the blame be cast upon Hippocrates for things that happened either through the fault of later men, by chance, or by the will of God. For since these two previously mentioned 
<margin>B</margin> parts of medicine were advanced to the highest perfection by him, immortal thanks must always be given to his divine hands. 

Furthermore, it should be committed to eternal memory that both branches of medicine, just as they are truly distinct, equally possessed different names. One was called <term>preventive <note>original Greek: φυλακτική (phylaktikē)</note></term>, or <term>hygienic <note>original Greek: ὑγιεινή (hygieinē)</note></term>, and the other was called <term>therapeutic <note>original Greek: θεραπευτική (therapeutikē)</note></term>. These names were adopted based both on the work performed and the subject matter they deal with. Because these terms were chosen wisely and truly, they have never undergone any change among any people. Just as even down to later times, this long-standing custom remained among physicians: that they all establish two primary parts of medicine, calling one curative and the other preservative. For this reason, they usually encompass both under the common name of "medicine." 

<margin>C</margin> The curative part, which was discovered first due to greater necessity, obtained that name [of medicine] for itself. The preservative part, having been joined to it later, not only shared that name but also acquired such authority among some people that they judged that this alone should be called "true medicine." They argued that the curative part was uncertain, false, or a mere imposture of men striving to deceive others—namely, because it first uses bare conjectures and the lowest sorts of arguments to recognize diseases. Furthermore, they claimed that in this branch, almost everyone employs accidental remedies and unknown medications for the most part, and finally, they are not infrequently deceived in both judgment and treatment. 

However, anyone who wishes to calmly consider the nature of human calamities and the hardships of diseases—and what they would be like if the curative art did not provide relief—will easily recognize that those people are wandering in the gravest error. It seems it was not without the highest reason that the Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate (reigned 361–363 AD), who issued various edicts regarding the status and education of physicians.</note> appears to have promulgated this law in favor of physicians.

### On the parts of preventive medicine, and what is to be discussed. Chapter II.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a man (possibly a physician or scholar) seated at a desk within a room, looking towards a window.</image-desc>
**S**ince, therefore, there are two parts of medicine—one curative, the other preventive, also called **hygienic** <note>original Greek: <term>ὑγιεινή</term> (hygieinē)</note>—this latter part has been divided by some into three branches: **prophylactic** <note>original Greek: <term>προφυλακτικήν</term> (prophylaktikēn)</note>, which turns away future and looming diseases; **preservative** <note>original Greek: <term>συντηρητικήν</term> (syntērētikēn)</note>, which guards current health; and **restorative** <note>original Greek: <term>ἀναληπτικήν</term> (analēptikēn)</note>, by which those recovering from illness are refreshed. Although these were discovered last, as we have already demonstrated, they have nonetheless acquired as much splendor from the additions of many men as the first inventors would have hardly dared to hope for. This is due both to the abundance of things asserted for this preventive branch and the incredible utility it has been seen to provide in both past and present times. Furthermore, the things devised and organized by physicians to establish this branch are encompassed by four names, each of which includes various and complex matters under it. For it was agreed upon by Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose systems dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> and other medical authorities that good health can be preserved by just so many safeguards. These are: **things taken in** <note>original Greek: <term>τὰ προσφερόμενα</term> (ta prospheromena)</note>, **things excreted** <note>original Greek: <term>τὰ κενούμενα</term> (ta kenoumena)</note>, **external encounters** <note>original Greek: <term>τὰ ἔξωθεν προσπίπτοντα</term> (ta exothen prospiptonta)</note>, and **activities performed** <note>original Greek: <term>τὰ ποιούμενα</term> (ta poioumena)</note>. Those things **taken in** are defined as drinks and food, whether used as nourishment or as medicine. Those under **excretion** include sweats, feces, phlegm, urine, and all other similar things. **External encounters** include water, air, saltiness, the sea, oil, and...

<margin>A</margin> [These] are established in this manner. The actions [required for health] are comprised of exercises, studies, vigils <note>Periods of wakefulness or staying up late for work or prayer.</note>, sleep, sexual activity, anger, care <note>Specifically mental worry or anxiety.</note>, baths, and others of the same kind. From these, there is no thing, nor any aid conducive to defending health, that is not included under one of the four aforementioned types, which complete the entire art of preservation through appropriate quantity, quality, and timing. But since almost all these matters have been treated copiously by both the ancients and the moderns, yet regarding gymnasia or exercises—from which the gymnastic art was so celebrated and named among the ancients—almost nothing, or very little, is found handed down (and that which exists is confused and accidental), I have therefore decided to produce a complete treatise on these matters. This will cover the gymnastic art, called the "art of exercise" by the Latins, a task perhaps never fully completed by another. I am more inclined to do this 
<margin>B</margin> because Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note> left it in writing that this is by no means the least noble part of the faculty of preservation. Almost all authors testify that the art of exercise brings incredible utility both for averting future diseases, for safeguarding present health, and for restoring the infirm (which three parts make up the whole of the art of preservation). We ourselves shall demonstrate this most abundantly when we declare all these things both distinctly and copiously in these books, as the subject itself demands. First, what gymnastics itself is: how and when it was invented, increased, and perfected, and how many species it has. Next, what exercise is: how many kinds there are, and how they were performed by the ancients. Then, what that "quality, quantity, and timing" are, by which this art contributes so much to preserving good health. Finally, what benefits or what harms are to be expected from each 
<margin>C</margin> kind of exercise by those devoted to gymnastics. Once all these things have been diligently explained, I hope nothing will be left that could be desired in a treatise of this kind. I predict that all those devoted to health will embrace this work more eagerly because the part we are treating seems to excel the curative part of medicine as much as exercise surpasses drugs themselves. Regarding this, Galen and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the "Prince of Physicians," whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook for centuries.</note>, the most celebrated writers of medicine, have handed down that exercises can both dissolve <term>waste products</term> <note>original: "excrementa"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to all metabolic leftovers the body needs to expel, not just feces.</note> and expel them through the pores of sweat. Exercise is as superior to both food and "thinning" medicines as it is better to remove what is redundant without any discomfort to our body, rather than thinning out the liquid flesh and solid parts at the same time. For such discomforts are associated with hot and thinning medicines. However, exercise is so far from causing such things that it instead brings firmness

Indeed, <margin>E</margin> Diogenes, according to Stobaeus, used to say that Medea <note>A mythological sorceress famous for her rejuvenative powers.</note> was actually a wise woman, not a sorceress; she took the soft and effeminate bodies of men and strengthened them through gymnasia and exercises, rendering them robust and vigorous. From this, the rumor spread that she restored people to youth by boiling their flesh <note>A clever historical interpretation suggesting that the "heat" of the cauldron was actually the heat generated by intense physical training.</note>.

### What Gymnastics is, and how many kinds there are. Chapter III.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a landscape scene with buildings and trees.</image-desc>
**S**INCE there are four things by which the entire faculty of preserving health is fulfilled, no sane person would deny that the art of exercise is a certain portion of the fourth part. Since exercises are <margin>F</margin> placed among those things to be done (along among many others) which were declared by us as the fourth part of preservation, it is consistent with reason that gymnastics, which is concerned entirely with exercise, belongs to that category. Therefore, no one can deny that knowing this art pertains to the one who professes medicine. This is in opposition to Erasistratus <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–250 BC) who often disagreed with the Hippocratic school.</note> and others who sought to separate gymnastics from medicine. This is especially true because it is frequently found in the writings of Hippocrates, Plato, and Galen that exercises provide as many and as great benefits for leading a healthy life as almost any other instruments of medicine. But if Hippocrates wrote in his book *On Places in Man* that gymnastics and medicine are opposites because one requires change and the other does not, he was speaking only of that part of medicine which later writers called "clinical" <note>From the Greek *kline* (bed), referring to the treatment of bedridden patients as opposed to the preventative care of the healthy.</note>, which is concerned solely with healing those who are bedridden. <header>FIRST</header>

<margin>A</margin> [Some] have claimed that there are two arts concerned with the human body: medicine and gymnastics. They did not separate them for the same reasons as Erasistratus <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician known for his work on the circulatory and nervous systems.</note> and his followers, but rather followed the common usage of speech. Because gymnastics was discovered and attached to medicine later, people treated them as distinct for no other reason than this historical sequence. However, to understand what this "gymnastic art"—called by a Greek name—truly is, we must look to its definition or description. Although we have a splendid explanation in Plato, I believe it was declared more briefly and clearly by our Galen, who said: <term>Gymnastic art is the science of the power inherent in all exercises</term>. <note>original: "ἡ τέχνη γυμναστική ἐστιν ἐπιστήμη τῆς ἐν πᾶσι γυμνασίοις δυνάμεως"</note> That is to say, gymnastics is the art that knows the faculties of every exercise; or rather, the gymnastic art is the knowledge of the potential of all physical movements. In this passage, it must be <margin>B</margin> noted <margin>In the book *To Thrasybulus*.</margin> that Galen did not use the word "science" in its strictest sense, but in the common way authors often do. This is because gymnastics has a practical result as its goal, and since pure sciences are not considered to have a "work" or physical output, it is technically excluded from being a true science—even though it frequently contemplates the causes of the strength found in exercise. Furthermore, it should be noted that Galen, through this definition, distinguished gymnastics from **physical instruction** <term>paedotribica: the practical art of a trainer who teaches the specific techniques and maneuvers of exercises</term>. Gymnastics stands as the "empress," observing all the qualities and causes of exercises and commanding them; the latter exists as its servant. In this way, the **gymnast** was the one who rightly understood the powers of all exercises and prescribed them to different people as he judged fit for their health and good condition. <margin>C</margin> The **trainer**, on the other hand, was the one who demonstrated in practice how those exercises should and could be performed. Polybus <note>A student of Hippocrates and often cited as his successor.</note> explained this enigmatically with these words: <term>Physical trainers teach how to break the law according to the law, to do wrong justly, to deceive, to steal, to snatch, and to use force most honorably and most disgracefully.</term> <note>original: "παιδοτρίβαι τοῖον διδάσκουσι παρανομεῖν κατὰ νόμον, ἀδικεῖν δικαίως, ἐξαπατέειν, κλέπτειν, ἁρπάζειν, βιάζεσθαι, τὰ κάλλιστα, καὶ αἴσχιστα"</note> For if anyone evaluates the actions of wrestlers and others who were taught by trainers, they will clearly see how closely they resemble what Polybus wrote. Thus, the gymnast and the trainer were quite different. Nevertheless, because occasionally one person might fulfill both roles, some have not wrongly thought these two arts to be one and the same—just as sometimes the same person performs the duties of both a soldier and a Commander. Yet Galen insisted they be distinct: gymnastics is the name given to the knowledge of the qualities of exercise, which is more noble than the execution itself; while **physical training**...

But that gymnastics is truly such as we have declared, and that the <term>gymnast</term> <note>The theoretical expert who understands the effects of movement on the body.</note> and the <term>paedotriba</term> <note>The physical trainer or coach who oversees the actual performance of exercises.</note> differ, can also be proved by the testimony of Aristotle. In the beginning of the fourth book of his *Politics*, he left this written: 

*In all arts and sciences that exist perfectly—not regarding a specific part but regarding a whole genus—it is for one art to consider what is appropriate for each genus: such as what kind of exercise is suitable for what kind of body, and which is best (for it is necessary that the best suit the one most naturally well-disposed and well-provided); and which single exercise is best for the majority of people. For this belongs to the gymnastic art. By these words, it is clear enough both that gymnastics is called a "science" by Aristotle in almost the same <margin>F</margin> way it is by Galen, and also that gymnastics is distinguished from the physical trainer. 

But lest a definition escape those who understand both roles under the single name of "gymnastics"—a definition that explains the power of both at once—we might say this: 

**The gymnastic art is a certain faculty that contemplates the powers of all exercises and teaches their varieties through the work itself, either for the sake of preserving good health, or for the sake of acquiring and protecting the best physical condition.**

I said such is the goal of this art, not only to provide a full and perfect definition as far as possible, but also to show how this science differs from others that possess a similar form. For all the games of the ancients, both Greek and Roman, as well as the whole of athletics itself and the exercises performed for the sake of war, are concerned with almost all the same physical exercises...

### *On the subject of gymnastics, and its praises. Chapter IV.*

<image-desc>A square decorative woodcut initial letter "C" containing a landscape scene with figures, likely illustrating a classical or biblical theme.</image-desc>
SINCE we have now (unless I am mistaken) sufficiently explained what gymnastics is, and have separated it from its related disciplines, it remains for us to consider what its **subject matter** is. For just as no art is found—whether it be a master art <note>original: "architectonica," referring to a primary or governing science.</note> or one subordinate to it—that does not have some **end** or goal for its operations, likewise there is no art to which one cannot assign a specific **subject** around which its entire operation revolves. And <margin>E</margin> although the same subject often appears to belong to several arts, if the matter is weighed exactly, it will appear that the subjects of all arts are distinguished by their specific goals. This is because the same thing is considered by each art in a different way, under different conditions and properties. Thus it happens that the human body, which is truly the subject of many arts and disciplines, is considered by one in a way that it is not by another. For instance, insofar as the body is a natural thing capable of movement, the Physicist <note>In the 16th century, a "Physicist" referred to a natural philosopher studying the laws of nature.</note> contemplates it; insofar as it is capable of health or disease, it is subject to the Physician; and insofar as it is <term>*euekton* <note>original Greek: *εὔεκτον*. This term refers to a "well-conditioned" state or a body in peak physical habit.</note></term>, that is, capable of a **good habit of body**, it is considered by gymnastics (specifically the preservative branch) which is subordinate to medicine, and about which we shall speak.

Therefore, we define the human body, insofar as it is born to receive a good habit and to preserve itself and its health, as the subject of gymnastics. <margin>F</margin> As Galen also most clearly declared in that short book written to Thrasybulus <note>Galen's *Ad Thrasybulum* is a foundational text discussing whether health belongs to the art of medicine or gymnastics.</note>. Nor should it be inferred from this that Galen contradicts himself when elsewhere he wished for gymnastics to be separated from medicine. He intended for gymnastics to be a part of medicine in such a way that, just as a part is in some way distinct from its whole, so gymnastics is distinguished from medicine. For medicine, considering health and disease in the human body, strives to expel the latter and to obtain and preserve the former. But gymnastics strives to generate a **good habit** in a healthy body, and to maintain it as either a part or a sustaining cause of health. On account of this, its reputation among the ancients was so great that Plato and Aristotle (not to mention many others) judged that a Republic could not be at its best...

Since care must always be taken of the soul <note>original: "animi," referring to the mind or soul.</note>, and because the soul is unable to achieve anything weighty or worthy without the help of the body, one must certainly strive for the health and <term>good habit of the body</term> <note>original: "bonoque habitui." Furthermore, regarding how much the gymnastic art contributes to attaining this habit, and to both preserving and restoring health—to pass over the most certain testimonies of Plato and Aristotle—I will bring forward Galen alone. He boasted that he had restored nearly infinite weak individuals to a good habit, and likewise preserved countless others from falling into diseases through gymnastics alone. <margin>B</margin> Thus, we should in no way be surprised if our ancestors valued bodily exercises to such an extent that they not only built public and most magnificent places for exercising bodies, such as the gymnasia and the Roman <term>baths</term> <note>original: "thermae."</note>, but also designated a certain place for exercises in almost every private house, where they were in daily use.

### *At what time, and in what manner, gymnastics began. Chapter V.*

<image-desc>A square decorative woodcut initial letter "V" depicting a figure in a boat or chariot moving across water, with a town visible in the background.</image-desc>
ALTHOUGH Galen—the prince of all physicians after Hippocrates—was of the opinion that the gymnastic art had not yet been discovered in the time of Homer, but only had its beginning shortly before the time of Plato, <margin>C</margin> it nevertheless seems likely that certain seeds of it were sown and its first beginnings shone forth during the Trojan War described by that very Poet. This is unless we also admit that it could easily have existed much earlier, but was either not named at that time, nor cultivated and reduced to rules and the form of an art, or that it lacked writers to rescue it from destruction and oblivion. That certain principles of <term>gymnastics</term> <note>While we think of gymnastics as acrobatics, to the ancients it meant all physical training and athletics performed in the gymnasia.</note> existed [in the earliest times] can be easily understood by those who, in reading the books of the poet <note>Homer is often referred to simply as "the poet" in Renaissance scholarship.</note>, have noticed that the Greek soldiers occasionally exercised themselves in the discus, wrestling, running, the bow, and other such activities which later passed into the gymnastic faculty. This is frequently read in the eighth and twenty-third books of the *Odyssey*. However, as to how and in what order this art came to be, although we have nothing plainly explained, we can nevertheless arrive at it through a certain conjecture from those things which Plutarch recorded in the fifth book of his *Symposiacs* <note>original: "Sympoſiacorum," also known as *Table Talk*.</note>, problem 3. There, he relates that contests were first simple affairs, in which they held only victory and the crown as their goal. From these, the practice was later transferred to sacrifices, when those about to perform sacred rites for a God—and wishing to delight the people coming to the festivals—instituted contests. These, I believe, were finally introduced from the sacrifices into the gymnasia by degrees. In those first times, while men <margin>E</margin> led a temperate life and enjoyed perpetual health, they had this one pursuit: that they might become most fit for waging wars and overcoming enemies. Therefore, when they were at leisure, lest they be utterly consumed by idleness <note>original: "inertia."</note>, they occupied themselves with those exercises. Prizes were even set out for the victors, so that, enticed by the pleasure of them and inflamed by the hope of rewards, they might be disposed more willingly and accurately to fight sharply against the enemy. For this reason, Homer in the second book of the *Iliad* fashioned it in this manner:

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 14 regarding the historical progression of exercise. Having established that the earliest exercises were military and spontaneous, the author now explains how they became formalized into religious festivals and eventually integrated into medical practice.</meta>

<page-num>15</page-num>
<header>B O O K   O N E</header>

<margin>A</margin> From these and all the following points, it is clear enough that in those first centuries the purpose of exercises was both a certain delight and the hope of obtaining rewards, as well as the agility and skill for winning wars and overcoming enemies. After those times, when the worship of the Gods and the celebration of sacrifices began to grow, these exercises were established during the festivals of the Gods so that the men flocking to them might participate more eagerly and willingly. There, they were considered pleasing to both Gods and men. Furthermore, so that there would be no lack of participants, rewards—which usually incite men to dare anything—were established for the contests, making them more desirable and excellent, as Aristotle suggests. In these exercises, since men competed solely for the sake of prizes, which are called <term>athla</term> <note>original Greek: "ἆθλα" (athla), meaning prizes or trophies of a contest.</note> by the Greeks, the practitioners were named <term>athletes</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀθληταὶ" (athletai).</note>, <margin>Proven in Aristotle's *Politics*, Book 3, Problem 8.</margin> who were also called <term>asketai</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀσκηταὶ" (asketai), meaning those who practice or train; this is the root of the word "ascetic."</note> by the Attic Greeks (as Erotianus records) and "Athletes" by the Latins. Among the Latins, the contest itself took the name of a "game" <note>original Latin: "ludi."</note>, because such contests were performed not only at the festivals of the Gods, but also in Amphitheaters, and (before theaters were built) in the forum or in private places for the amusement of the people, just as there were <term>agones</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀγῶνες" (agones), meaning assembly or contest.</note> among the Greeks. 
<margin>B</margin> For the Olympics at Pisa (or in Elis), the Nemean games at Cleonae, the Isthmian games on the Isthmus itself, and the Pythian games at Delphi were the same kind of events for them as the Capitoline, Secular, and other such games were for the Romans. In all of these, besides the prizes, such great honors were established for the victors that they not only received praise while standing in the assembly with a palm and a crown, but also (to use the words of Vitruvius <note>Vitruvius was a famous Roman architect and engineer whose writings often touched on the cultural practices of his time.</note>) when they returned to their own cities, they were carried through the city walls and into their homelands in triumph upon four-horse chariots, 
<margin>C</margin> and they enjoyed perpetual honors through established taxes paid from the public treasury. But since we are not meant to speak of these things here, let us return to our subject. So long as the life of men remained frugal, these were the only purposes for exercise. But in truth, as luxury increased and many were held back by long-lasting illness, exercises finally began to be established for the sake of restoring health, curing weakness, and acquiring a good physical constitution. This occurred a little before the age of Hippocrates, when that famous Herodicus <note>Herodicus of Selymbria was a 5th-century BC physician considered the father of sports medicine.</note> (as Plato writes) joined <term>gymnastics</term> to medicine. <margin>In the third book of the *Republic*.</margin> Previously, gymnastics held authority and a place only in sacrifices, games, and military training; in my opinion, this change was nothing other than the application of those contests and exercises—which were in use only for winning crowns and prizes, for military discipline, for pleasing the Gods, and for delighting men—toward the goal of preserving health and acquiring a good constitution.

The author explains how physicians and philosophers refined these practices into a structured art for the benefit of health.</meta>

<page-num>16</page-num>
<header>B O O K   O N E</header>

<meta>image quality: excellent</meta>

to bring it to its conclusion, which exercises—once those first gymnastics masters, and also <margin>D</margin> later ones, had been advised by physicians and philosophers (as is likely)—they learned contributed to the body in a wonderful way. They moderated some things, added others, and transferred the practices from public spaces to private and specific locations. Finally, they enclosed the practice within certain rules, precepts, and terms, and thus gave birth to the entire art called *gymnastics* <note>original Greek: "γυμναστικήν" (gymnastikēn)</note> from the word *to exercise* <note>original Greek: "ἀπὸ τοῦ γυμνάζεσθαι" (apo tou gymnazesthai)</note>, as if there were no other end than to exercise for the sake of obtaining a good habit of the body and preserving health. Galen, in the 58th chapter of his book *To Thrasybulus*, testified that Hippocrates, Diocles, Praxagoras, and Erasistratus were the first of all to achieve this. Therefore, from these facts, I believe it is clear how the gymnastic art took its beginning, its growth, and its status, as well as the time it arose.

Indeed, it first began to appear during the Trojan War, while the Greek soldiers, descending from their ships onto the sand—from which I believe the proverb "to enter the arena" <margin>E</margin> <note>original Latin: "In arenam descendere." The word "arena" literally means "sand," referring to the shoreline where they trained.</note> later emanated—exercised among themselves for war. At that time, it also received the names of the "agonistic" <note>competitive</note> and "gymnastic" art. Later, having been transferred to sacrifices and the pleasures of men, it not only retained the aforementioned names but also acquired the title of "athletics"; Galen even referred to this version as "faulty gymnastics." Finally, once it was brought to the gymnasia and specific places for the education of boys, for the protection of everyone's health, and for the preparation of a good physical condition, and was confined within formal rules, it truly earned the name of gymnastics. This occurred before the time of Plautus, in whose writings that Attic youth, Philolaches, speaks thus: *My heart aches when I consider what I am now, and what I once was; no youth was more industrious than I in the gymnastic art: the discus, spears, ball, running, weapons, and horse.*

Truly, however, this art (as Marcus <margin>In the second book on rural affairs, in the preface.</margin> Varro left recorded) flourished in use only among the Greeks as long as the Romans <margin>F</margin> were tilling the countryside and held highly productive fields through cultivation, and were themselves stronger in health. But after they preferred to idle in towns as laziness grew, rather than labor in the countryside, they promoted the urban gymnasia of the Greeks so frequently that the same Varro complained that in his time, hardly a single gymnasium was enough. Indeed, while Rome flourished under the Emperors, these were the largest and most beautiful of all. But thereafter, as the Roman Empire declined and other things fell into ruin, the gymnasia were destroyed together with them. At the same time, the art itself suffered no small loss. Anyone can understand that this art was in very frequent use from the times of Varro until the decline of the Roman Empire, if they observe from the surviving writings of all the physicians valued in Rome at that age, who everywhere employed the training art in curing diseases and preserving the healthy, or if they read Plutarch.

## -> On the Gymnasiums of the Ancients. Chapter VI. <-

<image-desc>A decorative historiated woodcut initial letter 'G' depicting a male figure (perhaps a gardener or laborer) holding a staff or branch, framed within an ornate architectural or floral border.</image-desc>
<margin>B</margin> Since we have established above that gymnastics, or the art of exercise, was accustomed to take place in specific locations, it is now consistent with reason to make clear what those places were and of what kind they were. For those places were nothing other than what were called "gymnasiums" <note>from the Greek *gymnasion*</note>, as is clearly proven by many sources, and especially by the words of Galen written in the second book of *On Preserving Health*. There, he relates that a gymnasium was a public place built in a separate region of the city, in which people were anointed with oil, rubbed down, wrestled, threw the discus, or performed some similar activity. These places were so named because the exercisers there were, for the most part, stripped naked. Indeed, the very ancient word "to exercise" <note>original Greek: "γυμνάζεσθαι" (gymnazesthai)</note> seems also to signify "to be stripped naked," as Martial indicates in his third book:
> The Gymnasium, the Baths, the Stadium are in this area; step back! 
> We are undressing; refrain from looking at naked men.
And Bardesanes, in the sixth book of Eusebius’s *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter eight, says that the Greeks could not be prevented by any power of the stars from <margin>C</margin> exercising with naked bodies in the gymnasiums. Nevertheless, sometimes the name "gymnasium" is found to encompass every place where people exercised. Later, this word was even transferred to other things, as can be seen in Josephus, who demonstrates in his books on the *Jewish War* that baths were sometimes called gymnasiums. There, speaking of Herod, he says: "For at Tripoli, Damascus, and Ptolemais, he built public baths, which are called gymnasiums, and at Byblos he built sitting-rooms <note>original Latin: "exedras"</note> and porticos." I find these places called "palaestras" <note>A *palaestra* was specifically a wrestling school, but often used interchangeably with gymnasium.</note> by Vitruvius, Celsus, Pliny, and other authors of the Latin language. From this, I also conjecture that in the time of Vitruvius <note>The famous Roman architect of the 1st century BCE.</note>, palaestras or gymnasiums in Italy were either very rare or non-existent, since he, being about to hand down the methods for their construction in his book on architecture, declares that they were not part of the Italian custom. For those who are believed to have first built gymnasiums were the Greeks, if...

<margin>In the dialogue *Anacharsis*.</margin> We should believe Solon in the writings of Lucian, and Marcus Tullius Cicero, who <margin>D</margin> writes in the second book of *On the Orator* that gymnasiums were first established by them <note>The Greeks</note> for the sake of delight and exercise. Among the Greeks, the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> were the first to stand out, as Athenaeus (following the opinion of Hippias) and Plato in the *Theaetetus* and the first book of the *Laws* have recorded. It can also be understood from the first book of Martial that the Lacedaemonians constructed those very gymnasiums that were the most excellent and beautiful of all, where he includes these verses:
> Let him sing of Thebes or Mycenae,
> Born among the Argive cities,
> Or of bright Rhodes, or of the lustful
> Wrestling-grounds of Leda’s Lacedaemon. <note>original Latin: "Argiuas generatus inter urbes / Thebas carmine cantet, aut Mycenas, / Aut claram Rhodon, aut libidinoſae / Ledacas Lacedaemonis palaeſtras."</note>

However, I cannot exactly determine how Plato, in the *Critias*, describes that Atlantean palace—which he says flourished nine thousand years before his own <margin>E</margin> age—and writes that gymnasiums existed there. He elsewhere makes them an invention of the Lacedaemonians, unless we believe that entire narrative of the *Critias* to be a fable. After the Lacedaemonians, the Athenians also erected their own gymnasiums. Pausanias and Suidas testify that three existed in their city: one called the *Academy* <note>original Greek: ἀκαδημίαν</note>, where Plato taught his philosophy; another called the *Lyceum* <note>original Greek: λυκεῖον</note>, where Aristotle taught, which we read in Lucian was originally a temple <margin>In the dialogue *Anacharsis*.</margin> of Apollo Lyceus; and a third called *Cynosarges* <note>original Greek: κυνόσαργες</note>, where the illegitimate, low-born, and all the more ignoble people exercised. Indeed, among the Greeks, the common and illegitimate were marked with such hatred and infamy that those who were truly legitimate and noble refused to have any social interaction with them or share a common place for exercise. Besides these three, Philostratus, in <margin>F</margin> his *Life of Herodes Atticus*, mentions another which he calls the Canopus. I said there were three gymnasiums "in" the city of the Athenians because, although they were technically outside the city walls, they were built so nearby that they could be said to be in the city. Indeed, it is written in Cicero that the Greeks also had a custom of burying the dead in these places; <margin>Book 4 of the *Letters to Friends*, epistle 12.</margin> Servius writes to him that he buried the murdered Marcellus in the Academy of the Athenians, the most noble gymnasium in the whole world.

As for the structures that Ligorio <note>Pirro Ligorio (c. 1513–1583), a famous Italian architect and antiquarian who excavated Hadrian's Villa.</note>, a man most skilled in all antiquity, writes he found represented in the ruins of the Emperor Hadrian’s villa at Tivoli—the Athenaeum, the Hermeum, and the Panathenaicum—I do not think these were gymnasiums where bodies were exercised. Rather, they were places where effort was devoted to the study of disciplines and other arts, or where certain festivals were celebrated, such as the Panathenaic festivals in the Panathenaicum. Corinth also had a gymnasium

<margin>A</margin> One was called the Craneum, as Laertius is the authority in his third book <note>Diogenes Laertius, a biographer of Greek philosophers.</note>. The Romans <margin>In the book *On Ancient Names*.</margin> were the last of all to begin building gymnasiums in the city—which they called *palaestras*—in emulation of the Greeks, according to the authority of Varro. Nor should I be silent about what Martial wrote concerning Nero’s gymnasium in his seventh book:

> What is worse than Nero?
> What is better than Nero’s warm baths? <note>original Latin: "Quid Nerone peius? / Quid hermis melius Neronianis?" Martial uses the term *thermae* or *hermae* to refer to the luxurious public baths built by the Emperor Nero.</note>

For no one among the authors of the Latin language doubts that entire gymnasiums were sometimes called Baths due to the frequent use of hot water there. Likewise, "Baths" sometimes signify that specific part <margin>B</margin> of the gymnasium in which people washed, where the furnace-room <note>original: *propnigeum*</note>, the steam-room <note>original: *laconicum*</note>, and the hot bath <note>original: *calda lauatio*</note> were located, as is clearly seen from many testimonies of authors, and especially from the verses of Martial recently cited. 

Gymnasium, baths, and stadium are all part of this. By all these points, everyone can now be persuaded how much my fellow citizen Blondus of Forlì <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), a pioneering Renaissance historian and archaeologist.</note> was mistaken—I admit this unwillingly—when he wrote in the second commentary of *Rome Restored* that baths were established solely for the purpose of washing. Furthermore, lest anyone be seized by wonder that I said Plato and Aristotle were accustomed to philosophize in gymnasiums, they should know that various types of people were accustomed to gather in places of this kind; all of these will be demonstrated by us point by point in the following chapter. For the capacity of such places was so great, and their spacious size so vast, that diverse and almost innumerable exercises for both <margin>C</margin> bodies and minds could be carried out without any hindrance, just as anyone moderately skilled in this matter will be able to see from the description provided by Vitruvius <note>The Roman architect whose *De Architectura* is the foundational text for classical building.</note>.

Although we presented a different version of this description in the first edition, based on the judgment of Octavius Pantagathus—a man of the highest caliber in our time—we now present a more refined version, having considered it more diligently (as second thoughts are usually better), which corresponds exactly to all the words of Vitruvius. ### On the building of palaestras and covered walkways, from Vitruvius, Book V, Chapter XI.

<image-desc>A large decorated initial letter N showing several men in classical robes, likely scholars or architects, engaged in a discussion or demonstration within an interior room.</image-desc>Now it seems right to me (although they are not of the Italian custom <margin>E</margin>) to hand down an explicit account of the buildings of palaestras, and to show how they are constructed among the Greeks. In the palaestras, the peristyles <note>courtyards surrounded by columns</note>, whether square or oblong, must be made in such a way that they have a walking circuit of two stades <note>approximately 1,200 feet</note>, which the Greeks call a *diaulos* <note>original Greek: δίαυλον, referring to a double-course race track</note>. Of these, three single porticoes <note>covered walkways or porches</note> should be arranged, and a fourth, which faces the southern regions, should be double, so that when there are windy storms, the spray and rain cannot reach the interior part. Within the three porticoes, spacious *exedrae* <note>semicircular rooms or recesses</note> are to be built with seats, in which philosophers, rhetoricians, and others who delight in studies may be able to sit and engage in debate. 

In the double portico <margin>F</margin>, however, these specific rooms should be placed: the *Ephebaeum* <note>a room for young men or 'ephebes'</note> in the middle (this is a very large room with seats, which should be one-third longer than it is wide); to the right, the *Coryceum* <note>a room for punching-bag exercises</note>, then next to it the *Conisterium* <note>a room where athletes were dusted with sand</note>; from the *Conisterium* at the turn of the portico is the cold wash, which the Greeks call a *loutron* <note>original Greek: λουτρόν</note>. To the left of the *Ephebaeum* is the *Elaeothesium* <note>the oiling room where athletes applied oil</note>, and next to the *Elaeothesium* is the cold room <note>original: *frigidarium*</note>, and from there a passage into the furnace-room <note>original: *propnigeum*</note> at the turn of the portico. Next, moving inward across from the cold room, a vaulted sweating-room <note>original: *sudatio*</note> should be placed, twice as long as it is wide, which has in its corners the *Laconicum* <note>a dry-heat room or sauna, named after the Spartans of Laconia</note> arranged in the same manner as described above. Opposite the *Laconicum* is the hot wash <note>original: *calida lauatio*</note>. In the palaestra, the peristyles (as written above) must be perfectly distributed in this way. Outside, however, three porticoes should be arranged: one for those exiting the peristyle, and two to the right and left...

<margin>A</margin>
...on the left should be colonnades a stade <note>a Greek unit of distance, approximately 600 feet</note> in length. Of these, the one that faces toward the North should be made double-wide and of very great breadth; the other should be simple, constructed in such a way that in the parts around the walls and those around the columns, they have margins serving as paths no less than ten feet wide. It seems these xysta <note>the open-air walks</note> should be made so that there are woods or groves of plane trees between the two porticos, and within these, walkways should be completed among the trees, with resting places made of tile-work <note>original: *opere fignino*, likely a variation of *opus signinum*, a waterproof Roman building material made of crushed tiles and lime</note>. Behind the xystus, a stadium is to be shaped so that large numbers of people can watch the competing athletes with plenty of room. I have now written down the things that seemed necessary for the proper arrangement of buildings within the walls.

**N** A vaulted sweating-room <note>original: "sudatio"</note> located further inside, facing the cold room, twice as long as it is wide, having: 
— on one side **P**, a <term>Laconicum</term> <note>a dry sweating-room or sauna, named after the Spartans/Laconians</note>
**Q** An exit from the peristyle.
— on the other side **O**, a hot bath.
**R** The first portico outside the <term>palaestra</term> for those exiting.
**S** A second portico looking toward the North, double-aisled, very wide, and a <term>stadium</term> in length.
**T** A third, single portico built to have:
**V** Edges around the walls.
**X** Edges at the columns.
**Z** A hollowed-out middle area with two steps for the descent, each a foot and a half high. <margin>F</margin>
**α** Open-air walkways next to the <term>xystus</term> <note>a covered portico for winter training</note> and the double portico, which the Latins called <term>xysta</term> and the Greeks called <term>peridromides</term> <note>original Greek: περιδρομίδας; literally "running-around places"</note>.
**β** Groves or groves of plane trees <note>original: "platanones"</note> between the two said porticoes.
**γ** Sitting areas or stations made of brickwork <note>original: "opere fignino"</note>.
**δ** A stadium shaped so that large crowds of people could watch the competing athletes with plenty of room.
**ε** Places which, though Vitruvius does not mention them, were nevertheless necessary in a wrestling school, such as a wood-store, a water-room, a vessel-room, latrines, servants' quarters, and similar things.
