### Chapter VII: On the various kinds of people who gather in the gymnasiums.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>10th Book of the Method <note>Referring to Galen's "Methodus Medendi" or "The Art of Healing."</note></margin>
The multitude of people spending time in the gymnasiums was so great and so varied that, according to Galen, disputes frequently broke out among them. Even a very loud and unpleasant noise, which <margin>Epistle 57.</margin> Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, a Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> complained about, was continuously heard there. Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar.</note> also testifies that this was customary in the baths during his time, using these words recorded in Nonius: "Just as we were accustomed to do in Rome, we began to clap and murmur in the baths." But, lest I wander too far from my purpose by describing every individual group, I shall pursue certain of their primary classes. The first class of those frequenting the gymnasiums were the Philosophers, Rhetoricians, and others who delighted in studies; <margin>B</margin> they read, conversed, and debated among themselves there, just as Juvenal <note>A Roman poet known for his "Satires."</note> demonstrates in these verses, in which he sets out the requirements for a Rhetorician and teacher:

<margin>Satire 7.</margin>
> But you, impose harsh laws upon him:
> That the teacher’s rule of words remains constant,
> That he reads histories and knows all authors
> As well as his own nails and fingers; so that if by chance, 
> while heading to the hot baths or the baths of Phoebus, 
> he is asked, he can name the nurse of Anchises and the homeland of his stepmother.
> <note>Anchises was the father of Aeneas in Roman mythology; these lines mock the obscure trivia teachers were expected to know.</note>

And this is also confirmed by the testimony of Galen, who mentions a <margin>13th Book of the Method</margin> certain Cynic philosopher named Theagenes, who disputed publicly every day in the Gymnasium of Trajan. From various books of Galen, it is <margin>In the book "On His Own Books"</margin> <margin>C</margin> known that there were three places in Rome where literary exercises were conducted: the Temple of Peace before it was destroyed by fire, the public gymnasiums, and the <term>upper halls</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνώγεια (anōgeia) — rooms on an upper floor used for lectures or gatherings</note>. Among these, if someone were to include the so-called "School of Physicians," in my opinion, they would not be far from the truth. It was built on the Esquiline Hill and was most highly decorated with many images and marbles, as has been observed by many from its ruins, and especially by Ligorio <note>Pirro Ligorio, a famous 16th-century architect and antiquarian.</note>. I have not yet read in any author exactly what was done in this school. However, I believe that besides the arrangements and other exercises of medical students, something similar was practiced there to what happens now in the institutions called colleges; especially since a marble found in Rome at the Church of St. Sebastian shows that such a school had its own secretary, bearing this inscription:

->TO MARCUS LIVIUS CELSUS, SECRETARY<-
->OF THE SCHOOL OF PHYSICIANS<-

It specifically highlights the "School of Physicians" on the Esquiline Hill as a precursor to modern medical colleges.</summary>

The second group consisted of **Young Men**, who approached the gymnasia in order to learn the rules and methods of the exercises; there, they were taught whatever exercises they desired by the gymnasium masters themselves. It is easily proven that free-born youths were accustomed to learning thoroughly in the wrestling-school <term>palaestra; a Greek-style wrestling school or the area within a gymnasium dedicated to physical training</term> from those words of Parmeno in Terence’s work, where he says, while offering Chaerea to Thais in the guise of a <margin>In *The Eunuch*.</margin> eunuch: *"Test him in literature, test him in the wrestling-school, in music; I will provide a skilled man in all that it is proper for a free-born youth to know."* I shall demonstrate this more clearly below. The third group were the **Athletes**, who exercised there so that they might delight the people in public games or sacred contests, and also to obtain victory and prizes. Aside from the authority of Vitruvius, Suetonius demonstrates this most clearly when he reports <margin>E</margin> that Nero used to enter the gymnasium from time to time to watch the athletes competing. The fourth group were all those, whether of noble or common birth, who devoted themselves to various types of exercise either for the sake of military discipline and bravery, or for the sake of preserving health and attaining a good physical condition. Concerning the former, there is a passage in Cassiodorus (Book 5, Letter 23), which was misunderstood by Pamelio in his notes on Tertullian’s book *On Spectacles*, where he writes: *"Our young men show in wars the valor they learned in the gymnasium."* Among the latter group, we can include our own Galen, since he writes <margin>In the 1st book *On the Joints*.</margin> that in the thirty-fifth year of his age he suffered a dislocation of the upper shoulder in the wrestling-school. The fifth group consisted of those who were **rubbed** <note>original: "fricabātur" — referring to the practice of medical or hygienic massage with oils.</note>; for although massages were performed by many before the rest of their exercises, nevertheless many others were rubbed alone, apart from the others and without any exercise—as Suetonius records of <margin>Book 2, *On the Preservation of Health*.</margin> Vespasian. This can be understood from <margin>F</margin> Galen, who distinguishes the massage used as a preparation for exercise from the other types. The sixth group were those who **bathed**, and these were both nobles and those of lower status. There was this difference, however: the wealthy and the elite had their own private basins <term>labra; large basins for washing</term> and swimming baths <term>colymbithras; from the Greek word for a diving pool or swimming bath</term> within the otherwise common rooms, where they bathed alone at different times. There were many who even carried with them mats—either wooden or silver (as Pliny recounts)—so that they would not place their bare feet where the lowest of the low stood. Nevertheless, some also report that the Emperor Hadrian was accustomed to bathe where the common people bathed, which Suetonius writes that Titus Caesar also did. Those who were only anointed were not found in the gymnasia, because they were anointed either for the sake of exercise or for the baths. Finally, from all these groups, not a few **spectators** (not to mention the attendants, whom we shall discuss below) gathered in the gymnasia for no other reason than to see those exer-

<margin>A</margin> ...reciters <note>original: "citatores", likely referring to "recitatores" or public readers</note>, since they were at leisure and occupied by no business, went there. In this place I also think it should be noted that on festival days the gymnasia were more crowded, when craftsmen or those held by other services, being idle, spent time in them for the purpose of relaxing from their labors and taking pleasure. Whether women also frequented the Roman Baths just as the men did, I would not dare to affirm for certain, except that it seems such a thing would have been unbecoming to Roman majesty. It could easily happen that some impure women, for the sake of both watching and playing—as Juvenal and Martial suggest—frequented the gymnasia publicly, as well as in separate places which were built there solely for women to wash. Just as in private baths, honorable women would wash, both those of low or middling birth as well as the more illustrious; for Pliny reports that Poppaea, the wife of Domitius Nero, <margin>Book 2. chap. 41.</margin> <margin>B</margin> used to bring five hundred pregnant she-asses everywhere with her, and she would soak her whole body in that milk in the bathtub to increase the whiteness of her skin. Juvenal understood this when he wrote:

> *...or the thick Poppaean creams.* <margin>Satire 6.</margin>
> *It smells and*
> *It begins to be recognized, and is cherished by that milk*
> *For which she leads out she-asses as her companions.*

For this use of whitening the body, Galen remembers that other women used bean flour, and others used nitre or foam of nitre <note>original: "aphronitrum"; a naturally occurring salt used as a cleaning agent</note> in the baths. However, Propertius, in his third book, among others, provides sufficient testimony <margin>First on the Properties of Aliments.</margin> that Spartan women were accustomed to exercising together with men in the wrestling-schools:

> *We admire many laws of your Sparta,*
> *But more so the many goods of the maidenly gymnasium,*
> *Because it does not practice shameful games with the body—*
> <margin>C</margin> *A naked girl among the wrestling men,*
> *When the ball eludes the swift throws through the arms,*
> *And the hooked key of the turning hoop rattles,*
> *And the dusty woman stands at the furthest markers,*
> *And endures wounds in the hard combat sport,* <note>original: "pancratio"; an ancient Greek martial art combining boxing and wrestling</note>
> *Now she binds her joyful arms to the boxing-glove with thongs,*
> *Now she rotates the weight of the hurled discus in a circle.*

Nor should anyone wonder at this custom of the Spartans, since Plato, in the fifth book of the *Republic*, proved with very serious arguments that it contributes greatly to the happy state of republics if women, both young and old, exercise naked together with men in the wrestling-schools and gymnasia. Whether this was decreed wisely, and whether it would contribute to achieving continence or temperance through habit—as was Plato's intention—this is not the place to examine.

### On the Various Parts of the Gymnasia. Chapter 10.

<margin>D</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial V showing a seated figure within a landscape.</image-desc>
**I**T is clear from his own words that Vitruvius, who flourished in the age of Augustus Caesar, described only the Greek wrestling schools (*palaestras*), since the Roman Emperors had not yet begun to build their own. Just as it is probable that those later Roman structures were similar to many Greek gymnasia, it is likewise likely that the Romans—as is the custom of those who refine things at a later date—added many things to their own that the Greeks either did not know or valued little. Therefore, in order to explain the main parts of the gymnasia, I will by no means bring forward only those indicated by Vitruvius. Instead, without following any particular order of placement, I will describe those parts which I find recorded scattered throughout various authors, or which the logic of the subject seems to require as having existed in both Greek and Roman schools. 

I have never thought that Vitruvius’s authority should be highly esteemed—indeed, I consider him <term>obscure and of little reputation <note>original Greek: "ἀδοξόλογον"</note></term> and minimally valued in his own time. <margin>E</margin> For he was appointed by Augustus to no distinguished works except for ballistas <note>ancient missile-throwing engines</note>, even while magnificent buildings were being constructed inside and outside the city. Furthermore, he is found named by almost no later author, except in the catalog of Pliny’s books—which some think is not by Pliny at all, or is at least corrupted—which certainly raises a justified suspicion about his reputation. 

Therefore, the first parts of the gymnasia were the porticoes full of *exedrae* <note>open semi-circular or rectangular seating areas for conversation</note> or open chambers. In these, philosophers, rhetoricians, mathematicians, and all lovers of learning were exercised by debating, reading, and teaching. We can guess that these were situated not far from the other exercise areas, both from their design and from a proverb born there: "They would rather hear the discus than the philosopher." <margin>F</margin> This was said of those who, while sitting among the philosophers in the gymnasium, would hear the clatter of the throwing-discs and abandon the school of wisdom to rush to the nearby place of competition. 

It is reasonable to believe that the youths and boys who were devoted to their studies spent time in the *exedrae* of the philosophers. These were like schools where, after exercising their minds, young men and boys could very easily exercise their bodies for health or strength and then wash. For the authority of Lampridius <note>an author of the Historia Augusta</note> exists, stating that Alexander Severus, after his reading, would give his effort now to the wrestling school, now to the ball court <note>original: "sphaeristirio"</note>, now to running, now to light wrestling, and soon after enter the bath. Among these I also count the schools of the physicians. The second part was the *Ephebaeum* <note>a room for youths or "ephebes"</note>, where it seems likely to me that they would gather and make agreements about prizes and types of exercise...

<meta>catchword: agreements</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the architectural layout of ancient gymnasia, specifically focusing on the integration of intellectual spaces (exedrae) with athletic ones. Mercuriale notably critiques the reputation and reliability of the Roman architect Vitruvius as a primary source.</summary>

<margin>A</margin> ...those who were accustomed to train and compete together. However, I am aware that <term>Philander <note>Guillaume Philandrier (1505–1565), a French architect and commentator on Vitruvius.</note></term> held the opinion that youths were exercised in the <term>Ephebaeum <note>A room in the gymnasium specifically for youths (ephebes).</note></term>. In this matter, I believe his judgment was much better than that of <term>Guillaume du Choul <note>A 16th-century French antiquarian known for his work on Roman religion and military matters.</note></term>, who recorded in his book on the exercises of the ancients that youths sat in the Ephebaeum for the purpose of study. Whether this was truly the case among the Romans—who forbade boys to have any social interaction with men before their sixteenth year—I would not dare to affirm. Nor can we deny that in <margin>Galen, *On the Care of the Health*, addressed to Posthumus.</margin> <term>Galen’s <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note></term> time, boys were commonly exercised in the wrestling school (*palaestra*), as he mentions a certain illness that Commodus (then a boy and the Emperor’s son) had acquired in the wrestling school. Furthermore, in the second book of *On Preserving Health*, he writes: <note>original Greek: "οὕτω δὴ ἥσις ἀναῤῥιχᾶται διὰ σχοινίου καθάπερ ἐν παλαίστρᾳ γυμνάζουσι τὰς παῖδας εἰς εὐτονίαν παρασκευάζοντες"</note> <margin>B</margin> **"Thus, whoever climbs up a rope, just as they exercise boys in the wrestling school, preparing them for physical vigor."** From these words, it is clear enough that boys were accustomed to being exercised in wrestling schools, even if <term>Plautus <note>A Roman playwright known for his comedies.</note></term> had not also testified to it most clearly in his play *The Bacchis Sisters*. In that work, Lydus, the tutor of Pistoclerus, criticizes the indulgence of fathers toward their sons in his own time and speaks thus of the customs of former days:

> *I deny that in your first twenty years you had the chance*
> *To move your foot a finger’s breadth away from your tutor from the house.*
> *Unless you had come to the wrestling school before the sun rose,*
> *You would pay no small penalty to the Prefect of the Gymnasium.*
> *And when that happened, bad was added to bad:*
> *Both the pupil and the teacher were held to be wicked.*
> *There, in running, wrestling, spear-throwing, the discus, boxing, and ball,*
> <margin>C</margin> *They exercised themselves more than in whores or kisses.*

From this, I am led to believe that it was prescribed for boys to go to the wrestling school very early in the morning so that they might avoid the company of the men (who were not yet there) and also because they would have leisure time remaining for the study of literature. Indeed, that there were men who sought to see boys naked and to win their forbidden love in the wrestling schools can be easily gathered from <term>Plutarch’s <note>A Greek-Roman historian and essayist.</note></term> book on love.

The third part was the <term>Coriceum <note>Likely a dressing room or a room for punching bags (korykos).</note></term>, which (in my opinion) served as the place for men to undress, whether they wished to exercise, to bathe, or to do both. Elsewhere it is called the <term>apodyterium <note>The primary undressing room in ancient baths and gymnasia.</note></term> by the Greeks and the <term>gymnaserium</term> by Galen. Unless the Coriceum in Vitruvius signifies such a place, one would have to say that the wrestling schools described by him lacked this most necessary part of all. I believe this room was present not only in public gymnasia but also in private ones, since <term>Pliny Caecilius <note>Pliny the Younger, a lawyer and author in ancient Rome.</note></term> mentions it in the descriptions of his villas... <margin>Letters, Books 2 & 5.</margin>

...among other things, he counts the <term>apodyterium <note>The room for undressing in an ancient gymnasium or bathhouse.</note></term> of his Laurentine and Tuscan villas. For this reason, I cannot approve of the opinions of **D** those who thought that the <term>Coryceum <note>A room containing a korykos, or punching bag filled with flour or sand.</note></term> in the text of <term>Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer whose works are the primary source for ancient building practices.</note></term> should be read as being named from the *corycus* (a type of ball), as if such a game were performed there; or that it was a <term>Coryceum</term> used as a barber shop; or a <term>Coryceum</term> because girls and young women, called *choraia* (<note>original Greek: χοραία</note>) by the Greeks, exercised in it. The fourth part was the <term>eleothesium <note>The oil-room where athletes were anointed.</note></term>, called the anointing-room (<note>original Greek: ἀλειπτήριον</note>) by
<margin>Book 2, Letters</margin>
Julius Pollux, and the anointing-room (<note>original Latin: unctuarium</note>) by Caecilius Pliny. In that place, those about to wrestle, or about to begin other exercises or baths, were anointed and re-anointed. But, since the opportunity of the subject seems to demand that I speak regarding this gymnastic duty of anointing—and because the book of Metrodorus of Scepsis, *On the Art of Anointing* (<note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς ἀλειπτικῆς</note>), cited by Athenaeus, does not survive today—I shall say four things: first, when and who were anointed; second, what was the material used for anointing; third, for what purpose they were anointed; and fourth, in what manner and by whom the anointing was administered. Those who came into the gymnasium either to bathe or to exercise **E** were, for the most part, stripped in the <term>apodyterium</term>. Afterward, some of these, and especially those who intended to enter into wrestling or the <term>pancratium <note>A brutal ancient Greek combat sport combining wrestling and boxing.</note></term> (for boxers, runners, and many others did not require anointing), would enter the <term>alipterium <note>The anointing room.</note></term> to be oiled. Having been thus anointed, they would pass to the place where the dust was (which I shall speak of below) and were sprinkled with powder; and so, one after another, they went out to their various exercises. After they had exercised **F** as much as they pleased, they returned again to the anointing-room. There, they were cleaned by the <term>Mediastini <note>Low-ranking bath slaves.</note></term> and the Re-anointers with iron <term>strigiles <note>Curved metal tools used to scrape oil, sweat, and dirt from the skin.</note></term>, about which <term>Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his Epigrams.</note></term> wrote:
> Pergamum sent these to divide the dirt with curved iron,
> The cleaner will not have to rub your linens so often.

In this cleaning, the oil, dust, and sweat that were scraped off were mixed together and preserved for medical use. This was called *konisalōs* (<note>original Greek: κονίσαλος</note>) by the
<margin>Book 1, ch. 3.
Book 34, ch. 8.
On Simple Medicines 81 & 4, On Preserving Health.
Book 5 & 10, On Simple Medicines & Book 2, ch. 17.</margin>
Athenians, and *rhūpos* (<note>original Greek: ῥύπος</note>) by others, as can be very easily confirmed from <term>Dioscorides</term>, <term>Pliny</term>, <term>Galen</term>, and <term>Aetius</term>. Nevertheless, <term>Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and influential physician of the Islamic Golden Age.</note></term> in his second book also makes mention of the "dry sweat" of athletes, which I think was that which contained neither oil nor dust. And although in Galen’s time scrapers were used for the purpose of the bath, nonetheless, the scrapers of the baths were mostly sponges or linens; nor were they always provided for everyone in common, but each person carried his own with him, especially anyone who avoided sharing tools with others, as <term>Persius <note>A Roman satirist.</note></term> suggests in his fifth Satire:
> Go, boy, and carry the scrapers of Crispinus to the baths.
The scrapers were of iron, or gold, or silver, or horn, or ivory, or bronze, with which the scrapings and filth of the exercisers were scraped from their bodies. The bronze scrapers, the illustration of which is placed here, are those which were once found among the ruins of the Emperor Trajan’s baths.

### BOOK ONE
<page-num>32</page-num>

Finally, having been wiped clean, those who were more diligent regarding their health, or for the sake of luxury **D**, were anointed again. Sometimes, having been anointed, they entered the baths, but after coming out they were anointed once more—sometimes with plain oil, sometimes seasoned with various scents, and sometimes with a **scented powder** <term>diapasmate; a finely ground aromatic powder used to dry the skin or suppress sweat</term> to restrain <margin>Book 21, Ch. 19</margin> sweat, as Pliny writes. Thus, there were various times for anointing: sometimes after the bath, which we read was observed in the times of Homer, as in *Odyssey* Book 3: *But when she had washed him and anointed him with rich oil* <note>original Greek: Αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ' λούσάν τε καὶ ἔχρισεν λίπ' ἐλαίῳ</note>; and again in Book 4 and 17: *When the handmaidens had washed them and anointed them with oil* <note>original Greek: τοὺς δ' ἐπεὶ οὖν δμωαὶ λοῦσαν, καὶ χρῖσαν ἐλαίῳ</note>. Sometimes they were also anointed before bathing, as Galen reports in the sixth book of *On Preserving Health*. Some things worth knowing about **Archimedes** <note>The famous Greek mathematician of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BCE)</note> are read in Stobaeus: namely, that while he was leaning over his calculation tablet and drawing certain figures, he used to be dragged away by force by his servants to be anointed, and even on his body—once anointed—he was accustomed to frequently **E** draw mathematical figures.

The material used for anointing before exercise was varied. In Aristotle's time, they were anointed with both plain oil and oil mixed with water. Indeed, in the fifth section of his *Problems*, he wrote that water mixed with oil, when applied to those who have exercised, removes fatigue more effectively than plain oil, because by penetrating more deeply it moistens the dried-out limbs. I add also from Hippocrates in his eleventh book *On Diet* that such anointings do not allow bodies to heat up more than is proper. <margin>Book 1, Ch. 4</margin> Pliny is the authority that the Greeks—the fathers of all vices—were the first to bring oil into the gymnasia. Regarding this, **Anacharsis** the Scythian <note>A 6th-century BCE philosopher who traveled to Athens and was known for his outsider's perspective on Greek customs</note> used to say it was a "drug for madness," because once thoroughly anointed with it, the athletes would act like madmen. Pliny left it on record, and after him Galen, that among some barbarian nations who perhaps lacked oil, **butter** was sometimes used for <margin>Book 11, Ch. 14 & Book 28, Ch. 9. Book 3 of On the Properties of Foodstuffs, Ch. 15</margin> anointing the bodies of those exercising. There was also another kind of mixture found later **F**, composed of oil, powder, and wax, with which they were anointed. I find this called **ceroma** <term>ceroma; a thick, waxy unguent used by wrestlers to make the skin supple but also to provide a grip</term> by Pliny, by which he says the Roman youth, in exercising their bodies, lost the strength of their minds. This is also seen in Martial, Book 4:
> *Whether you rub the sticky ceroma* <margin>and Book 5</margin>
> *Nor do you stretch your twisted arms with ceroma applied* <margin>and Book 7</margin>
> *And the disciplined ceroma of the Lydian wrestling floor.*

Pliny likewise writes that the oil in the gymnasia was seasoned with scents, though usually the cheapest ones. All these things should be understood as referring to anointings applied before exercise. Indeed, after exercise and after baths, almost infinite types of various ointments seasoned with scents are recorded as being used—these served only luxury and lust. And I think these were indicated to us by Plutarch in his *Dialogue on Love*, when he wrote that Solon forbade slaves from "dry anointings" and the

### BOOK ONE
<page-num>33</page-num>

**A** ...love, but not likewise the marriage of women, unless he understood rather the anointings made outside the baths, or scented powders. Regarding the purpose for which those going to the gymnasiums were anointed with the aforementioned ointments, I find various explanations handed down by authors. **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BCE)</note> recorded in the third book of *On Diet* that the dust of the earth was customarily mixed with oil so that, by its own coldness and dryness, it might temper the heat and humidity of the oil. **Alexander** <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle</note> wrote in the first volume of his *Problems* <margin>Problem 119</margin> that athletes were accustomed to be thoroughly anointed with oil before exercises so that their softened limbs might sustain labors without any danger of rupture—an opinion also followed by **Lucian** <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist and rhetorician (c. 125–180 CE)</note> in his dialogue *On Gymnasia* <note>original Greek: περὶ γυμνασίων</note>. **Lucan** <note>A Roman poet (39–65 CE)</note> seems to have felt that wrestlers were accustomed to sprinkle themselves with dust so that their bodies might be made stronger. For when speaking of **Hercules and Antaeus** <note>In Greek mythology, Hercules wrestled the giant Antaeus, who gained strength from touching the earth</note>, he says:
> He pours hot sands as an aid to his limbs.

**B** **Plutarch** <note>Greek philosopher and biographer (c. 46–119 CE)</note>, in his short book *On the Principle of Cold*, seems to have been of the opinion that athletes used powder in their anointings both to cool their heated bodies and to restrain sweat, so they would not become so exhausted. I, however, agree with Lucian that the primary use of the powder was so that hands would not slip because of the oil, but rather that the trainers might be able to grip each other more easily, and so that they would not be drenched in sweat, or so that winds would not enter their open pores. And for this reason, that powder was called *aphe* <note>original Greek: ἁφή; meaning "grip" or "touching"</note> by **Martial** <note>Roman poet known for his Epigrams</note>, as in the passage: "the grip-dust turns yellow" <note>original: "flavescit aphe"</note>. From this, if any athletes defeated opponents who were anointed but competing without the dust, they were held worthy of greater glory; such was **Dioxippus** in the writings of **Pliny**, and **Dioreus** in **Pausanias**, who earned the name *akoniti* <note>original Greek: ἀκόνιτι; literally "without dust," meaning a victory won without a struggle</note>. **Horace** made mention of this matter, writing thus to Maecenas:
<margin>Book 1, Epistle 1</margin>
> What pugnacious man, haunting the villages and crossroads,
**C** > Would scorn to be crowned at the great Olympics, who had the hope,
> Who had the sweet condition of the palm of victory without dust?

Because of this, I cannot marvel enough at **Budé** <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French humanist scholar</note>—certainly a most learned man—that he did not see this in his annotations on the *Pandects*, and preferred to say that *akoniti* meant "without a contest" <note>original Greek: ἀνὸὺ ἀγῶνος</note>. There are others who believe trainers were anointed with oil to ward off cold and relieve fatigue. **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire (129–c. 216 CE)</note> feels that oil was conducive to releasing past fatigue and <margin>On Preserving Health, book 6, last chapter</margin> mitigating future fatigue, as well as for preparing for movement. I agree with Galen that wax was added to this, so that the otherwise fluid oil would adhere longer. No one doubts that the anointings used after the baths were intended to prevent the humidity acquired in the baths from evaporating, or to keep the natural heat from escaping through the pores opened by the heat of the bath. Although, some more delicate people did this for the sake of pleasure and luxury with fragrant ointments, or dry powders to compress immoderate sweat.

<margin>Pliny, Natural History, Book 13, ch. 2; Book 21, ch. 19; Book 1.</margin>
As **Pliny** <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus (23–79 CE), author of Natural History</note> writes, they were anointed after the baths, concerning which **Martial** <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis (c. 38–104 CE), a Roman poet known for his Epigrams</note> writes: **D**
> What of the fact that the stench smells even worse when mixed with scented powder? <note>original: "Quid quod olet grauius mixtum diapasmate virus"</note>

However, I find nothing defined for certain as to how they were anointed. Yet it is very probable that some, after first rubbing themselves, did this with their own hands, or were anointed by one another in turn—which **Lucian** <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist</note> writes regarding the Gymnasiums. It was also permitted for them to be anointed by gymnasium slaves, called <term>reunctoribus</term> <note>literally "re-anointers" or massage attendants</note>. These attendants themselves, to ensure a better penetration of the ointment, would first rub the person and then finally smear the whole body, pressing sometimes gently and sometimes otherwise. According to the requirements of the season, they applied a liniment that was sometimes lukewarm, sometimes hot, and at other times cold. All these things were mostly done in the <term>Alipterium</term> <note>the anointing room in a Roman bath or Greek gymnasium</note>. Those who rubbed themselves with <term>nitrum</term> <note>native soda</note> and <term>aphronitrum</term> <note>literally "froth of soda," a lighter form of saltpeter or soda used as a detergent</note>, as **Cyprian** mentions in Letter 7, Book 4, and Martial in Book 14, I believe did so to better wash away the dirt from the body and to dry it; for no one is ignorant of how much <term>aphronitrum</term> **E** is able to wipe away.

Nearby was the <term>Conisterium</term> <note>the "dusting room" from the Greek 'konis,' meaning dust</note>, called *konisea* <note>original Greek: κονίσεα</note> by **Pollux** <note>Julius Pollux, a Greek grammarian and sophist</note>. This was the fifth part of the gymnasium, in which the stored dust was kept so that those who had been anointed could immediately be sprinkled with it. We read that powders were brought from various regions for this purpose, but two held the prize: the **Puteolan** <note>from Puteoli, modern Pozzuoli near Naples, famous for its volcanic sand</note>, about which **Sidonius Apollinaris** <note>A poet and diplomat of the 5th century</note> says,
> For the dust of the Dicarchean sand was brought over, <note>original: "Namque Dicarcheae translatus puluis arenae" — Dicarchea is the ancient name for Puteoli</note>

and the **Egyptian** sand, which **Suetonius** <note>Roman historian (c. 69–122 CE)</note> records was usually brought to Rome for this purpose in the time of **Nero**.
<margin>Pliny, Book 35, ch. 15.</margin>
Similarly, **Pliny** relates that **Patrobius**, a freedman of Nero, brought a very fine sand from the Nile—not much different from the Puteolan dust—for the purpose of "subduing the bodies" <note>an idiomatic way of referring to the hardening or preparation of the skin</note> for the studies of the wrestling school. He also notes that the same sand was carried by **Leonnatus, Craterus, and Meleager**, generals of **Alexander the Great**, along with other military supplies. Perhaps the sand described by **Ovid** when depicting the fight of **Achelous** <note>A river god who wrestled Hercules</note> was not unlike this: **F**
> The restless color turns yellow from the trail of golden sand. <note>original: "Inquies vicem fuluae tractu flauescit arenae"</note>

For **Martial**, mocking **Philenis** <note>a female character often satirized by Martial for behaving like a male athlete</note> for entering the exercises of the wrestlers, said that she herself turned yellow from this sand, which we have said was called *aphe* <note>meaning "the grip" or "the touch"</note> because it served the physical contact of the trainers. For no one is ignorant that *haphen* <note>original Greek: ἁφήν</note> signifies "touch."

<margin>In the *Bacchides*. Book 2 on *Preserving Health*, chapter 9.</margin>
The ancient man was sharp-witted when (as that character Lydus from **Plautus** <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BCE), a Roman playwright</note> used to say) they exercised themselves more in running, wrestling, the spear, the discus, boxing, ball-games, and jumping than in consorting with mistresses or exchanging kisses. **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> writes that these exercises were usually performed there: wrestling, boxing, hanging by the hands from ropes, an exercise where they stood with their feet and their hands bound into a fist while offering them to another to be pried open, the lifting of weights with the hands while remaining still—a type of equipment called <term>halteres</term> <note>ancient Greek dumbbells</note>—shadow-boxing, and fighting with weapons. Agreeing with Galen, **Oribasius of Pergamum** <note>A 4th-century Greek medical writer</note> confessed that there were not only these, but six hundred other types of exercises in the <term>palaestra</term> <note>specifically the wrestling school or the area of the gymnasium dedicated to it</note>. 

From this, it should be noted that the "palaestra" signifies many things among authors of both languages <note>meaning Greek and Latin</note>. First, it can mean the entire gymnasium itself, as can be seen in the works of **Vitruvius** <note>The famed Roman architect</note>. Second, it can mean any place suitable for exercising the body; this is how **Cicero** spoke in the first letter of his third book to his brother Quintus, and in the second book of *On the Laws*, where, describing his villa at Arpinum, he names a "palaestra" there. **Virgil** does the same in the fifth book of the *Aeneid*:
> Part exercise their limbs in grassy wrestling-grounds <note>original: "Pars ingramineis exercent membra palaestris"</note>,

<margin>Collection 6, ch. 14. *De Berecithim* <note>Likely a reference to a specific treatise or section</note>, book 1, ch. 36. *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, book 5. *On the Laws*, book 1. *On Famous Orators*. *Natural History*, book 27, ch. 4.</margin>
and Geta in **Terence's** *Phormio*, where he says: "Look, he is coming out from his wrestling-school [palaestra]." Third, it refers to a certain part of the gymnasium in which, according to the opinions of Plautus, Galen, and Oribasius, we previously mentioned so many exercises were performed. **Pliny** and **Theodorus Priscianus** <note>A 4th-century medical writer</note> wrote that the grime collected from its walls and applied to a cloth could ripen and heal boils. I believe **Catullus** used the word in this sense when he said:

Pliny records that these scrapings were sometimes sold by the masters of the games for eight hundred sesterces <note>a very large sum of money for what was essentially gymnasium dirt</note>. I find also that the exercise of the palaestra itself is sometimes called "palaestra," just as **Marcus Tullius [Cicero]** sometimes seems to have understood "palaestra" metaphorically to mean actions performed in an orderly and graceful manner. He does this on the authority of **Lucilius** <note>The satirist</note>, whose verse is read in Porphyrio: *The judge Hortensius has a "palaestra" [skill] born for that matter*. Moreover, **Plato** in the *Charmides* used "the palaestra of Taureas" to signify a place where learned men gathered for conversation and debate. To these points, **Plutarch** in the second book of his *Symposiacs* writes that the place where athletes were trained was called a "palaestra," and in that place only wrestling and the <term>pancratium</term> <note>a "no-holds-barred" combat sport combining wrestling and boxing</note> [were performed], not run-

...running about, and not boxing, were performed. This is how **Galen** <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 CE), an influential Greek physician</note> sometimes used the name "palaestra" <note>a wrestling school or the area of a gymnasium dedicated to it</note> when referring to a place where only athletes, those studying the thickening of the body, were exercised. I believe it is understood in this same way by **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–c. 370 BCE)</note> when, at the beginning of the first book of the *Epidemics*, he relates that tumors arose in those who exercised in the palaestra and the gymnasia. Perhaps, however, someone might doubt whether dust was spread in this palaestra, since Galen <margin>Book 2, *On Preserving Health*, chapter 9.</margin> seems to have separated it from the place where the dust was located with these words: <note>original Greek: "ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν τοιαῦτα καὶ χωρὶς παλαίστρας, ἢ βαθείας κόνεως δύναται γίγνεσθαι καθ’ οτιουν χωρίον ἐπίκροτον ὀρθῶν ἑστώτων. ὅσα δὲ παλαίοντες εἰς ἀλλήλους δρῶσιν ἀσκοῦντες τὸν τόνον, ἢ κόνεως βαθείας, ἢ παλαίστρας δεῖται"</note> "But such movements can occur even without a wrestling school or deep dust in any hard-packed ground while standing upright; however, those things which wrestlers do against one another while practicing their strength require either deep dust or a wrestling school." 

To this I wish to respond that even in the palaestra, dust was indeed spread, but it was low and moderate, so that there were two types of places spread with dust: one within the palaestra and another outside the palaestra. In the former, the dust was shallow; in the latter, it was deep and plentiful. The use of dust in both places served several purposes: first, so that the contestants could stand more firmly and not slip with their feet; and second, so that those who were thrown to the ground would be less injured. However, deep dust had this further advantage: while men fixed their feet deeply into it, they required greater effort and force to lift them, and thereby acquired greater strength. **Lucian** <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–after 180 CE), a Hellenistic satirist and rhetorician</note> indicated all these things in his booklet on exercises. For I think Galen was speaking <margin>Book 11, *On the Use of the Parts*, and the book *On Procatarctic Causes*.</margin> of this deep dust when he writes that he frequently saw athletes in danger of suffocating from the dust, and where he tells of a certain youth who, due to vigorous movement performed through deep and sandy places, became greatly dried out and betook himself to the gymnasium; this was because he was one of those who delighted in that kind of exercise and wished to exercise there repeatedly.

As for the claim that the "palaestra" was also the name for the art of training orators in their delivery—as **Budé** <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a French humanist also known as Budaeus</note> attempts to prove in his notes on the *Pandects* <note>A massive compendium of Roman law compiled under Emperor Justinian</note>—I truly do not see it.

We have already sufficiently proved in the previous sections that this is not the *coryceum* <note>a room containing a punching bag or heavy bag</note> described by **Vitruvius** <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80–15 BCE), Roman architect</note>. <margin>Book 2, Epistle 5; and Book 17, Chapter 16 <note>These are likely references to the Pandects or Digest, a compendium of Roman law.</note></margin>
That the same [sphaeristerium] could encompass circles <note>likely referring to circular exercise patterns or circuits</note> can also be confirmed from that passage of the *Pandects* <note>a massive collection of Roman legal writings</note>, where these words of **Ulpian** <note>a famous Roman jurist, c. 170–223 CE</note> are read: "When it was said that **Aurelius Quinctus** had commanded his guest, a physician, to build at his own expense—in his gardens which he held at Ravenna, and to which he was accustomed to retire every year—a <term>sphaeristerium</term> <note>a room or court for ball games</note>, <term>hypocausts</term> <note>an ancient Roman underfloor heating system</note>, and certain other things suitable for his own health." From this, it is also easily conjectured that not only ball games, but indeed other exercises were accustomed to take place in the sphaeristerium, since **Vespasian** <note>Roman Emperor, reigned 69–79 CE</note> also used to rub his throat and other limbs there to a rhythmic beat (as **Suetonius** relates). The eighth part consisted of those paths which, as I believe, were situated between the porticoes and the walls, bare of all buildings, as well as the entire area of the <term>peristyle</term> <note>a courtyard surrounded by a colonnade</note> which were made both to provide light to the porticoes and chambers, and for walking or performing other exercises which could not be done in the wrestling school, nor in deep dust, nor in the <term>xysti</term> <note>covered walkways</note> or other places. I believe these were the "beaten ground" mentioned by us a little earlier from **Galen**, so-called because they were not paved with any stones or bricks, but were rugged and consisted only of leveled soil.

In these areas, I believe running took place, and for that purpose both <term>diauli</term> <note>a "double-pipe" race, involving a turn at a post</note> and <term>dolichi</term> <note>a long-distance race</note> were held; the forms and boundaries for the <term>dolichodromi</term> <note>long-distance runners</note> and <term>diaulodromi</term> <note>double-lap runners</note> were established there, even if in **Vitruvius** <note>Roman architect and author, 1st century BCE</note> the *diaulos* was nothing other than the circuit of the square peristyles defined by two <term>stadia</term> <note>about 370 meters</note>. In these same places, jumping and discus exercises—which Galen denied to the wrestling school—were (in my opinion) sometimes held. The ninth part was the *xysti* and *xysta*; for both terms hold no small distinction among the Greeks and Latins. Indeed, the Latins call *xysti* the covered porticoes where athletes exercised during winter and summer when the time was unsuitable for wrestling. The *xysta*, however, were open-air walkways where, in mild winter weather, they would come out from the portico to exercise and walk, as they almost always did in summer. Vitruvius writes that these were called *exomides* <note>original: "ἐξωμίδας" - likely a scribal or printer error for "paradromides," the term Vitruvius actually uses for open-air walks</note> by the Greeks. These were of two kinds: some were bare, others were planted with plane trees or other trees to provide a pleasant environment and shade for those who were <margin>Book 12.</margin> offended by the sun. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of Natural History</note> was speaking of these when he writes that the plane trees in the walkway of the Academy at Athens were famous. **Pliny the Younger** <margin>In the place cited.</margin> also spoke of these when, in describing <margin>In the *Oeconomicus*.</margin> his Tuscan and Laurentine villas, he so often praises the *xysti*. ### On the Baths of the Gymnasia, and also on the Stadium. Chapter X.

<image-desc>A historiated initial 'D' depicting a nude male figure (possibly Hercules or a gymnast) in an athletic pose within a rectangular frame decorated with scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>

THE TENTH part of the gymnasia was the Bath, which it is certain was most highly valued by everyone for the sake of both pleasure and health. In my opinion, it stood out as larger and more beautiful than all the other parts. This was because (as Galen <note>The most famous physician of the Roman Empire, c. 129–216 CE</note> laments regarding his own times) almost all men bathed daily. In the time of Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine," c. 460–370 BCE</note> and of almost all the ancients up until the age of Asclepiades <note>A Greek physician who brought Greek medicine to Rome</note> and Pompey, this was not the case; as Hippocrates and Galen write <margin>3rd commentary on *Regimen in Acute Diseases*</margin>, public baths or suitably built private ones were not yet seen, and men bathed only rarely. Furthermore, the baths required many rooms for the various conveniences of the bathers, which necessarily required a larger space; for this reason, they were constructed with columns and the most magnificent marbles. 

I should not omit how much magnificence private individuals employed in building private baths, about which Seneca wrote <margin>Epistle 87</margin> that every man seemed poor and filthy to himself unless the walls of the baths shone with large and precious discs; unless Alexandrian marbles were inlaid with Numidian crusts; unless an elaborate border, varied like a painting, was applied to them on all sides; unless the chamber was roofed with glass; and unless silver faucets poured out the water. I will not even silence the ornament of statues and columns that supported nothing, which the baths of freedmen possessed, to the point that they wished to tread on nothing but gemstones. Anyone who has read the "Bath of Etruscus" most elegantly described by Martial and Statius <margin>Book 6; Book 1, *Silvae*</margin> will not be able to sufficiently admire the magnificence and luxury of our ancestors in constructing baths; but enough on these matters. However, so that a slightly fuller knowledge of the baths of the gymnasia may be had, I offer these points for the present (since Andreas Baccius of Elpidio <note>Andrea Bacci (1524–1600), a famous physician and contemporary of the author, who wrote an exhaustive study on ancient baths</note>, a man of great reading and learning, after the first edition of these commentaries...)

First, what they were and which places were designated for bathing; Second, which vessels were used and the arrangement of the air where they washed; Third, for what purpose they washed; Fourth, who washed and when. For everyone knows the substance in which they washed was usually fresh water, either collected from rain, or channeled from aqueducts, rivers, or elsewhere. <margin>Book 3, Letter 1 to his brother Quintus</margin> I find that the places constituting the bath complex as a whole were called "Balnearia" by Cicero; these included a cold wash <note>original Greek: λοῦτρον (*loutron*)</note>, a cold room (*frigidarium*), a warm room (*tepidarium*), a hot sweating room, and a hot wash. Those areas that served the baths were the <term>hypocaust</term> <note>an underfloor heating system</note>, the water-chamber (*aquarium*), and the vessel-room (*vasarium*). Anyone who wishes to contemplate the ruins of the Roman baths can see that all these places were vaulted and built in the manner of arches. No one should be surprised that we list more bath locations here than are found described by Vitruvius <note>The famous Roman architect of the 1st century BCE</note>; for those he described were almost all adopted from the Greeks, at a time when the Romans had not yet begun to build those admirable structures of the <term>thermae</term>, in which they arranged even more locations, being far more decadent than the Greeks. 

The cold wash, or <note>Greek: λοῦτρον</note>, was the place where the cold water baths were located, and especially the pool—otherwise called a <term>baptistery</term> <note>from the Greek *baptisterion*, meaning a place for dipping or plunging</note> by Pliny the Younger. Such a person was Alexander Severus, of whom Lampridius writes that he very rarely washed in the hot rooms, but almost always in the swimming pools. More on the use of this can be seen in Oribasius, following the opinion of Galen, in the tenth book of his *Collections*. Lampridius is the authority for the fact that Heliogabalus <note>A Roman emperor infamous for his eccentricities and luxury</note> never allowed himself to be washed in the pools unless they had been infused with saffron or other precious ointments. 

Adjacent to this was the cold room (*frigidarium*), built for those who wished to enjoy cold air immediately after exiting the warm room or the hot room; for no water vessels were found there, so that more people could gather in the summer. There have been those who believed that in this part, a pool was placed for those fond of swimming (which we shall treat extensively in Book 3). It is possible that those about to bathe also undressed there, both because the <term>apodyterium</term> <note>the undressing room</note>—the common place for athletes to strip—was located a considerable distance away, <margin>D</margin> so much so that if bathers had left their clothes there, they would have been forced to walk naked through the <term>ephebaeum</term> <note>a large hall for exercise and education</note>, the cold bath, and other areas. Furthermore, it is probable that people were frequently found in the <term>ephebaeum</term>, and it was by no means honorable for those about to bathe to be seen naked by them. To avoid all these issues, it is easy to conclude that they undressed in the <term>frigidarium</term> <note>the cold room</note>, especially since <margin>Varro, On Agriculture, in the prologue; Pliny, Letters, Book 3.</margin> Varro and Pliny have testified that in both the city and the countryside, the undressing room was a part of the bath itself. <margin>On the Preservation of Health, 10, column c, chapter 6.</margin> Galen and Oribasius also seem to indicate this; when explaining at what hour a young man of temperate constitution ought to use the bath, they mandated that the "gymnastic room" must be tempered, which can be nothing other than the <term>frigidarium</term> itself, where sweat was also wiped away. Indeed, Galen, in the tenth book of his *Method of Medicine*, enumerates the parts of the bath and establishes four: the <term>calidarium</term> <note>hot room</note>, the hot bath <margin>E</margin> (which he calls <note>original: "loutron"</note> *the washing*), the cold bath, and a fourth part in which sweat was wiped away. However, this is understood more by conjecture than by any certain judgment. Nor should anyone doubt here why Vitruvius calls one part and Galen another part the <note>original: "loutron"</note> *washing*, since it is not contrary to reason that both were designated by that name, as people washed in both.

It should also be mentioned in this place that public baths had this area built quite vast and accessible to anyone, so that the clothes of those who were bathing could easily be stolen. Because of this, it was provided by law that "bath-thieves" should be punished more severely, as Aristotle taught more copiously than others in Section 29, Problem 14. Nevertheless, I know that bath-attendants and others used to hire out those called <term>capsarii</term> <note>slaves who guarded the "capsa" or clothes-box</note> for this purpose, to keep the clothes of the bathers safe from thieves. > *Whom a home-born slave follows, guarding the narrow clothes-box.*

And Ovid in Book 3 of *The Art of Love*:
> *While a guard outside keeps watch over the girl's dress,*
> *The many baths may provide for secret jests.*

And Martial in Book 12:
> *When recently a home-born slave, empty-handed, was carrying the linens for the boar,*
> *And a one-eyed old woman sat atop the little toga.*

The <term>tepidarium</term> <note>warm room</note>, annexed to the <term>frigidarium</term>, served two kinds of people: those who wished to enjoy a moderate temperature of air or water (or both) for pleasure or health, and those who sought to bathe in either cold or hot water. # BOOK ONE

<margin>Book 3, Letter 1 to his brother Quintus.</margin>
As people might shudder when moving from one extreme to another in the bathing process, or otherwise be physically shocked, they used the <term>tepidarium</term><note>The lukewarm room in a Roman bath.</note> as a middle ground. In this space, those exiting a cold or hot area would remain until they had prepared themselves to enter the other without harm. However, it is also possible that in private baths, the <term>tepidarium</term> and the <term>apodyterium</term><note>The dressing room.</note> were the same room, either due to a lack of space or because it was more convenient. Indeed, Cicero, when he visited his Arpine villa (which was being built under the supervision of his brother Quintus), writes that he moved the <term>assa</term><note>Dry heat or "sweat-room" pipes.</note> into another corner of the dressing room in the baths. In this, he demonstrates clearly enough that the dressing room and the <term>laconicum</term><note>A circular sweating room with dry heat.</note>—or the hot, dry sweating-room, as he and Celsus call it—were joined together. This is similar to how we believe the <term>tepidarium</term> and <term>laconicum</term> were sometimes joined, at least after the time of Vitruvius, even though he, in Book 5,

<margin>Book 5, chapter 14; Book 2, chapter 16.</margin>
<margin>Book 3 to Quintus, Letter 1; In the preface to the book on Agriculture.</margin>
chapter 10, seems to support this opinion entirely. The <term>calidarium</term><note>The hot room.</note>, which was called the <term>laconicum</term> by Vitruvius and Celsus, was a chamber containing no water within it, established primarily to provoke sweating. For this reason, it was called a "hot sweating-room" by some, and <term>assa</term><note>Literally "dry."</note> by Cicero and Cornelius Celsus. Speaking of this, Columella wrote the following against the customs of his own time: *“Soon after, so that we may come to the gluttonous feasts with an appetite, we cook away our daily indigestion in the Laconica, and having squeezed out our sweat, we seek a thirst.”* In this room, trapped hot vapor or dry heat provoked sweating, not unlike the myrtle groves above Baiae, where in the time of Celsus, hot vapor pouring out of the earth and trapped by a building stirred up great sweats. ...since it seems irrational to me that he would practice ball games and other exercises—which Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman author and administrator</note> records as being customary in the *sphaeristerium* <term>sphaeristerium: a large hall or court for ball games</term>—in a hot place built for sweating. For that would have been (as the proverb goes) "adding oil to the furnace," if they had performed exercises that are inherently very heating to the body in the hottest of locations. Regarding the *laconicum* <term>laconicum: a dry sweating room, similar to a modern sauna</term>, the words of Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet</note> can be understood if the verse is restored as follows, whatever others may have said:
->*He who lubricates the Lacedaemonian circle with a preliminary drink:*<-
<note>original: "Qui Lacedaemonium proptysmate lubricat orbem." The author interprets this as a critique of someone spitting excessively on the floor of the Spartan-style sweating room, making it slippery.</note>
For he censures a certain man because, by spitting copiously on the floor of the *laconicum*, he made it so that the feet of those walking could not find firm footing. After the *laconicum* there followed the "hot room" filled with basins placed to hold water, which, because people washed there, was given the name *loutron* <note>original Greek: λουτρον, meaning a bath or washing place</note> by Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer</note> and Galen <note>An influential Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note>. I believe Archigenes <note>A Greek physician practicing in Rome</note>, cited in Galen’s eighth book on the *Composition of Medicines according to Places*, called this the *zeson* <note>original Greek: ζησὸν, meaning "boiling" or "very hot"</note>. This was indeed the primary part of the bath, and therefore no one has raised any controversy regarding it.

Why Vitruvius, in describing the construction of the baths in gymnasia, makes no mention of the *tepidarium* <term>tepidarium: the warm room, used as a transition between hot and cold zones</term>—which he clearly mentions when teaching about private baths—I am not entirely certain. For if he intended it to be understood as part of the "vaulted sweating-room," it would follow that it was also customary to sweat in the *tepidarium*, yet in a previous chapter he distinguished between the sweating-rooms and the *tepidarium*. If one prefers to think the *tepidarium* was included by him under the "hot wash," how then did he make the *calidaria* <term>calidaria: hot rooms</term> and *tepidaria* distinct at the beginning of the tenth chapter of that same book? Thus, it must perhaps be said that the "vaulted sweating-room" encompasses both the *laconicum* and the "hot wash," while the *tepidarium* was omitted because the Greek *palaestrae* <note>Wrestling schools or gymnasia</note> did not have it.

Furthermore, as for what Pollux <note>A Greek grammarian and sophist</note> wrote in his seventh book—that the *aleipterion* <term>aleipterion: an unctuarium or room for oiling the body</term> was a part of the baths according to Alexis—I am in no way able to prove this, since elsewhere he himself numbered it among the parts of the gymnasia. Unless we wish to believe that among the Ancients, the word *balaneion* <note>original Greek: βαλανεῖον</note> signified the entire gymnasium itself. And let these remarks suffice concerning the parts of the public baths in the gymnasia. There were also almost innumerable private baths, which likely lacked some of the aforementioned parts and possessed others; but it is not our purpose to speak of such things.

As for the places that were not within the baths but merely served them, they first contained the *hypocaustum* <term>hypocaustum: an underfloor heating system</term>, which according to Vitruvius’s description was a furnace or a vaulted subterranean structure placed beneath the *calidarium*, the hot wash, and the vessel-room. In this, a fire was kindled to heat both the water and the aforementioned places. To prevent it from being extinguished, it was frequently stirred by the "furnace-slaves"—called so by Papinian in the *Pandects* <note>A compendium of Roman Law</note>—using poles and balls smeared with pitch. Regarding the wood used for this purpose, Plutarch relates in the tenth problem of the third book of his *Symposiacs* that the aediles <note>Roman officials in charge of public buildings</note> took care that the bath fires were not kindled from olive wood...

<margin>A</margin> ...nor should darnel <note>original: "lolium," a weed often found in grain that can be toxic or cause dizziness when burned or ingested</note> be thrown into the furnace when it is lit, because the fumes of these things bring on a heaviness of the head and vertigo to those who are washing. From this, it can be manifest to anyone in how grave an error those people are who believed the *Hypocaustum* <term>hypocaustum: the underfloor heating area</term> and the *Laconicum* <term>laconicum: a dry, sauna-like sweating room</term> were the same thing. <margin>B</margin> Our authority is Seneca in the third book of *Natural Questions*, chapter 23, and also in his 91st Epistle: he says that in his own time, tubes pressed into the walls were invented, through which heat would be circulated to warm both the bottom and the top of the room equally. > *rolls the exhaled flames through the hollow plaster-work,*
> *gathering the enclosed vapor as the heat breathes out.*

Traces of these tubes can still be seen in many places in Rome, such as in the gymnasiums <note>The massive public bath complexes</note> of Diocletian and Caracalla. In front of the hypocaust was a passage called the *propnigeum* <term>propnigeum: the room in front of the furnace where the heat was regulated</term>, which Vitruvius also called the *praefurnium*. The "water room" <note>original: "aquarium cella"</note> was a chamber for hot washing, connected <margin>C</margin> to the hot room <term>calidario: the room containing the hot bath</term>, in which a large basin was built to hold water brought in from aqueducts or elsewhere, to be channeled from there through pipes into the cold and hot washing areas. Not far from this was located the *vasarium* <term>vasarium: a room for vessels and equipment</term>, where the vessels necessary for the bath services were kept, and where the water for them was heated. Vitruvius described it this way: <margin>Book 5, Chapter 10</margin> three bronze vessels were placed above the hypocaust—one hot <note>original: "calidarium"</note>, the second warm <note>original: "tepidarium"</note>, and the third cold <note>original: "frigidarium"</note>—and so arranged that as much hot water as flowed out of the hot vessel would be replaced by water flowing in from the warm one, and from the cold into the warm in the same manner. Regarding the air of the baths, which was admitted from the outside (as Vitruvius indicates), these were located in the warmest place, away from <margin>Book 9, Chapter 10</margin> the North and the North-wind; thus the hot and warm rooms received light from the winter sunset. ### BOOK ONE

...so that a wide opening was left in the middle of the ceiling, under which a basin <term>labrum: a large, raised water basin, often circular</term> was constructed. Around this basin were spaces of a certain size, like margins or porticoes, which were called *scholae* <note>original: "scholae," literally "schools" or "places of leisure," here referring to the standing room or waiting areas around the bath</note> by Vitruvius. In these areas, while the bathing spots were occupied by those who arrived first, the rest could stand properly and look on; because they stood around the perimeter, they did not block the light coming from the opening above with their shadows.

Furthermore, concerning the condition of the air inside the bath, I find it written by the most serious authors Seneca and Plutarch that the ancients used soft and moderately warm baths. For instance, Alexander the Great bathed even while suffering from a fever; and the women of the Galatians <note>a Celtic people living in central Asia Minor</note> would carry pots of porridge into the baths to wash and eat along with their children. But in their own time <note>Seneca's and Plutarch's era, the 1st century AD</note>, extremely hot baths were held in high value, so much so that it could be said of them: <margin>Epistle 87. Book 8, Table-Talk, Problem 9.</margin>

> ->*Hither flow Cocytus and Phlegethon, seeking the Acheron.*<-
> <note>original: "Huc Cocytus, Phlegetonq. fluunt Acheronta petentes." These are the names of the burning or freezing rivers of the Greek Underworld, used here as a humorous exaggeration of the bath's extreme heat.</note>

Perhaps the Baths of Nero were of this sort, about which Martial writes in his fifth book:

> ->*If you wish the boiling bath of Faustina to be tempered,*<-
> ->*into which Julian could scarcely enter,*<-
> ->*ask the Rhetorician Sabinus to bathe there;*<-
> ->*he cools down the Neronian baths.*<-
> <note>This is a satirical jab by the poet Martial; Sabinus was apparently such a "cold" or boring public speaker that his presence alone could lower the temperature of the hottest steam rooms.</note>

Nevertheless, in the time of Galen—who flourished a little after Seneca and Plutarch—baths were by no means used at such extreme temperatures. Indeed, I hold it as certain that the custom of using very hot baths was not common to everyone then, but was a preference of some individuals. Seneca testifies that among the ancients, even the most noble Aediles <term>aediles: Roman officials responsible for the maintenance of public buildings and order</term> performed the duty of entering the bathhouses used by the public to demand cleanliness and to ensure a useful and healthy temperature was maintained. But he relates that by his own time, that practice had fallen into disuse, and the baths had become so hot they were like a fire. Pliny relates in Book 33, Chapter 9, that those recovering from illness would place salt under their tongues so that they could endure the intense heat of the bathhouses.

The vessels in which people washed were either fixed or mobile. Those that were not moved were made of brick or marble. The tanks <term>alvei: deep, sunken tubs for immersing the body</term> and basins <term>labra</term> were used for hot washing, while for cold washing they were called pools <term>piscinae</term> or "baptistries" <term>baptisteria: from the Greek 'baptizein', to dip or immerse</term>. These were so large that swimming was even permitted within them to some extent; traces of these can still be seen today in some of the ruins of the great Imperial baths <term>thermae</term> in Rome.

As for the mobile vessels, although they were mostly used in private baths, I believe they also existed in public ones, perhaps for the use of private citizens. These had various shapes: some were square, others oblong-square, some somewhat round, and others oval, as is apparent from the ancient examples that still survive in Rome. Here, however, we provide only one form, shared by Pirro Ligorio <note>A famous 16th-century architect and antiquarian</note> from his excellent records of ancient monuments; we believe this form is the most beautiful and the most suitable for the wise reader to understand many things. <margin>Epistle 87.</margin>

# BOOK ONE

->**A Representation of the Roman Bathing Rituals**<-

This page presents a detailed illustration of the interior of a Roman bathhouse, identifying the various instruments and vessels used by the ancients to maintain their health and cleanliness.

The central focus is the **Oceanic Basin or Labrum** <note>original: *Lavacrum Oceanum vel Labrum*; a large, ornate stone basin usually positioned in the warm or hot rooms of the bath</note>. This massive tub, fed by lion-head spouts, serves as the primary communal washing area where men gather to soak. 

To the far left, we observe the use of the **strigil** <note>original: *strigili*; a curved metal tool used to scrape oil, sweat, and dirt from the skin after exercise</note>. This was a vital part of the Roman cleansing process, as they used oil rather than soap to lift impurities from the body. Nearby, a man rests upon a **Stone Throne** <note>original: *solium*</note>, a high-backed seat designed for bathing in a seated position or for receiving a pour-over wash.

The attendants and bathers utilize several specific vessels:
*   The **Small Pitcher** <note>original: *orceolum*</note> is used for pouring water over the limbs.
*   The **Boiling Kettle** <note>original: *caccabus*</note> is used to heat and transport water to the basins.
*   The **Bathing Ladle** <note>original: *trulla balnearia*</note> allows for the precise scooping and splashing of water during the ritual.

The architecture, characterized by sturdy pillars and wide doorways, suggests a grand public space, emphasizing that bathing was not merely a private necessity but a central social activity of the Roman world.

There were also those who attempted to make wooden basins for the baths, such as Tucca, who was mocked by the poet Martial <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis, a Roman poet known for his witty and biting epigrams</note> in these words:

<margin>E</margin>

The purpose for which they bathed was not just one. (I am speaking here of healthy men and those devoted to the gymnasia; for this is not the place to discuss the washings of the sick and the infirm.) I have always believed that the primary institution of the baths was to wash away daily filth <note>original: *sordes*</note> so that they could dine with a clean body, as they bathed every single day. In ancient times, the use of linen cloths—which protect the body from dirt—had not yet been invented, or at least was uncommon. Because they went about with their bodies largely bare, they were defiled by dust and all other sorts of grime. Consequently, they were compelled to wash at least three or four times a month, or even every single day if they took pleasure in always dining clean. 

It is reasonable to conclude that later generations—who were anointed before exercises in the gymnasia and became covered in dust and sweat—always practiced this to wash away the filth, and for this reason, the use of baths was introduced within the gymnasia themselves. For just as those first ancestors established the place where Roman youth exercised near the Tiber <note>The main river of Rome</note>, so that they would not be forced to travel too far to strip away the filth contracted during exercise (as Vegetius writes in <margin>Book 1 on Military Matters</margin>), so too, after gymnasia were established for exercises, it was only right to build baths there for cleansing the body. From this practice of dining only once a day and reclining on couches while they ate—as I shall demonstrate more fully below—this custom was introduced.

<margin>F</margin>

# BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin>
...they used to soothe parts of the body burning from exercise, the sun, or the cold. Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, a prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> testifies at the beginning of his third book on local medicines that people used not only fresh water but also medicated waters for the sake of luxury. Plutarch <note>A Greek philosopher and biographer</note>, in his book <margin>In the book *On Preserving Health*.</margin> *On Preserving Health*, records that some were accustomed to using the baths because they could not—and would not—take food unless they had first washed; he reports that the Emperor Titus died for this very reason, according to the accounts of those who attended him during his illness. The physician Posidonius also related that those who had stomachs too weak to digest food would bathe for the sake of strengthening the stomach and processing their meals. Thus, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the encyclopedic *Natural History*</note> was not without reason when he attacked physicians for persuading people that food is "cooked" within the body by hot baths—baths from which <margin>Aetius, Book 6, Chapter 10. Book 29, Chapter 1.</margin> no one ever emerged feeling stronger, and the most obedient patients were often carried out dead. Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian</note> writes that, in short, baths existed for four reasons: "either for cleanliness, or warmth, or health, or finally, for pleasure" <note>original Greek: ἢ καθαριότητος ἕνεκα, ἢ ἀλέας, ἢ ὑγείας, ἢ τὸ τελευταῖον ἡδονῆς</note>. 

<margin>B</margin>
Our ancestors used hot baths to relieve fatigue and to soften the body; for this reason, they called them <term>anthropognapheia</term> <note>From the Greek for "human laundries" or "man-fullers," suggesting the bath processed the body like a fuller softens cloth</note>. They used hot and lukewarm baths to induce sleep. They bathed in cold water both for pleasure and to make themselves more robust, so that the natural heat, driven inward, might become greater. Pliny reports in Book 25, Chapter 7, <margin>Book 3 of the *Pedagogue*, Chapter 9.</margin> that the brothers Euphorbus and Antonius Musa—physicians to King Juba and Augustus respectively—were the first of all to demonstrate this practice of using cold water after hot baths. Likewise, Charmis, a physician from Massilia <note>Modern-day Marseille</note>, condemned the use of hot baths and urged people to wash in cold water even in winter, plunging the sick into lakes. On this matter, there exists the testimony of Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, the Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero</note>, who called himself a <term>psychrolutres</term> <note>A Greek term meaning "cold-water washer" or "cold-bather"</note>. Furthermore, as Pliny and Agathinus (cited in Oribasius <note>A Greek medical compiler</note>) report, many believed that cold bathing contributes to prolonging life and provides many other benefits; Agathinus records these things from his own experience:

<margin>C</margin>
"Indeed, many times when I have difficulty falling asleep after dinner because of the heat, <margin>Book 28, Chapter 4. Book 10 of the *Collections*, Chapter 7.</margin> I am accustomed to go down into cold water; and it is marvelous what a pleasant night I سپس pass." Juvenal <note>A Roman satirical poet</note> testifies that those who entered the public baths paid nothing before their fourteenth year:
> "Nor do boys believe it, except those who do not yet bathe for a coin."
<margin>Satire 2.</margin>

Others gave a <term>quadrans</term> <note>The smallest Roman copper coin, worth a quarter of an *as*</note> to the bath-keeper, and for this reason Seneca called the bath a "farthing affair" <note>original: *rem quadrantariam*</note>, about which Horace <note>The poet Quintus Horatius Flaccus</note> wrote:
> "While you go to bathe as a king for a farthing."
And Juvenal:
<margin>Satire 6.</margin>
> "To slaughter a pig for Silvanus and bathe for a farthing."

Furthermore, Gaius Gracchus <note>A Roman Reformer and orator of the 2nd century BC</note>, in his speech on the promulgated laws, seems to confirm the same; his words are read in Aulus Gellius <margin>Book 10, Chapter 3.</margin> as follows: "For modesty did not allow both sexes to wash together, but convenience required the buildings be joined." Unless we say that all these points are to be understood not as referring to public baths—which at that time either did not exist or were very narrow and cheap—but to private ones. This is perhaps how Vitruvius <margin>Book 5, Chapter 10.</margin> understood it when he showed that the washrooms for both sexes should be joined together. Truly, however, it can be proven by the testimony of many highly respected authors that in later centuries women used mixed baths.
