# BOOK ONE

...for a long time, the custom persisted both in Rome and elsewhere for <margin>D</margin> women and men to wash in mixed baths. Even so, there were some who occasionally attempted to restrain this unchaste boldness of women; such as the Emperor Hadrian <note>Reigned 117–138 AD; he was known for his administrative reforms and interest in Greek culture</note>, whom Cassius Dio <note>A Roman historian of Greek origin who wrote a massive history of Rome</note> writes wished for men to wash separately from women. Likewise, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus <note>Often known as the "Philosopher King" (reigned 161–180 AD)</note> abolished mixed baths; and although Elagabalus <note>An emperor notorious for his eccentric and often scandalous behavior</note> reinstated them, Alexander Severus <note>Emperor from 222–235 AD, noted for his more conservative moral reforms</note> prohibited them again, as reported by Capitolinus and Lampridius <note>Authors within the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of biographies of Roman emperors</note>. For this same reason, it is recorded that a censorial law <note>A law enacted by the Censors, the Roman officials responsible for public morality</note> was once passed requiring women to abstain from mixed baths, and not to enter common washing places with men for the sake of lust, under the penalty of divorce and the loss of their dowry. This was later accepted into the final law under the title *On Divorces* and in the decree *Concerning Marriages*. 

By this reasoning, it is possible that certain women's baths were built specifically for the use of women only, <margin>E</margin> such as those of the Empress Agrippina <note>The mother of Emperor Nero</note>; likewise those of Olympias in the Subura <note>A crowded, lower-class district of ancient Rome</note>, and those which Victor <note>Publius Victor, a 4th-century writer who cataloged the buildings of Rome</note> records that Ampelis and Priscilla held across the Tiber, perhaps to avoid the sight of men. The time for bathing among the ancients, as Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Stoic philosopher</note> relates, was such that <margin>Epistle 87.</margin> they washed their arms and legs daily, but only bathed their whole bodies on market days <note>original: *nundinis*. The Roman market day occurred every eight days, used here to mean a weekly thorough cleaning</note>. However, after the age of Pompey the Great, they began to wash the whole body every single day. From the time of Homer <note>The legendary Greek poet of the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*</note> until roughly the present, the hour for bathing observed by most was shortly before taking food. Nevertheless, there were some in the time of Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> who would bathe even after eating, <margin>Book on tremors, shivering, and spasms.</margin> without any consideration for their health. Because of this, he relates that he saw cases of shivering without fever in his own time—a condition he writes was not seen in the age of the older physicians, since in that era few people bathed after a meal. 

For the most part, however, the majority of free-born men would exercise first and then <margin>F</margin> enter the baths; some, however, bathed without exercise. Galen noted that the ancients were accustomed to washing in hot baths after playing ball games; <margin>In the book on the small ball game. Book 4.</margin> Martial <note>A Roman poet famous for his witty and often biting epigrams</note> seems to have observed a similar custom before him, in this verse:

> Return the ball, the bronze bell of the baths is ringing; do you still go on playing?
> Do you wish to go home having washed only in the Virgin water. <note>original: *Virgine*. This refers to the Aqua Virgo, an aqueduct that supplied cold water to several baths; the poet implies that if the player stays too late, the hot baths will be closed, leaving only the cold water.</note>

For when the hour for the baths approached, it was signaled by a certain bell <note>original: *tintinnabulo*</note>, at which point the ball players and other exercisers would immediately run to them. Otherwise, they would have to wash in the freezing Aqua Virgo—which Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the *Natural History*</note> reports is most pleasant to the touch, just as the Aqua Marcia is to the taste—once the <margin>Book 31, chapter 3.</margin> hot baths were already closed. For Capitolinus writes that before the time of Alexander Severus, the hot baths were never opened before dawn and were always accustomed to be closed before sunset, and that the Emperor himself [supported] the public baths...

<margin>Book 5.</margin>
> Tired, as I follow you to the baths of Agrippa at the tenth hour <note>The Roman "tenth hour" was late afternoon, roughly 3:00 or 4:00 PM</note>, or even later, while I myself wash at the baths of Titus. <note>original: "Lassus ut in thermas decima, uel serius, hora / Te sequar Agrippae, cum lauer ipse Titi"</note>

This much is certain, as Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer</note> recorded in the passage previously cited: the time for bathing was chiefly established from midday until evening. Since our ancestors used to eat their fill only once a day, no time was considered more opportune than this, which was around the eighth hour of the day, shortly before dinner, as Martial has left on record.

> The eighth hour is enough for the sleek wrestling-grounds; the ninth... <margin>Book 4. Book 11.</margin>

<margin>B</margin> The Emperor Hadrian, according to Spartianus <note>One of the authors of the *Augustan History*</note>, wished for no one except the sick to bathe before the eighth hour. We can infer that Julius Caesar also observed this same hour in earlier times from a Letter of Cicero to Atticus, where, speaking of Caesar, he says: "On the third day of the Saturnalia, he was at the house of Philippus <margin>Book 13. Last Letter.</margin> until the seventh hour, and admitted no one—I believe he was reviewing accounts with Balbus; from there he walked on the shore; after the eighth hour he went to the bath; then he heard news of Mamurra <note>A Roman officer under Caesar; the news was likely an insult or a setback</note>, but did not change his expression; he was anointed and took his place at the table; he was acting <term>ἐμετικῶς (emetikos)</term> <note>literally "emetically"; following a medical regimen involving induced vomiting</note>, and so he both ate and drank <term>ἀδεῶς (adeos)</term> <note>without fear or anxiety</note> and pleasantly." 

However, whether Caesar always maintained that way of life is not clearly held from that passage, since Cicero is explaining the routine of only that single day, in which Caesar had intended to vomit according to the custom of many. Because of this, he had eaten and drunk <term>ἀδεῶς (adeos)</term>—that is, without fear—and pleasantly, so that (as was the precept of physicians) <margin>Hippocrates in the book *On Healthy Diet* and Galen's commentary there.</margin> <margin>C</margin> he could vomit while going to sleep, being filled with various kinds of food and drink. For in my judgment, that passage ("he was acting emetically") ought to be understood in this way: just as <term>διαιτητική (diaitetike)</term> <note>dietetics</note> is the name given by the Greeks to that branch of medicine situated in things pertaining to human diet, and <term>κενωτική (kenotike)</term> <note>evacuative</note> to that which pertains to purging, so too <term>ἐμετική (emetike)</term> <note>emetics</note> is that <term>ἀγωγή (agoge)</term> <note>regimen or discipline</note> or method which is placed in the things and manners that prepare one for vomiting. 

Let these brief remarks suffice concerning the baths of the gymnasia and private baths. In earlier times, their use was rarer, until Asclepiades of Prusa <note>A Greek physician who became famous in Rome in the 1st century BC</note>, who was considered an orator in the time of Pompey and drew no profit from that art, turned to medicine. In a short time, he acquired great glory and authority in that field because of the soothing charms with which he cured the sick, because of his own perpetual vigor of health, and because he had recognized that a certain man in Rome—who had been carried out for burial as if dead—was actually alive, much to the wonder of the nations, as Celsus, Pliny, and Apuleius have recorded. <margin>Pliny, Natural History Book 2, ch. 6, 27; Book 7, ch. 37. Florus.</margin>

I believe all these things were omitted by Vitruvius in describing the *xysti* because they were either obvious or more conveniently explained elsewhere. I find that <term>popinae</term> <note>Small cookshops or snack bars providing quick meals</note> were built next to the public baths, which Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville, an encyclopedist of the early Middle Ages</note> records in Book 15, Chapter 2 of his *Etymologies* <note>original: "lib. etymolog. xv. cap. ij."</note> were included so that those who were quite exhausted or weakened by exercise or bathing would have a place where they could be immediately refreshed. And perhaps Pliny <note>Pliny the Younger, a Roman statesman and writer</note> understood these in Book 1, Letter 3 <note>original: "Epist. iij. lib. j."</note>, when he mentions the cookshops after the bath and the dining rooms. So much for the gymnasia of the ancients.

### On the origin of the custom of reclining at dinner among the ancients, and of dining only once a day. Chapter XI. <margin>F</margin>

SINCE the occasion of explaining the baths now encourages us, and as we promised above to have a discussion about the origin of the ancient custom of eating only once a day and of reclining at dinner; even if it seems outside our main subject, and we have no explanation from Galen <note>A highly influential Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> regarding reclining, it must not be overlooked; rather, we shall put forward our opinion for consideration, being most willing to change it at another time if someone endowed with better judgment and learning demonstrates another view that is truer and more consistent with reason. <margin>A</margin> Aristotle wrote that this was the case, and—excepting the Syracusans, whom Plato records were stuffed with food twice a day as if it were some strange novelty—it has been sufficiently proven by Horace, Martial, Plutarch, and Galen (to name but a few) <margin>3rd part, Problem 32. Epistle to Dion.</margin> that people ate only once a day. But I have treated this more fully and better in my *Various Readings*. Regarding the fact that almost everyone similarly reclined on couches <note>The Latin *accumberent* refers to the practice of "reclining" at a meal, a posture associated with luxury and formal banquets</note> while they dined, the most learned Philander <note>Guillaume Philandrier (1505–1565), a French humanist whose commentary on Vitruvius was a standard reference for Renaissance scholars</note>, in his commentaries on Vitruvius, has made this clear through the testimony of ancient authors and Roman stone monuments, so much so that he has spared me all the labor of further proof. However, as to the origin of these two customs—reclining and the single daily meal—and exactly how they reclined, no one I have seen, whether among the ancients or more recent writers, has explained it so aptly and diligently that they did not leave posterity with reasons to doubt or a desire for more information. Whether this has happened because <margin>B</margin> of the obscurity of the subject or through neglect, I do not know. I, for my part, believe that both of these customs—reclining and the habit of eating one meal a day—arose from the use of baths. First, to explain my view on reclining, I am led by several conjectures that are not to be dismissed. The first is that in the time of Homer, when baths were not used so frequently, those about to dine would sit, as is apparent in the banquet of the Suitors:

-> Sat in order on benches, and in order on thrones <-

<margin>C</margin> > They sat on thrones near Menelaus, the son of Atreus. That is,
-> They sat on thrones near Menelaus, the descendant of Atreus. <-
Thus, in the time of the elder Scipio and Plautus, as the use of baths gradually increased, this type of reclining also began to grow, especially among the Romans. Plutarch narrates in his biography of Acilius <note>The author likely refers to Manius Acilius Glabrio or a similar figure from Plutarch’s *Parallel Lives*</note> that he was murdered at a banquet by the very men who had conspired against him. To show that among the ancients, reclining at table occurred in this specific manner, we can rely not only on the very rich testimony of writers but also on two illustrations which we have taken care to place below. One of these was shared from ancient monuments by Ligorius <note>Pirro Ligorio (c. 1513–1583), a famous Italian architect and antiquarian</note>, an antiquarian of the greatest authority, showing diners at a tripod table, as was most common. The other we have had accurately and faithfully represented from a very ancient and most rare marble, which can be seen in the magnificent house of Paullus Rhamnusius in Padua, a man of excellent character and a most devoted student of literature and all beautiful things. From this latter piece of evidence, our own opinion regarding the true form of reclining is most clearly confirmed—a theory which we perhaps were the first of all to propose in Rome to Octavius Pantagathus, Onuphrio Panvino, and other most serious men, and finally to Ligorius in Padua, based on conjecture alone and defended by the authority of books without the evidence of any marble. Through this, the nature of the ancient dining rooms <term>triclinia<gloss>A dining room typically consisting of three couches arranged around a square table</gloss></term> is clearly understood. Indeed, the opinions of Lambinus <note>Denys Lambin, a major 16th-century French classical scholar</note> and others, who attempted to describe the reclining posture in various ways based on their own wits, are refuted. At the same time, many obscure and famous passages by ancient writers are illuminated, so that all lovers of the fine arts and antiquity ought rightly to give immortal thanks first to the spirit of the most learned Jo. Baptista, who acquired the stone, and then to his son Paullus Rhamnusius, who guarded it excellently and pointed it out to us. For it is now no longer obscure how wonderfully the illustration of the Rhamnusian dining arrangement fits with what Plutarch discussed concerning the "consular place" <margin>1. From *Table Talk*, problem 3.</margin> and the three couches of the dining rooms. Let us now consider wedding feasts, at which—since a great crowd of people would gather—the specific number of those reclining could by no means be strictly maintained. This is gathered from Plutarch 
<margin>1. Symposiaca, book 5.</margin>
and the Rhamnusian stone <note>A marble relief belonging to the Rhamnusio family, used here as archaeological evidence</note>, which undoubtedly represents either a public banquet or a wedding feast. Because of this, Chaerephon, in the sixth book of Athenaeus <note>Athenaeus of Naucratis, author of *The Deipnosophists* (The Learned Banqueters)</note>, seems to allow only thirty guests at a wedding. In such large gatherings, it is probable that the "caller" <term>uocatorem<gloss>An usher or servant who announced guests and directed them to their assigned seats</gloss></term> was necessary, whom Seneca mentions in the third book of *On Anger*, chapter thirty-seven, and who called the guests to their proper places according to each person's dignity. 

As for the fact that Turnebus and Lambinus <note>Adrianus Turnebus and Denys Lambin, prominent 16th-century classical scholars</note> interpreted this same role as a boy offering water, I certainly do not disapprove. Yet perhaps it would not be absurd if the words of Horace <note>The text refers to "Flacci," the cognomen of Quintus Horatius Flaccus</note> were applied to that boy whom almost all ancient carvings of tables, as well as the testimonies of poets, show always offering cold and hot water at banquets. Everyone was careful to respect this boy, lest they be poorly treated by him, and it is likely they refrained from "biting" <note>original: "mordendo"; here meaning to snap at or criticize</note> him. 

Now, indeed, one can easily perceive how Mary Magdalene stood behind the feet of Christ as he dined to wash them, and how John reclined upon Christ's own chest. This is easily understood from this same figure of the Rhamnusian dining room <term>triclinij<gloss>A dining room with three couches arranged in a U-shape</gloss></term>, quite contrary to the depictions of modern painters who are ignorant of ancient matters, and contrary to the useless commentary of Cardinal Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio (1469–1534), a philosopher and theologian</note>. Indeed, that the Hebrews and Christ observed the Roman custom of reclining can be testified—beyond the name of the "Master of the Feast" <term>Architriclini<gloss>The headwaiter or steward of a banquet</gloss></term> and the term for reclining frequently used in the Gospels—by what I have frequently seen: when people lived in Rome, or similarly Romans in Judea, it became standard practice for the manners of the leading people to be frequently emulated. Likewise, it is not difficult to perceive what Martial intended to signify with this couplet:
<margin>Book 5.</margin>

->Since you hand all the food back to the boys,<-
->Why is the table not placed at your feet?<-

For since the diners lay high up, spaces were left behind them in which it was easy for servants, who were tending to various needs, to offer many things and take away what had been removed. That servants used to stand at the feet of the diners can be understood from the writings of many. Seneca in the third book of *On Benefits* says: "The servant who had stood at the feet of the diner narrates what [the master] had said while drunk during dinner." Martial writes: "He fills the bottle with mixed wine at the feet." Suetonius, in his life of Galba, chapter 22, writes: "During a dinner that was so abundant, you ordered the leftovers heaped upon your hands to be carried around and scattered to those standing at your feet." 

But besides these things just mentioned, this dining room shows us three things that are not so commonly known. One is what Varro recorded: namely, that in the time when the use of finished ceilings was unknown, veils <note>original: "uela"</note> were used to catch dust so it would not be sprinkled over the tables and the feast at the same time...

...so that he might not simultaneously defile the guests. It is known that the tapestries usually hung in dining rooms, called *aulaea* <note>original: "aulaea," referring to ornamental hangings or canopies</note> by Horace, are described in these verses:

We have found that Princes and Monarchs maintain this custom today; we often see their tables prepared under certain silk canopies, as if in tents. 

The second point is what we have taught in our various readings: in those ancient times, before crowns made of flowers, herbs, and gold came into use, those about to dine were accustomed to bind their temples and foreheads with wool or linen bands. This was done both to ward off <term>auerruncandos<gloss>A ritual term meaning to avert or ward off a potential evil or ailment</gloss></term> the headaches caused by food and drink, and to restrain drunkenness. I think this was devised for good reason, since the veins, arteries, and other passages of the head—the more they are compressed and constricted—receive fewer of the vapors rising from wine and food, which simultaneously cause various discomforts. 

The third point is that which Athenaeus has treated most brilliantly. In his writings, it is found 
<margin>The Learned Banqueters, book 11.</margin> 
and proven that those ancients first drank from the horns of oxen. From this, the term *to mix* <note>original Greek: κεράσαι (kerisai)</note>—that is, to temper wine with water—was called so *from the horns* <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τῶν κεράτων (apo ton keraton)</note>. Later, those horns were not only decorated with gold and silver, but were even made entirely of silver and gold, and guests were accustomed to toast one another with them. 

From all these details, it seems rightly concluded that the Rhamnusian stone is of the greatest antiquity. On it, the tapestries, the foreheads of guests bound with wool or linen bands, and the toasting done with horns are most clearly represented, along with several other instruments shown in the right margin. I leave the explanation of these to others more practiced in explaining antiquity. I also wish to advise them that if any figures of the reclining guests or tables in this very dining room appear less than complete, they should not be seized with wonder. Since the marble itself is today corroded by age and nearly erased, we thought it better to represent it as it is, rather than risking our credibility by adding or removing anything.

<vocab>Reclining</vocab> <note>original Latin: *Accubitus*, referring to the specific posture of leaning on one's side during a meal</note>

This illustration captures the essence of the ancient banquet. Unlike modern customs where we sit upright, the Greeks and Romans practiced the **reclining position** upon couches arranged around a central table. This tripod table, often called a <term>delphica<gloss>A three-legged table modeled after the tripod of Apollo at Delphi</gloss></term>, is shown here with legs carved to resemble the powerful limbs of lions. The servants are depicted in the midst of their duties: one presents a roasted beast—likely a sacrificial pig or boar—while others prepare the wine and water, continuing the traditions of mixing and service described in the preceding pages. This posture was not merely for comfort but was a mark of status and a requirement for the leisurely, intellectual discourse that defined the "Learned Banquet."

# BOOK ONE

<margin>D</margin>Now, therefore, returning to that which I proposed above, I say that since the customs of bathing and reclining were introduced and began to increase at the same time, it is likely that one took its origin from the other. It should not be said that baths took their origin from reclining, as baths are far more ancient; therefore, it remains that reclining had its beginning from the baths. 

The second reason is that the ancients, as far back as the times of Homer <note>The legendary Greek author of the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*.</note>, used to dine immediately after bathing. Indeed, from the passages of Homer cited by us above, it is clearly gathered that tables were usually prepared near the place where they washed. From this, if we consider the reasons of convenience, pleasure, and health, it was very much in accordance with reason that those—especially those who had private baths at home—having already been washed and dried, would enter their couches so as not to incur any harm but to escape weariness. They would not leave these couches, but soon see to it that tables and dinner were prepared nearby, and so they would eat. 

This is much like the majority of those physicians of our own time command to be done, who order either the infirm or even the healthy to bathe. For those <term>klismoi<gloss>original Greek: κλισμοὶ; a type of ancient chair or couch with a curved back</gloss></term> in which Homer depicts the suitors sitting after they have washed while they dine, were not much different from reclining couches. From this we are also able to conjecture that the custom of reclining then had a certain obscure beginning, which, gradually growing in later centuries, resulted in that form <margin>Book 14, Chapter 22</margin> which we see. 

For Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), author of *Natural History*.</note> also seems to have wished to hint at this when he disapproves of some who were too devoted to wine because they would not allow themselves to enter the beds first and put on a tunic after the bath, but ran naked immediately to drink. 

There is a third reason: since they did not begin to recline in this way for the sake of any other pleasure, convenience, or honor—for if we compare those sitting and those reclining while dining, the former enjoy far greater convenience, ease, dignity, and respectability than those reclining—it seems we must conclude that this custom was introduced for some other just reason. In my opinion, this was none other than because they bathed daily. Lest they be harmed by the washing or incur fatigue, and so they might better enjoy the moistening effect of the bath, they entered their beds. There, dressed either in a <term>lacerna<gloss>A coarse outer cloak worn by Romans</gloss></term> or what was otherwise called a wedding garment—or even naked, as they are shown in some marbles—they ordered tables to be set up for them. 

As this kind of custom gradually grew, it happened that not only were tables and couches always prepared together, but it even became a great disgrace if someone dining did not recline. This is gathered from these words of Plautus in his play *Stichus*: "We shall be received on a bench like Cynics <note>Followers of the Cynic school of philosophy who lived with extreme simplicity and rejected social comforts.</note>, rather than on couches." And as Martial indicated when he condemned Syriscus because he would dine in "sitting-taverns" <note>Low-status establishments where patrons sat on stools (*sellulae*) rather than reclining on couches.</note> without reclining. 

But if anyone should wish to oppose our opinion by saying that it does not seem at all likely in public banquets, in weddings, or in private dinners—

<summary>The author argues that the Roman custom of reclining while dining originated from the practice of bathing, as reclining protected the bather's health and comfort immediately following the bath. He supports this with references to Homeric chairs, Pliny's critiques of drinkers, and the social stigma against sitting while eating as mentioned by Plautus and Martial.</summary>

### BOOK ONE

<margin>A</margin>It is argued that among the ancients, baths were always used before dinner so that the guests might then lie upon the couches; and because a great part of the people washed in the public baths of the **gymnasiums** <note>In antiquity, gymnasiums were large complexes for both physical exercise and public bathing.</note> but dined in private homes, it was necessary for them to dress themselves upon leaving the baths. Furthermore, some believe it is hardly credible that craftsmen and all those who dined by reclining always washed beforehand. This is especially argued because we know from the plays of Plautus and Terence, and from Roman inscriptions, that it was the custom for those about to recline to have their <term>socci<gloss>light, slipper-like shoes</gloss></term> and <term>soleae<gloss>sandals</gloss></term> removed. This is used as an argument that guests did not always come directly from the baths. It is also established that the **triclinia** <note>The formal dining room in a Roman house, named for the three couches arranged around a central table.</note> were separated from the baths, and that the couches for reclining to eat and the beds for sleeping were distinct from one another.

To this I first respond that it is not at all clear to me that everyone, without distinction, always reclined. It is certainly true of the nobler and wealthier citizens who had private baths at home. <margin>B</margin><margin>Book 1, Satires; Epistle 6</margin> However, when **Horace** <note>A leading Roman lyric poet during the time of Augustus.</note> explains his own private way of living, he makes no mention of reclining; and **Martial** <note>A Roman poet famous for his short, witty epigrams.</note> indicates that those who ate in the so-called "seated" taverns did not recline at all. He speaks of **Syriscus** <note>A character portrayed as a spendthrift who squanders a fortune.</note> in this manner:

->Syriscus, having recently been poured a full<-
->ten million sesterces by his patron,<-
->wandering through the little seated taverns<-
->around the four baths, O Maximus, spent it all.<-
->O how great a gluttony to eat ten million!<-
->How much greater still not even to recline?<-

<margin>C</margin>But even granted that they reclined—and indeed that everyone washed—it can hardly be denied that mention is very rarely or never made of reclining among ancient authors without washing also being mentioned in some way. Regarding public banquets and wedding feasts, I admit that everyone then reclined on spread couches; however, no one can rightly deny that even then, everyone washed beforehand, either separately or together, in private or public baths. Indeed, it is likely that those about to attend public or private banquets of friends washed themselves first, lest they, carrying the filth contracted by necessity during the day, should disturb the other guests who were cleaner. For this reason, couches were always prepared for them.

Furthermore, the custom of removing sandals and shoes for those about to recline is a certain argument that they were accustomed to wash themselves beforehand. Lest their feet become soiled while walking from the baths to the couches, they were accustomed to cover them; then, while they reclined, they always took them off. Perhaps the **Apostles**, having been washed while they went to recline with **Christ**, had neither sandals nor shoes (which they used very little), and for that reason heard from Christ that they had indeed been washed, but still needed their feet to be washed <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 13:10, where Jesus tells Peter, "He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet."</note>. I add to this that it was by no means...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Roman dining habits, specifically the transition from reclining for rest after a bath to reclining as a standard, often luxurious, posture for eating.</meta>

<header>B O O K</header>

<meta>catchword: or</meta>

<margin>D</margin>...than for me to think that in later centuries everyone reclined while dining because they came straight from the baths. Rather, I believe the origin of reclining emanated from this: the ancients, upon leaving the baths, would enter their beds after a short interval to avoid the fatigue they had already contracted or to prevent future exhaustion. There, sometimes naked and sometimes dressed in cloaks or other garments prepared for that purpose, they would dine. From there, as the custom of bathing increased, the habit of reclining grew to such an extent that the nobility, holding it as the height of luxury, saw to it that couches were constructed separately for this purpose—sometimes made of marble, other times of silver (as they say of **Heliogabalus** <note>The Emperor Elagabalus, notorious for his extravagant and eccentric lifestyle.</note>). Nor did they wish to sleep on those dining couches—on which, however, many people used to sleep (as **Capitolinus** <note>One of the authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> records of the Emperor **Lucius Verus**, and as I believe the poor especially were accustomed to do)—but rather they preferred to sleep in beds called <term>cubicularii<gloss>bedroom couches</gloss></term>. This custom of reclining was later adopted by the common and poor people in imitation of the wealthy, occurring so frequently both after bathing and even while unwashed, <margin>E</margin><margin>Book 11 on Agriculture, chapter 1.</margin> that **Columella** <note>A prominent Roman writer on agriculture.</note> was forced to command that the <term>villicus<gloss>farm manager or overseer</gloss></term> should not dine reclining except on sacred feast days. In this matter, the result was no different than what is seen to have happened with baths and many other things: they were first invented for honest use and a kind of necessity, but were subsequently turned toward luxury, decadence, pleasure, and other such uses. 

Who is there who does not know that the ancients devised almost every pleasure for their banquets, leaving nothing out that might serve to soothe the mind? For they invented dinner-table conversations with great zeal to stimulate the intellect; they employed various kinds of music to delight the hearing; and they dedicated the most precious ointments to the sense of smell. Likewise, they held crowns woven from leaves and flowers <margin>Table Talk, Book 3, Problem 1.</margin><margin>On Simple Medicines, Book 6, chapter on dill.</margin><margin>The Instructor, Book 2, chapter 8.</margin>—which they wore sometimes on their hands, sometimes their necks, and sometimes their heads, as **Roman inscriptions**, **Plutarch**, **Galen**, and **Clement of Alexandria** testify; <margin>F</margin> they did this so that the fragrance and color would please the nose and eyes, induce sleep, and ward off drunkenness. Furthermore, how much effort they applied to seeking out the most delicate foods and drinks is proven not only by those sixteen types of foodstuffs brought to Rome from distant regions (as **Gellius** <note>Author of *Attic Nights*.</note> reports from **Varro** <margin>Book 7, chapter 15.</margin>), and many others named by **Julius Pollux**, but also by the many and nearly innumerable commentaries by authors on the culinary art cited by **Athenaeus** <note>Author of *The Learned Banqueters*, an encyclopedic work on ancient dining.</note>. 

Regarding the custom of the ancients of filling themselves with food only once a day, I am also of the opinion that since the ancients were compelled to wash every day before eating to cleanse their bodies (as we said in the previous chapter) and entered their beds directly from the washing, they would hardly have enough leisure to eat more than once a day. For if we look at each person's private business, and consider the time required for exercises, baths, and the preparation for reclining, a great part of their day was consumed. Thus, if they had wished to be satiated twice a day, they would have had to either omit their business...

<margin>A</margin>...or were forced to sometimes enter the baths with a full stomach, and to commit many other errors, both regarding their health and in other matters of lifestyle. > Having eaten not greedily, only as much as to prevent 
> lasting the day on an empty stomach. <note>Original Latin: "Pransus non auide, quantum interpellet inani Ventre diem durare."</note>

Furthermore, I believe the reason they dedicated the evening hour to dinner was primarily for the convenience of life; indeed, it would have been difficult to apply oneself to doing business after exercise, baths, and food. <margin>B</margin> Moreover, since they dined while reclining, some were seized by sleep immediately, while others, after staying awake for a short span of time, went to bed. For this reason, no hour was found more suitable for all these things than the evening, although I also suspect that some people, and especially physicians, looked to the requirements of health in this matter, since food is better <term>concocted<gloss>digested</gloss></term> at night than during the day, and it is clear that one should eat more at the time when more can be digested. These are the things I wished to say <term>incidentally<gloss>Greek: παρεργῶς (parergōs)</gloss></term> regarding the origin of reclining and the dinner of the ancients.

### On the Authors of Gymnastics, and the attendants of the gymnasts. Chap. XII.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'V' depicting a seated scholar or teacher figure, possibly an ancient physician or philosopher, gesturing towards text.</image-desc>

<margin>C</margin>JUST AS other arts had their own authors who committed their capabilities, rules, and use to writing, it is similarly certain that gymnastics was by no means lacking in those who illustrated it with volumes and rescued it from oblivion. But it happened that these authors also suffered the same loss that many human affairs have undergone, since in these times we have none of those whom we know for certain Galen and other more ancient writers saw and read often. For who in our age has seen the writings of **Hippocrates**, **Diocles**, **Praxagoras**, **Philotimus**, **Erasistratus**, **Herophilus**, and **Asclepiades** <note>A list of foundational figures in ancient Greek medicine and physiology.</note> on this subject, though they are cited by Greek and Latin authors? If their most distinguished commentaries were not missing today, perhaps this art—which has already been nearly abolished for a long time—would have no less dignity and splendor than the others; nor would we have to take up this labor of bringing it back to light. I pass over the books of **Theon** on this same subject, and the commentaries of the gymnast **Diotimus** on exercises and sweats, which were celebrated by **Theophrastus**. When I consider that we lack these works...

**B** After these followed the **Gymnast** (*Gymnastas*), whom Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire.</note>, in the second book of *On the Maintenance of Health*, maintained was the master of all exercises. He was skilled in knowing their strength and power as they relate to health; he taught athletes and all other exercisers how the exercises should be performed, for how long, and which ones were suitable for whom. This was because he was either a physician himself, or equal to a physician in many respects, as is gathered from the eleventh book of Plato's *Laws*. There, Plato argues that if someone sells a sick slave to a physician or a gymnast, the sale cannot be revoked <note>Latin: *redhibendum*, a legal term for returning a defective purchase for a refund.</note>, as if both of them ought to know how to distinguish the ailing from the healthy. Indeed, Basil, in his eleventh homily on the *Hexameron* <note>A series of sermons by Basil of Caesarea on the six days of creation.</note> regarding the nature of man, teaches that the Gymnast and the physician are equally accustomed to observe and investigate. Cicero, in a certain letter to Lentulus <note>Publius Cornelius Lentulus Spinther, a Roman consul and friend of Cicero.</note>, wrote the following: **D** 
> "But I would have wished that they [the physicians] had taken thought not only for my health, as doctors do, but also for my strength and complexion, as the **trainer-anointers** <note>Original Latin: *aliptae*. These were specialists in the gymnasium who used oils and massage to improve an athlete's physical condition.</note> do."

From this, Clement of Alexandria stated in the sixth book of his *Miscellanies* that health is obtained through medicine, but a good bodily condition is acquired through the art of anointing. I am aware, however, that the term *alipta* is also sometimes used for the common anointer himself, or for the master of the anointers, as can be seen frequently in Plutarch’s book *On Preserving Health* and in the works of Caelius Aurelianus. In such cases, Galen notes in his *Explanation of Terms* that Hippocrates preferred to use the word <term>exaleipto</term> <note>Original Greek: *ἐξαλείπτω*, meaning to smear or anoint thoroughly.</note>. 

After the Gymnast came the <margin>In the book *To Thrasybulus*.</margin> **Physical Instructor** <note>Original Latin: *Paedotriba*.</note>. Although according to Plato this role did not seem to differ from that of the Gymnast, Galen nonetheless writes that they were quite distinct. He likens the Gymnast to a physician or a General, while he compares the Physical Instructor to a soldier or a cook, calling the instructor a mere servant to the Gymnast. Just as a **E** soldier knows nothing of the science of war, and a cook knows nothing of the science of medicine—but both merely execute the commands of the General or the physician—likewise the Physical Instructor was ignorant of the full power of all exercises. He only carried out the Master Gymnast’s instructions, for although he understood the use, the differences, and the methods of exercises through a kind of practical experience, he would frequently go astray due to his lack of theoretical knowledge. This is what Galen intended to imply in his short work *On the Epileptic Boy*, where he remarked that it was difficult to find a prudent Physical Instructor. 

The philosopher Aristotle also seems to have recognized this difference between the Gymnast and the Physical Instructor when, in the eighth book of the *Politics*, he concludes that youths should be handed over to the arts of gymnastics and physical instruction; for one of these creates a certain habit of the body, while the other <margin>Chapter 3.</margin> oversees its operations. Furthermore, in the fourth book of the *Politics*, in a passage cited earlier, he says: **F** **"one should care no less for the physical trainer and the gymnast, even in accordance with this capacity."** <note>Original Greek: *μηδὲν ἧττον τοῦ παιδοτρίβου καὶ τοῦ γυμναστοῦ φροντίσαιτε, καὶ ταύτην ἐπὶ τὴν δύναμιν*.</note>

Thus, the Gymnast was the overseer of exercises, while the Physical Instructor was the servant. The instructor corresponds proportionally to the baker, the cook, or the builder: they know how to make bread, prepared dishes, or houses, but they do not understand what is best or least optimal within those things, nor do they discern what power each of them holds for the preservation of health. Galen remarks that these two names do not exist in the works of Homer because, as we explained before, only the "seeds" of the gymnastic art were visible at that time; the art had not yet been reduced to rules and a formal system, and therefore there was neither a master artist nor a servant. 

There was also the **Ball-game Instructor** <note>Original Latin: *Sphaeristicus*.</note>, the teacher of those who played with the ball. <margin>Book 2, *On the Maintenance of Health*.</margin> He was like a Physical Instructor who, according to Galen, was skilled in every throw, catch, or strike of the ball, yet he did not know in the least which...

**A** As for what the **Morning Games** and **Great Games** were, I find it recorded that the spectacles given to the public were held partly in the morning and partly after the midday meal, which was provided publicly to the people in the city. In the morning, matches between wild beasts, or between men and beasts, were presented, as can be seen in Seneca's 7th Letter, as well as at the end of the third book of *On Anger*. After the midday meal, combat between men was joined; this type of gladiatorial service is frequently mentioned by historians, and the same Seneca mentions it in his 7th Letter. It is easy to understand that those who fought against beasts were called <term>beast-fighters</term> <note>original Latin: *bestiarios*</note>, while the gladiators were called <term>midday fighters</term> <note>original Latin: *meridiani*</note> by Suetonius in his life of Claudius. As for why the midday spectacle was called the **Great Game**, I believe the reason is that a larger crowd of spectators flocked to see the combat of men than that of beasts; thus, everyone, **B** and especially Seneca, rightfully attacked this delight of the people in watching homicides. Nevertheless, one should not be ignorant of the fact that certain schools in Rome were called the Great and Morning Games, perhaps because men exercised in the former at midday and in the latter in the morning. I conclude, therefore, that the gymnasiums had all these attendants: the **gymnasium leader** <note>original Greek: *gymnasiarcham*</note> as the head of the place; the **master of the portico** <note>original Greek: *xystarchum*</note> as the teacher of athletes; and the **gymnast** <note>original Greek: *gymnastam*</note> as the overseer of all exercises, a man of no small status, since he understood their capacity for health, the manner and time of use, and other such matters. Subject to the gymnast were many attendants: the **physical trainer** <note>original Greek: *paedotriba*</note> who served the wrestling school and oversaw wrestling exercises; the **ball-game master**; the **rubber** <note>one who performed massages</note>; the **anointer**; the **menial servant**; the **ball-player**; the **hair-plucker**; the **doorkeeper**; and the **furnace-stoker**. Let these things we have said regarding the gymnasiums of the ancients suffice.

**D** ...of the whole kind: the true or legitimate gymnastics (to speak in the manner of Galen), the military type, and a third which Galen called "corrupt" <note>original Latin: *vitiosam*; referring to the unhealthy or excessive training of professional athletes</note>. Although all of these involve nearly the same physical exercises and movements for the human body, they differ greatly in their goals—the purposes for which each was established—as we have also shown above. For simple gymnastics, which is a branch of medicine, cares only for this: that through moderate exercise, men might acquire and maintain health and achieve a good physical condition. <margin>In the book *On Philosophy*</margin> "I admit," Plato said, "that it is not excessive but moderate exercise that produces a state of well-being <note>original Greek: *euexia* (εὐεξίαν)</note> in men." Because Galen demonstrated this truth as extensively as he did clearly, both in his short work *To Thrasybulus* and in his books *On Protecting Health*, and since we also declared matters pertaining to this **E** branch above, I will not linger any longer in praising it with words, but will move on to **Military Gymnastics**. Its purpose since ancient times was to prepare and adapt boys—and among some peoples, even women—through these same exercises, so that they might conduct themselves bravely in war, repel enemies, protect their homelands, and finally possess all military skill. For although this type, like the former, also provided a good physical condition and protected health to some degree, it is clear that they are not the same; its specific goal was to make men fit and strong for waging war. To prove that military gymnastics has no nature other than what I have explained, I bring forward Plato as a most wealthy witness, who, in the seventh book of *The Laws* (after declaring that the education of the young and children occupies the greatest part of public affairs), **F** decrees that public teachers should be employed to teach gymnastics to boys, girls, and young women. He believed that for achieving military skill, nothing better could be found than the **wrestling** <note>original Latin: *palaestrica*</note> and **dancing** <note>original Latin: *saltatoria*</note> branches of gymnastics, a point he also pursued most elegantly in the third book of *The Republic* and often elsewhere. After Plato, Aristotle similarly explicitly identified military gymnastics in the eighth book of the *Politics*, where he criticizes both those cities that try to deform the bodies of youths with the habits of athletes and hinder their growth, as well as the **Spartans** <note>original Latin: *Lacones*</note> who make their adolescents wild with excessive labor. He advises that boys should be given a type of gymnastics that can make them robust and truly brave in military affairs through milder labors and gentler exercises. Regarding this gymnastics, it was clearly spoken...

**A** I do not find this specifically in Galen, unless we wish to believe that he includes it under "legitimate gymnastics" when he celebrates it, because it also focuses on achieving a good physical condition, even though it directs all its efforts toward military skill and fitness. Indeed, those who apply themselves to the study of medical gymnastics may also be capable of performing military duties when necessary. Among Latin writers, Vegetius taught clearly in his books on military matters how much this gymnastics contributes to warfare, and how it should be learned and practiced. Thus, there is no doubt that an art of this kind was held in high esteem among both the Greek and Latin nations. 

Besides these two, there is another "corrupt" gymnastics, called "athletic" by Galen, which focused on making men exceptionally strong. Such a man was Milo of Croton <note>A famous Greek wrestler of the 6th century BCE, known for his legendary feats of strength</note>, and that athlete of whom Olympiodorus wrote (in the fourth book of his *Meteorology*, in the chapter on hard and soft things) that he was accustomed to crushing clods of earth <note>original Greek: *ta bōlia* (τὰ βώλια)</note>. These men exerted themselves so that they might win in competitions and earn **B** prizes and crowns. 

I find this art called by many names among ancient authors. The Greeks sometimes call it "agonistic" <note>original: *agōnistikēn* (ἀγωνιστικήν); from the word for a struggle or contest</note>, sometimes "sacred contests," sometimes "athletic," and sometimes "gymnic." The Latins call them "gymnic contests," sometimes "sacred games," or "athletic art." Because these contests were celebrated in honor of one of the Gods, they were called either "sacred contests" or "holy games" <note>original Greek: *hieroi agōnes* (ἱεροὶ ἀγῶνες)</note>. I find that those who trained for them were sometimes called "athletes of the sacred games," as in Xenophon’s book on the sayings and deeds of Socrates: "Just as the athletes of the gymnic contests who easily hold the first place neglect their practice" <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ οἱ τῶν γυμνικῶν ἀγώνων ἀθληταὶ ῥᾳδίως πρωτεύσαντες ἀμελοῦσι τῆς ἀσκήσεως</note>. 

However, they were called by other names when they were performed in amphitheaters and circuses for the amusement of the people, or when they took place in gymnasiums or other public places merely for the sake of exercise. Nevertheless, according to the opinion of Julius Pollux <margin>Book 2</margin>, all such competitors are found to have a common name: they are most often simply called "athletes." This is either from the goal they pursued, which was the "prize" <note>original Greek: *athloi* (ἆθλοι)</note>, or from the "contest" <note>original Greek: *athlou* (ἄθλου)</note> itself. 

Galen, however, preferred to say <margin>In his *Art of Medicine*, comment 60</margin> that the name is derived from "wretched" <note>original Greek: *athliou* (ἀθλίου)</note> or from "wretchedness" <note>original Greek: *athliotētos* (ἀθλιότητος)</note> to signify the incredible misery of this class of men—though it is not necessary to believe this is the true origin. I have said that any such trainers who compete for the sake of a prize were called "athletes" by that simple name, because even Plato occasionally uses that term for teachers of military gymnastics, but he almost never uses it alone; he nearly always adds a qualifier, as in the third book of the *Republic*...

**D** where, distinguishing true athletes from those of war, he [Plato] says: <note>original Greek: κομψοτέρας ἄτ’ ἴσως μοι δοκεῖ ἀσκήσεως δεῖ τοῖς πολεμικοῖς ἀθληταῖς, οὕς γε ὥσπερ κύνας ἀγρύπνους τ’ ἀνάγκη εἶναι</note> "I think military athletes require a somewhat more refined training, as they must be like sleepless guard dogs." And again in the seventh book of the *Republic*: <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ δ’ ἐννοῶ λέγον ἅμα, οὐκ ἀθλητὰς μέντοι πολέμου ἔφαμεν τούτους ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι νέους ὄντας?</note> "But this comes to my mind as I speak: did we not say these youths must be athletes of war?" He speaks similarly in other places. From all of this it is apparent that whenever Plato calls those practicing military gymnastics "athletes," he always adds the qualifier "military," "of war," or something similar. For example, at the end of the seventh book of the *Laws*, he mentions "the athletes among us" for no other reason than to distinguish them from the true [professional] athletes.

Therefore, in conclusion, I say that the practitioners of the first [medical] and second [military] types of gymnastics are never properly called "athletes." That name belongs **E** only to the practitioners of the third type. Galen, in the first book of *On the Properties of Foodstuffs*, admits that <term>palaestritae</term> <note>wrestlers who trained in the palaestra or wrestling school</note>, boxers, <term>pancratiasts</term> <note>competitors in the pancratium, an ancient martial art combining boxing and wrestling</note>, and others who compete for a prize are ubiuquitously but less properly called by this name. Since these wrestlers and the rest had only one goal—to prepare themselves for contests in which they were forced to wrestle or fight the <term>pancratium</term> for an entire day—they required food that was difficult to break down and slow to digest. This was the sort of food provided by the meat of swine, which only true athletes ate. Such were the men who competed in the games, in the amphitheaters, and in other places for prizes and glory. They differed from others in this: they studied only how to win and attain the crown, whereas others intended either to acquire a good physical condition and maintain health, or to acquire military fortitude and skill. I find these latter groups are simply called **F** "gymnasts" or "the trained," or sometimes "military athletes."

From this we gather that a "simple athlete" is one thing, and a "simple gymnast" is another. Furthermore, there were three arts involving physical exercise called by the common name of gymnastics. Of these, the medical art was most properly called by that name; the second, the military art, was less so (I say this among physicians, though others might perhaps make the military art primary); and the third was the least proper of all. Indeed, this third art, degenerating from the others, is called "corrupt" or "vicious," because it devotes its effort to sheer strength rather than health. Aristotle is a witness that strength requires a different physical constitution than health, as he writes in the eighth section of his *Problems*, number six. In that place, he writes that a fleshy, thick constitution is suited for strength, but a lean and sparse one is suited for health.

# ### ## Concerning Corrupt Gymnastics, or Athletics. Chapter XIV.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'P' featuring leafy scrollwork and a small face or floral element in the center.</image-desc>

<margin>In his *Exhortation to the Good Arts*</margin>
**A**FTER we have sufficiently discussed military gymnastics, and even simple gymnastics, as far as the present business was concerned, it will now be appropriate to have a discourse on athletics. Because this practice had claimed for itself the greatest authority during the time of Galen, and even in earlier ages, it was necessary for him to attack it with a very long oration and with the most foul and insulting words. How wisely and justly he did this will, I hope, be very easily clarified from what I am about to say regarding the character and other conditions of its practitioners. To begin at the beginning, Pliny is the authority for the fact that gymnastic games were invented by Lycaon, and athletics by Hercules <margin>Book 7, chapter 56</margin> at Olympia. Thus, this whole art had two parents who, although they were distinguished and originally founded an illustrious art worthy of admiration, **B** it was nevertheless so corrupted and adulterated by the wicked habits of men over a long interval of time that Galen said the name <term>kakotechnia</term> <note>original Greek: κακοτεχνίας; meaning a "fraudulent craft" or "evil art" rather than a true science</note> was more suited to it than "art." Indeed, <margin>In the book *To Thrasybulus*</margin> its practitioners, while they applied themselves too much to thickening the body and acquiring strength in the hope of victory and a prize (for whose sake, as we have properly taught, all those who competed were called "athletes"), they also rendered their minds thick and all their senses dull, torpid, and sluggish. For this reason, Plato not undeservedly called athletes sleepy, sluggish, lazy, <margin>Third book of the *Republic*; First book of the *Aphorisms*</margin> idle, prone to dizziness, and finally diseased. In this, he followed the physician Hippocrates, who everywhere detested the physical condition of athletes as dangerous and subject to the greatest illnesses. Similarly, Plutarch <margin>In the book *On Preserving Health*</margin> likened them to the columns of the gymnasium—sturdy but immobile—and elsewhere confessed that nothing else brought softness and slavery upon the Greeks except this **C** corrupt gymnastics. Through its influence, becoming sluggish and weak, they fell away from the use of arms, content to be called "good wrestlers" and "athletes" instead of strenuous and brave soldiers. Furthermore, no sane person will doubt that this is the case if they consider the entire nature of the matter as explained by Aristotle in a very brief statement. In the first book of the *Rhetoric*, concerning <term>Agonistica</term> <note>the art of competition, which we said above was also called athletics</note>, he left these words written: <margin>Chapter 5</margin> <note>The following is a translation of the Greek quote: "The excellence of the body in competition consists of size, strength, and speed; for the swift man is also strong. He who can throw his legs far, and move them quickly and far, is a runner; he who can squeeze and hold down is a wrestler; he who can shove with a blow is a boxer; he who can do both these things is a pancratiast; and he who excels in all is a pentathlete."</note> "The excellence of the body in competition consists of size, strength, and speed; for the swift man is also strong. For the one who is able to throw his legs Gymnastica. forward..."

...can throw himself forward and move swiftly and far is a **runner**; **D** he who can squeeze and hold fast is a **wrestler**; he who strikes with a blow to drive his opponent back is a **boxer**; he who excels in both of these is a **pancratiast** <note>A practitioner of the *pancratium*, an ancient Greek sport combining boxing and wrestling with very few rules.</note>; and he who excels in all of these is a **quinquertio** <note>The Latin term for a pentathlete.</note>. From these examples, it is clearly evident that the training and discipline of all athletes was directed toward this single goal: to acquire body size, strength, and speed, through which they alone could overcome other antagonists and obtain the prize and honor. Although they competed in many types of contests, there were five principal ones in which they competed—either always or for the most part—both in sacred contests and in games, amphitheatres, and public spectacles, but especially in the stadium, which was almost exclusively destined for athletes: wrestling, boxing, running, jumping, and the discus. Hence they were called wrestlers, boxers, runners, jumpers, and discus-throwers, if they excelled in each separately; just as a **pancratiast** was the name for one who was strong in wrestling and boxing; but he who was strong in all **E** five was called a **pentathlete**, or in the Roman term, a **quinquertius**, as Festus teaches. 

However, the same Festus writes that among Livius Andronicus <note>A Greco-Roman dramatist and poet (c. 284–204 BC).</note> the term *quinquertiones* signified athletes in general; among whom also he was said to have "won the circuit" <note>original: *perihodon uicisse*</note> who had won at the Pythian, Isthmian, Nemean, and Olympic games, taking the name from the "circuit" or cycle of those spectacles. Later there were jumping weights <note>original: *halteres*; these were held in the hands to increase the distance of a jump.</note>, javelins, and several other things whose contests athletes also undertook, but in the celebration of public games and sacred contests, those were rarely performed, with the exception of single combat <note>original: *monomachia*</note>, which Galen recorded <margin>Book 3, distinction 23</margin> that Greek priests were accustomed to practice in Pergamon during the summer time. 

Although I know that among the ancients "single-combatants" <note>original: *monomachos*</note> or gladiators were distinct from athletes, as Marcus Cicero testified in his *Letters to Friends* [Book 7, Letter 1] with these words: "For why should I think you long for athletes, when you have despised gladiators?" **F** Unless we say what is recorded by Dionysius of Halicarnassus in *Roman Antiquities* [Book 10], that some athletes were of the lighter contests and others of the heavier contests, and that these latter were the gladiators. 

Concerning these, I find it written by Ulpian in the *Digest* [Book 9, Title 2, *Lex Aquilia*]: "If in a wrestling match, or in a pancratium, or while boxers are training among themselves, one kills another, the Aquilian law <note>The *Lex Aquilia* was a Roman law providing compensation for damage to property or injuries caused by negligence.</note> does not apply, because the harm is seen to have been given for the sake of glory and valor, not out of malice." From this, I think it is clear that among our ancestors this athletic art was held in the highest esteem; the reason for which was that men are always accustomed to extol and make worthy of honor those things from which they strive to obtain pleasure and delight. Because athletics brought the greatest public pleasures in the public games and other spectacles, it was held in honor and sought after by many; so much so that when <margin>Book 16, chapter 4</margin> athletes entered the games, as Pliny reports, everyone would stand up, even the Senate, and they sat next to the Senate, as well as with their fathers and paternal grandfathers...

**A** They were exempt from any public duties, and victors were carried into their homelands in triumphs; indeed, Sextus Empiricus <note>A skeptical philosopher and physician (c. 160–210 AD) who recorded ancient customs.</note> in the third book of the *Outlines of Pyrrhonism* <note>original: *iij.hypot. Pyrrhon.*</note> is our witness that it was not only permitted but even considered honorable for athletes to strike and even kill well-born citizens—acts which the laws forbade to others. Not to mention that Eusebius <note>A Greek historian of Christianity (c. 260–339 AD) who argued against pagan practices.</note>, in the fifth book of *Preparation for the Gospel*, condemns the ancients at great length for having reached such a point of superstition and madness as to count boxers and athletes among the gods. For all these reasons, it can be clearly seen that athletics held great authority in ancient times; and therefore Galen <note>The most famous physician of the Roman Empire, who wrote a famous "Exhortation to the Arts" criticizing the unhealthy life of professional athletes.</note> did not attack it without reason, as he noticed how much damage the reputation of the athletic art caused to the human race. Indeed, not only were all the virtues of the mind but even the goods of the body so corrupted that nothing could be found more detrimental to men than that art, which they sought from every side for the sake of glory and prizes, as Euripides also most elegantly testified in these words:

**B**

> There is nothing worse than the race of athletes.
> First, they do not even learn how to live well at home;
> Nor could they, for how can any man
> Who is a slave to his jaw and a servant to his belly
> Acquire wealth to support his fatherland?
> Nor, again, do they know how to be poor and serve fortune’s turns.
> For men not accustomed to good habits
> Hardly change for the better when times are tough.

Which is to say, 

> When countless evils creep through Greece,

> Who first do not learn to live well in their homes,

**C**

> Can anyone devoted to gluttony and indulging his belly
> Prepare riches to nourish his family?
> Nor likewise do they know how to be needy and serve their fortunes:

> Habits, they are not easily changed for the better.

In my judgment, nothing reveals the state of athletics more than these words. Yet, there have been some who strove to celebrate this pernicious art in their commentaries, such as Tryphon and Theon of Alexandria—the latter of whom, though he excelled in athletics, eventually abandoned it for gymnastics <note>The author distinguishes between *athletica* (professional, prize-seeking competition) and *gymnastica* (exercise for health and virtue).</note> once its wickedness was known. Nor should I be silent about Plato, whom Servius and Laertius record was an athlete, but who left it behind to devote himself to philosophy. But because it did not escape notice that athletes were accustomed to compete for the sake of a prize and to expose their lives to a thousand kinds of death...

## *On the Regimen of Athletes. Chapter XV.*

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut initial letter 'V' featuring a bearded scholar or physician in classical attire, seated at a desk and working with books in an arched architectural space.</image-desc>

**S** **INCE** many things have been argued both excellently and eloquently by Hippocrates, Plato, and Galen regarding the "athletic depravity" <note>original: *athletica prauitate*. In early medicine, this refers to the unhealthy, overdeveloped, and unstable physical state of professional athletes compared to a naturally healthy person.</note>, and we ourselves have said a few things in imitation of them, I have now decided to set forth the way of life of those athletes who were specifically called *palaestritae* <note>Wrestlers or those trained in the wrestling school (palaestra).</note>. Once this is understood, it will be easy for anyone to judge what kind of men they were, what their art consisted of, and how wisely those acted who attempted to explode that art and condemn it with reproachful speech. But, because a person's entire way of life is situated in six things which physicians have chosen to call the "non-naturals" <note>A foundational medical concept: six external factors that influence health but are not part of human nature itself—air, food/drink, sleep/waking, motion/rest, evacuations, and emotions.</note>—namely food and drink, sleep and waking, rest and motion, air, the passions of the mind, and the evacuation of wastes—I shall explain how they conducted themselves in each of these categories. First, then, in food and drink, they are seen to have erred in four ways: in quality, quantity, order, and timing. Regarding quality, I find that athletes used different foods at different times. Indeed, Pliny and Oribasius write that the earliest ancestors were prescribed to eat dried figs <note>original: *caricis*; specifically figs from Caria in Asia Minor.</note>, which I believe they did in order to become fat. However, authors disagree among themselves as to who first allowed them meat. Pliny writes that a certain trainer named Pythagoras first offered meat to be eaten by athletes. Oribasius of Pergamon <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler and personal physician to the Emperor Julian.</note> records that a man named Goras abolished the use of figs and the ancient custom of living, and first served meat to Euramenes of Samos, and that such a way of life then passed down to posterity. However that may be, athletes were eating meat before the time of Hippocrates, and especially pork, as he himself reports concerning the boxer Biantes in the fifth book of the *Epidemics*. Furthermore, they did not always live on just one kind of meat, since they sometimes ate goat meat—as in the case of a certain Theban athlete whom Clitomachus of Carthage (a famous follower of the New Academy) reports surpassed the other athletes of his time in strength because he ate goat...

<margin>Pliny, Book 13, ch. 7. Oribasius, Book 1 of the Collections, ch. 40.</margin>

**A** ...that he ate goat meat. Martial <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis (c. 38–104 AD), a Roman poet known for his Epigrams.</note> implies in his third book that boar glands were also used as food for athletes; while describing the insolence and obscene habits of a certain Zoilus, he says:

> Among the little dogs licking the entrails of geese,
> He distributes boar-glands to the wrestlers.

However, it is well established from Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note> that they made more frequent use of both beef and pork. He writes that they lived on these meats and on bread made with cheese without leaven, which was called *Coliphium* <note>original: *Coliphium*. A type of coarse, nutritious bread or diet specifically intended to make the limbs of athletes firm.</note>, so that through the hardness and density of the nourishment they might not only be more abundantly nourished, but also remain full for longer. When the boxer Biantes, a "glutton" <note>original: πολυβόρος (*polyboros*), meaning "much-devouring" or "gluttonous."</note>, used this type of diet immoderately, he fell into those diseases reported by Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460–370 BC).</note> in the fifth book of his *Epidemics*.

Pliny <margin>Book 4, On Medical Matters, chapter 27.</margin> and Valerian write that no food for athletes existed without dill (*anethum*), perhaps because they believed solid nourishment was produced by it, or so that other foods might be seasoned with the scent of such a herb and thus taste better to them, or so that a deeper sleep might be provoked in them for the purpose of digesting heavy foods; for doctors know that dill provokes sleep. 

**B** How much the quantity of food for athletes exceeded the measures of other men can be known from those things which Galen committed to writing in the second book of *On the Prognosis of Pulses*. Specifically, he notes that two *minae* <note>original: *minas*. A Greek unit of weight; two minae would be roughly two pounds or nearly a kilogram.</note> of meat was considered "little food" for athletes. 

**C** Thus, we are able to some extent to give credit to that legendary story celebrated concerning the athlete Milo of Croton <note>A legendary 6th-century BC wrestler known for his incredible strength.</margin> and the boxer Heraclides. They say that one of them swallowed twenty *minae* of meat and the same amount of bread, and drained three *choes* <note>original: *choas*. A Greek liquid measure; three choes equals roughly 9-10 liters.</note> of wine; and once, he alone consumed a whole bull which he had carried through the stadium while holding his breath. They say the other was capable of nearly infinite food and drink, and stood equal to no one. 

From this it becomes clear how truly Aristotle <margin>Chapter 3.</margin> spoke in the fourth book of *On the Generation of Animals*, saying that the limbs of athletes are frequently affected by various deformities. This occurs because, on account of their great voracity, nature is not equally able to digest all parts of the food throughout the whole body and distribute the digested parts evenly. Similarly, in the eighth book of the *Politics*, he called the food of those who exercised athletically sometimes "violent nourishment" <note>original: βίαν τροφοῦ (*bian trophou*)</note>, and sometimes "forced eating" <note>original: ἀναγκοφαγίαν (*anagkophagian*)</note>. Likewise Galen, in the third book of *On Preserving Health*, called it "eating by necessity" <note>original: ἐδωδὴν πρὸς ἀνάγκην (*edodēn pros anagkēn*)</note>, as if they were forced to eat more than they could bear. I know, however, that there have been those who interpreted that phrase in Aristotle differently. Clement of Alexandria <margin>Book 7, Method.</margin> also uses this term in the second book of the *Paedagogus*, chapter one. 

It can be sufficiently clear from the above that athletes similarly observed no order, or very little, in eating, and had no regard for time—except for what Galen reports: that they were not accustomed to take their strongest foods equally in the morning and evening, but only at dinner. They were taught this not only by reason, but also by experience, that such foods...

...foods are more easily digested in sleep, when the internal heat is more active within, while otherwise these foods are very difficult to digest, both because of their quality—which strongly resists heat—and because of their immense quantity. However, Pliny <margin>Book 11, chapter 53.</margin> seems to have felt differently; he writes that athletes always preferred to complete the digestion of their food by walking rather than by sleep, believing that sleep contributed more to bulkiness than to actual firmness. Yet, if Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and historian (c. 46–120 AD).</note> in the fourth book of his *Symposiacs* <margin>Problem 4.</margin> records that these same men lived on the simplest foods and avoided all variety entirely, we ought to accept his opinion in this way: he meant that athletes used only one kind of meat and bread, whatever and however much it might be. We do not deny this, as we stated above that their most frequent foods were only beef, or more often, pork.

Furthermore, Plato most clearly demonstrated what kind of moderation athletes applied to sleep and wakefulness—corresponding to the other parts of their lives—by calling them "sleepy" everywhere in his writings. Galen also testifies <margin>38. part, problem 5.</margin> that athletes were accustomed to observing no measure in movement or rest; he relates that they were used to working sometimes all day—specifically when they underwent the "complete" <note>original: τέλειον (*teleion*)</note> exercise or the "preparation" <note>original: κατασκευὴν (*kataskeuēn*), referring to a rigorous training cycle.</note> mentioned by Galen in the third book of *On Preserving Health*—sometimes at night, sometimes at dawn, and sometimes before noon. It is as if they held it as their purpose to despise these precepts of Hippocrates concerning universal health (namely: moderation in labor, food, drink, sleep, and sex), and instead proposed for themselves to work immoderately, always, and without any rule.

When Aristotle understood this, he sought the reason why those who sweat moderately are immediately cheered by a pleasant color after exercise, while athletes turn out quite pale. <margin>In the book on the timings of diseases.</margin> He said this happens because athletes work altogether too much; indeed, excessive labor drives out the healthy color along with the sweat and the breath, and induces paleness. In contrast, moderate heat slightly retains the color at the surface of the body and invites it outward, just as happens to those who are warmed or those who blush from shame. Therefore, since they always worked without measure, it is not at all surprising that Galen said athletes lasted at their "peak strength" <note>original: ἰσοθενεῖς (*isostheneis*)</note> for five years at most.

Now we can also believe that they made no distinction regarding the air, because they exercised under the burning sun and took no account of the winds or other conditions of good air. However, while they were training for future contests, the ancients took care that this was done in healthy air, as is evident from the *xysti* <note>Covered porticos or galleries used by ancient Greeks and Romans for exercise.</note>. Vitruvius <note>A Roman architect and engineer of the 1st century BC.</note> writes that these were built in gymnasiums so that in winter, athletes could exercise more comfortably in healthier air to avoid the injuries of the weather. During this time, as Basil the Great <note>An influential 4th-century theologian and bishop.</note> records <margin>Homily 54.</margin>, they endured many blows from the trainers <note>original: *paedotribis*, the physical instructors in a gymnasium.</note> and followed a diet that was hardly pleasant, but rather prescribed by the masters of exercise.
