In Strabo <margin>Geography, Book 5.</margin> we read that ancient athletes were accustomed to being sent to Ravenna, so that they might be exercised more conveniently in the healthier air there. No one will deny that athletes were affected by the passions of the mind more vehemently than is proper, if one considers how easily all competitors flare up in anger for the slightest reason, how greatly the defeated are saddened, how much the victors exult, and finally, in what a constant state of mind they live who are tortured now by immoderate gluttony and now by hunger, as athletes are. Regarding the evacuation of waste (which was the sixth and last point), few things need be said, because perhaps they erred less in this than in other matters; but since sexual activity <note>original: "venus"</note> is placed by doctors among the evacuations necessary for health, let us see how they conducted themselves in that matter. For while both Hippocrates and Galen taught that sexual activity should be moderate, they are judged by all who are even moderately learned in medicine to have condemned both those who use it immoderately and those who use it too sparingly. Hence, athletes are seen to have sinned greatly in this regard, as they perpetually forbade themselves intercourse, although they perhaps had more need of it than others due to their excessive abundance of nourishment and blood. For Galen spoke of these men in the sixth book of *On Affected Places*, chapter 5, <margin>On Affected Places, Book 6, at the end.</margin> when he wrote that he had seen many of a hot and moist nature become torpid and sluggish because of training <note>original: ὑπὸ ἀσκήσεως (*hypo askēseōs*)</note> (not out of shame or sobriety, as most interpreters translate) when they abstained from sexual use. Furthermore, that athletes abstained entirely from sexual activity is recorded not only by Plato <margin>On the Laws, Book 8.</margin>—who handed down to memory that Astylus, Diopompus Crisson, and Icous of Tarentum were such men—but Galen also testified to it. After Galen, Basil the Great <note>A 4th-century Christian bishop and theologian.</note> wrote in his 52nd homily that the trainers <term>paedotribas</term> <note>Ancient Greek physical trainers who supervised the exercises of youths.</note>, considering that the body is rendered weaker and sluggish for necessary tasks by sexual pleasures, promulgated a law of temperance. This law was intended to keep the bodies of young men safe from pleasures and not even permit the competitors to look at beautiful forms. Martial also indicated this when, speaking of a certain athlete named Blatara, he left these words:

<margin>Book 11.</margin>
> Why does he drench his body, yellowed with Spartan wrestling-oil <term>ceromate</term> <note>A mixture of oil, wax, and dust used by wrestlers.</note>,
> With cold virgin water? Lest he engage in sex.

For athletes not only washed themselves with cold water to inhibit sexual desire, but even applied lead plates to the regions of the kidneys and loins to ward off nocturnal emissions and break the impulses of lust, as Pliny and Galen testified <margin>Pliny Book 34, ch. 18; Galen on the preservation of health, last chapter.</margin>. I believe Saint Paul also wished this to be understood when he said: "Those who run in a stadium abstain from all things; and they indeed to receive a mortal crown, but we an immortal one." <margin>To the Martyrs</margin>
Explaining this more fully, Tertullian <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note> said the following: "Indeed, since athletes are set apart for a stricter discipline, so that they may devote themselves to building up their strength, they are kept away from luxury, from richer foods, and from more pleasant drinks; they are forced, they are tortured, and they are worn out." Clement of Alexandria likewise, in the third book of the *Miscellanies*, and Simplicius in his commentary on Epictetus, understood this, writing that athletes abstain from sexual activity <note>original: "a venere"</note> out of their zeal for the victor’s crown. However, elsewhere Pliny <margin>Book 28, chapter 6.</margin> seems to feel that athletes occasionally made use of sexual intercourse, noting that they were restored when they grew sluggish, and that the voice—when it falls from a bright tone to a husky one—is recovered through it. This, then, was the established way of life for athletes. Regarding how much damage this brings to health—to say nothing of Hippocrates, who said the athletic condition was not according to nature—the things that Galen records as being prone to happen to them daily can serve as proof. These include sudden loss of speech, loss of sensation and movement, suffocation, and the bursting of blood vessels. It was not without great reason that Saint Jerome <margin>In the Persuasion to Honorable Arts; In the book to Thrasybulus; Book 2 against Jovinian.</margin> wrote that athletes could by no means live for a long time, using the authority of Hippocrates and Galen. Therefore, I cannot wonder enough at the reasoning of Cornelius Celsus—a physician otherwise most learned and eloquent—who advises that an "athletic diet" should be used in cases of chronic pain in the sides; unless we interpret this, as Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540) was a French humanist scholar who commented extensively on ancient weights, measures, and customs.</note> does, as referring simply to a strong type of food suited to strengthening one’s powers. But since it does not pertain to our current purpose to say more about the profession of athletes, these things will suffice, if I add one more thing which Clement of Alexandria <margin>The Pedagogue, Book 3, chapter 9.</margin> recorded almost playfully: that athletes possessed this one image of decency, that they never came forward in public to compete without loincloths <note>original: "subligaculis"</note>. It is recorded that this custom was first introduced by Hercules, just as the custom of covering the private parts among women who exercised in running and other sports was introduced by Palaestra, the daughter of Mercury. Although Dionysius of Halicarnassus <margin>Roman Antiquities, Book 1.</margin> writes that it can be gathered from Homer that the ancients considered it shameful to compete naked, he notes that first of all, in the 15th Olympiad, Neanthum the Spartan <note>Historically usually identified as Acanthus of Sparta.</note>, while running in the Olympic stadium, stripped his whole body, with only his private parts covered by a field-loincloth <note>original: "subligaribus campestribus"</note>.

->*Here ends the First Book.*<-

# THE SECOND BOOK OF THE ART OF GYMNASTICS

### *What exercise is, and how it differs from labor and motion. Chapter I.*

<margin>B</margin>
<note>The ornamental letter 'P' depicts a figure in a natural landscape, symbolizing the connection between physical activity and the natural world.</note>
After we have sufficiently explained what Gymnastics is, its origin, and the difference between the true and the false forms of the art, it follows that—without entirely omitting the other aspects—we should primarily pursue in our discourse that branch which pertains to medicine, and which we promised to treat. Indeed, when we previously set forth the definition of a gymnast, we indicated that it is a certain art possessing knowledge of the faculties of all exercises, and teaching their varieties through practice for the sake of health. Therefore, the right method of instruction seems to demand that we first learn what exercise is, then divide it into its proper types, and explain each of them individually. For once this is done—since art (as Aristotle said) is the right reasoning of doing <margin>Aristotle, Ethics, Book 6</margin>—we shall see what this right reasoning is in performing exercises, and how each of them contributes either to acquiring a good physical condition or to defending one's health.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>Aetius, Book 3, Chapter 2</margin>
Exercise, therefore, was defined by Galen <note>Galen (129–c. 216 AD) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire; his works on health and exercise remained authoritative for over a millennium.</note> in the second book of *On Preserving Health*, and followed by Aetius, as a **vigorous motion that alters the breath**. In that work, he demonstrates how <term>gymnasion</term> <note>original Greek: γυμνάσιον; exercise</note>, <term>kinesin</term> <note>original Greek: κίνησιν; motion</note>, and <term>ponon</term> <note>original Greek: πόνον; labor or toil</note> differ from one another. This is because motion is something more general and applicable to more things than exercise is; for many people move often without being said to "exercise," whereas exercise does not occur unless the motion is vigorous. Similarly, although labor <note>toil or hard work</note> may be a vigorous motion, not all labor is properly called exercise. For instance, those digging or reaping are said to labor, but they are not properly said to be exercising—even though sometimes, by a certain common naming, labor is called exercise. Galen considers that it was called such by Hippocrates <margin>On Popular Diseases, Book 6, Ch. 4, Text 31</margin> <margin>Aphorisms, Book 2, 16</margin> <margin>In the Lexicon</margin> when he said, "Labor should precede food," and "Where there is hunger, one must not labor." In those instances, Galen judges that this word <term>ponos</term>—which usually signifies pain, labor, or even "harm" (as Erotianus preferred), as well as exercise—ought to be understood strictly as exercise. Therefore, exercise shall be nothing else, according to the opinion of Galen and Aetius, <margin>On Preserving Health, Book 2; Aetius, Book 3, Chapter 2</margin> but a vigorous motion that alters the breath, called *gymnasion* by the Greeks...

...[so] called <note>original: "pellatus", likely completing "appellatus" (named) from the previous page</note>, because they generally exercised naked, or at least with very few clothes; just as we abundantly showed in the previous book that the place where this activity occurred was called a <term>gymnasion</term> <note>original Greek: γυμνάσιον; a place for physical training</note>. But since someone in the gymnasiums could be moved violently by another through external force, yet could in no way be said to be "exercising," for that reason this Galenic definition of exercise—if I may say so with all due respect to him—is by no means 
<margin>Avicenna, The Canon of Medicine, Book 1, Fen 3, Doctrine 2, Chapter 1.</margin> 
complete. And therefore **Avicenna**, the most learned of all the Arabs, when he had noticed that exercise had not been fully defined by Galen, brought forward another definition: namely, that **exercise is a voluntary movement, because of which large and frequent breathing is necessary.** In this passage, he also rightly condemns those who call any slight walking by the name of exercise; he did not need to add the word "vigorous" because, where breathing is large and frequent, it always necessarily follows that the movement is vigorous. 

But neither does this definition by Avicenna fully satisfy me. For although it may apply to all the various types of gymnastic exercises, it does not properly encompass those which it pertains to the physician to treat, and of which we have undertaken to speak. Indeed, it by no means encompasses all four types of <term>causes</term> <note>The author refers to Aristotle's "Four Causes": the material, formal, efficient, and final. To define a thing perfectly in this era, one had to identify all four.</note>, as neither the "material" is explained, nor the "cause for the sake of which" <note>the "final cause" or purpose</note>. Furthermore, there is the fact that many people are moved voluntarily, vigorously, and with increased breathing who in no way would be said to be "properly exercising"—such as servants executing the commands of their masters with speed, or those who, fleeing either the attack of enemies or 
<margin>Averroes, Colliget, Book 6, Chapter 2.</margin> 
some other sorrowful event, both move vigorously and breathe frequently and greatly. From this, it is clear that Avicenna's definition does not perfectly embrace the whole nature of exercise; nor does that of **Averroes**, who said in his book *The Colliget* <note>original: "libro collectaneorum"; Averroes' "Colliget" was a major medical encyclopedia</note> that exercise is a movement of the limbs made by some act of will. 

Therefore, defining it otherwise, let us say that exercise, which it is in the interest of the physician to treat, is properly **a vigorous, voluntary movement of the human body, with altered breathing, performed for the sake of either preserving health or acquiring a good physical condition.** <note>original Latin: "motus corporis humani uehemens, uoluntarius, cum anhelitu alterato uel sanitatis tuendae, uel habitus boni comparandi gratia factus."</note> For in this way, the definition includes all the causes and applies only to the thing being defined. 

Truly, someone might rightly ask me whether movement performed by riding or sailing deserves the name of exercise, since it seems to depend not freely on the human will, but on another force? To which I respond that those riding and sailing should no less be said to be "exercised" by others—if not "properly," at least in a general sense—provided they do it for the sake of health or even for military training. For those who undertake the exercise we have just defined are said to be "properly" exercised; whereas to those whom some...

<header>BOOK TWO</header>

<margin>A</margin>When any of the necessary conditions are missing, these activities are said to be practiced in a "common" sense rather than in a "proper" or strict sense, whether the individuals are moved by themselves or by others. An example is a person riding a horse; they move voluntarily because the movement of the horse—by which the rider is moved—is both directed and completed by the rider's own desire. This principle must always be understood for other similar activities. That this was the opinion of **Galen** himself is indicated by his words in the second book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: "de tu. ual.", short for the Latin title *De tuenda valetudine*</note>. There he says that those who dig and those who ride do not only perform labor, but also "exercise," at least under the common name of exercise. He establishes this even more clearly in the fifth book, chapter 11, where he calls all motion "exercise" in a common sense, but specifically refers to "vigorous motion" as exercise in the proper sense. **Paul of Aegina** <note>A 7th-century Byzantine physician whose medical encyclopedia was a standard textbook</note> also seems to have named it thus in Book 2, chapter 49, where he distinguishes exercise from being carried <note>original: "gestationibus," referring to passive exercise like riding in a carriage or boat</note>, walking, and vocal exercises. 

Furthermore, since I mentioned that exercise was called <term>gymnasion</term> <note>original Greek: γυμνάσιον</note> by the Greeks, just like the place in which it occurred, someone might wonder whether exercises performed outside of gymnasiums were "properly" considered as such? My answer is that since the definition of exercise does not include a specific location, it indicates that a particular place is by no means necessary for exercise. Therefore, vigorous voluntary movement with altered breathing, performed for the sake of maintaining health or attaining the best physical condition, must be called "exercise" regardless of where it is performed, just as much as if it were done in the gymnasiums. For who of sound mind would not call walking along the roads, playing ball, throwing javelins, and similar things "exercises"? This holds true even if they are done in the countryside or in villages, provided they do not lack the other required conditions. Since this is the case, it must be said that the treatment of all exercises—whether they occur in gymnasiums or outside—pertains to the gymnastic art. This is especially true because **Galen**, who is otherwise very observant of the proper use of words, recorded in his fourth book of *On the Affected Parts* that <term>gymnastic games</term> <note>original Greek: γυμνασικὰς παιδίας; refers to athletic play or training</note> were commonly practiced by boys in the water during his own time.

<margin>

2nd book of *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: "d tu. ua.", referring to Galen's *De tuenda valetudine*</note>.

Both **Plato** and **Galen** have rightly written that this most excellent principle is received from nature, as even the brute animals provide proof: for as soon as they come into this worldly light, they are seen to move, stir, and leap about. Children do the same thing; although they emerge into this life weaker than the animals in their ability to enjoy it, they nevertheless strive to move themselves as much as is permitted, and they receive no small amount of pleasure from these movements. When these movements later receive the conditions described above as the years grow, they are clearly nothing other than the very works of the gymnastic faculty. Thus, we are compelled to say that this faculty, if not created by nature itself, is at least according to a natural propensity. Since **Plato** established two primary and universal parts of this faculty, we shall set forth the division of gymnastics proposed by him—not because the species of all exercises are perfectly contained within it, but because it has not yet happened that any other person has divided this art better. Nor should anyone criticize us for placing such high value on the authority of **Plato**—whom no sane person regards as a physician—in treating a medical matter. For the great **Galen** (whom physicians are bound to believe no less than the disciples of **Pythagoras** believed their master) left it in writing that **Plato** was an imitator of **Hippocrates** and never departed from his views. Indeed, we cannot follow **Galen** in this particular place because, where he attempted a similar division, he seems to have instituted a partition of the exercises themselves rather than of the art of gymnastics. **Plato**, therefore, in the seventh book of *The Laws*, after demonstrating that nature makes the left hands no weaker than the right, and that their apparent weakness should be ascribed to custom and exercise rather than a natural defect, teaches that it pertains to those in charge of nourishing and educating children to accustom them to exercising their left hands as well. Later, teaching which disciplines children should be cultivated by, he writes that one is music and the other is gymnastics. He then makes two members of gymnastics: one he calls *wrestling* <note>original Greek: τὴν πάλην (tēn palēn)</note>, the other *dancing* <note>original Greek: τὴν ὄρχησιν (tēn orchēsin)</note>. Of *dancing* <note>original Greek: ὀρχήσεως (orchēseōs)</note>, he says one kind belongs to those who imitate shameful things with their movements, while the other belongs to those who devote their efforts to <term>good physical habit</term> <note>original: "bonae corporis habitudini", referring to a state of fitness and health</note>, agility, and the beauty of the limbs. In this passage, although **Plato** may seem to speak only of military gymnastics, it is nonetheless nearly the same as medical gymnastics, differing only in its end—and not entirely in its end, because **Plato** also intends to prepare a good bodily habit and preserve health just as the physician does, but he adds another goal: namely, that by the help of this exercise, they may be more fit for waging wars.

S E C O N D [B O O K]

<margin>A</margin> ...that men might become more fit. We should say, then, that according to Plato, gymnastics is divided into dancing and wrestling, understanding under the name of wrestling that whole series of exercises that were performed either in the wrestling-schools of the gymnasia or in a place serving as a wrestling-school. For since the gymnastic faculty exists—as we have often said—to understand the nature and qualities of exercises and to prescribe the methods and rules for using them for the sake of health or a good physical condition, almost all exercises performed with skill (which are nothing other than certain movements of human bodies) are defined and categorized as either dancing or wrestling. This is perhaps what Galen intended to suggest when he wrote in his second book on the movement of muscles: **dancers and wrestlers** <note>original: ὀρχηστικούς καὶ παλαιστικούς</note> are the only ones who can easily bend their legs. For I am not unaware (as

<margin>B</margin> I said a little earlier) that this division of gymnastics is by no means perfect, nor can every single species of exercise be included within it, since walking, horse-riding, and similar activities are gymnastic exercises, yet they are in no way subject to dancing or wrestling. Nevertheless, we will follow this division to some extent, as it is ancient and handed down by a most serious author. But if we, illustrating the matter more clearly, say that gymnastics is twofold—one part considering the movements of people made by themselves, the other considering movements made by others—and then divide the first part into both wrestling and dancing, we will not only agree with Plato’s view but perhaps also achieve the truth of the matter itself. Indeed, no one could think of any exercise that we cannot show is contained under one of these aforementioned types. Nor will anything

<margin>C</margin> stand in the way of our opinion regarding what Galen wrote in the book titled <term>The Physician<note>original: ἰατρός (Iatros). A medical handbook traditionally attributed to Galen, though often debated by scholars.</note></term> (if that is Galen's genuine work, or rather, as others believe, the work of the physician Herodotus). There, he placed wrestling and dancing under one kind of art, and medicine under another—of which the ancients made gymnastics a part. This is because there he speaks of dancing as a type of theatrical acting, as we shall explain below, and not the kind we are discussing. Similarly, he speaks of the corrupt form of wrestling, which we call <term>athletics<note>The author distinguishes between healthy gymnastics and "athletics," which in this period often referred to professional, over-strained, or "vicious" training for competition.</note></term> and which we, along with Galen, establish as being entirely separate from medicine; he is not speaking of the wrestling or the dancing understood by Plato and by us.

### On the Art of Dancing. Chapter III.

<margin>D</margin> <image-desc>Historiated initial 'V' containing a portrait of a bearded man in profile.</image-desc> **S**ince, therefore, the whole of gymnastics is divided into that which examines the movements of men made by themselves and that made by others; and the first part is further divided into the art of dancing and the art of wrestling, we shall first explain the art of dancing, so that our treatment does not become confused. Then we shall explain the art of wrestling, which encompasses all exercises performed in the wrestling-school <term>palaestra; an ancient Greek wrestling school or gymnasium</term> or similar places. Finally, we will attach that part of gymnastics which concerns movements made by others. Once these have been treated, the whole of gymnastics will become known. Those who have read the books of Homer can easily understand that he knew of three species of the art of dancing, or **orchestics** <note>original: ὀρχήσεως</note>. The first is **acrobatics** <note>original: cubistica</note>, which Xenophon and Suidas write was a certain art in which men, twisting their feet and hands in various ways, danced upon their heads, in the same way

<margin>E</margin> that some itinerant performers <note>original: circulatores</note> do in our own time, who wander through various cities reciting comedies and deceiving people for the sake of profit. Lucian called this **tumbling** <note>original: κυβίστημα</note>, and in the glossary it is held that *he tumbles* <note>original: cernulat / κυβιστᾶ</note>—a word which Seneca also used in his eighth Epistle, although many manuscripts have "falls headlong" <note>original: cernuat</note>. The second species is **ball-play** <note>original: sphaeristica</note>, or the game of the ball. For that those playing with balls also danced is clear, besides the testimony of Homer, who relates these things in the sixth book of the *Odyssey* concerning Nausicaa:
> **They played with the ball, having cast aside their veils,**
> **And among them white-armed Nausicaa led the dance.** <note>original: σφαίρῃ δ᾽ ἔπαιζον ἀπὸ κρήδεμνα βαλεῦσαι / τῇσι δὲ Ναυσικάα λευκώλενος ἤρχετο Μολπῆς.</note>
> *that is:* They played with the ball, their ribbons and garments removed,
> And among them Nausicaa, visible for her snowy arms,
> Gave the beginning to the game.

<margin>F</margin> Athenaeus also testifies to this on the authority of Demoxenus, as we shall indicate below. The third species is **dancing** <note>original: ὄρχησις</note> simply so-called; we may simply call it "the dance." Although our ancestors used this entire art of orchestics for the most part for pleasure and wantonness rather than for anything else—a custom which persists even to these times—it is nevertheless established that it was not entirely without military, athletic, and medical gymnastic applications. Indeed, I shall demonstrate that no exercise was omitted by almost any of these three branches when I attempt to indicate, in declaring the individual species of exercises, how each one used those parts of gymnastics separately. For we have Plato as a most wealthy witness that the military art was not without the art of dancing; in the seventh book of the *Laws*, he divided dancing into three types: the military, that suited for peace, and a middle type. He called the military type the dance of those who, now with leaps into the air, now

-> SECOND BOOK <-

<margin>A</margin> ...sometimes by lowering themselves, and sometimes by leaning, they imitated the attacks and evasions of enemy incursions. These dancers, through various movements, simulated those who throw javelins or strike blows. Plato valued this practice so highly that he wished for masters to be established in his Republic, who, supported by public funds, would teach this art to both men and women alike. He believed that this practice alone would provide no small benefit in acquiring military skill. That athletic gymnastics once included dancing among its other exercises can be proven from the writings of Pliny. He recorded that Stephanio, the first inventor of the Roman-style dance <note>original: togatae saltationis</note>, performed at both the Secular Games and the games of the Divine Augustus and Claudius Caesar. Similarly, in the passage recently cited, Plato mentions an "intermediate" dance, which he called "disputed" <note>original: ἀμφισβητουμένην</note>. This was customarily performed during sacrifices and rites of purification. Xenophon reports that this same dance was performed by the Mantineans and Arcadians in the presence of Cyrus.

<margin>B</margin> <margin>Book 6, The Expedition of Cyrus.</margin> By handing down this account, Xenophon seems to clearly suggest that the athletic art—which we have already determined encompasses both public games and sacred celebrations—included dancing. Furthermore, Galen confesses that medical gymnastics did not reject dancing as if it were useless for health or physical fitness. Indeed, in the final chapter of the second book of <margin>Last chapter.</margin> *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: περὶ ὑγιεινῶν</note>, he reports that many weak people were restored to health by him through wrestling, the *pancratium* <term>pancratium; an ancient Greek martial art combining boxing and wrestling</term>, dancing, and other exercises of this kind. This was likewise testified by Antyllus <margin>Oribasius, Book 6.</margin>, who places dancing among the other exercises that contribute to human health. He describes it as holding a middle nature between choral dancing <note>original: chorea</note> and "shadow-boxing" <note>original: umbratilem pugnam</note>. For this reason, he writes that it is beneficial for children, women, and the elderly, whose bodies are remarkably weak and slender. Whether this is indeed the same dance that Plato called "peaceful" <note>original: εἰρηνικήν</note>, or suited for peace—which he wrote was practiced by those who remain temperate in times of prosperity

<margin>C</margin> and moderate in their pleasures—I do not dare to affirm with certainty. Let it suffice for us to have shown thus far that no branch of gymnastics lacked this element of dancing, into which (along with the art of wrestling) we have already noted that Plato divided gymnastic exercise.

# BOOK II

<margin>D</margin> Ball-play acquired such variety that it earned a place in the gymnasiums known as a **ball-court** <note>original: σφαιριστήριον / sphairisterion</note>, as well as a dedicated official called a **ball-instructor** <note>original: σφαιριστικόν / sphairistikos</note>. Regarding who first invented this ball-play—or "the game of the ball"— <margin>Book 7, chapter 56.</margin> writers hold different opinions. Among the Latin authors, Pliny attributes the invention to a certain Pytho. Agallis of Corcyra, a female grammarian, claims in the works of Athenaeus that Nausicaa <note>The princess in Homer’s Odyssey</note> was the inventor of the ball game, though I do not know on what grounds she bases this. Hippasus attributed the invention to the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note>, while Dicaearchus credited the Sicyonians. Because of this, we cannot arrive at any certain conclusion, especially since we lack the commentaries of Timocrates the Laconian and others on this game. Perhaps from those, we might understand the reasons for such great variety and recognize with more certainty the almost unknown types of ball games. In explaining these types, writers have been quite confused until now and have occasionally wandered far from the truth. We shall strive, as much as possible, to make this treatment clearer 

<margin>E</margin> and less contradictory to the writings of the ancients. I find that only four types of ball games existed among the Greeks: the **large ball**, the **small ball**, the **hollow ball**, and the **corycus** <note>original: μεγάλην σφαῖραν, μικρὰν σφαῖραν, κενὴν σφαῖραν, & κώρυκον</note>. I include the *corycus* <note>A heavy hanging bag or ball used for exercise</note> among the types of balls, for although Galen, Oribasius, and Paulus differentiated it from them, that instrument—as we shall demonstrate—was either a ball or very similar to a ball. According to Antyllus, the game of the small ball had three distinct species. The first was with a very small ball; those who exercised with it played with their bodies held very upright and moved their hands very close to their teammates. The second used a somewhat larger ball, where the players moved their elbows together while playing; they did not cling to one another nor did they simply nod, but moved in various ways, stepping here and there because of the various throws of the ball. The third used a ball 

<margin>F</margin> even larger than the second, in which men played at a distance from each other. In this type, there was a "stationary" and a "mobile" role; those who remained in place threw the ball with great force and grace. I judge that the type of game called **harpaston** and **phenis** <note>original: ἁρπαστὸν & φενίς</note> in Athenaeus should be counted among these species. This is partly because Galen explained it along with the others in his booklet *On the Exercise of the Small Ball*, and partly because <margin>Book 3 of the Paedagogus, chapter 10.</margin> Clement of Alexandria—a most serious writer—makes it clear that this was a species of small ball. While demonstrating that the game of the small ball, and especially **pheninda** <note>original: φενίνδα</note>, was an exercise very well suited for men, he says: **"I also know of those playing the game of pheninda with the small ball, especially in the sun."** This is also confirmed by Pollux, who suggests it was also called *harpastum*. Indeed, Juba the Mauritanian wrote that the inventor of this game was Phanaestrius the physical trainer, whose description...

<margin>A</margin> Antiphanes <note>A Greek comic playwright</note> provided a description in this manner: **"Taking the ball, he delighted in giving it to one while at the same time fleeing from another. He knocked the ball away from one, but raised another player up again with ringing shouts."** <note>original Greek: Σφαῖραν λαβὼν, τῷ μὲν διδοὺς ἔχαιρε τὸν δ᾽ ἔφευγ᾽ ἅμα. τὸν δ᾽ ἐξέκρουσε, τὸν δ᾽ ἀνέστησεν πάλιν κλαγκταῖσι φωναῖς.</note> Antiphanes called this game **pheninda**, named **from the 'sending' of the ball-players** <note>original: φενίνδα, ἀπὸ τῆς ἀφέσεως τῶν σφαιριζόντων / pheninda, apo tēs apheseōs tōn sphairizontōn</note>, as if those playing in this way were mutually entrusting the ball to one another. Or perhaps it was named after its first inventor, Phennidus, or **from the word for deceiving** <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ φενακίζειν / apo tou phenakizein</note>, which is to say, from trickery. This is because players feint toward one person while throwing in another direction, thus deceiving a gullible opponent, as Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century scholar and lexicographer</note> has recorded. In his writings, we read that the game of **episcyrus** <note>original: ἐπίσκυρος; a team game involving a center line</note> was commonly played where equal numbers of players were arranged in two teams. A middle line was drawn, which they called the **scyrus** <note>original: σκῦρον / skyron</note>, upon which the ball was placed. Each side would then compete to drive the ball past two other lines drawn behind the ranks of the opponents—these were the goals—and victory was claimed by whoever could touch them with the ball. Indeed, while the players were catching the ball

<margin>B</margin> and throwing it to one another, they would flee from one, drive away another, and lift another up with loud shouts, or perhaps knock them down. It is likely that this provided great delight to the spectators and to the players themselves, even more so because they sometimes focused on the gracefulness of their movements. On this point, <margin>Athenaeus, *The Deipnosophists*, Book 1.</margin> Demoxenus <note>A comic poet</note>—intending to explain the elegance and joy born from such a game—recorded these words: **"A certain youth was playing ball, perhaps seventeen years of age. He was from Cos (for that island seems to produce gods); whenever he looked at the spectators, whether catching or giving the ball, we all cried out together. Such was the rhythm, the character, and the order that appeared in everything he said or did. It was beyond beauty. O men, I have never before heard of nor seen such grace. I would have suffered some ill-effect had I stayed any longer, for even now I do not seem to be quite sane."** <note>original Greek: Νεανίας τίς ἐσφαίριζεν... καὶ νῦν δ᾽ ἐκ ἐμοὶ ὑγιαίνειν δοκῶ.</note> That is to say, a young man about seventeen years old played with the ball. His homeland was Cos (for 

<margin>C</margin> that island seems to produce gods); when he gazed upon the seated crowd while either catching or handing over the ball, we all shouted at once. For such elegance, order, and charm existed in whatever he said or did that it surpassed all beauty. O men, never before have I heard of or seen such charm; certainly, some harm would have befallen me if I had remained there longer, for I do not feel quite right in the head. From these words of Demoxenus, it is clear that ball players were accustomed to play with refinement and grace. These, then, are the types of **small-ball** games of which I know mention was made by the Greeks. In these games, the philosopher Epigenes and also Ctesibius of Chalcis <note>A philosopher and friend of kings</note> are said to have excelled; many of the associates of King Antigonus used to strip for exercise to play with the latter. Furthermore, Pollux proposes other types of small-ball games: **Aporraxis** <note>A game involving bouncing the ball on the floor</note> and **Ourania** <note>The "sky-game"</note>. In the latter, players would lean back and throw the ball into the sky, attempting to catch it before it touched the ground.

<margin>D</margin> ...reached for the ball, they would catch it. Furthermore, Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical writer and physician to Emperor Julian</note>, citing Antyllus <note>A celebrated 2nd-century Greek surgeon</note>, testifies that the **large ball** also produced two modes of play that differed from the previous ones—not only in the size of the ball itself, but also in the positioning of the hands. In one, they played with a large ball; in the other, with one even larger. Both modes shared this common feature: whereas in the other games mentioned earlier the players always kept their hands lower than their shoulders, in this game they always held them higher than their heads. Sometimes they even walked on their tiptoes so they could lift their hands even higher; at other times they would jump, specifically when the ball was carried above them, moving their arms with great vigor when throwing it.

Furthermore, as for the **hollow** or **empty ball**, which we established as the third type of ball, its exact nature is not sufficiently explained. However, if one may gather anything by conjecture from the words of Antyllus, I believe this ball was sewn from leather like the others, differing only in this: while those were filled with feathers or other material, this one was filled only with wind or <margin>E</margin> air. It was of such a great size that it was difficult to play with.

But as for what the **corycus** <term>corycus: from the Greek kōrykos, a leather bag or sack used as a swinging weight for exercise, much like a modern punching bag</term> was, or how that game was performed, since Antyllus (as cited in Oribasius) has expressed it most clearly, I have decided to translate his discourse here as it appears in the Vatican manuscript:

**"For weaker individuals, the *corycus* is filled with fig seeds or flour; for the stronger, it is filled with sand. Its size should be adapted to the strength and age of the participant. It is suspended in the gymnasiums from above, hanging from the ceiling, and stands at such a distance from the ground that its bottom reaches the navel of the one exercising. Holding this with both hands, the participants swing it, first gently and then more violently, so that they follow it as it recedes and yield to it as it returns, driven back by its force. Finally, they release it from their hands and push it away so that, when it swings back, it strikes the body more forcefully upon its return..."** <note>original Greek: Κόρυκος ἐπὶ μὲν τ' ἀθενεστέρων ἐμπίπλαται καὶ κεχριμίδων, ἢ ἀλύρων, ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἰσχυροτέρων ψάμμῳ... / Kōrykos epi men t' asthenesterōn empipletai kai kechrimidōn, ē alyrōn, epi de tōn ischyroterōn psammō...</note>

<margin>F</margin> ...and having set it in motion at its furthest point, they send it back, so that from its approach—unless one prays fervently to turn away—it strikes them. Sometimes they resist it with their hands as it approaches, sometimes with their chest while spreading their arms wide, and at other times turning away and catching it <margin>Book 6, Collections</margin> upon their back.

<note>The following is the Latin version of the Greek quote provided in the original text:</note>
> "The *corycus* is filled with fig seeds or meal for weaker bodies, and with sand for the more robust; its size is indeed accommodated to the strength of the body and to one's age. It is suspended from the roof of the gymnasium and is so far from the ground that its base reaches the navel of the one being exercised. Holding this with both hands, those being exercised carry it first quietly, then more vehemently, so that they follow it as it recedes and yield to it as it returns, compelled by its violence. Finally, they release it from their hands and send it forth so that when it returns, it strikes the body more vehemently from its approach..."

...it meets them from its own path, and at the very end they most often let it go, returning it to its original position, so that from the impact, if they do not pay close attention, it might move backward. <margin>A</margin> This results in them sometimes meeting it with their hands as it approaches, sometimes with their chest while their hands are spread wide, and sometimes with their hands folded behind their backs. Thus far Antyllus. Although he does not describe the shape of the **Corycus**—seeing as it was a device known to everyone at that time—we can nevertheless infer that it was spherical, or at least round, and made of leather. Otherwise, if it had been angular, it would have injured the hands and chest upon impact. If **Fuchs** <note>Leonhart Fuchs (1501–1566), a German physician and botanist.</note> had seen these things, he certainly would have understood that **Valeriola** <note>François Vallériole (1504–1580), a French physician who wrote on medical theory.</note> contended against him with good reason: that the air-filled ball <note>original: "follis"</note> and the punching bag <note>original: "corycus"</note> differ from each other as much as heaven and earth. 

I also cannot wonder enough at that ancient writer **Caelius Aurelianus**, who in Book 5 of *On Chronic Diseases* <note>original: "tardarum passionum"</note>, the last chapter, says that a variety of rolling in the wrestling school was called by the Greeks *celadian* and *choricomachian*, unless there is an error in a very corrupt manuscript, as I suspect. <margin>B</margin> Regarding this, one should understand the adage: "to exercise against the punching bag" <note>original: "πρὸς κόρυκον γυμνάζεσθαι"</note>, a type of contest in which Apuleius competed in Thessaly. **Hippocrates**, or perhaps **Polybus**, also spoke of this exercise where he recommended the "punching bag fight" <note>original: "κορυκομαχίαν"</note>—which **Cornarius** <note>Janus Cornarius (1500–1558), a physician famous for his translations of Greek medical texts.</note> falsely interpreted as an air-filled ball—for slimming down the body. Just as **Aretaeus** <note>A prominent Greek physician of the 1st century AD.</note> understood it, where he recommended "throwing the punching bag" <note>original: "κορυκοβολίας"</note> for the exercises of those suffering from elephantiasis. That "good translator" (I know not what he was thinking) quite ineptly translated it as "throwing a wallet" or "a small sack." I believe Caelius Aurelianus also understood this same thing when he recommended the "punching bag fight" (for so it must be read) for reducing obesity, using nearly the same remedies proposed by Hippocrates in the cited passage. From this, I argued that the Author, just like other things, borrowed the "punching bag fight" from Hippocrates, even though the text in my judgment is corrupt. <margin>C</margin> 

Some have thought that the place where this was played is called the *Coryceum* <note>A dedicated room in a gymnasium for the punching bag.</note> in **Vitruvius**. Since I have already refuted their opinion in earlier sections, nothing more needs to be said. And so, these are the four types of Greek ball games: namely the **small ball**, the **large ball**, the **hollow ball**, and the **corycus**. That all these were distinct from one another is clear not only from the descriptions just provided but also from the words of **Galen** in the second book of *On Preserving Health*. There, among other gymnasium exercises, he lists the corycus, the small ball, and the large ball separately; **Paul of Aegina** did the same, imitating him. They certainly would not have done this unless these were distinct types of balls and diverse exercises were performed with them. Whether all of these were practiced in the Greek gymnasia matters little to know; let it suffice to understand that medical gymnastics, as well as military...

For the custom of speaking among both the ancients and the moderns, both Greeks and Latins, has prevailed such that they call many exercises *paidiai* <note>original: "παιδιαὶς", meaning games or childish play</note> and "games," either because they were mostly performed by boys—who are called *paides* in Greek—or because those who exercise seem to act not in earnest but in jest, whether they do it for the sake of health or some other reason. However, those games which we say belong to athletics were properly so called because they were performed during festive leisure for the sake of solace and pleasure alone. <margin>E</margin>

->On the game of the Ball according to the Romans. Chapter V.<-

<insert>A</insert>FTER we have sufficiently explained the types of ball play common among the Greeks, it remains to explain those that are found both used and handed down in writings by the Romans. From this, I hope it will become clear in what ways they both agreed and in what ways they differed. I find, therefore, that there were four types of balls with which they played even among the Romans: the *follis*, the *trigonalis*, the *paganica*, and the *harpastum*. Some believe all of these were encompassed under the name of the "Italian sphere" by the physician **Caelius Aurelianus**. The **follis** was a large ball made of soft leather <note>original: "aluta"</note>, filled only with air. If it was larger, it was struck with the arms, and was sometimes simply called a "ball," as in **Nonius** <note>Nonius Marcellus, a 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note> quoting **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar.</note>: "Know that it has been cleared, since <margin>F</margin> you will see in Rome, in the forum before the butcher shops, boys playing ball by driving it out." <note>original: "expulsim ludere," a style of play where the ball is hit away quickly rather than caught.</note> And in **Propertius**, Book 3:
> When the ball escapes the swift throws through the arms.
Sometimes it is also called the "swift ball," as in **Horace**, *Satires* Book 2, Satire 2:
> Whether the swift ball
> gently deceives the harsh labor with enthusiasm,
> or the discus occupies you.
Indeed, one can see an exercise of this kind of ball on the coins of the Roman Emperor **Gordian III**, which we have placed here depicted, and from which it is possible to conjecture that each of the players had his own ball, and that this game was used in the **Pythian sacrifices** among the people of Apollonia, as is not difficult to gather both from the word *PYTHIA* and from the palm and the sacrificial vessels.

->On the game of the Ball according to the Romans. Chapter V.<-

<insert>A</insert>FTER we have sufficiently explained the types of ball play common among the Greeks, it remains to explain those that are found both used and handed down in writings by the Romans. From this, I hope it will become clear in what ways they both agreed and in what ways they differed. I find, therefore, that there were four types of balls with which they played even among the Romans: the *follis*, the *trigonalis*, the *paganica*, and the *harpastum*. Some believe all of these were encompassed under the name of the "Italian sphere" by the physician **Caelius Aurelianus**. 

The **follis** was a large ball made of soft leather <note>original: "aluta", a type of leather softened with alum</note> which, when inflated with air, was the largest of all the balls, but also the lightest. Because of its lightness, it was struck with the arm or the hand, and was especially suited for old men and children, as it required less exertion. This is the ball about which **Martial** <note>A Roman poet famous for his short, witty epigrams</note> says: "Keep your distance, you youths! The gentle ball <note>original: "follis"</note> becomes my age." It was called "gentle" because, being filled only with air, it did not strike with any great weight or force. <margin>A</margin> 

Next was the **trigonalis**, which took its name from the three people <note>original: "trigonum", or triangle</note> who stood in a triangular formation to play. This game was more demanding than the *follis*, requiring the players to catch and toss the ball with great speed and often using both hands. 

The **paganica**, according to the same Martial, was a ball stuffed with feathers. It was firmer than the *follis* but softer than the *trigonalis*, making it a medium-weight option. It was called "paganica" because it was frequently used in the rural villages <note>original: "pagis"</note> by the common people. <margin>B</margin>

Finally, the **harpastum**, which the Romans adopted from the Greek game called *pheninda*, was a small, hard ball. This game was much more strenuous and involved snatching the ball away from opponents...

<page-num>90</page-num>

If the ball was somewhat smaller, it was struck with the fists and called a "punching ball" <note>Latin: *pugillaris follis*</note>, as seen in the works of <margin>D</margin> **Plautus** <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright famous for his comedies.</note> in his play *Rudens*: "By Hercules, I shall turn you into a punching ball right this instant!" <note>original: "ex templo Hercle ego te follem pugillatoriū faciā"</note>. I believe this same ball was also called a *folliculum* [little ball], as mentioned by **Suetonius** in his *Life of Augustus*, where he relates that the Emperor was greatly delighted by this game of ball. However, **Martial** in his fourth book wrote:

>Whether you share the feathery weights of the loose ball, <note>original: "Plumea seu laxi partiris pondera follis"</note>

Even though this ball was sewn from leather and filled with air, and not feathers—as almost all Latin authors agree with one voice—whatever others may argue, I believe Martial called them "feathery weights" because of the ball's extreme lightness. Thanks to this lightness, neither children nor the elderly (who are otherwise physically weak) would be overly exhausted while playing. For this reason, Martial also left this written elsewhere: <margin>Book 14.</margin>

>Stay far away, young men; a gentle age suits me,
>It is fitting for boys to play with the follis, and for the old. <margin>E</margin> <note>original: "Ite procul iuuenes, mitis mihi conuenit aetas, Folle decet pueros ludere, folle senes."</note>

Indeed, so that weaker bodies could be exercised by this type of game, they not only made the ball light but also ensured the area dedicated to the play was not paved with stones or bricks. This was done so that players would not slip, and if they happened to fall, they would not suffer injury from the impact. Consequently, since the ground was not paved at all, dust was stirred up by the continuous friction of feet. However, it is also possible that they played on a paved floor, but it was sprinkled with a small amount of dust so that the bounce of the ball was not hindered while the players' feet were more firmly planted. Martial implies in his twelfth book that this exercise was usually performed on dusty ground, where he mocks a certain Menogenes, who could not bring himself to leave the Baths for the sake of his amusement:

>Though you wish to escape Menogenes at the Baths
>And around the bathing-houses with all your art,
>He will snatch the warm *trigon* ball with right and left hand, <margin>F</margin> <note>The *trigon* was a fast-paced game played by three people in a triangle.</note>
>So that he may often credit you with the balls he has caught;
>He will gather and return the *follis* fallen from the dust,
>And though already washed, he will be back in his sandals.

Now, whether this game was one of those we described above according to the Greek authors has been a matter of various opinions. For some have believed that the "large ball" of the Greeks and the *follis* of the Romans were the same thing. Among these was **Thomas Linacer** <note>A famous 16th-century English humanist and physician who translated Galen from Greek to Latin.</note>, who, having translated *corycus* <note>A leather bag usually filled with flour, sand, or grain, used like a modern heavy bag or speed bag.</note> as *follis* in his second book of *On the Preservation of Health* <margin>2. On the Preservation of Health</margin>, later in his sixth book translated "large ball" again as *follis*. He acted as if the *corycus* and the large ball did not differ in the works of **Galen**, though Galen explicitly distinguished between the small ball, the large ball, and the *corycus*. Others preferred the view that the *corycus* of the Greeks was the *follis* of the Romans. This opinion was held by the majority of more recent writers, among whom were some who, in the works of **Oribasius**, titled the chapter on the *corycus* as being about the punching ball...

## B O O K  S E C O N D

<page-num>91</page-num>

<meta>The marginal letters A, B, and C serve as markers for the author's primary arguments regarding the distinction between different types of balls and games.</meta>

<margin>A</margin> ...have judged it should be written. However, all these authors are greatly mistaken. First, those who believed the *follis* <note>An air-filled ball, similar to a modern light exercise ball.</note> and the *magna pila* [large ball] were the same thing are refuted by two reasons. The first is that those playing with the "large ball" always held their hands higher than their heads, and sometimes even walked on their tiptoes so they could keep their hands higher. The second reason is that **Oribasius** <note>A Greek medical writer of the 4th century AD and personal physician to the Emperor Julian.</note> judged the game of the large ball to be useless not only for the sick, but even for those recovering or in good health. It is easy to judge from the preceding pages that neither of these conditions applied to the *follis*. 

Furthermore, those who thought the *follis* was the same as the *corycus* <note>A heavy punching bag used by athletes.</note> are also found to have erred for many reasons. First, because the *corycus* was suspended from the ceiling of the gymnasiums, whereas the *follis* was thrown freely. Second, the *corycus* was filled with fig seeds, flour, or sand, while the *follis* contained only air. Third, the *follis* was used for exercise in the dust <note>This refers to the *palaestra* or outdoor exercise ground.</note>, but the *corycus* was not. There were also those who believed the *follis* was the "hollow ball" described earlier by us from the works of **Antyllus** <note>A famous Greek physician from the 2nd century AD, known for his writings on surgery and physical therapy.</note>. 

<margin>B</margin> I would willingly agree with them, except that **Martial** <note>A Roman poet (c. 38–104 AD) famous for his Epigrams which provide details of daily Roman life.</note> said the *follis* was suited to a "milder age" <note>Meaning children and the elderly.</note>, while Antyllus judged the exercise of the hollow ball to be not at all easy or suitable, and therefore something to be omitted. I conclude, therefore, from all of this, that since the *follis* was neither the hollow ball of the Greeks, nor their large ball, nor the *corycus*, it must be that they were ignorant of it; for no one considers a small ball to be a *follis*. 

Furthermore, the *Trigonalis* ball <note>The ball used in the game of *trigon*.</note> used for play was small, so named either from the place where it was played—which some claim was a triangular space—or more likely from the number, formation, and positioning of the players. I find that this was sometimes simply called "the ball" [*pila*], as in the seventh book of Martial:

> Neither the ball, nor the air-ball, nor the feather-ball <note>original: "paganica"</note> 
> Prepares you for the Baths, nor the blunt strike of the bare post;
> Nor do you stretch your arms out smeared in oil,
<margin>C</margin> > Nor do you, wandering, snatch the dusty snatch-balls. <note>original: "Non pila, non follis, non te paganica Thermis / Praeparat, aut nudi stipitis ictus hebes: / Vara nec iniecto ceromate brachia tendis, / Non harpasta vagus puluerulenta rapis."</note>

Indeed, if we only recognize four types of balls, and the others are named specifically, then the *Trigonalis* must be included under the simple name of "ball." I believe **Celsus** <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus (c. 25 BC – 50 AD), a Roman encyclopedist known for his medical treatise *De Medicina*.</note> spoke similarly when he said that for those troubled by bowel issues <margin>Book 1, chapter 6.</margin>, "the ball and other exercises of the upper parts are suitable," since in this kind of game the lower parts of the body remained almost always stationary, while the upper parts were in constant motion. 

How this exercise was actually performed can easily be gathered from Martial’s words. He shows that players used to play together in a triangular formation so that they were able to strike and catch the ball in turn with both hands—now the left, now the right—so that it never fell. It is likely that the highest praise for players was found in this skill, just as in Book 7, where he praises a certain **Polybus** for the agility of his left hand in throwing and catching the ball.

<summary>This page distinguishes the Roman air-filled ball (follis) from Greek exercises like the heavy bag (corycus) and the large ball, while introducing the "trigon" game played in a triangle where ambidexterity was highly prized.</summary>

From these verses, by Hercules, it is clear that those playing <term>trigon</term> <note>A game played by three people standing in a triangle, notorious for requiring quick reflexes and the use of both hands.</note> were accustomed to send the ball to one another and receive it, now with the left hand, now with the right. This was done in much the same way that our own people play with a small ball over a cord, and in the way **Antyllus** <note>A famous Greek physician of the 2nd century AD.</note> described the third type of small-ball play. However, why **Martial** <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century AD famous for his satirical epigrams.</note> called it the "warm trigon," both in the passage cited above and in Book 4:
> Whether you rub the sticky wrestling-oil, or the warm trigon:
I am not entirely certain. Nevertheless, if one is allowed to speculate, I would say he called the trigon "warm" either because the men playing <margin>E</margin> grew more heated due to the intense labor of using both hands and the steady, continuous movement of the ball; or perhaps because the place where they played was near the <term>tepidarium</term> <note>The warm room in a Roman bath complex.</note> in the gymnasiums, and therefore the players felt a certain warmth from the location as much as from the ball itself. That this was the case seems likely, since we have demonstrated above, through the opinions of both **Galen** and **Martial**, that players were accustomed to enter the hot baths immediately after a ball game. Unless, of course, we prefer to say the poet called it "warm trigon" because the ball itself became warm from the continuous movement in the hands. This is similar to how **Propertius** <note>A Roman elegiac poet of the 1st century BC.</note> in Book 1, in the *Elegy of the Complaining Door*, spoke of the "warm threshold," which became warm from people constantly standing upon it:
> Will there be no end granted to our grief?
> And shall there be base sleep upon a warm threshold?
An example of the trigonal ball seems to me to be the one that appears on the coins of **Marcus Aurelius Antoninus** <note>Commonly known as the Emperor Caracalla.</note> minted by the Byzantines in this manner. It is also recorded that this same game was traditionally played during the sacrifices to **Apollo Pythius Actiacus**. I believe nearly the same or a similar game of <term>paganica</term> <note>A "country" ball stuffed with feathers, firmer than the air-filled follis but larger than the hard small ball.</note> is described by **Petronius Arbiter** <note>A Roman courtier and novelist under Nero, author of the Satyricon.</note> in his satires, where he writes as follows: "We saw a bald old man dressed in a reddish tunic playing ball among long-haired boys. It was not the boys who drew our attention, although they were worth the sight, but the master of the house himself, who, wearing sandals, exercised with a pea-green ball. He never picked it up again if it touched the ground; instead, a slave held a bag full of balls and supplied them to the players. We also noticed something new: for two eunuchs were standing at opposite sides of the circle, one of whom held a silver chamber pot, while the other counted the balls—not those which were vibrating as they were struck between hands in play, but those which fell to the ground."

Next follows the "country ball" <term>paganica pila; a ball stuffed with feathers, often used in rural areas</term>, so named because it was quite common among the ordinary people <margin>D</margin> and used in the country villages called *pagi*; or perhaps because it was very frequently used in the city districts <note>The author is distinguishing between rural "pagi" (villages) and the administrative "pagi" (districts) within the city of Rome.</note>. For Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian of Rome.</note> relates in the fourth book of his *Antiquities* that Rome was once divided into four tribes, which were called *pagi*, just as their inhabitants were called *Pagani*. Whether the ball was named after these city districts or from the country villages, I believe it matters little. It is enough that it was a ball made of leather stuffed with feathers, wider than the three-cornered ball <note>The *pila trigonalis* discussed on the previous page.</note>, but not as loose as the air-filled ball <term>follis; a large, inflated bladder-ball similar to a modern exercise ball</term>; rather, it was harder. 

Indeed, while the air-ball, which was filled with wind, was easier to play with the harder it was inflated, and more difficult the looser it was—as our daily experience in this age confirms—the country ball was stuffed with feathers to make it even harder. It was not stuffed in a way that left it loose anywhere, but was very hard throughout, and for that reason, it was difficult to play with, as Martial shows most elegantly in this couplet from his fourteenth book: <margin>E</margin>

> This country ball, swollen with tight feathers,
> Is less loose than the air-ball, and less compact than the small ball.
> <note>original Latin: "Haec quae difficilis turget paganica pluma, / Folle minus laxa est, & minus arcta pila."</note>

As we indicated a little earlier, the simple name "ball" (*pila*) can sometimes refer to the air-ball and sometimes to the three-cornered ball. Furthermore, I do not want it to be overlooked here that the exercise of the country ball was also in use in the gymnasiums, as the same Martial left on record in his seventh book:

> Neither the small ball, nor the air-ball, nor the country ball
> Prepares you for the baths, nor the dull blow of the practice-post.
> <note>original Latin: "Non pila, non follis, non te paganica thermis / Praeparat, aut nudi stipitis ictus hebes." The "stipes" or practice-post refers to sword-fighting practice against a wooden pole.</note>

Since we have frequently pointed out that almost everyone who exercised with the ball in the gymnasiums usually played first and then immediately entered the baths, Martial’s words demonstrate that the country ball was also numbered among the other ball games used by those exercising in the gymnasiums as a preparation for the baths.

The last and fourth type of Latin ball <margin>F</margin> we have identified is the *harpastum* <term>harpastum; a "scramble" or "snatching" game, often considered a precursor to rugby or football</term>. Because of the similarity of the name, it seems to be exactly the same as the Greek *harpaston* <note>original Greek: "ἁρπαστὸν," meaning "snatched."</note>: for it was a ball that players would snatch from one another. However, what its size was and what material it was made of is not explained by any author, except that Athenaeus makes it clear with these words that the *harpastum* was round: <margin>„ „</margin> "The game called *harpaston* by means of the sphere <note>original Greek: "σφαίρας" (sphairas), meaning a ball or globe.</note> was once called *pheninda*, which I delight in most of all." <note>original Greek: "τὸ δὲ καλούμενον διὰ τῆς σφαίρας ἅρπασον, φενίνδα ἐκαλεῖτο, ὃ ἐγὼ πάντων μάλιστα ἀσπάζομαι."</note> Just as it also seems likely it was made of leather like the other balls. Authors likely neglected to write about these details because they were unknown to no one at that time. Furthermore, Galen seems to have fully explained its size; while in his book *On the Game of the Small Ball* he describes the *harpastum* most aptly, calling it...

paruam <note>catchword: small</note>

<margin>A</margin> ...it is proved to have been a small ball, and not halfway between small and large, as some have claimed. From this, the game which today is named from the "heel" <term>calce; likely referring to Calcio or a form of football played with the feet</term>, although it resembles the <term>harpastum; a "snatching" ball game involving intercepting a ball in the air</term> in some respects, nevertheless seems to differ from the *harpastum* of the ancients in this: that the ancient ball was small, whereas the ball with which our people play the kicking game is larger. For even the ancients played with this ball on dusty ground, as Martial testified in his fourth book:
> Whether you seize the dusty *Harpasta* with your hand. <margin>& book 7.</margin>
> You do not, wandering, seize the dusty *Harpasta*. <margin>& book 14.</margin>
> Swift Draucus <note>A famous athlete mentioned by Martial</note> snatches these in the dust of Anteus <note>A mythological giant who gained strength from the earth; here referring to a wrestling or exercise ground</note>, he whose great neck strains with vain labor.
All of these can serve as evidence that this exercise was very arduous and suited only for the strongest of men. Indeed, <margin>B</margin> women were by no means strong enough to play this kind of game, according to the testimony of Ovid, who writes thus concerning the games of men:
> To girls, a weak nature granted these trifles;
> Men play with more substantial material.
> They have swift balls, the javelin, and hoops,
> And weapons, and the horse forced to run in circles. <margin>3. On the Art of Love.</margin>
The verses of the same poet prove this when he reproaches a certain Philaenis <note>A name often used in classical poetry to describe a woman who took on masculine roles</note>, a masculine woman, because she performed almost all the duties of men; as if she were doing something particularly unusual for women above all others, he said after many things:
> She also plays *Harpastum*, wearing a loincloth. <note>original: "Harpasto quoque subligata ludit."</note>
Therefore, I am usually surprised why Caelius Aurelianus <note>A Roman physician of the 5th century AD</note>, in treating epilepsy in children, wishes for nurses to be exercised by a game of ball or some kind of dance: <margin>Lib. 1. ser. 3. trac. 2. cap. 2.</margin> unless the "ball" he refers to is the air-ball <term>follis; a large, light ball filled with air</term>, which I showed above was used by both children and the elderly. <margin>C</margin> Avicenna <note>A famous Persian polymath and physician (980–1037 AD)</note> mentions a certain wooden ball, which I shall speak of later, since it pertains very little to the present treatment of the "spheric" <note>The art or science of ball games</note> as the other part of the art of movement, concerning which enough has been said.

### On Orchestics, or the third part of the art of movement. Chapter VI.

**T**he three parts of the art of movement—the "cubistic" <note>The art of tumbling or acrobatics</note>, the "spheric" <note>The art of ball games</note>, and that which is simply called by the name of the genus, "dance"—we have established in the preceding sections. Since two of these have now been explained, the third must now be brought forward. Concerning this, we shall explain the following: first, what it was; second, how many species it had; third, why our ancestors used it; and fourth and finally, in what place and by whom it was practiced. Aristotle, therefore, in the beginning of his *Poetics*, when he had said that all kinds of poetry agree in this, that they are imitations, divides imitations...

-> BOOK TWO <-
<page-num>96</page-num>
<header>B O O K</header>

...[he taught] that some of these arts imitate in different ways, such as by harmony, by rhythm, or by bare speech; others imitate different subjects, such as things better, similar, or worse [than reality]; others in a different manner, such as by acting, introducing characters, or narrating, and either assuming a different persona or remaining unchanged; regarding dancing, he concludes this: <margin>Chapter 4</margin> <note>Aristotle, *Poetics* 1447a</note> "Dancers imitate by rhythm alone without harmony; for they, through rhythms given shape, imitate passions, characters, and actions." <note>original Greek: αὐτῷ δὲ τῷ ῥυθμῷ μιμῶνται χωρὶς ἁρμονίας οἱ τῶν ὀρχηστῶν, καὶ γὰρ οὗτοι διὰ τῶν σχηματιζομένων ῥυθμῶν μιμοῦνται καὶ πάθη καὶ ἤθη καὶ πράξεις.</note> Indeed, dancers imitate by rhythm <note>original: *numero*; in ancient music theory, "number" refers to rhythmic measure or meter</note> itself without harmony: for these men imitate characters, passions, and actions through a rhythmic variety of gesturing. 

From this discourse, it appears that <term>orchesis; the ancient Greek word for dancing</term>, or dancing, was nothing other than a certain ability to imitate human character, emotions, and actions through bodily movements and gestures, performed with a certain skill, rhythm, and reason. For he <note>Aristotle</note> who had said in the seventh book of the *Politics* that there is nothing in the nature of things that expresses the likenesses of things more than rhythm and song, also wisely wrote that dancers use rhythm in imitating actions. 

How this imitation might be achieved through rhythmic movements was expressed most clearly of all after Aristotle by Plutarch, who wrote in the ninth book of his *Table Talk* <margin>Problem 15</margin> that dancing had three parts: motion, figure, and indication. He says this because the whole art consisted of movements, postures, and rests, just as harmony consists of tones and intervals. He defines <term>motion; Latin: *lationem*</term> as nothing other than a movement representative of some emotion, action, or power. The <term>figure; Latin: *figuram*</term>, however, was the posture and arrangement in which the movement or motion ended; namely, when the dancers, coming to rest, persisted for a short time like a painting <note>original: *graphice*</note> in bodily forms arranged according to the figure of Apollo, or Pan, or some Bacchante (as found in Plato’s <margin>Book 7 of the *Laws*</margin> seventh book of the *Laws*). 

The <term>indication; Latin: *indicationem*</term>, moreover, was not strictly an imitation, but a declaration of some thing—namely the earth, the sky, or bystanders—made through rhythmic and ordered movements. For just as poets, while imitating, use sometimes invented names and sometimes metaphors, but use proper names when they are indicating something directly; similarly, dancers use figures and postures when imitating, but use the aforementioned "indications" when pointing out the things themselves. Thus, according to Plato, Aristotle, and even Plutarch, this entire art of dancing consisted in imitation performed by movement alone. And the dancers themselves performed nothing else except that, moving in rhythm and gesturing with order, they either imitated character and emotions through motions and figures, or declared things through indications, or represented human characters, passions, and actions through all these together. Hence, not without the highest reason, Simonides...

[Simoni]des the poet <note>The text begins with the end of the name Simonides of Ceos, a Greek lyric poet.</note> used to call dance silent poetry, just as he called poetry speaking dance. However, Plutarch reports <margin>In the place cited.</margin> that in his own time, true dance had been corrupted from the music with which it was associated; and falling away from that heavenly origin, it held sway like some tyrant in tumultuous and unlearned theaters. All sensible men recognize that this corruption has subsequently persisted until our own times, in which all dance is debased. 

Regarding who first demonstrated this kind of dancing to men, it is not sufficiently certain, except for what Theophrastus reports in Athenaeus: that Andron of Catana, a flute-player, while he played, performed movements with a rhythmic body, and for this reason, dancing was called *sicelissare* <note>original: "siceliſſare"; to dance in the Sicilian manner</note> among the ancients. <margin>8th book of the *Deipnosophistae*</margin> After him, Chleophantus of Thebes and Aeschylus invented many figures of the dancing art, which Athenaeus suggests were called *ballismos* <note>original Greek: βαλλίσμους; a rhythmic leaping or skipping</note> in the Sicilian dialect, on the authority of Epicharmus. From this, the name *Ballo* [Dance] still persists today among many nations of Italy. 

Furthermore, this dancing was held in such high esteem and honor among the ancients that they called Apollo a dancer, just as Pindar did:
> *Dancer, lord of splendor, Apollo of the wide quiver.* <note>original Greek: Ὀρχηστὰ Ἀγλαΐας ἀνάσσων εὐρυφάρετρ’ Ἄπολλον</note>
->*Dancer, king of splendor, and Apollo of the quiver.*<-
This was performed sometimes to the sound of flutes, or the lyre, or another instrument, or to singing, or without any accompaniment at all. Indeed, Homer, Plato, Xenophon, Aristotle, Strabo, Plutarch, Galen, Pollux, and Lucian have recounted almost innumerable species of it. Those which were considered more excellent and illustrious took their name either from the regions in which they were used (or where they were discovered and made famous), or from their inventor and the manner in which they were performed. 

From regions, they were called Laconic, Troezenian, Epizephyrian, Cretan, Ionic, Mantinean, and Gaditane <note>From Gades, modern Cadiz in Spain, famous in antiquity for provocative dancers</note>, of which Juvenal writes thus:
<margin>Satire 11</margin>
> *Perhaps you expect that a Gaditane girl will begin to frolic with a melodic*
> *chorus, and, praised by applause, sink to the ground with trembling thighs,*
> *a provocation for a fading Venus, and sharp*
> *stings for the wealthy.*

And there were other such kinds. From the inventor and the manner of performance, others were called Pyrrhic, invented by a certain Pyrrhichus of Laconia, or, as others prefer, by Pyrrhus the son of Achilles. In these, armed men danced with singing and without singing, as can be seen from the image taken from ancient stones, which we have taken care to place here.

### THE PYRRHIC DANCE
