<page-num>99</page-num>
<header>B O O K S E C O N D</header>

(In our own times, those types of combat dances which are popularly called **Morescas** <note>Also known as "Morris dances"; a traditional folk dance involving rhythmic stepping and often choreographed swordplay</note> resemble the ancient **Pyrrhic** dances.) These dances obtained various names, such as the *Orsitis* and *Epichiedios* among the Cretans, and the *Carpaea* among the Aenianians and Magnetes, which Xenophon describes in the sixth book of his *Expedition of Cyrus*. There was also the *apochinos* or *mactrismos*, which women used to dance and were thus called *Martypiae*. Other dances were more stable and possessed greater variety, such as the *dactylic*, *iambic*, *molossic*, *emmelia* <note>a grave and stately dance used in Tragedies</note>, *cordax* <note>a provocative dance used in Comedies</note>, *sicinnis* <note>a vigorous dance used in Satyr plays</note>, the *Persian*, the *Phrygian*, the *nicatismus*, the *Thracian*, and the *calabrismus*. The *Telesias* was named after a man called Telesias, who was the first to dance it in full armor; it was this dance that the soldiers of Ptolemy used when they overthrew Alexander, the brother of Philip. Others were called "turning" or "whirling" dances because the performers danced while turning in a circle. Erotian—who was a contemporary of Nero’s chief physician Andromachus, as Galen writes—records that these dances were called *dineis* <note>original: δίνεις; "whirls" or "revolutions"</note>. Others were considered "insane" dances, such as the *caudifer* <note>tail-bearer</note>, the *mongas*, the *Thermaustris*, and the *anthema* <note>flower dance</note>, which the dancers performed while singing, "Where are my roses? Where are my lilies? Where is my celery?" Still others were "ridiculous," such as the *igdis* <note>the mortar</note>, the *mactrismos*, the *apochinos*, the *phobas*, the *morphasmos* <note>transformation dance</note>, the *Glaux* <note>the owl</note>, and the *Leo* <note>the lion</note>. Some were for the stage, such as the tragic, comic, and satyric; others were lyrical, such as the *pyrrhic*, *gymnopaedic*, and *hyporchematic*. It is not the purpose of this present treatise to declare exactly how all these were performed; let it suffice to understand that this third category of dance possessed these and many more diverse species (to which Lucian dedicated a specific book), just as it utilized diverse movements of both the feet and the hands. For since all motion, according to the opinion of Aristotle <margin>7th book of the *Physics*</margin> is composed of pushing and pulling, dancers either pushed their bodies or pulled them; and this was done upward, downward, forward, backward, to the right, or to the left. From these basic motions were later composed the simple walk, the turn, the forward run, the leap, the spreading of the legs, the limp, the kneeling, the lifting of the body, the tossing of the feet, and the exchange of positions—by which the entire dance was completed.

### On the Purpose of Dance, and on the Location. Chapter VII.

<insert><image-desc>Decorative drop-cap initial 'V' containing a woman's portrait.</image-desc>Since</insert> the ancients almost always focused on the exercise of the feet in their contests and hunts, and paid no attention to moving the hands, it is likely that the art of dance was first invented to exercise only the lower parts of the body. Afterward, <term>cheironomia</term> <note>original: χειρονομία; literally "hand-law," referring to the art of expressive gesticulation or "hand-dancing"</note>, which taught organized hand movements, was added to it. Thus, along with the other aforementioned movements, there was included the connecting, joining, intertwining, and extending of the hands...

...the dancers would perform complex movements and alternating steps; in this way, the entire dance was composed of movements of both the hands and the feet, shaped to represent various subjects. Because dancers primarily move their arms, Ovid also indicated this when he said:
<margin>1st & 2nd [books] of *The Art of Love*</margin>
> *If you have a voice, sing; if your arms are supple, dance.* <note>original: "Si uox eſt, canta, ſi mollia brachia, ſalta."</note> &
> *Admire the arms of the dancer, and the voice of the singer.* <note>original: "Brachia ſaltantis, uocem mirare canentis."</note>
Although the primary goal of this art was (as we have said) imitation, I find that it nevertheless had other purposes as well. For it was used in theaters and games for the sake of pleasure, and also for religious reasons in sacrifices. Besides Plato and Plutarch, this is attested by Galen <margin>at the locations cited.</margin>, who at the beginning of his work on the *Art of Healing* vehemently inveighs against the men of his time for devoting too much effort to the art of dancing, as if they were neglecting the noble arts by being devoted only to pleasures and games. Our ancestors likewise used this same dancing to seek physical strength and military skill. Even though this has already been proven above from Plato, it must be added that every armed dance, called the **pyrrhichia** <note>The Pyrrhic dance; a famous Greek martial dance performed in armor</note>, was invented for no other reason than that boys, men, and women might learn to escape or attack enemies and master other gestures necessary for conducting war. Thus, in the writings of Xenophon, when the Paphlagonians saw a little female mimic dancer commanded by a Mysian to dance the *pyrrhichia*, they asked the Greeks in wonder whether they also used women in battle. Indeed, when Phrynichus <note>A 5th-century BCE Athenian tragic poet who was famously elected as a general</note> performed excellently in this kind of dance in a play, the Athenians chose him as their General. Nor is it difficult to show that this same dancing contributed not a little to both attaining a good physical condition and preserving health. Regarding the gesturing of the hands, <margin>2nd [book] *On Diet*; 1st [book] *On Method of Healing*, Ch. 1.</margin> which the Greeks call <term>cheironomia</term> <note>original: χειρονομίαν; literally "hand-law," referring to a system of rhythmic gestures or shadow-boxing used for exercise</note>, it is found in the writings of Hippocrates, Aretaeus, and others that it was employed for exercising both healthy and sometimes sick bodies. In our own times, no one would deny that other dances performed with timing, order, and a certain method provide such benefit, just as Galen confesses that he restored many to health and preserved others in it by the aid of dancing alone. He similarly counted the exercises of dancers among other things sought from a physician when he said: *the vigorous movements of dancers in which they jump the highest, and whirl around turning most quickly, and having crouched down they spring up, and they drag forward and spread their legs to the greatest extent.* <note>original: ὀρχηστῶν αἱ σκληραὶ κινήσεις ἐν αἷς ἄλλονται μέγιστα, καὶ περιδινῆνται στρεφόμενοι τάχιστα, καὶ ὀκλάσαντες ἐξανίστανται, καὶ προσύρεσι, καὶ διασχίζεσιν ἐπὶ πλεῖστον τὰ σκέλη.</note> That is, the intense movements of dancers, in which they jump most high, and are turned round and round very swiftly, and also flection the knees to rise upward, and draw in their legs very much...

**A** they hunt and branch out, so that no one should doubt that we have rightly placed the Art of Dancing <note>original: "Orchesticam"</note> within the category of medical gymnastics. This is especially true since Socrates, in Xenophon’s *Symposium*, openly professes that he practiced the art of dancing both to achieve and preserve health, as well as to acquire physical strength; it is for this reason, they say, that he desired a spacious house. I find that those who practiced this art of dancing were of various kinds. Plautus indicated that "cinaedi" <note>In this context, specialized rhythmic dancers or pantomimes, though the term often carried more derogatory connotations in other Roman contexts.</note> devoted themselves to the art of dancing more than all others; in his work, the old man Periplectomenus says: "Then for dancing: no *cinaedus* ever dances better than I." <margin>In the *Braggart Soldier*, Act 3.</margin> However, Nonius Marcellus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note>, citing the testimony of Lucilius and even Plautus, maintains that the ancients called the dancers themselves and the pantomimes *cinaedi* from the Greek phrase *apo tou kinein to sōma* <note>original: "$\alpha\pi\mathrm{o}$ $\tau\omega$ $\kappa\iota\nu\epsilon\iota\nu$ $\tau\mathrm{o}$ $\sigma\omega\mu\alpha$"; meaning "from moving the body".</note>. Similarly, all the poets not only taught the actors the choreographed movements, but they themselves

**B** also danced at times. Indeed, the poets Thespis, Pratinas, Cratinus, and Phrynichus were all called "dancers" for this reason: they not only represented their own dramas among the dancing choruses, but they also willingly taught anyone who wished to dance outside of their own poems. Children and women were also most frequently involved in dancing; after them, effort was devoted to dancing by anyone who had been commanded to do so by doctors or physical trainers <note>original: "gymnastis"</note> for the sake of health and strength. As for the places in which dances were performed: at first, while they were not yet refined, they took place in villages and public streets. Later, when they had received greater dignity and adornment, they were moved to certain parts of the theaters, which were called "orchestras" by both Aristotle and Pollux for that reason; from this, the very elegant name for a dance, the *chorea*,

**C** also emerged. Athenaeus is the authority who claims that these dances were transferred from theaters to the *palaestras* <note>wrestling schools or training grounds</note> or gymnasia. <margin>Book 14 of the *Deipnosophistae*.</margin> Plutarch seems to agree with this in the ninth book of his *Table Talk* <note>original: "symposiacon"</note>, where he mentions a certain man who had danced the **pyrrhic** <note>A traditional martial dance performed in armor.</note> so excellently that he seemed to surpass the boys gesturing in the *palaestra*. In that same passage, he appointed Meniscus the *paedotriba* <note>A physical trainer or master of a gymnasium.</note> as the judge of the dance, from which we can clearly surmise that the *paedotribae*, the ministers of the gymnasia, possessed no small knowledge of the art of dancing. Likewise, Xenophon left it clearly recorded in his *Symposium* that dancing was customarily practiced at banquets, just as Plutarch and Pliny have recorded that the theaters did not reject it either. Therefore, I conclude that dancing was accepted by all of gymnastics, just like ball-play <note>original: "sphaeristica"</note>; these were the two parts of the art of dancing <note>orchestica</note> into which, along with the whole of athletics <note>palaestrica</note>, we have divided gymnastics itself. And this is enough concerning this matter.

**D** <insert><image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'D' containing a seated classical figure, possibly a scholar or philosopher.</image-desc>D</insert> ELIVERED now sufficiently, at least as far as this treatise is concerned, is the subject of dancing. It is now worthwhile to approach the <term>Palaestric art: the branch of gymnastics dedicated to wrestling and physical combat</term>, which was the other part of gymnastics. To this, we shall subsequently join the remaining exercises, both those performed within the gymnasia and those outside of them. It was demonstrated above that the *Palaestra* <note>The wrestling school or square</note> comprised many exercises, among which wrestling—called *palē* <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\lambda\eta$"</note> by the Greeks and sometimes *katablētikē* <note>original: "$\kappa\alpha\tau\alpha\beta\lambda\eta\tau\iota\kappa\eta$", meaning "the art of throwing down"</note> or "the dejectory art" by the Spartans—consistently held the first place. This was nothing other than a certain exercise performed in a specific part of the gymnasium, namely the *palaestra*, or a covered portico which was called a *xystus* <term>Xystus: a long, covered walkway where athletes could exercise in bad weather</term>. In this place, wrestlers in pairs—naked, anointed with oil, and sprinkled with dust <note>Dust was applied over the oil to allow wrestlers to grip one another's slick bodies.</note>—would entwine their arms and contend with one another.

**E** Each contended to throw the other to the ground. To accomplish this, certain maneuvers known as *embolae*, *parembolae*, *paratheses*, and *systases* <note>These Greek terms refer to technical wrestling maneuvers: thrusts, counter-insertions, strategic placements, and standing engagements.</note> were necessarily required. Above all else, they sought to catch the feet first, which the drunken character Pseudolus in Plautus’s play indicated when speaking of wine: "It catches the feet first; it is a crafty wrestler." <margin>Act 5.</margin> Before they entered the contest, they would first warm up their muscles and smooth them out with rubs and gentle movements. For if they ever neglected to do these things, certain parts of their bodies would be ruptured or wrenched, as Galen records in his fourth book on *The Affected Parts*. He also left written elsewhere <margin>Chapter 8.</margin> that this order was observed by the gymnastics masters in wrestling: they never entered into violent movements unless they had first been taught easy and simple ones. Nor were they accustomed to approach these movements before being rubbed, nor rubbed before they were anointed with oil. I said they wrestled in "pairs" because, although

**F** many might contend in wrestling at the same time in the same place, nevertheless, one was always entwined with only one other. Among some people, not only did man contend with man, but girls also contended with young men, as was the custom among the Spartans and as Athenaeus reports concerning the people of Chios. Wrestling—which Galen, not without reason, believed to be no small part of the gymnastic art <margin>2. On the Differences of Pulses.</margin>—did not lack those among the ancients who argued it was the oldest of all exercises. They were led to this by the quality of its name, since *palai* <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\lambda\alpha\iota$"</note> among the Greeks seems to signify nothing other than "antiquity" or "long ago." Indeed, it is well established that the place for exercises, now called the *palaestra*, was first named *palēn* after wrestling. However, as Plutarch reports, there were also those who did not wish the name of the *palaestra* to be derived from *palē* <margin>2. Symposiacs, Problem 4.</margin> as if wrestling were the most ancient thing, but rather because only this exercise...

**A** <note>original: "$\pi\eta\lambda\epsilon$" (pēle)</note>—meaning it would be derived from clay, dust, and wrestling-wax. To further challenge that idea, they added another reason: it seems in no way likely that wrestling—which is the most skillful and cunning of all exercises—was also the oldest of all. It is clearly apparent that those things which are simple, lacking art, and following a natural path rather than a refined method, are the first to be put into use. For this reason, Sosicles preferred the theory that the word for "to wrestle" <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\lambda\epsilon\iota\nu$" (palein)</note> was derived from "to trip" <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\lambda\alpha\iota\epsilon\iota\nu$" (palaiein)</note>, which means to throw someone down through trickery and snares. Philinus, however, suggested it came from the *palaistē* <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\lambda\alpha\iota\sigma\tau\eta\varsigma$"</note>, which is a measure of the four fingers joined and bound together. He argued that wrestlers work chiefly with this part of the hands, and so the sport was named for them, just as the art of the <term>Pugillatory: the sport of boxing, named from "pugnus" (fist)</term> is named from the fists. Julius Pollux clearly seems to refute this opinion, writing that the name signifies only the specific measurement of four fingers; to derive the name of the exercise from a unit of measurement is quite a long-distance stretch.

**B** Therefore, those who believe that *palē* <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\lambda\eta$" (wrestling)</note> was born and named from the word for "shaking" <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\lambda\lambda\omega\alpha\iota$" (pallesthai)</note> seem to have a better sense of it; or perhaps from the terms for "hurling" and "being tossed" <note>original: "$\pi\alpha\lambda\lambda\epsilon\nu$ $\&$ $\pi\alpha\lambda\lambda\epsilon\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$"</note>. Among the poets, the former means to throw down, to hurl, or to scatter—the last of which the scholar Erotianus testifies was used by both Homer and the physician Hippocrates. The latter term, according to Plato in his *Cratylus*, means to lift something from the earth or in one's hands, both of which are clearly the goals of wrestlers. Unless, as others prefer, we wish it to be named from "approaching" <note>original: "$\pi\lambda\eta\sigma\iota\alpha\zeta\epsilon\iota\nu$" (plesiazein)</note> and "becoming near" <note>original: "$\gamma\iota\nu\epsilon\sigma\theta\alpha\iota$ $\pi\epsilon\lambda\alpha\varsigma$"</note>. This is because runners always kept their distance and never drew close; likewise, boxers were never permitted by the <term>Designators: officials or referees who organized and supervised the matches</term> to become entangled. Only wrestlers performed in this way. We can see all of this represented more clearly on the coins of the Syracusans, in which wrestlers are shown in various positions, as the antiquarian Ligorius <note>Pirro Ligorio (c. 1513–1583), a famous Italian architect and antiquarian known for his studies of Roman and Greek remains.</note> has pointed out to us.

**A** This entire discipline in the gymnasia <note>The ancient Greek centers for physical and intellectual education.</note> had three goals, and in the time of Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire (c. 129–216 AD).</note> his expertise grew in a marvelous way; specifically, as he himself reports in the first part of *On the Joints*, chapter 23, the masters of wrestling discovered various and manifold distortions and entwinings of the limbs. The first goal was so that **Athletes** might be trained in them, so that when they went out to the games, sacrifices, and amphitheaters, they could achieve victory. Plato writes that the authors of this style of wrestling were Antheus and Cercyon. The second goal was so that men might be trained for **war** <margin>Plato, *Laws*, Book 7</margin>, a type of exercise which some say was first put into use by Theseus, the prince of the Athenians, and others say by Phorbas, the physical trainer <term>paedotriba <note>A specialist in physical education and gymnastics.</note></term> of Theseus. The third goal was so that men and boys, through wrestling, might acquire the best physical condition and thus maintain their **health**. They worked so hard at this and struggled with all their might that it was not rare for those wrestling in this way to break or dislocate some bones; Galen testifies that these men were accustomed to resetting them in a specific "palaestric" <note>Referring to the techniques used in the wrestling school or *palaestra*.</note> way that differed from others.

**B** However, I believe it should be noted that Galen <margin>Galen, *On Machines*</margin> not only disapproved of "athletic" wrestling—which he writes that well-ordered republics should hate—but even when discussing those striving for health, he praised it only sparingly. This is because, while strength is indeed increased by it, the danger of dislocation, bone fractures, and even suffocation is imminent. Similarly, Clement of Alexandria, who flourished in Rome during the time of Galen, in the third book of *The Instructor* <note>original: "Paedagogus"</note> where he discusses exercises, disapproves of all wrestling. Nevertheless, he considers that form to be more honorable and more worthy of a man which is performed "with seemliness" <note>original: "$\mu\epsilon\tau$' $\epsilon\upsilon\sigma\chi\eta\mu\mathrm{o}\nu\mathrm{o}\varsigma$"</note> and for the sake of good and useful health. Furthermore, since Plutarch writes that only wrestling and the "rolling pancratium" <note>A combat sport combining wrestling and boxing where the fight continues on the ground.</note> were usually practiced in the *palaestra*, two things must be considered. First, that the term *palaestra* sometimes signifies the entire gymnasium, as we declared above, and sometimes a specific place

**C** in the gymnasium where all the exercises we enumerated in the first book were performed; and sometimes a place where only wrestlers and "rolling" pancratiasts exercised. Their contests are called "heavy" by Galen in the third book of *On Preserving Health*, chapter 2. Plutarch hints at this here, and Galen also seemed to hint at it at the end of his book *On Exercise with a Small Ball*. The second consideration is that the pancratium was of two kinds: the first, which we will discuss below, was composed of wrestling and boxing. The second was called "rolling" <note>original: "uolutatorium"</note>, and was a species of wrestling. For in standard wrestling, the contestants sought to throw each other down while remaining upright; but in the "rolling" pancratium, they were flattened on the ground. There, tangled together and rolling each other around, each strove to get the other beneath him. This is most clearly shown on the coins depicted here of a certain Sallustius <note>Likely referring to a high-ranking official or usurper in the late Roman period.</note> who, having seized the kingdom of Africa during the reign of Valentinian and the Empress Placidia, put on these and other games to celebrate his victory.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, *On the Gait of Animals*.</margin>
Regarding this exercise, it seems likely to me that Aristotle was speaking of it when he demonstrates that no one who is upright and standing can walk continuously and safely if they move in the same manner as wrestlers, who advance by sinking onto their knees in the dust. Regarding this same matter, it might seem probable to some that Martial was speaking when he said:
> *I do not love the one who wins, but the one who knows how to yield,*
> *And has better learned the leaning-back wrestle <note>original: τὴν ἀνακλινοπάλην (tēn anaklinopalēn)</note>.*
unless one should rather interpret "leaning-back wrestling" as a defensive maneuver, by which a wrestler, with his chest pulled back, would pull back his adversary and avoid his blow; or rather (as that Poet was always a lover of obscenities) we might interpret it as that "couch-wrestling" <note>original: κλινοπάλην (klinopalēn)</note> which Suetonius records that Domitian <note>Roman Emperor known for his eccentricities and vices.</note> called it. Antyllus also spoke of this same thing in the works of Oribasius, <margin>Oribasius, *Medical Collections*, Book 6, Ch. 27.</margin> while he established a twofold division of wrestling: one performed upright, and the other upon the
<margin>B</margin>
floor. By "wrestling upon the floor," he understands nothing other than the "Rolling Pancratium," which was nevertheless quite different from the other form of rolling signified by Hippocrates under the name "rolling exercise" <note>original: ἀλινδήσιος (alindēsios)</note>, by which men prostrated on the ground in the wrestling school <note>term: palaestra (a Greek wrestling school or gymnasium)</note> rolled themselves about either alone or with others. <margin>Hippocrates, *On Diet*.</margin> Coelius Aurelianus also spoke of this, <margin>Aurelianus, *On Diet*, Book 6.</margin> where he praised rolling in the wrestling school for the purpose of "diminishing the flesh" <note>An ancient medical term for weight loss or reducing body mass.</note>; for in that exercise they neither competed nor became entangled, but only rotated themselves quickly upon the polished floor or a floor sprinkled with dust. For this reason, Galen placed it among the "swift motions," not without good cause. <margin>Galen, *On the Preservation of Health*, Book 2.</margin>

### On Boxing, the Pancratium, and the Cestus. Chapter IX.

**B**OXING, called *pygmikē* <note>original: πυγμικήν</note> by the Greeks, was in use before the times of the Trojans, as Pliny testified, and before Pliny, Homer. Plutarch also observed this in the second book of his *Symposiacs*, <margin>Plutarch, *Table Talk*, Problem 5.</margin> noting that Homer continually places boxing before wrestling and running for the reason that this kind of exercise took its origin before the others—just as Lucretius also seems to suggest in this verse:
> *The ancient weapons were hands, nails, and teeth.* <margin>Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things*, Book 3.</margin>
What this exercise truly was, however, and how it was carried out, few (as far as I know) have explained diligently; and those who have wished for "cestus-fighting" <note>term: cestus (a battle-glove often weighted with lead or iron)</note> and "boxing" to have been entirely the same thing have understood this matter less than others. Nevertheless, from the writings of authors we can reach a conjecture: in this exercise, men were accustomed to contend naked, and with fists clenched—either bare, or filled with a bronze or stone sphere, from which comes the term "sphere-fighting" <note>original: σφαιρομαχεῖν (sphairomachein)</note>—or bound round with leather thongs or metal plates, they struck one another, seeking now the head, now the back, now the arms, and never entangling themselves with one another. Athenaeus, in the fourth book of the *Dinner Philosophers* <note>original: *Dipnoſoph.*</note>, relates the opinion of Eratosthenes that the Tyrrhenians <note>The Etruscans, whom the Greeks and Romans often depicted as luxury-loving and eccentric.</note> were accustomed to box <note>original: πυκτεύειν (pykteuein)</note> to the sound of the flute. <margin>Plutarch, *Table Talk* <note>original: 2. Symp. Prob. 5.</note></margin> Plutarch certainly left it on record that this contest served the purpose of exercising the body. However, I am of the opinion that boxing was numbered among exercises by Galen in his second book *On the Preservation of Health* <note>original: *de tu. ual.*</note>, but it was very little used in the gymnasiums for the sake of preserving health or for acquiring a good physical condition. I am led to believe this by two primary reasons. The first is that Galen named boxing only two or three times; and Antyllus, who treated this subject most diligently, had almost not a word to say about this exercise, just as no other trustworthy physician did, except for Aretaeus, who seems to recommend boxing for those suffering from vertigo—unless (as I suspect) the Greek manuscript is corrupted. If boxing had existed as a type of medical gymnastic exercise, it would certainly be right that it should not be passed over in silence by everyone. <margin>E</margin>

The second reason is that if we look exactly at the nature of boxing—since it imitates the strikes and evasions necessary for war, as Plutarch said, and teaches them—we cannot deny that it greatly assists military skill. But since it only exercises the arms and fists, and occasionally harms the body with blows and heavy strikes, I do not see how it can contribute to the preservation of health and the acquisition of a good physique. Thus, it can be safely said that boxing had very little use in medical gymnastics, but much in military training, and the most in athletic competition. Plato and Galen record that the chiefs and authors of this sport were Amycus and Epeius; it was also a sport in which Glaucus of Carystus <note>A legendary Greek boxer said to have used his hand like a hammer to drive a plowshare into the ground.</note> so excelled that, having been crowned in the twenty-fifth Olympiad, he deserved to be called by the name of "the Boxer" <note>original: *pictae*, likely a printing error for *pyctae*</note> par excellence. <margin>F</margin>

We read in Terence <margin>In *The Eunuch*, act 2, scene 3.</margin> that these boxers devoted their efforts to acquiring fat. This they did so that they might be able to strike more heavily and feel the blows inflicted upon them less; for it is proven by experience and reason that obese people feel injuries to their flesh less. Furthermore, it is not very difficult to guess why that character Thesprio in Plautus, when asked by Epidicus how his master's son was doing, replied "in a boxing and athletic way" <note>original: *pugilice atq. athletice*</note>. <margin>Galen, *On the Properties of Foodstuffs* <note>original: 1. de alim. fac. c. 2.</note>, book 1, ch. 2.</margin> Galen also left it written that wrestlers were primarily called the "true athletes," but a little before his own time, boxers and pancratiasts were also called by the same name. <margin>Plautus, *Epidicus*.</margin> For this reason, it is possible that in the age of Plautus, boxers were distinct from athletes, yet both aimed for strength and thickness of body; and therefore that slave rightly separated boxing and athletics, signifying that his master was robust and "fat-bellied." <margin>A</margin> A third kind of exercise was also established, which all gymnasts commonly called the **pancratium** <note>An ancient combat sport combining boxing and wrestling; the name literally means "all powers" or "all-mastering."</note>. In this exercise (as Aristotle testifies in the first book of the *Rhetoric* <margin>Ch. 5.</margin>), those who trained strove to strike their adversaries with their fists, and to squeeze, restrain, and throw them down. For boxers fought with fists alone and never became entangled; thus, we should commend the wit of Horace, who in the third Satire of his second book <note>Horace, *Satires* 2.3.298.</note> very charmingly called those suffering from fits of madness "boxers" because they struck their servants and bystanders. Wrestlers, on the other hand, entangled and squeezed each other in order to throw them down, but they hardly ever struck with their fists. Pancratiasts used both methods, and even any other means—such as teeth, knees, heels, flicking fingers <note>original: *talitris*, a snapping or flicking motion of the fingers used as a strike.</note>, and finally the whole body (as Pausanias said <margin>Book 5, *Elis*</margin>)—striving to overcome their opponent. In this, they differed from boxers in that boxers fought with clenched fists, while pancratiasts fought with their fingers only slightly 
<margin>B</margin> bent. Galen intended to signify this where he wrote <margin>1. *On the Motion of Muscles*</margin>:
> "But if each of the fingers is bent, the shape of the hand would become most similar to those who extend it in the pancratium." <note>original Greek: "εὶ δ᾽ ἕκαστος τῶν δακτύλων καμφθῇ, τὸ σχῆμα τῆς χειρὸς γένοιτο μά λιστα τοῖς ἐν παγκρατίῳ προτετακόσιν αὐτὴν ὅμοιο"</note>
Indeed, such a shape of the hands was very well suited for grasping adversaries, which was the pancratiasts' primary aim, as the name itself seems to signify. For these reasons, this exercise was sometimes called **pammachion** <note>original: παμμάχιον, meaning "all-out fight."</note>, just as Plato called Euthydemus a **pammachon** <note>original: πάμμαχον, an "all-fighter."</note>. It was also considered a more difficult contest than both boxing or wrestling; because of this, Galen, in his commentary on the sixth book of *Epidemics* where Hippocrates recommends exercise for those with kidney ailments, believes that the pancratium should not be understood as a suitable exercise under such conditions because of the sheer magnitude of the labor involved.

I believe Plato was moved by a similar reason when, in the eighth book of <margin>C</margin> *The Laws*, led by his own method of exercising women (which was little approved by some), he advised that women should only practice the pancratium after they had reached a marriageable age. In my opinion, Galen was speaking of some specific type of pancratium when, in his commentaries on the book *On Salubrious Diet*, he said that gymnasts who wished to bulk up were often set to "touching" <note>original: προσάπτεσθαι (*prosaptesthai*), a light form of sparring.</note> and "body-fighting" <note>original: σωματομαχεῖν (*somatomachein*), an intense form of wrestling.</note>—for these were types of exercises—so that they might be joined and fight with the whole body, but naked and without the clinch. Panaetius also, as cited by Gellius in the thirteenth book, chapter 26, depicted the gestures and play of the pancratiasts in this manner:
> "Like those athletes who are called **pancratiasts** (more accurately than 'pancratiae'), for just as they are called to the contest and stand with their arms held high, they protect their head and face with their hands held out as if by a rampart; all their limbs, even before the fight begins, are cautious either to avoid blows or prepared to deal

...arranged, and so forth. Propertius clearly indicated that this exercise was among those performed in the gymnasia <margin>D</margin> when, praising the exercises of the Spartan wrestling-schools <term>palaestrae</term> <note>An ancient Greek wrestling school; the term is often used for the athletic grounds themselves.</note>, he said:
> *And he endures wounds in the hard pancratium.* <note>Propertius, *Elegies* 3.14.8.</note>

However, one should not conclude from this that the **pancratium** was much used by physicians for the sake of health. For if boxing and wrestling were only rarely approved by them for exercising the body, it must be believed that the pancratium—consisting of both boxing and wrestling—could be of even less use for health. <margin>2. *On preserving health*, last chapter.</margin> As for the fact that Galen once wrote that he had restored many to health through the pancratium, or preserved them in it, he achieved this only in those who were dedicated solely to such exercises, and even then, it was done with great wisdom and skill. Thus, it should by no means be inferred that the pancratium held any special place in medical gymnastics; nonetheless, its authority was very strong in athletics <margin>E</margin> and even in warfare. Indeed, in games and contests, the spectacle of the pancratiasts was so delightful and esteemed that even noblemen did not refuse to practice it. Such a man was Phrynon, the most famous Athenian general and pancratiast, whom Pittacus of Mitylene <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece, known for his military and political leadership.</note>, while contending in a single combat, entangled in a rope hidden beneath a shield and thus overcame him. Another such man was Autolycus, to whom a statue was erected in the Prytaneum <note>A public hall in ancient Greek cities, often used to honor distinguished citizens and athletes.</note> in Athens, a most worthy place, on account of his glory in the pancratium. I also find a certain kind of fight among the ancients called the *pancrapum* <note>Likely a variant of *pancarpium*, a spectacle or combat involving various beasts.</note>, but this was only undertaken against beasts, as may be seen in Cassian, book of *Conferences* 5, chapter 14. Truly similar to boxing, or rather a certain species of it, was that contest performed with the **cestus** <note>A combat glove used in ancient boxing, often made of leather strips weighted with metal.</note>. These were bronze plates tied to the hands; the things they were tied with <margin>F</margin> were certain leather thongs marked with points, which were bound all around the hands and arms. Thus, those competing with the cestus might strike each other not only with weight and thickness, but also with the hardness of the metal. From this it is clear that these men were in some part different from those properly called boxers <term>pugiles</term>, who fought only with their hands joined into fists. However, I know that those who fought in this manner were also sometimes called boxers, as in Marcus Tullius Cicero, the second book of the *Tusculan Disputations*. Propertius testified that those who wear the cestus <term>cestiphoros</term> were also accustomed to be exercised in the gymnasia; he writes in his third book that among the Spartan wrestling-grounds, even girls used to exercise with the cestus, in this manner:
> *Now she binds her joyful arms to the cestus with thongs.* <note>Propertius, *Elegies* 3.14.9.</note>

But that this kind of contest was practiced by athletes rather than those seeking health can easily be [known] from those things we wrote above regarding boxing.

## On Running. Chapter 10.

**A**mong the other gifts that nature granted to animals for the preservation of life, everyone who wishes to consider their condition will easily understand that the power of running is paramount. Indeed, while other means by which animals protect themselves are either not present immediately at birth or are unable to perfectly defend the body from those lying in wait without some injury occurring, the ability to run is granted to almost all from the very beginning of their existence. It protects their bodies from the harms of predators and all things capable of causing offense, so that they suffer no injury. For this reason, man would have much to complain about, as he remains unfit for running for a long time after birth, were it not for the fact that he—whose legs were crafted by nature in that specific shape for the sake of walking and running, as 
<margin>Aristotle, *On the Movement of Animals*; Galen, *On the Use of the Parts*, Book 1.</margin>
Aristotle and Galen have recorded—readily compensates for this loss through the care of his parents, under whose protection he then lives. Man alone, or more than any other animal, knows how to use nature's gifts not only to preserve his life, but also to spend it pleasantly and healthily at the same time. This can be seen in running; although it was granted to man solely for the purpose of preserving life, he nevertheless did not hesitate to use it to achieve glory, pleasure, and health. Who does not know that our ancestors, among other exercises—as Plutarch discusses in the second book of his *Table Talk*—included running among the spectacles instituted for military training and for acquiring a healthy physical condition? One cannot find a specific place assigned to this in the gymnasiums because this exercise could be performed on the common roads when they were not occupied by others, or even sometimes in a place where deep dust was spread, if we believe 
<margin>In the dialogue *Anacharsis, or On Gymnasia*.</margin>
Lucian. For we know from previous discussions that "peridromides" <term>peridromides</term> <note>Ancient Greek: *peridromides*. Covered walkways or galleries in a gymnasium intended for strolling rather than sprinting.</note> were not established for running, even if the name suggests it, but for the use of walking. The athletes who represented the famous gymnasium games and contests sometimes valued the power of running so highly that (as Pliny reports) 
<margin>Book 11, chapter 37.</margin>
they would have their own spleens cauterized <note>original: "lienem sibi ipsis inurendum curarent". In ancient medicine, the spleen was believed to cause side stitches and slow down runners; cauterizing it was thought to "dry it out" and improve speed.</note>, so that it would not hinder their speed in running, as it usually does. Pausanias is the authority that the people of Elis instituted the contest of running, as well as the first contests of wrestling, without any prior 
<margin>Books 5 and 6 of the *Description of Greece* (*Eliaca*).</margin>
example from ancient memory. In his writings, one similarly reads that Endymion proposed such a contest in Olympia to his sons to decide who should rule. Furthermore, the custom of running in the Nemean and Isthmian games, which had been discontinued, was restored by Hadrian. From this passage, we can know that both slaves and freeborn citizens contended in running matches in ancient times—even more so because Lampridius records that Alexander Severus...

<margin>8. On the Laws</margin> ...that he intended no one but a slave to be a runner, because, as he said, a freeborn man ought not to **D** run except in a sacred contest. On the other hand, Plato so highly recommended running for military exercises that he wanted not only men and youths, but even young women, boys, and adult women—all of them, whether naked or in armor—to be trained in running. He wanted this not only in the stadium <note>A track roughly 185 meters long.</note> but also in the *dolichos* <note>a long-distance race</note>, the *diaulos* <note>a double-length race, down and back</note>, and even on horseback. Thus, it is rightly debated in Plutarch’s second book of *Table Talk* whether wrestling and boxing, or running, is the older practice in military and competitive use. Following Plato’s opinion, Vegetius, in his commentary on military training, left it written that youths devoted to military discipline must especially be accustomed to running. This allows them to charge the enemy with greater force, to occupy advantageous positions quickly when the need arises, or to seize them before the enemy can do the same. It also ensures they go out to scout with vigor and return even more swiftly, and that they can more easily overtake the backs of those in flight. **E** Sallust reports regarding the training of Pompey the Great <note>Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, a leading Roman general and statesman.</note> that he competed with the agile in jumping, with the swift in running, and with the strong in lifting weights <note>original: "uecte" (lever/bar)</note>; he would never have been a match for Sertorius <note>A Roman general who led a rebellion in Spain.</note> had he not prepared himself and his soldiers for war with frequent exercises of this kind. From these examples, it is gathered that running was of the greatest importance in military gymnastics. Just as the athletic variety had four principal types: the *stadium*—of which Saint Paul spoke when he said that those running in the stadium compete for a corruptible crown <note>1 Corinthians 9:24-25</note>—the *dolichos*, the *diaulos*, and the armored race. In this <margin>Book 1, chapter 9.</margin> last category, Pausanias writes that Callicrates won twice. From these races, the trainers were called <term>stadium runners</term> <note>original: "σταδιόδρομοι"</note>, <term>long-distance runners</term> <note>original: "δολιχοδρόμοι"</note>, <term>double-track runners</term> <note>original: "διαυλοδρόμοι"</note>, and <term>armored runners</term> <note>original: "ὁπλιτοδρόμοι"</note>. Furthermore, anyone who has carefully read Aristotle’s first book of *Great Ethics* and the physician Galen’s second and sixth books on *The Preservation of Health* can easily understand that running held a significant place among exercises contributing to health and a good **F** bodily condition. Even Seneca, among the physical exercises he thought should be considered, gave the first place to running. <margin>Letters, Book 2, xv.</margin> However, I do not quite perceive what he intended to indicate in his third letter when he says that he "made himself a *Hiera*" <note>A reference to the *hiera gramme* or "sacred line," the finish line or a middle boundary in a race.</note>—something that rarely happens to runners. For if (as the most learned Muretus <note>Marc-Antoine Muret, a renowned 16th-century humanist scholar.</note> thinks) we understand *Hiera* to mean the middle line of the stadium, I do not quite follow how he can say that runners rarely reach it. I find that Antyllus <note>A famous Greek physician of the 2nd century AD.</note> established only three types of this exercise: one of running forward, another backward, and another in a circle. However, I know that in Galen both the *dolichos* and the *diaulos* are found; he himself reports that the former signifies a long-continued run among the Greeks (which the majority of authors, however, believe was a distance of twelve stadiums), while nearly everyone defines the latter as a race in which they ran the length of the stadium once and then ran back. Therefore...

**A** The *stadium* was a race of only one stadium length; the *dolichus* <note>original: "dolichus"</note> was a long-distance race, while the *diaulus* <note>original: "diaulus"</note> was also double the stadium's length, but run by turning back at the post. I believe it possible that the circuit of an interior peristyle <note>a courtyard surrounded by columns</note>—which Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer.</note> records was called a *diaulus* because of its two-stadium measurement—was used for this kind of race. For this reason, the claim found in the writings of Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist.</note> is discovered to be false: he suggests that stadium-runners <term>stadiodromos</term> cover a longer distance in their race than long-distance runners <term>dolichodromis</term>, when the opposite is clearly understood from an epigram by Parmenion:

> I say in an epigram of many thousands that it is in the middle;
> do not seek the long-distance race <note>original: "dolichon"</note> in a single stadium-length <note>original: "stadio"</note>.
> The course of the *dolichos* circles back many times, but in the stadium-length
> there is the sharp, driven tension of the breath.

The same point is further confirmed by a proverb cited by Pollux in his third book, **B** <term>do not seek the long-distance race in a stadium-length</term> <note>original: "μὴ ζήτει ἐν σταδίῳ δόλιχον"</note>, which signifies that one should not look for a greater thing within a smaller one. In addition to these, running had many varieties based on the diversity of locations; for whenever people ran outside the gymnasiums—as necessity or convenience demanded—they ran across flat ground, or rough terrain, or level paths, or uneven ones, or through meadows, or over mountains. Nor should anyone wonder here that those concerned with their health would also run outside the gymnasiums. Because specific locations could not possibly provide all the forms of exercise suitable for every need, men were sometimes compelled, as their health required, to go outside the gymnasiums, where they ran just as they did inside, sometimes clothed and sometimes naked. On all these matters there exists an opinion of Aristotle: that those who run naked become more healthy in color <note>tanned or vigorous-looking</note> than those who are clothed; for all who live in open and <margin>2. partic. prob. 30. & partic. 38. 5</margin> **C** airy places are better colored than those who stay in obstructed and still places.

He held this opinion: that leaping up and jumping differ from one another, because <term>to leap up</term> <note>original Greek: πηδᾷν</note> is a certain movement similar to running, specifically when the body remains in the same place while bending the knees and swinging around; whereas jumping, or <term>halma</term> <note>original Greek: ἅλμα</note>, is a nearly continuous movement upward, either toward a middle point or toward a goal, bounded by no certain laws or imitations. For this reason, it clearly differs from dancing, which we have shown uses laws, rhythms, and imitations. I believe Seneca understood these types of jumping when he recommended jumping for exercising the body— **F** <margin>Seneca, Book 2, Epistle 15.</margin> either that which lifts the body high, or that which sends it far, or that which was called the "Salian" or "Fuller" jump <note>The Salii were "leaping priests" of Mars; fullers jumped on cloth to clean it.</note>. Long ago, Spartan women used "leaping up" by jumping to strike their buttocks; they jumped with their legs bent back so that they touched their buttocks with their heels, sometimes with the legs bent alternately, and sometimes both at one and the same time. **A** ...for the sake of the parade, they are accustomed to hold back the riders and not allow them to go forward; those who move in this way quickly tire and feel fatigue. In another form of the exercise, they took small weights in their hands so that, being steadied by them, they might jump more vigorously. Although I know these weights are called *halteres* <term>halteres <note>original Greek: ἁλτῆρας</note></term> by Aristotle and by Theophrastus in his book <margin><term>On Weariness</term> <note>original Greek: περὶ κόπων</note></margin>, I will demonstrate further below that *halteres* also existed as a different kind of exercise. Meanwhile, it is pleasing to note the error of Cornarius <note>Janus Cornarius (1500–1558), a German humanist and translator of Greek medical texts.</note>, who, in his commentaries on the second book of Galen’s *On the Composition of Medicines according to Places*, being ignorant of this matter, thought Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a French scholar who wrote extensively on ancient weights and measures.</note> should be condemned for saying that jumpers in competition used weights. For even if I were to grant what he says regarding the difference between *halteres* and *halcteres*, Aristotle (in *Problems* 5.8) and Theophrastus (in *On Weariness*) nonetheless state—contrary to what he denies—that pentathletes and others jump better if they carry a stone or hand-weights in their hand than if they swing **B** empty arms. From this, perhaps, in both Galen’s second book of *On Protecting Health* and in Artemidorus, we should read not *alkteres* <note>original Greek: ἀλκτῆρες</note> and *alkteria* <note>original Greek: ἀλκτηρεία</note>, but *halteres* <note>original Greek: ἁλτῆρες</note> and *halteria* <note>original Greek: ἁλτηρεία</note>; especially since I have not happened to find this word *alkteres* used by any other author.

As for how this jumping was performed by both athletes and others, I conjecture this: that they sometimes jumped across level ground with continuous leaps. In those cases, they had a limit from which they took the starting point of the jump, called the *bater* <term>bater <note>original Greek: βατῆρα</note></term>, and a measure called the *canon* <term>canon <note>original Greek: κανόνα</note></term>. Similarly, there was a finish line which it was a great honor to reach, and a supreme honor to pass, called the *skamma* <term>skamma <note>original Greek: τὰ ἐσκαμμένα; literally "the dug-up ground"</note></term>. From this comes the proverb used against those who leap beyond the goal: *not even beyond the skamma* <note>original Greek: μηδ᾿ ἂν ὑπὲρ τὰ ἐσκαμμένα; a Greek idiom for overstepping boundaries or exceeding expectations.</note>. At other times they jumped from a low place to a high one, and sometimes from a high place to a low one. Among these, **C** the jump performed from the low to the high ground required greater effort, since Aristotle and Theophrastus <margin>See *Problems* and the book *On Weariness*.</margin> have declared that it is consistently more laborious simply to ascend than to descend.

I find that they did not only hold hand-weights while jumping to exercise themselves better, but indeed they sometimes carried even heavier loads above the head, sometimes upon the shoulders, and occasionally on the feet—just as can be seen from the picture on this ancient tablet, in which jumpers are very aptly represented, and which we received as an ancient and authentic image from Ligorio <note>Pirro Ligorio (c. 1512–1583), a famous antiquarian and architect who provided Mercurialis with many drawings of ancient Roman and Greek life.</note>.

<margin>A</margin> There were also those who would dance with their feet upon wine-skins <note>skins made from animal hides, usually goats, used to hold liquids</note> that had been anointed with oil and filled with wine. Among these, those were judged the winners who conducted themselves so skillfully that they did not fall to the ground because of the slipperiness. These winners would carry away the wine-skin full of wine as a victory prize; however, those who struck the ground with their buttocks moved the spectators to great laughter and delight. It is recorded that this was observed in ancient times during the games dedicated to Bacchus <note>the god of wine and festivity, known as Dionysus in Greek</note>, which the Greeks called *askolia* <note>original: ἀσκώλια</note>. In these games, wine-skins made from goatskins were trampled upon with leaps as a sign of contempt for goats, who are believed to be so harmful to grapevines. Regarding this, Aristophanes says in the *Plutus*: "Here, jump upon the wine-skin under the open sky" <note>original: ἀσκωλία ζ' ἐνταῦθ’ α πρὸς τὴν αἰθείαν</note>. And Eubulus, as cited by a commentator on Aristophanes, says: "Therefore, having placed a wine-skin in the middle, jump upon it, and mock those who slip off with loud laughter" <note>original: ὥς πρός γ' εἴτ' ἀσκὸν εἰς μέσον καταθέντες εἰσάλλεσθαι, καὶ καγχάζετε ἐπὶ τοῖς καταῤῥέουσιν</note>. Virgil also writes of these in the second book of the *Georgics*:
<margin>B</margin>
> And joyful amidst their cups,
> They leapt over oiled wine-skins in the soft meadows.

But it should not be ignored that it is written in Julius Pollux that the term *askoliazein* <note>original: ἀσκωλιάζειν</note> was also used by the ancients for those who dance on only one foot while the other is lifted up.

### On the Discus and Hand-Weights. Chapter XII.

<margin>2. d Vitruvius,
Book 3.
Book 7. ch. 5.</margin>
**T**hat the throwing of the discus <term>discus <note>a heavy circular plate of stone or metal thrown as an exercise of strength</note></term> held by no means the lowest place among the exercises of the gymnasium has been affirmed not only by Galen in the clearest words and predicted by Propertius, but indeed Vitruvius also seemed to imply this openly through a most elegant story. There it is read that when Apaturius of Alabanda had designed a stage setting at Tralles with excellent skill, and everyone’s sight was being enticed by its beauty due to its intricate detail, and they were already prepared to approve the work, then Licinius the Mathematician came forward. He said that the Alabandians were considered sharp enough in all civic matters, but because of a minor flaw of indecency, they were judged unwise; for in their gymnasium, all the statues are
<margin>C</margin> of people pleading legal cases, while in the forum <note>the central public square and marketplace</note>, there are statues of people holding discuses, or running, or playing ball. The mathematician noted that just as statues pleading cases are proper for the forum, so those holding the discus belong to the gymnasium. Because of this impropriety regarding the nature of the locations, he said the placement of the statues had brought a flaw to the city's reputation. Thus, the discus was an exercise of the gymnasium for those ancients. Whether those studious of military skill practiced it among other things is not entirely clear to me, unless Plato intended the throwing of the discus to be understood among those various hurlings which he greatly recommends for future elite soldiers. This is likewise signified by Homer in the *Iliad*, where he imagined that Achilles, angry at Agamemnon, had withdrawn his Myrmidons <note>the legendary soldiers commanded by Achilles</note> from the fighting, and they exercised themselves on the seashore with discuses and javelins—as tools suited for soldiers—lest they grow sluggish. It was as if this kind of exercise were adapted, if not for wounding enemies, then at least for providing them with a variety of agility. That athletes indeed practiced it, and even competed in public contests, is made manifest by the common opinion of authors, who with one voice number the discus among the athletic competitions, and besides these, by the illustration which we provide here.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the definition and physical form of the ancient discus, moving from its mention in medical texts on the previous page to its etymology and various physical iterations as described by classical authors and observed in archaeological finds.</meta>

<page-num>123</page-num>
<header>B O O K T W O</header>

<margin>A</margin> ...the discus was a certain round instrument, which was sometimes so heavy that it could scarcely be lifted by a single man—just as St. Jerome <note>Jerome was a 4th-century scholar and priest best known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate)</note> wrote concerning himself. Indeed, I believe Solon <note>An Athenian statesman and poet, here appearing as a character in a dialogue</note> was speaking of this in the works of Lucian <note>A Syrian-Greek satirist of the 2nd century AD</note>, where he asks Anacharsis whether he had seen in the gymnasium a certain smooth, round, bronze globe lying there, shaped like a small shield, having neither a thong nor a handle, which was heavy and difficult to grasp, and which some were accustomed to hurl into the air with an upward twist of the hand. He adds further: I find that sometimes that instrument had a shape similar to the body of the sun, because the body of the sun is called a "discus" <note>original: δίσκος</note> by Alexander in his second book of *Problems* (whether he was Alexander of Aphrodisias or Alexander of Tralles, which I more strongly suspect). Similarly, the "discus" was the name for a round platter on which feasts were carried to the tables. From this, those appointed to carry these platters were called "discus-bearers" <note>original: δισκοφόροι</note>.
<margin>B</margin> Thus we read that the head of St. John the Baptist was offered to the dancing girl on a "discus" <note>often translated as a platter or charger in biblical contexts</note>. Finally, the discus is found to designate a type of instrument of which we are speaking. Furthermore, I find it recorded what sort of instrument it was. Eustathius <note>A 12th-century archbishop and scholar who wrote extensive commentaries on Homer</note>, the interpreter of Homer, explaining those words in the second book of the *Iliad*, "they delighted in the discuses" <note>original: Δίσκοισιν τέρποντο</note>, says: "the discus is a heavy stone, which those exercising used to throw, but they call the iron one a *solos*" <note>original: δίσκος ἐστὶ βαρὺς λίθος, ὃν ἐῤῥίπτεον οἱ γυμναζόμενοι, τὸν δὲ σιδηροῦν σόλον προσαγορεύουσι</note>. From this, according to his opinion, it can be seen that the discus was a heavy stone which those exercising threw away from themselves; and when it was made of iron, they called it a "mass" <note>a *solos* or lump of metal</note>. Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his Epigrams</note> seems to testify to this in these verses:
> When the gleaming weights of the Spartan discus fly, 
> Stay far away, boys; let it be dangerous only once.

Others, with whom I agree, believed that the discus was a certain plate three or four fingers thick, a little more than a
<margin>C</margin> foot long, sometimes made of stone, sometimes of iron (the most learned Ligorio <note>Pirro Ligorio, a famous 16th-century architect, painter, and antiquarian who studied Roman ruins</note> testified to us that he had also seen a bronze one from the tomb of Marcus Mannius Philopator, an athlete, located on the Via Salaria). I believe the greater part of them were made of such materials so that they would not break when falling from a height. It resembled a flat species of lentil, which they would hurl into the air, but in a manner different from the throwing of javelins. For in throwing javelins, they would extend their arms and then push forward; by contrast, with the discus, the hand was brought toward the chest, then drawn back and down, and they would hurl it into the air with a rotation, just as Propertius <note>A Roman elegiac poet of the 1st century BC</note> very beautifully explained in this verse:
> Now he whirls the missile weight of the discus in a circle.

That the discus had the shape we have described, similar to a lentil, is confirmed here—besides Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist whose *De Materia Medica* was the primary source on herbs for 1,500 years</note> calling the lentil a "diskos" <note>original: δίσκον</note>—by the marble statue of the Discus-thrower <note>the famous *Discobolus*</note>, which is kept today in Rome in the house of Giovanni Battista Vittorio, in whose hand one can see the discus placed in the shape we have described.

<summary>This page defines the discus as a heavy, round object made of stone, iron, or bronze, distinguishing its athletic use from its meaning as a food platter. It also details the technical throwing motion—a circular rotation—contrasting it with the linear throw of a javelin.</summary>

painted [it] excellently, as <term>Pliny</term> <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman author of Natural History</note> reports. If that <term>William Choul</term> <note>Guillaume du Choul, a 16th-century French antiquarian known for his studies of Roman religion and military life</note> had seen and carefully examined this form of the discus along with the aforementioned 
<margin>D</margin> evidence, he certainly would never have dared to assert that the discus was a round ball perforated in the middle; unless that good man understood any spherical object by the name of "pila" [ball], contrary to the usage of the Latin language. And I say this because <term>Saint Cyprian</term> <note>An early Christian bishop and author</note>, in his book *On Spectacles*, calls the discus a "bronze orb," and on certain coins of the Emperor <term>Marcus Aurelius</term> struck at <term>Apollonia in Illyria</term> <note>An ancient Greek city in modern-day Albania</note>, an example of which was placed above, this kind of game of the <term>Discus-throwers</term> <note>original: *Discobolorum*</note> is represented, in which it appears that the discus was a certain rounded square, perforated in the middle. From this I may conjecture that there was not just one form of discus, whether it was used in sacrifices or in the <term>gymnasia</term> <note>public places for athletic training in ancient Greece</note>. However, it should not be overlooked that in throwing the discus, a certain skill was necessary, as the interpreter of <term>Pindar</term> <note>The great Greek lyric poet</note> shows; otherwise, the throwers were cheated of their praise and mocked, and they often brought significant harm to the 
<margin>E</margin> spectators, which was what happened with <term>Phoebus</term> <note>The god Apollo</note>, who is fabled to have killed <term>Hyacinthus</term> <note>In Greek mythology, a beautiful youth and lover of Apollo, accidentally killed by a discus during a game</note> with a discus. Another type of exercise was similar to the discus, called *halteres* <note>original Greek: *ἁλτῆρες*</note> by the Greeks, which <term>Galen</term> <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note> writes was commonly practiced in the <term>palaestra</term> <note>A wrestling school or gym</note>. That this was different from the "halteres" mentioned above—which we demonstrated dancers were accustomed to grip in their hands to jump more vigorously—was clearly declared by <term>Antyllus</term> <note>An ancient Greek surgeon</note>, whose words are found written in <term>Oribasius</term> <note>A Greek medical compiler and personal physician to the Emperor Julian</note> in the chapter *On the throwing of Halteres* <note>original: *περὶ ἁλτηροβολίας*</note>:

> There is a difference between the halteres themselves; for they are either thrown with the hands extended and bent in turn, or they are merely held while the hands are extended and still, moving for the most part with a short motion while the exercisers step in and shake them much like boxers do, or they bend themselves in turn with their hands according to the motion of the back. <note>original Greek: Διαφορά δ' ἔστιν αὐτῶν τ' ἁλτήρων, ᾗ γ' βάλλoνται παρὰ μέρος τ' χειρῶν ἐκτεινoμένων, καὶ συγκαμπτoμένων, ἢ κρατoῦνται μόνoν ἐν προτάσει τῶν χειρῶν ἡσυχαζoυσῶν ὡς τὰ πολλὰ βραχεῖά τινι κινήσει κινoυμένων αὐτῶν τε τ' γυμναζoμένων ἐμβαινόντων, καὶ ἀνασειόντων τοῖς πύκταις ὁμοίως, ἢ κατὰ σύνευσιν τῆς ῥάχεως ταῖς χερσὶ παρὰ καμπτόντων τῶν γυμναζoμένων.</note>

i.e., On the throwing of Halteres. There is a difference, however, in the halteres themselves, for either they are projected 
<margin>F</margin> with the hands extended and alternately bent, or they are only held in the extension of the hands, which remain still, and for the most part are moved with a brief motion; while those who were exercising entered and shook them just like boxers, or those who exercised bent themselves in turn with their hands according to the movement of the back. From these words, it seems clearly judged that, although halteres of this kind could be of the same material and the same form as the weights of the dancers, they nevertheless differed from them because they were not only held in the hands, like the dancers, but were also thrown in various ways, just as is practiced among many in our own times, who exercise themselves by throwing either a ball, or a stone of either earth or lead, with hands and arms extended and swung around, into the air; about which <term>Aretaeus</term> <note>A famous Greek physician from Cappadocia</note> spoke, an author no less esteemed than he is ancient, where he recommended the "throwing of halteres" <note>original Greek: *τ' ἁλτήρων βολίω*</note> for a headache. And so that a more certain knowledge of the form of this exercise may be had, we have taken care to place here the images of the <term>halterists</term> <note>those who exercise with halteres</note>, which were sent to us by <term>Pyrrhus Ligorius</term> <note>Pirro Ligorio, a famous Italian architect, painter, and antiquarian who provided the author with archaeological drawings</note>, taken from ancient engraved gems.

And so that no one may take an occasion for error from the ambiguity of names, we wish it to be noted that there is no small difference between a *weight-thrower* <note>original: "ἁλτῆρος" (haltēros)</note> and a *wanderer-dancer* <note>original: "ἁλητῆρα" (alētēra)</note>. For while the *weight* <note>original: "ἁλτὴρ" (haltēr)</note> signifies the type of exercise already described by us, as well as the weights usually grasped in the hands by jumpers, Athenaeus records that the *alētēr* <note>original: "ἁλητῆρα"</note> was a type of <term>orchestic</term> <note>the art of rhythmic movement or dance in ancient Greece</note> or dance common among the Sicyonians. By this same name, the people of Ithaca also practiced a dance, which I believe was established not without the fortune and hardships of Ulysses <note>the Roman name for the Greek hero Odysseus</note>; since indeed, from the verses of Homer, the usage of Hippocrates, and the interpretation of Galen, the word *alētēr* <note>original: "ἁλητὴρ"</note> signifies a beggar and a wanderer. Furthermore, as to what kind of weights these <term>halteres</term> were, I find nothing else explained except what Pausanias wrote in the fifth book of his *Description of Greece* <note>original: "Eliacorum"</note> in this manner: *“These weights have the following shape: they are somewhat oblong, and do not reach a perfect circle but are half-rounded; they are made so that the fingers of the hands may pass through them, just as through the handles of a shield.”* <note>original: "Οἱ δὲ ἁλτῆρες οὗτοι παρέχοντο σχῆμα τοιόνδε κύκλῳ προμήκεσέ ρ' κ, καὶ ἐπ' ἐς τὸ ἀκριβέστατον περιφερεῖς εἰσιν ἥμισυ, πεποίηται δὲ ὡς καὶ τοὺς δακτύλους τῶν χειρῶν διίεναι, καθάπερ δι' ὀχάνων ἀσπίδος."</note> That is, these halteres have the shape of an oblong circle, and do not achieve a perfect roundness even in half their form. Indeed, their shape is made so that the fingers of the hands are inserted as if through the handle of a shield.

<margin>Book 4, chapter 2 of the *Chronicles* <note>Referring to the works of Caelius Aurelianus, a 5th-century Roman physician.</note></margin>

Caelius Aurelianus, a physician among the ancient Latins, seems to have held a slightly different view on this, where he writes that it is beneficial for those suffering from arthritis to be given wax to be softened by the fingers, or to hold "handfuls" <note>original: "manipulos"</note> which the wrestlers call <term>halteras</term>. These were to be moved as waxen or wooden objects, at first with a little lead poured inside, then made heavier according to the degree of progress. From these words, it is gathered that the halteres were certain small masses or bundles made from various materials—sometimes lighter, sometimes heavier—of such a size that any of them could be gripped by the hand. In my opinion, these were thrown not only by the hands alone but even by cords wrapped around the weights themselves, which were then unfurled during the throw, just as many do in these times who compete by throwing either iron wheels, or cheeses, or something similar. Whether indeed *halteres* <note>original: "ἁλτῆρες"</note> are named by Plato among the other exercises devised for acquiring military fortitude, nothing is certainly explained. I am of the opinion, however, that where he writes in the eighth book of the *Laws* <note>original: "8. de legibus"</note> regarding the specific exercises of women, *“and of those competing with stones thrown from the hand and with slings,”* <note>original: "καὶ λίθοις ἐκ χειρός τε, καὶ σφενδόναις ἁμιλλλομένων"</note> he conceived of nothing else than that they should compete among themselves both with stones cast from the hands and those sent from slings. For even the *halteres* were sometimes stones, which we have indicated practitioners of exercise were accustomed to cast from their hands; hence, it is not entirely contrary to reason that Plato understood the *halter* under the name of a stone cast from the hand. Just as it is certain that a sling is different from weights by its cord...

**A** certain sling existed, which was held by the hand at two ends: one with a loop so it would not slip out, and the other without a loop so it could be released. It was wider in the middle to contain the stone, which the slingers would hurl violently by swinging the cord strongly and releasing it from one end. <margin>Pliny, Natural History, book 7, ch. 56.</margin> I believe this form of projection was invented by the Phoenicians—whom Pliny identifies as the inventors of the sling—for two reasons: first, so that less harm would come to the hands from touching rough stones, and second, so that stones might be thrown further and with greater force. For this reason, I believe David chose to use a sling to strike down Goliath, as he realized that against a most powerful Giant, there was a need for the greatest force and the most powerful momentum of arms. This type of contest was so celebrated among the people of the Balearic Islands <note>an archipelago in the western Mediterranean, famous in antiquity for providing elite slingers to various armies</note> that mothers would not allow their sons to eat any birds for food unless they had struck them down for themselves with a sling.

**B** And for this reason, Virgil called the sling by the name "Balearic" in this verse:
<margin>Virgil, Georgics, book 1.</margin>
> *The hempen lashes of the Balearic sling are whirled.*

And Statius in his first book:
> *The oak-staves and the heavy reins of the Balearic sling;*

Ovid in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*:
> *He burned no differently than when the Balearic sling*
> *hurls lead: it flies, and grows hot as it goes.* <note>Ancient writers often believed that lead sling bullets traveled so fast they could melt or glow red-hot from air friction.</note>

Indeed, anyone can easily learn from the commentaries of Vegetius <note>a late Roman writer on military matters</note> that military gymnastics made use of this type of exercise.

**C** ### On Javelin-Throwing. Chapter XIII.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial letter V, featuring a person in a garden setting within a circular frame.</note>

**A**LTHOUGH we may understand by the name of <term>throwing in general</term> <note>original: "τῆς πάσης ῥίψεως" (tēs pasēs rhipseōs)</note> or all casting, as used at times in Plato, the throwing of a stone, <margin>Plato, Laws, book 7.</margin> or a javelin, or any other object, he nevertheless seems to have established two primary species of it in the eighth book of his *Laws*, calling one <term>archery</term> <note>original: "τοξικὴν" (toxikēn)</note> and the other <term>javelin-throwing</term> <note>original: "ἀκόντισμα" (akontisma)</note>. Galen records that Apollo and Aesculapius presided over these two; following almost all Latin authors, we shall call the first "archery" and the second "javelin-throwing." I find that archery was traditionally practiced in three principal ways: by throwing-straps alone—concerning which Silius says in book 14:
> *the spear is aided by the strap* <note>original: "amentum"; a leather thong attached to the shaft of a javelin to give it spin and greater range</note>

as well as with bows, and with ballistas, into which they fixed thin and slender arrows—

...and first tensioning, then releasing them, they shot the arrows; and <meta>marker: D</meta> these were called by the common name *toxentai* or *toxotai* <note>archers; from the Greek $\tau o \xi \epsilon \upsilon \tau \alpha \imath$ or $\tau o \xi \acute{o} \tau \alpha \imath$</note>. From this, the physician Paul of Aegina writes that a certain poison was named *toxikon* <note>original: $\tau o \xi \iota \kappa \grave{o} \nu$; the root of the modern word "toxic"</note> because barbarians would infect their arrows with it to strike more lethally. Javelin throwing, however, was performed not only without a strap, bow, or ballista, but also required larger arrows, thicker rods, and frequently heavy stakes. Indeed, while archers moved only their arms, the *akontizontes* <note>original: $\alpha \kappa o \nu \tau \acute{\iota} \zeta o \nu \tau \epsilon \varsigma$; javelin-throwers or hurlers</note> or hurlers would contort and extend their arms during the throw, and furthermore, they would flex and move their backs and thighs while keeping their feet still—just as we see those who are called "stake-hurlers" practicing in our own times. Both groups, however, required no small amount of strength to perform these exercises. <margin>On Airs, Waters, and Places.</margin> For this reason, Hippocrates quite rightly recorded that many of the Scythians <note>nomadic people of Central Eurasia known for their archery skills</note>, due to an "impotence of humidity" <note>a humoral imbalance making the joints too soft or weak</note> in the shoulder, were unable to draw a bow <meta>marker: E</meta> or hurl a weapon. Likewise, at the beginning of his book *On Fractures*, he said that the posture of the arm is different in "natural javelin throwing," different in "slinging," different in "stone-throwing," and different in "boxing" <note>original: $\epsilon \nu$ $\alpha \kappa o \nu \tau \iota \sigma \mu \tilde{\omega}$ $\kappa \alpha \tau \grave{\alpha}$ $\phi \acute{v} \sigma \iota \nu$ (javelin), $\sigma \phi \epsilon \nu \delta \acute{o} \nu \eta \sigma \iota \nu$ (slinging), $\lambda \iota \theta o \beta o \lambda \acute{\eta} \sigma \iota \nu$ (stone-throwing), $\pi v \gamma \mu \tilde{\eta}$ (boxing)</note>. Those who exercised in this way had marks and targets set before them, which each man attempted to either pass or hit for the sake of victory, as Horace explained in this verse:

->*Often with the discus,*<-
<margin>Odes, book 1, ode 8.</margin>
> *Often noble for the javelin sent speeding beyond the mark.*

<margin>On Military Matters, book 10, ch. 15.</margin>
Furthermore, I do not wish to overlook here that the "balista" was also a type of engine which, according to Vegetius, hurled stones and arrows; and Vitruvius wrote that the ancients similarly used catapults and "scorpions" <note>a type of heavy crossbow or siege engine</note> to shoot arrows. However, treating such machines <meta>marker: F</meta> pertains very little to our purpose. The types of archery and hurling we are discussing are those which the gymnastic art embraces as its own proper exercises. That gymnastics used archery and javelin throwing as aids to health (though it is rarely found written among authors) can nonetheless be inferred from the fact that the ancients, as Galen reports, <margin>In his Exhortation to the Liberal Arts.</margin> made Apollo and Aesculapius the gods of both medicine and archery or javelin throwing. Plato is a most substantial witness that both types of hurling—with or without a bow—had a primary use in military gymnastics among the ancients. He took care that both women and men who were to be fit for war should be exercised in these things above all, knowing that the women of the Scythians used to do this; <margin>In the place cited above.</margin> Hippocrates noted that they used bows and shot arrows both on foot and from horseback.
