<meta>This page continues the technical and historical discussion of throwing exercises, specifically focusing on the military and athletic applications of archery and the javelin. It transitions from the physical mechanics discussed on page 130 to the historical figures and inventors associated with these practices.</meta>

<page-num>131</page-num>
<header>B O O K S E C O N D</header>

...that they were accustomed to this, he left written; to say nothing of Homer, who depicted the Myrmidons, the soldiers of Achilles, exercising themselves in throwing whenever they were free from war, lest they lose their military skill. How greatly the practice of throwing and archery aids that skill, and how much strength it brings to the arms, was clearly indicated by Vegetius <note>Renatus Vegetius, a late Roman author of a famous treatise on warfare</note> in the first book of *On Military Training*. That athletics was not lacking in throwing exercises can be proven by its founder, Hercules, of whom Seneca and others record that he was most skilled in archery; with that ability, he pierced the Centaur Nessus from a great distance, as well as the bronze-footed hind, and slew the winged Harpies in mid-air. Furthermore, those diverse and manifold beasts, which athletes used to kill in public spectacles and games—sometimes with arrows, sometimes with other weapons—provide the clearest evidence that athletic competitors also practiced throwing. This included not only men of low birth but even the most illustrious men, and even the Emperors themselves. Among these are numbered two: namely, Commodus (the son of the Prince Marcus and Faustina, who was the daughter of Pius and the elder Faustina) and also Domitian. Of the latter, Tranquillus <note>Suetonius Tranquillus, a Roman biographer known for his lives of the Caesars</note> writes that he frequently pierced a hundred wild beasts of various kinds with arrows at his Alban retreat, with many looking on. Of the former, Herodian <margin>Book 1</margin> records that he laid low a hundred beasts in the arena with as many shots, with such powerful force that he killed many with a single <margin>B</margin> blow. He similarly writes that the Emperor’s hand was so steady that whatever he aimed his eye at, he would strike with javelin or arrow. Therefore, it is established that throwing had its place in warfare, athletics, and medical gymnastics. We have said that there were two primary instruments for this throwing: the bow and the arrows, which some say were invented by Scythes, son of Jupiter, while others attribute them to Perses <margin>C</margin>, son of Perseus. <margin>Pliny, Book 7, Ch. 56</margin> Now indeed, we have identified many species of arrows: some subtle and slender, which were shot from bows and ballistae <note>large ancient missile launchers</note>, and which we believe were lead-weighted <note>original: *plumbatas*; Roman darts weighted with lead for extra momentum</note>. We are led to this by many authors, especially Pacuvius in his *Paullus*, who speaks thus: "It hails and snows arrows, lead, and stones"; and also by the authority of Aristotle, who wrote in the second book of *On the Heavens* that arrows carried through the air ignite the air itself, and that the heat subsequently melts the lead contained within them. Others are thicker, called javelins <note>original: *iacula*</note> by the Latins and *akontia* <note>original: $\alpha\kappa\acute{o}\nu\tau\iota\alpha$; light throwing spears</note> by the Greeks; Pliny believes their inventor was Aetolus, son of Mars. Still others, thicker and heavier yet, our people call "stakes" <note>original: *palos*</note>.

# ON THE ART OF GYMNASTICS
## BOOK THREE
### *On what is to be done, and on the method of the present treatment. Chapter 1.*

---

<note>A large decorative woodcut historiated initial 'M' depicts a landscape with a river, classical buildings in the distance, and a seated figure. This style of initial was common in 16th-century printing to signal the start of a major new section of text.</note>

<margin>E</margin>
**W**e described many types of exercises used by the ancients in the previous book with all the clarity we could; many still remain that are perhaps no less worthy of being known than those. Although the greater part of these were not primarily performed in the gymnasiums, nor did they belong to the <term>saltatoria</term> <note>original: "saltatoriam"; the art of dance or rhythmic movement</note>, or the <term>palaestrica</term> <note>original: "palaestricam"; the art of wrestling and physical combat practiced in the palaestra</note>—into which two categories we seemed to divide the whole of gymnastics in the previous book—we nevertheless deemed it necessary that they all be treated. We do this because even if they are not called "exercises" in the strictest sense, they certainly deserve the name in common usage, and therefore should by no means be excluded from the study of gymnastics. Furthermore, all physicians admit that these same activities contribute to a good <term>bodily constitution</term> <note>original: "habitum corporis"; the general state of health, muscle tone, and physical fitness</note> and to health. Since our study is primarily concerned with passing down all those bodily exercises which are judged to both aid health and produce the best bodily constitution, and since we have decided to consider gymnastics in each of these categories, it would be against the proper order and against our original plan to leave even one thing untreated. Nor indeed should it be held against us as a fault that, while intending to speak only of <term>medical gymnastics</term> <note>original: "medicinae gymnastica"; exercise prescribed for health and longevity rather than competition or war</note>, we have mixed in many things concerning <term>athletics</term> <note>original: "athletica"; training for professional competition and public games</note> and very many things concerning <term>warfare</term> <note>original: "bellica"; military drills and combat training</note>, and will continue to do so in the following sections. This is because our first and foremost plan was to speak of medical gymnastics; but afterwards, 

<margin>F</margin>
we added the rest for three reasons. First, so that by briefly knowing the conditions of the other two branches, the entire nature of that third branch—medical gymnastics—would be more clearly understood. Second, so that those things which were delivered confusedly regarding each branch together, or at least indistinctly, by both Greek and Latin authors, could be perfectly distinguished by our classifications, leaving the readers no occasion for error. Third, because the same exercises are found to be used by athletes, by those studious of military service, and finally by the professors of health. If we had spoken only of medical gymnastics, it would almost necessarily have followed that readers would believe either that this branch alone existed, or at least that the other types took their rules and origin from this one alone. How many errors this would have produced in reading authors...

<margin>A</margin>
...it shines forth, and no one even moderately well-versed in the liberal arts can fail to see this. Furthermore, if anyone chooses to compare what we have written about *medical gymnastics*, and what we shall say more fully in the following pages, with those things said by us regarding the other two types of gymnastics, they will certainly recognize that those others held only the smallest part. Therefore, it can never be rightly denied that we clearly intended to treat the art of gymnastics as it is subject to medicine, and not any other. For this is the gymnastics which, although it seems to devote its effort solely to the care of the body, nevertheless manages the exercise of both the body and the soul together, as *Plato* advised in the *Timaeus*. It does not allow the body, through sheer strength and thickness, to become insolently ferocious; rather, it subjects the body to the motions of the mind to be tamed, corrected, and directed according to reason. <margin>B</margin> *Galen* often proclaimed that <term>athletic training</term> <note>original: "athleticam"; Mercuriale distinguishes between healthy medical gymnastics and the extreme, often harmful training of professional athletes.</note> failed to achieve this, and for that reason, it was most strongly condemned and ignominiously exploded by all well-ordered republics. For this reason, we should be rightly excused if we have spoken more about it than someone might judge fitting; we did so so that its nature might be "estimated from the claw" (as the saying goes) <note>original: "ex ungue... aestimata"; a Latin proverb similar to "judging the lion by its claw," meaning to understand the whole from a small part.</note>, allowing one to recognize the depravity of athletic habits in both exercise and in living and social conduct, and having recognized it, to detest and avoid it.

### On walking. Chapter II.

<margin>C</margin>
<margin>3. *On the Use of the Parts*</margin> <note>original: "3. de usu partium"; a reference to Galen’s anatomical work *De usu partium corporis humani*.</note>
<note>A large historiated woodcut initial letter Q, featuring a seated figure in classical robes surrounded by foliage. This ornamental letter marks the beginning of the chapter on walking.</note>
**H**ow much benefit <term>walking</term> <note>original: "deambulatio"</note> provides to this human life, most wise Nature has shown clearly enough. By a certain wonderful craftsmanship and a singular, almost divine providence, she fashioned feet for us for no other reason than that we might be able to walk, and while walking, to perform those actions for which we were born. When that famous pirate near Coracesium in Pamphylia <note>A coastal city in ancient Asia Minor.</note> noticed this, he used to cut off the feet of the men who fell into his hands—as *Galen* records as a memorable example of cruelty—so that they could no longer walk or fully and honorably perform the other duties of life. Therefore, everyone sees with what great zeal walking—which either Nature or God granted us as necessary and especially beneficial—must be preserved and assisted. This is especially true because, if any bodily exercises are found that can preserve health, drive away the weakness contracted from disease, and provide a good <term>bodily constitution</term> <note>original: "habitum"; referring to the overall physical state or "habit" of the body.</note>, and which are in frequent use among all men and all nations, walking is surely the one.

<margin>B</margin> **for the sake of health** <note>original: "sanitatis gratia"</note>; they performed it in such a way that they were necessarily compelled to have various locations according to the changes of the seasons, so they might complete their walks without injury to their well-being. **Pliny** (Book 36, Chapter 12) reports that **Sostratus of Cnidus**, a most celebrated architect, was the first of all to build a "hanging" (elevated) walkway at Cnidus. We ought to believe that athletes never used these walkways, based on the fact that one never reads of them contending by walking in the games, nor in amphitheatres, nor in sacred contests—all of which they served. ...reason identifies many species of walking, derived partly from its nature, partly from the location, and partly from its purpose. Regarding its nature, since Galen <margin>3. On the Use of the Parts.</margin> <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the most influential physician and medical researcher of the Roman Empire.</note> defined walking as consisting of the motion and rest of the legs, that motion—and consequently the walk—was either large or small, fast or slow, or intense or relaxed. Regarding the location, the types of walking varied similarly: sometimes they took place in the city or in gymnasiums, and sometimes outside the city, as Phaedrus and Prodicus did in the works of Plato, as well as Ischomachus in Xenophon. <margin>In the Oeconomicus.</margin> <note>Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus* is a Socratic dialogue about household management and agriculture.</note> Ischomachus, while following his servant who led his horse into the field on foot, said he was engaging in better exercise than if he had walked in a **covered portico** <note>original: "xysto" — a xystus was a shaded colonnade where athletes exercised in winter.</note>. Sometimes walking occurred on level ground, sometimes on rough or sandy ground (which Asclepiades, Erasistratus, and Themison <margin>Caelius Aurelianus, Chronic Diseases, Book 2, Chapter 3; and the book *On Procatarctic Causes*.</margin> wrongly recommended for those suffering from paralysis), sometimes on even ground and sometimes uneven, sometimes long and sometimes short. Aristotle discussed all of these most copiously in the fifth part of his *Problems*.

Finally, walks were categorized by their purpose: namely, when they were used as aids to health and a good physical condition, or when they were performed for the recreation of the body. For after people had completed more strenuous exercises, they would employ a few more relaxed walks so that the transition to rest would not happen too suddenly—moving from one extreme to its opposite. They also did this after taking medicines or vomiting; they called this entire restorative class of exercise **apotherapia** <note>original: "ἀποθεραπείαν" — a Greek term for a "cool-down" or post-exercise therapy intended to restore the body to its natural state.</note>. The trainers of gymnasts also sometimes used this "cool-down" in the midst of labors, especially for those who had undergone what were called the "heavy exercises," <margin>3. On the Preservation of Health, Chapter 2.</margin> which Galen judged to be highly praiseworthy. According to Varro, as Nonius recalls, some even used walking to stir up a thirst. For in the Maenian law <note>A reference to ancient Roman sumptuary or conduct laws.</note> it was written: *"I practiced by walking, so that my throat might come to dinner more capable of thirst."*

### Whether Standing Upright is an Exercise. Chapter III.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' (used as U) set within a square frame featuring floral scrollwork.</note>

**T**hose who have only lightly examined the nature of things have judged that nothing is more unlike walking and motion than standing upright on one's feet. However, those searching more deeply come to the opinion that those standing upright on their feet, even if they do not walk, are moving in some fashion; therefore, this type of standing should by no means be excluded from the category of exercises. I have decided to speak on this matter for this reason, especially because many people, led by false reasoning, have soaked this opinion into their minds so thoroughly that they stubbornly believe that those standing on their feet are in no way...

<margin>A</margin> From this point, they engage in exercise, proving their opinion in this manner: namely, that it is found defined among all authors that exercise exists as motion, to which motion "standing" is clearly the opposite state. This is what Plato proclaims everywhere—especially <margin>In the *Sophist*.</margin> <note>In the *Sophist* (254d), Plato identifies Motion and Rest as two of the "Greatest Kinds" of being, treating them as fundamental opposites.</note> where he places "rest" and "motion" as two opposites among the first principles of things. However, it is easily proven that those who think this way are clearly hallucinating; for even if all those who stand upright on their feet do not seem to move in any perceptible way, reason itself most certainly persuades us that they move in some fashion. For it was also the opinion of many of the ancients that it is not only those things that *seem* to move that are in motion, but that many things appear immobile while occupying one and the same place, which are nevertheless demonstrated to be moving by most effective reasoning, and almost by the evidence of the senses themselves. For birds are thought to be in motion <margin>B</margin> not so much when they fly now up, now down, but while they occupy one place in the air almost immobily. This is proven thus: because if a bird that seemed to stand immobily in the air should die at that very instant, it immediately falls to the earth. 

This is seen in that "footless" bird, the **Manucodiata**, <note>The *Manucodiata* or Bird of Paradise was long believed by Europeans to have no feet and to live its entire life floating in the air, only falling to earth when it died. This was a common myth in 16th-century natural history.</note> which they say is never seen on the ground except when dead, and always remains in the air while alive. This happens for no other reason than because that body was sustained on high by the help of some <term>motion</term> <note>original: "motus" — here referring to the internal vital force or muscular effort required to maintain posture.</note> created by the soul within the body. Once the body is deprived of this motion and left to its own nature, it sinks toward the center <note>The "center" refers to the center of the Earth, which in Aristotelian physics is the natural place for heavy elements.</note>; just as while it is sustained upward against its natural inclination, it by no means falls, nor does it rest perfectly, but is agitated, as it were, by two contrary motions: one of the body being driven downward by nature, the other of the soul moving the body upward against nature. Almost the same thing happens in men standing upright, in whose <margin>C</margin> bodies—as nature inclines them toward the earth and the soul strives to sustain them upward against it—a certain motion arises that is imperceptible to the senses. 

The evidence for this is that if the soul should leave a body standing upright, it immediately collapses to the ground, because that motion fails—the very benefit by which the soul held the body, naturally inclined toward the earth, elevated on high. By these reasons, anyone should be entirely persuaded that those who stand upright on their feet move in some fashion due to the continuous and contrary struggles of the soul and the body. Furthermore, all their **muscles** carrying the body, lifting it from the earth, and erecting it, are intensely tensed. By the merit of this tension and also of this hidden motion, it later results that standing produces greater labor and more troublesome <term>fatigue</term> <note>original: "lassitudinem" — a specific medical term for the weariness caused by physical exertion.</note> than walking, as was most excellently recorded in the writings of Galen. <margin>Book *On Tremor and Rigidity*.</margin> <note>Galen's *De tremore, palpitatione, convulsione et rigore* explores the physiological causes of involuntary movements and the strain of maintaining posture.</note> Nor should Plato, where he places "rest" among the principles of things as if it were the opposite of 
->motion<-

<meta>This page continues the argument from page 137, transitioning from the theoretical definition of "motion" to practical medical and historical examples of how standing upright functions as a form of physical exertion.</meta>

# BOOK #

<margin>D</margin>
When [Plato] placed rest as the opposite to motion, he spoke quite truly; however, Aristotle, in the fifth book of his *Physics* <note>original: *Physicorum*; Aristotle’s *Physics* is a foundational text of natural philosophy where he explores the nature of change and movement.</note>, argued at length that it is not a state of rest that is contrary to motion, but rather another motion that is its true opposite. Unless, perhaps, one might say that Plato understood another "mystical" kind of motion and rest (as is his habit), since he asserts that even divine natures consist of these principles. Therefore, if it is sufficiently proven by so many arguments that those standing upright are moved in some way and occasionally exert themselves significantly, it seems appropriate that standing should not be removed from the category of exercises simply because exercise is defined as motion and standing itself might seem to hardly deserve the name of motion. On the contrary, just as many movements judged to contribute to health and a good physical condition are commonly shown by us above to be exercises (even if they are not "exercises" in the strictest sense), similarly, we judge that standing upright is an exercise according to common understanding.

<margin>E</margin>
Hence the most wise Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" (c. 460 – c. 370 BCE).</note>, who elsewhere proclaimed that ulcers require rest to be cured, wrote that standing and sitting are harmful to them. It is as if he wished to suggest that while the body is held upright—either by sitting or standing—the muscles are greatly strained, and a certain "motion" is generated between the soul and the nature of the body which does not allow the ulcers to knit together into a scar. And this, I believe, is why standing is called an "exercise" by Caelius <note>Caelius Aurelianus, a Roman physician of the 5th century CE, known for his work on chronic and acute diseases.</note> in the treatment of <term>Epilepsy</term> <note>Then known as the "falling sickness."</note>. Whether the ancient gymnastics masters accepted this kind of standing among other bodily exercises, I dare not affirm with any certainty. For the <term>athletes</term> <note>In antiquity, "athletes" specifically referred to professional competitors in the public games.</note> had almost no use for standing, except when the imitators of Milo <note>Milo of Croton, a legendary wrestler of the 6th century BCE known for his incredible feats of strength.</note> would present themselves standing upright to be pushed from their place by others as a display of strength, or used the position not for its own sake, but for another purpose; therefore, it seems unlikely to me that they exercised themselves in this specific way.

<margin>F</margin>
For what contest, I ask, could be seen or achieved in standing alone that would bring delight to spectators, or serve sacrifices, or be useful in the amphitheatres or stadiums, such that we might say athletes were accustomed to exercise or compete while standing still for the sake of these things? However, those who watched the athletes competing did stand, but for no other reason than that those wooden amphitheatres might hold a greater multitude of people. Indeed, in ancient times, everyone brought their own <term>benches</term> <note>original: *subsellia*; small portable seats or stools.</note> with them, which they used to watch comfortably and without annoyance, and sometimes even used as weapons while they fought for a spot. This custom first grew during the consulship of Marcus Messalla and Cassius, until soon, during the censorship of Publius Scipio Nasica, it was provided by a <term>Decree of the Senate</term> <note>original: *S. C.* or *Senatus Consultum*.</note> that no one in the city, or within a thousand paces of it, should be allowed to set up benches or sit to watch the games. Furthermore, it is handed down that it was cautioned by law for the ancient Romans that they should stand upright when worshipping, and should sacrifice to Jupiter while standing, just as...

### BOOK THREE ###
<meta>Catchword: [distribu-]tion</meta>

<margin>A</margin> When Valerius Martial <note>A Roman poet (c. 38–104 AD) known for his epigrams.</note> writes of a certain man:
> While he greets Jupiter with many prayers,
> Standing bent backward on the very tips of his toes.
->Aethon,<-

I believe this practice hardly pertained to athletes who were accustomed to playing in sacred contests or celebrating sacrifices. Rather, I hold it as certain that it was practiced for a deeper and more sensible reason: namely, so that they would not be overcome by sleep (which often happens to those engaged in intense contemplation) while sitting or lying down during worship. Instead, they could persevere in their prayers more attentively and vigilantly for a longer time. We might also say that the ancients did this equally to show greater reverence to the gods themselves. For many such things were regarded as signs of greater respect by our ancestors, which are seen differently today; for instance, sacrificing with the head covered was considered a sign of the highest reverence,

<margin>B</margin> as Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and historian (c. 46–119 AD).</note> left written in his *Roman Questions* <note>original: *Romanis probl.*; Plutarch's *Quaestiones Romanae* explores the origins of Roman customs.</note>, and as that character Curculio suggests in Plautus <note>A Roman playwright (c. 254–184 BC) known for comedies.</note> when he says: "Who is this who greets Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine and healing.</note> with a covered head?"—since he always walked with his head bare. In the same way, they regarded standing upright to pray as the greatest demonstration of honor, just as we regard kneeling. Nevertheless, Pythagoras <note>A famous Greek philosopher and mathematician.</note>, or according to Plutarch, Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome.</note>, wished for prayers to be made while sitting, so that the vows might be signified as fixed and firm. Therefore, the fact that they sacrificed while standing is by no means evidence that athletes were accustomed to using that posture in sacrifices. Similarly, it seems very reasonable to me that lovers of military

<margin>C</margin> discipline could have gained little utility from standing for the purpose of training in that field. Indeed, except for the quality of endurance—which is certainly necessary for soldiers—I do not see how a standing posture can either produce or assist any other military virtue. Furthermore, neither Plato, nor Xenophon, nor Aristotle, nor Vegetius <note>Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus, author of the influential Roman military manual *De Re Militari*.</note> commanded future warriors to exercise themselves by standing still; although we have heard it said that Flavius Vespasian <note>Roman Emperor (r. 69–79 AD).</note> the elder used to say that an Emperor ought to die standing. <note>original: *Imperatorem stantem mori oportere*.</note> However, I would never deny that the gymnastic physicians <note>term: *gymnastas* — experts who used physical exercise for medical treatment, distinct from athletic coaches.</note> sometimes exercised both the healthy and the sick by standing, since I see that it has many uses both for maintaining health and for providing strength to the legs. For while all the muscles are stretched, and the soul works in opposition to the body, both are made stronger; meanwhile, the humors <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed to govern health.</note> and wastes are more promptly carried to the lower channels, and food is more properly settled in the bottom of the stomach, where perfect digestion <note>original: *concoctio*; the process by which food is "cooked" or transformed by bodily heat into nutrients.</note> is completed. From this, I gather that this one form of exercise...

# BOOK THREE #

This seems to be confirmed by that common and not entirely absurd opinion: "stand after lunch, walk after dinner." <note>original: "a prandio standum a cena ambulandum"</note> However, I do not wish to overlook a distinction in this place: whether one stands upright under the sun (which Galen calls <term>sun-therapy</term> <note>original Greek: ἡλιωθεραπεῖσθαι; the practice of sunbathing for health</note>) or in the shade. Those in the shade undergo no other physical change except that which we have shown to arise from the posture itself. But those who persist in standing under the sun are changed considerably by the heat of the sun, in addition to the effects already mentioned. <margin>Part 5, Problem 34.</margin> For Aristotle wrote that such people grow even more intensely hot than those who are moving, because they lack that cooling of the air which everyone experiences daily through the effort of movement; not to mention the physicians, by whom it is believed that fevers are generated from standing under the sun in this manner. <margin>Letters, books 3 and 6.</margin> For this reason, I am often quite amazed by what Pliny Caecilius <note>Pliny the Younger (61–113 AD), a Roman lawyer and author.</note> recorded: that his uncle, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), the famous naturalist.</note>—who was otherwise most diligent in his way of life—often used to lie in the sun (which I interpret as "stand") in the summer if he had any leisure, after a meal which he took lightly and easily during the day according to the ancient custom. He even made use of the sun and drank cold water shortly before he perished from the eruption of Mount Vesuvius. Furthermore, it should not be ignored that standing upright, just like other exercises, is also beneficial before a meal. Our opinion, that the ancients were accustomed to stand after meals, should be interpreted to mean that this specific exercise was practiced *more frequently* after dining, not that it was never used before food. Indeed, anyone can easily recognize that those who are not at all fit for undertaking other exercises—whether they are healthy or infirm—can exercise themselves by standing in place of other activities, if not equally well, then at least slightly less effectively for the preservation of health. One may use a long period of standing before meals as a substitute for a light walk, provided that the other conditions which we will demonstrate below are observed.

<margin>A</margin> ...[athletes] might pursue the crowns of victory in contests and spectacles, delighting the people; or that they might acquire and preserve the best physical condition and health itself. I believe these men were called <term>combatants</term> <note>original Greek: μαχητὰς (machētās)</note> in Eusebius (*Church History*, book 8, chapter 18), so those who translated "pugiles" <note>boxers or fighters</note> in that passage were ineptly mistaken. As for how this exercise was practiced, since anyone can sufficiently conjecture for themselves, I will by no means dwell on explaining it. I only wish not to omit that, according to Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical writer and physician to Emperor Julian.</note>, there were two types of fighting in medical gymnastics: one always with weapons, and the other mostly without weapons, which the Greeks called <term>shadow-fighting</term> <note>original Greek: σκιαμαχίαν (skiamachian)</note> and our writers call "shadowy combat." The combat with weapons was performed when individuals competed against each other with wooden weapons, or those that strike and stab, from which it anciently derived the name <term>single combat</term> <note>original Greek: μονομαχίας (monomachias)</note>. It was also categorized as, and

<margin>B</margin> <margin>S. Chro. Pa. last chapter</margin> called <term>armed fighting</term> <note>original: hoplomachia</note>—that is, a feigned clashing of weapons—by Caelius Aurelianus, and was praised for reducing <term>excessive flesh</term> <note>original Greek: πολυσαρκίαν (polysarkian), referring to obesity or a heavy build</note>. But shadow-fighting occurred when a man fought against a shadow with both arms and legs. Besides Plato—who in his *Apology* and elsewhere spoke of <term>shadow-fighting</term> <note>original Greek: σκιαμαχεῖν (skiamachein)</note> regarding those who fight without an opponent—Oribasius is our authority. He records, from the opinion of Antyllus, that those training in this way were accustomed not only to fight a shadow with hands and legs, but even against a column, or against a post—which Juvenal <margin>Satire 6</margin> mentioned—or a wall. Sometimes, the boxers would also imitate the movements on the tips of their feet, at times as if jumping, at times as if retreating. I believe the ancients used this primarily when a partner or opponent was missing, or when the person to be exercised was so delicate that they could not suffer the slightest harm, which often happens to those who compete against another with any kind of weapons.

<margin>C</margin> <margin>Laws, Book 7</margin> For Plato seems to have first hinted at this where he said:
> "And furthermore, if we were lacking all things, both living and inanimate, so that for want of fellow gymnasts we should even dare to truly shadow-fight against ourselves." <note>original Greek: καὶ ἔτι πάντων, τῶν τε ἐμψύχων, καὶ τῶν ἀψύχων ἀπορήσαντες ὥστε, ἐρημίᾳ συγγυμνασῶν, ἆρ' ἄγε οὐκ ἐτολμήσαμεν αὐτοὶ πρὸς ἡμᾶς αὐτοὺς ὄντως σκιαμαχεῖν</note>

This means: If we lack all animate and inanimate things, shall we not dare to truly compete in a shadowy fight against ourselves because of the scarcity of those to exercise with us? And after him, Plutarch in the 7th book of his <margin>Table Talk, Problem 10</margin> *Table Talk*:
> "But I see," he said, "that you who are present are already prepared to shadow-fight against phantoms." <note>original Greek: ἀλλ' ὁρῶ, εἶπεν, ὑμᾶς οἰκεῖοντας ἤδη σκιαμαχεῖν πρὸς τὰ εἴδωλα</note>

Nor should anyone wonder that I claim the ancients fought with shadows (as if it were a ridiculous thing), since even in these times not a few are found who, for the sake of exercise, compete by themselves against the air with fists, arms, and weapons, either when an opponent is absent or when they prefer to be seen by no one. Speaking of this, the Apostle Paul said:
> "I box in this way, not as one beating the air." <note>original Greek: οὕτω πυκτεύω, ὡς οὐκ ἀέρα δέρων</note>

Therefore, these were the two species of combat that our ancestors are found to have used as a form of exercise: so much so, that no system of <term>gymnastics</term> <note>The ancient art of physical training for health and competition.</note> existed that did not include this among other exercises. As for the fact that <term>athletics</term> <note>original: athletica</note> in the most ancient times employed combat with weapons during training, we have a most wealthy witness in <margin>2. Probable</margin> Plutarch, who left written in the fifth book of his *Symposiacs* that anciently, <term>single combat</term> <note>original Greek: μονομαχία (monomachia)</note>—that is, a duel—was customary in the city of Pisa and in Elis, a region of the Peloponnese near the Alpheus river. Around that area every fifth year—that is, as the commentator on Pindar testifies, in alternating <term>Olympiads</term> <note>The four-year cycles between Olympic Games.</note>, or every forty-eight or fifty months—the Olympic games sacred to Jupiter were celebrated, and these combats used to proceed until the death and the cutting of the throats of those who were conquered and fell. <margin>D</margin>

Furthermore, Galen relates that the priests in Pergamum retained an ancient custom of practicing so-called "single combats" during the summer. Lest anyone believe these were unique only to the Greek nation, one should consult Athenaeus, who, in the fourth book of the *Deipnosophistae*, reports on the authority of Nicolaus of Damascus, the Peripatetic philosopher, that the Romans employed spectacles of <term>single combatants</term> <note>original: monomachorum</note> not only at festivals and in amphitheatres, but even at banquets, having borrowed the custom from the <term>Tyrrhenians</term> <note>Another name for the Etruscans.</note>; although the Romans preferred to call all of these men <term>gladiators</term> rather than single combatants. Pliny writes that these men fought most recently in the Forum during the age of Julius Caesar, and that Nero watched them fighting through an <term>emerald</term> <note>original: Smaragdo; Pliny the Elder famously recorded that Nero watched gladiatorial matches through a large cut emerald, perhaps to reduce glare or as a corrective lens.</note>. <margin>E</margin> <margin>Book 15, ch. 18 & Book 37, ch. 5</margin> Since these men practiced an art full of many absurdities, I shall briefly set forth a few things about them so they may be clearly distinguished from other exercises of combatants.

For first, they held to a clearly detestable practice: those competing strove to strike one another as severely as they could. And they did not only suffer bruises during their struggles (as written by Scribonius Largus, who practiced medicine in Rome during the age of Tiberius Caesar and Messalina), but often the contest was extended until the death of one, or even both, of the combatants. <margin>F</margin> <margin>3. On the Composition of Medicines, ch. 3</margin> As, besides Athenaeus and Plutarch, Galen also testifies; he writes that he treated severely wounded gladiators and, for that reason, was chosen by the high priest of his city to be their physician. Indeed, Gellius is the authority that for a gladiator matched for a fight, this lot was proposed: either to kill if he took the initiative, or to die if he yielded. Thus we ought to believe what Marcus Tullius Cicero recorded in the second book of his *Tusculan Disputations*: that even when athletes were consumed by wounds, they were accustomed to send word to their masters to ask what they wished; if their masters were satisfied with their performance, they were willing to "lie down" <note>A technical term for a gladiator accepting the death blow with dignity.</note>. **A** They faced death and wounds so fearlessly that they neither groaned nor significantly changed their expression. When the most excellent Emperor Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (r. 161–180 AD), known for his Stoic philosophy and attempts to reform the cruelty of the games.</note> could no longer bear to watch such wicked slaughter of men with his own eyes, Cassius Dio relates that he issued an edict. This decree mandated that gladiators should not fight with sharpened steel, but with blunted and rounded swords—much like those who devote themselves to learning the art of fencing do today. A second kind of shame by which this profession of <term>monomachia</term> <note>original: monomachiae; from the Greek for "single combat."</note> was marked concerned their diet. Indeed, Pliny recorded that gladiators were called "barley-eaters" <note>original: hordearios</note> because in ancient times they lived on barley, just as Galen wrote after Pliny that they were accustomed to eating beans and <term>tisane</term> <note>original: ptisana; a medicinal porridge or gruel made from crushed grain, usually barley.</note>. A third abominable practice of the gladiators was to drink the blood from an opponent's wound during the contest itself, as if it would effectively grant them strength and courage. Furthermore, Pliny reports that after a fight, they would drink ashes as a form of medicine.

**B** Therefore, regarding these men, the following was very famously declaimed by Saint Cyprian <note>Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an early Christian bishop and martyr who wrote extensively on the morality of Roman culture.</note>:
> A gladiatorial game is prepared, so that blood may satisfy the lust of cruel eyes. The body is filled with juices through stronger foods, and the robust mass of the limbs grows fat with muscles destined for ruin, so that, having been fattened for punishment, it may perish at a higher price. A human is killed for the pleasure of a human; and that one might be able to kill is considered a skill, a practice, an art. Crime is not only committed, it is taught. What could be said that is more inhuman, what more bitter? It is a discipline that one might be able to destroy, and it is a glory that he has destroyed. What of this, I ask you: what kind of thing is it where men whom no one has condemned throw themselves to wild beasts? In the flower of their youth, of handsome enough form and dressed in precious clothing, while still living they are adorned for a voluntary funeral; the wretches boast of their own evils. They fight beasts not because of a crime, but out of madness. Fathers watch their own sons. A brother is in the arena, and a sister is nearby; and although a more lavish display of the games may increase the price of the spectacle, it is so that a mother might be present at her own sorrows. In these impious spectacles, alas, a mother even pays for her place, and they do not consider themselves to be parricides <note>A term for one who kills a near relative; here used metaphorically for parents who "kill" their children by watching and funding their deaths.</note> with their own eyes.

**C** Thus far the words of that Christian man, whose speech I have chosen to transcribe here because nothing more brilliant could be found to show the wickedness of gladiatorial exercise. Yet, it occurs to me that something even more shameful than that wickedness is this: both during the time of the Republic's liberty and under the Emperors, there were few—whether nobles or commoners, consuls or emperors—who did not watch such inhuman spectacles, full of every disgrace and cruelty, willingly and with the greatest pleasure. However, I am quite uncertain whether men of every class practiced the gladiatorial art, or only the most low-born. <margin>Book 1, on military matters.</margin> **A** Those competing think they have defeated their adversaries themselves. In addition to these points, it has been abundantly demonstrated by both Plato and Aristotle that martial gymnastics was by no means lacking in exercises for both types of armed combat. Aristotle, in his books on Politics, showed certain women **B** participating in this exercise, and perhaps perfected it in those writings which all learned men know are now lost to us. However, it is credible that while they were learning these skills, wooden weapons <note>original: "rudia tela"; blunt or wooden practice swords, from which the term "rudius" (the wooden sword given to a retiring gladiator) is derived.</note> were mostly put to use. No one who has observed the teachers of these arts in our own times would deny that such contests provided the greatest utility for military skill, since Plato similarly valued them so highly that he preferred them over other types of exercises for both offense and defense, and wished for both women and men to work hard at them. I am inclined to believe that this military single-combat <note>original: "monomachiam"</note> performed with blunt weapons was the very thing that Hermippus writes the Mantineans invented and the Cyreneans emulated. Likewise, I believe that what the common people call <term>skirmishing</term> <note>original: "scrimiam"; an early term for the art of fencing or swordplay.</note> is this very thing, and not merely "shadow-fighting" <note>original: "umbratilem pugnam"; a simulated or "shadowy" practice without a real opponent.</note> as Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a leading French humanist scholar.</note> in his *Commentary on the Pandects*, Guillaume du Choul, and several others have falsely **C** claimed. It is this, in my opinion, that Plato seems to have spoken of when he wrote in the *Laches* that it is profitable for youths to learn to fight with arms, since a robust physical condition is acquired this way, and no other exercise is inferior to this or less laborious. In this practice, the competitors did not strike one another to the death as the gladiators did, but by using blunt weapons as if pretending to attack one another, and sometimes even truly striking, they learned both how to inflict and how to parry blows. Sometimes, however, they also fought with shadows while armed, which Posidonius records the Celts were accustomed to do after dinner. Yet most frequently of all, those who desired to acquire military discipline practiced fighting against the stake. ...just as against an adversary with a shield, and a club used as a sword, each man would **D** exercise himself—now as if seeking the head or the face, now threatening the sides, occasionally striving to strike the hamstrings and legs, retreating, lunging, leaping—and just as if an opponent were present, he would test the stake with all his might and every art of war. How medical gymnastics <note>original: "medicinae gymnastica"</note> adopted this type of exercise will be easily recognized by anyone who has weighed the discourse of Antyllus <note>Antyllus was a renowned Greek surgeon of the 2nd century AD.</note> found in the works of Oribasius. <margin>Book 6 of the Collections.</margin> He writes that the ancient Greeks by no means used armed combat for the sake of the infirm, but only to make soldiers more ready for war. He adds that the Romans were the first to discover that it could be practiced for the sake of health; it is likely they first practiced this in any suitable location with wooden weapons <note>original: "rudibus telis"; blunt or wooden practice tools used to prevent injury.</note> and then brought it into the gymnasiums. This is supported by Galen, who, among other duties of the physical trainer, lists weapon exercise as being conducive to a **E** good bodily constitution. For Galen showed clearly enough that practitioners of gymnastics used both armed combat and shadow-fighting <note>original: "sciomachiam"; literally "fighting with shadows," a form of solo sparring.</note> with health as the goal. <margin>On the Preservation of Health, Book 2, chapters 11 & 12.</margin> In that work, he recommended shadow-fighting to exercise the arms and legs, and he handed down that "hoplomachia" <note>original: "hoplomachiam"; training in heavy-armed combat.</note>, which was invented by Dameas, contributes to the excellent condition of many parts of the body. That the exercise they performed with weapons was called *hoplomachia* is attested not only by the logic of the name itself, but Galen also left testimony of it. Furthermore, Caelius Aurelianus demonstrated this (as we showed a little earlier), as did <margin>Book 8 [of the Epigrams].</margin> Martial, who criticized a certain doctor for practicing hoplomachia poorly—or rather, for striking his adversary severely and particularly in the eyes—with these verses:

> *Now you are a gladiator, though you were an eye-doctor before;*
> *You have done as a doctor what you now do as a gladiator.* **F**
<note>original: "Hoplomachus nunc es, fueras ophtalmicus ante / Fecisti medicus, quod facis hoplomachus." Martial’s epigram (8.74) is a dark joke: the doctor was so bad at healing eyes that he blinded or killed his patients, just as he does now as a fighter.</note>

Therefore, from all these things it may be clear to anyone that both types of armed combat, as well as shadow-fighting, had a place in every branch of gymnastics. Now let us pass on to the other exercises of the ancients that remain to be described.

->K ij<-

<margin>A</margin> <term>To exercise the hands: *cheirizesthai*</term>, <term>to move across the field: *ekplethrizein*</term>, and <term>to move rapidly: *pytilizein*</term> mean, specifically, to climb up by a rope, to struggle with the hands, and to perform the specific rhythmic movements known as *plethriffare* and *pytilissare*. <note>These Greek terms refer to specific repetitive training drills; *ekplethrizein* involves covering a set distance (a *plethron*, roughly 100 feet), while *pytilizein* refers to rapid, fluttering motions of the hands or limbs.</note> How they used to exercise themselves by climbing up ropes can be understood without much effort from the description seen on the engraved gems of the ancients. From this, one correctly concludes that Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician whose work formed the basis of Western medicine for centuries.</note> rightly categorized similar exercises among the "vigorous" or "intense" types. For the ancients also employed <term>rope-walkers: *funambuli*</term>—called *schoenobatae* <note>From the Greek *schoinos* (rope) and *bates* (treader).</note> by Martial in his third Satire—who even now wander the world for the sake of profit. That the ancients used them to entertain the populace is recognized not only from the aforementioned imagery, but is also confirmed by this very rich testimony from Terence in his play *The Mother-in-Law*: "The people, stunned by their own enthusiasm, had their minds entirely occupied by the rope-walker." <note>original Latin: *Ita populus studio stupidus in funambulo animum occuparat.*</note>

Not entirely unlike the rope-walkers was a type of game found in the writings of Hesychius and Pollux called the <term>*skaparda*: *σκαπάρδα*</term>. <margin>B</margin> In this game, a beam was fixed upright in the ground with a hole at the very top, through which a rope was passed. One person was tied or looped into one side of the rope with their back turned, while the other person pulled from the other side. If the puller managed to drag his companion all the way to the top, he was immediately declared the winner; however, if the other resisted and could not be pulled up at all, the victory was judged to be his.

### THIRD [BOOK] ###

K iij

<margin>A</margin> There have been some who thought that <term>finger-wrestling</term> <note>original: <term>ἀκροχειρίζεσθαι</term> (akrocheirizesthai)</note> was a specific part of wrestling, in which the wrestlers tested their strength by interlocking only the tips of their fingers. However, Galen <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician.</note> alone proves that they are mistaken, for in his second book of *On Preserving Health*, chapter 8, he immediately distinguishes wrestling from <term>finger-sparring</term> <note>original: <term>acrochirismo</term></note>. This exercise was, therefore, a kind of skirmish performed with only the extremities of the hands, in which no other part of the body was touched by the fingers, continuing until the opponent gave out. Athletes very rarely competed in this during public spectacles, though they occasionally revived its use. Indeed, we read in Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer.</note> that a man named Sostratus, a practitioner of the <term>pancratium</term> <note>An ancient "all-powers" martial art combining wrestling and boxing.</note>, achieved the highest praise in this kind of contest. Because of this, he was nicknamed the <term>Finger-Crusher</term> <note>original: <term>ἀκροχειριστὴν</term> (akrocheiristen)</note> as a mark of excellence, for he would grip the very tips of his opponents' hands so powerfully that he would not let them go until he realized they were overcome with pain from their fingers being crushed. Those who watched over military glory were also accustomed to <term>finger-sparring</term> from time to time, as they persuaded themselves that both their arms would be made stronger and more agile by such means. Posidonius <note>A Stoic philosopher and polymath.</note> reports of the Celts that, being trained in arms, they competed among themselves in this finger-sparring. Furthermore, both Galen and Paul of Aegina <note>A 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician.</note> agree that those concerned with health devoted themselves to this exercise, following Hippocrates (or perhaps Polybus), who recommended finger-sparring for various bodily ailments in his books *On Diet*.

<margin>Pausanias, Book 6, *Elis*.</margin>
<margin>Galen, *On Preserving Health*, book 2. Avicenna, book 1, fen 3, doctrine 2, chapter 2.</margin>

As for what <term>shuttle-walking</term> <note>original: <term>τὸ ἐκπλεθρίζειν</term> (to ekplethrizein)</note> was, both Galen and Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (980–1037 AD), whose medical works were standard in European universities.</note>—the most learned of all the Arabs—explained it. Both wrote in clearly the same words that this exercise consisted of running back and forth within a <term>plethron</term> <note>A Greek unit of measure equal to 100 feet, or one-sixth of a stadium.</note>. A person would run forward and backward repeatedly in both directions without turning around, and with each lap, they would shorten the distance slightly until finally they came to a stop in a single step—or, as Avicenna said more clearly, until they stood still in the middle of the finish line.

<margin>In his *Miscellanies*.</margin>

Furthermore, Politianus <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Renaissance humanist scholar.</note> was of the opinion that <term>rhythmic arm-swinging</term> <note>original: <term>πυτιλίζειν</term> (pytilizein)</note> was the same as gesticulating and moving the hands with frequent motion. However, it is easily proved from the discourse of Galen and Avicenna that Politianus—otherwise a most learned man—was "entirely wide of the mark" <note>original: *toto caelo aberrasse*, a Latin idiom meaning to be completely wrong.</note>. By them, this exercise is defined as follows: it is when someone, either walking on their tiptoes or standing still (as Avicenna believes), moves their outstretched hands upward very quickly, one forward and the other backward. They were especially accustomed to using this exercise while standing before a wall, so that if they occasionally lost their balance, they could easily steady themselves by grabbing the wall. Plutarch <note>A Greek biographer and essayist (c. 46–119 AD).</note> may have been speaking of this when he said that Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note> once issued a decree forbidding those exercises performed with the hands raised high, so that no one would become accustomed to being exhausted by the labor.

<margin>In his *Life of Lycurgus*.</margin>

### BOOK THREE ###

<page-num>153</page-num>
->T E R T I V S<-

<margin>A</margin> The muscles of the chest <note>original: "thoracis musculi"</note>, which are located around the ribs, are stretched and contracted to such an extent that the action called expiration cannot be completed. For there are two actions that fulfill the whole process of breathing: namely, inspiration and expiration. Inspiration occurs when air is drawn into the spaces of the breast to temper the heat of the heart and to generate vital spirits. On the other hand, expiration takes place when the "sooty" wastes <note>original: "fuligines," referring to the metabolic byproducts thought to be produced by the heart's "fire"</note> generated in the heart are led out through the hollows of the breast itself. Thus, when the chest and other instruments serving respiration are compressed by the muscles so that neither air can enter nor sooty residues can exit, we say that respiration is intercepted or restrained <note>original: "spiritus cohibitio"</note>. Medical gymnasts especially, as well as athletes, frequently used this restraint as both an exercise and a remedy. Physicians, or those gymnasts trained in medicine, utilized two types of breath restraint.

<margin>B</margin> In the first type, all the muscles of the chest were tensed while those in the diaphragm <note>original: "septo transuerso"</note> and abdomen were relaxed, so that waste materials <note>original: "excrementa"</note> might be more easily pushed downward. In the second type, the abdominal muscles are also tensed, so that the internal organs <note>original: "uiscera"</note> located below the diaphragm might feel the benefit of the exercise. In both types, however, they applied certain bandages <note>original: "fascias"</note> with which they cinched the chest, the ribs, and even the belly to more successfully achieve their goal. Their purpose in this kind of exercise was sometimes to confirm the heat acquired during training (or to strengthen the innate heat itself), sometimes to assist the respiratory organs <note>original: "spiritualia membra"</note>, and sometimes to purge waste from the breast. Indeed, when the spirit <note>the vital pneuma</note> is compressed from all sides during such a restraint, it is forced to retreat into narrow passages; if it is then propelled further and more forcefully, it passes through them entirely, carrying away some of the thinned-out waste.

<margin>C</margin> Furthermore, the more violently the spirit is forced and driven onward, the more it pushes some things and pulls others along. It pushes what it encounters in front of it and attracts what is positioned at its sides, both being driven by the force of the movement itself. Thus, no one who has examined these reasons should wonder that the physician Erysimachus, in Plato's *Symposium* <note>original: "conuiuio"</note>, primarily recommended the restraint of breath to cure Aristophanes’ hiccups. Aristotle later proved at greater length—not only for the reasons mentioned above—that this extinguishes hiccups and also warms the internal parts of the body. Galen asserted the same and confirmed it with a most clear discourse. In this manner, and for these reasons, the restraint of breath was established by the gymnastic masters. I believe they also observed this rule to ensure the practice succeeded better: namely, that they should begin lightly and briefly, and thereafter more vehement-

<margin>Aristotle, *Problems*, section 33.
Galen, *On the Causes of Symptoms*, Book 3.</margin>

### BOOK THREE ###

<page-num>154</page-num>

...they commanded that breathing be held more forcefully and for a longer time with puffed-out cheeks, and finally ordered it to be relaxed. For in this way, according to that Hippocratic precept <note>Referring to the medical teachings of Hippocrates of Kos</note> that all things should be done **gradually** <note>original Greek: "ἐκ προσαγωγῆς" (ek prosagōgēs), meaning by degrees or step-by-step</note>, I find that the ancient physicians desired it. 

However, although athletes perhaps did not use this kind of exercise—certainly because it served them nowhere in achieving glory or the delight of spectators—I nevertheless believe they used breath retention among other exercises to be undertaken for two reasons: first, so they might be refreshed from fatigue, and at the same time the body might be rendered "perspirable" <note>referring to the skin's ability to "breathe" or release vapors through the pores</note> and pure for subsequent labors, as Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> seems to have indicated; second (which is more consistent with reason), so that they might acquire greater strength in pushing, squeezing, jumping, and the like from the retained breath. For in performing all these things, greater strength is produced in some way if the breath is held; this is shown daily by those carrying heavy loads, as well as all other heavy laborers, whom we see restraining their breathing so they can more easily sustain the greatest labors. It is as if, through such retention, the breath is increased within, causing strength to grow and rendering their efforts more effective. 

Added to this is what Aristotle used to say: that retained breath fills the veins and thus does not allow the humors <note>the bodily fluids, such as blood, phlegm, and bile, which were central to ancient medicine</note> to exit or be blown away. <margin>On the parts of animals, book 2.</margin> Hence, with those humors retained, laborers neither dissolve in sweat nor become exhausted, nor does that power—which all physicians admit consists in the humors, spirits, and solid members—tend to weaken or diminish in any part. 

<margin>2. Problems, section 1.</margin> Plutarch writes in his book on the *Precepts of Health* that the *aliptae* <note>trainers who massaged and anointed athletes with oil</note>, while rubbing the athletes, used to command them to intercept their breath, and thus resist the rubbing, as if they were distending the anointed and handled parts of the body. In this passage, where the Greek reads **holding the breath** <note>original Greek: "τηρῶντας τὴν πνοήν" (tērontas tēn pnoēn)</note>, all logic persuades that this is how it should be read, even if the good Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Renaissance scholar and translator</note>, a most diligent translator, did not see this. From all these things it is made clear that athletic gymnastics was accustomed to take no small help from the retention of breath, just as it has been (unless I am mistaken) abundantly proved that medical gymnasts valued the same very highly. 

Indeed, even athletes sometimes exercised themselves in breath retention for the sake of ostentation and the pleasure of spectators. From this one may gather that we read of the famous Milo <note>Milo of Croton, a legendary Greek wrestler known for his incredible strength</note>, with his head—and especially his forehead—and also his ribs and chest bound with strong bands, holding his breath so long until the veins, swelling from the force, burst those bindings. This can be sufficiently confirmed by the images which Ligorio <note>Pirro Ligorio, an Italian architect and antiquarian</note> found among the bronze statues of the most illustrious Prince of Ferrara, the supreme patron of all good things, and from these [he has taken] these...

...they commanded that breathing be held more forcefully and for a longer time with puffed-out cheeks, and finally ordered it to be relaxed. For in this way, according to that Hippocratic precept <note>Referring to the medical teachings of Hippocrates of Kos</note> <margin>Hippocrates, *On Regimen in Acute Diseases*, Book 2</margin> that all things should be done **gradually** <note>original Greek: "ἐκ προσαγωγῆς" (ek prosagōgēs), meaning by degrees or step-by-step</note>, I find that the ancient physicians desired it. 

However, although athletes perhaps did not use this kind of exercise—certainly because it served them nowhere in achieving glory or the delight of spectators—I nevertheless believe they used breath retention among other exercises to be undertaken for two reasons: first, so they might be refreshed from fatigue, and at the same time the body might be rendered "perspirable" <note>referring to the skin's ability to "breathe" or release vapors through the pores</note> and pure for subsequent labors, as Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire</note> seems to have indicated; second (which is more consistent with reason), so that they might acquire greater strength in pushing, squeezing, jumping, and the like from the retained breath. It is as if, through such retention, the breath is increased within, causing strength to grow and rendering their efforts more effective.

Furthermore, Galen, in his second book *To Glaucon* <note>original Latin: "Ad Glauconem", a work focused on the art of healing</note> <margin>Galen, *To Glaucon*, Book 2</margin>, employed the use of breath retention for this same preparation when he wanted some medication to be diffused throughout the whole body. He also wanted the same to be done when we attempt to purge pus or corrupt discharge <term>saniem</term> <note>original Latin: "saniem", referring to a thin, often blood-stained discharge from a wound or infection</note> from the chest; namely, so that by holding the breath and driving it downward toward the diaphragm, the capacity of the chest is made larger, and by that same action, greater power is acquired for expelling harmful substances and purging those things that have settled in the lungs and chest.

### On Shouting and Laughter. Chapter VII. ###

<margin>
Book 1, Sermon 3, Chapter 5.
Book 1, Sentence 3, Doctrine 2, Chapter 2.
<note>These refer to the medical encyclopedias of Aetius and Avicenna</note>

Among the many other necessary uses that breathing <note>original: "spiratio"</note> has in human life, shouting <note>original: "vociferatio," meaning loud calling or yelling</note> occupies a significant place. Since this is nothing other than a "vehement striking of the air," both Aristotle and Galen—in the most excellent commentaries published on the subject—have proved that its substance, its driving force, and its form are supplied either by respiration alone or, at the very least, not without it. Therefore, I thought it would not be out of place if, after speaking about the retention of breath, I immediately added a treatise on shouting. Nor should I be deterred from this by the fact that Galen, the prince of physicians, handed down either nothing or very little in his writings concerning shouting, as if he did not judge that it should be numbered among exercises. This is because Antyllus <note>An important Greek surgeon of the 2nd century AD</note>, a most celebrated physician cited in the works of Oribasius, not only wished for it to be considered an exercise but also wrote that it was highly valued both for the cure of various diseases and for the refinement of the voice itself. Similarly, Aetius of Amida and the Arab Avicenna <note>A Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age</note> confirmed this with one voice in later centuries. Whether the professors of athletics or those devoted to military discipline actually made use of this kind of exercise, even if I have noticed it recorded by no specific author, I am nevertheless persuaded that neither group practiced shouting as something specifically suited or necessary to their own profession. But if someone should say that both athletes in contests and soldiers in joining battle used shouts to great benefit—since Caesar writes that it was not in vain that it was established in ancient times that signals should sound from all sides and everyone should raise a shout when committing to war, by which things...

<margin>A</margin>...they thought the enemies would be terrified and their own men incited; because of this, it by no means follows that the exercise of shouting, which we are discussing, contributes to learning military discipline. I find that only two types of men have diligently applied themselves to the exercise of the voice: namely, professors of the stage <note>meaning actors and theatrical performers</note> and the gymnastic trainers of physicians. For those professing the theatrical arts—among whom I place heralds, choir members, reciters of tragedies and other similar plays, and also those competing with their voices—were accustomed to being exercised by shouting. A most rich witness to this is <margin>Parts 11 and 19.</margin>Plato in his *Ion*, and Aristotle in his books of *Problems*, in which we read that Phrynichus <note>A famous early Greek tragic poet</note>, and also in even more ancient times, tragedies, comedies, dithyrambs, and the laws themselves were accustomed to being recited in song. Because of this, vocal exercise was held in such high esteem that—just as we showed regarding athletics—public contests of shouting were established with prizes proposed for the winner, which Coelius Au<margin>B</margin>reliano understood under the name of "agonistic modulation" <note>Competitive vocal performance</note>. <margin>Book 5, Chron., last chapter.</margin> We can infer that this custom lasted until the time of Galen from the fact that in the seventh book of *On the Composition of Medicines according to Places*, he reviews many medicines which ancient physicians used for those who had to compete with their voice, both before and after the contest. There he similarly relates that in his own time all voice trainers <note>original: "phonascos"</note>, cithara-players, heralds, as well as those representing masked characters in tragedy and comedy—who used great exercise of the voice—were accustomed to using many baths and light, laxative foods if they had ever damaged their voice by straining it. From these words, anyone may understand that stage performers did not simply use the voice and song (as Plato said) in reciting dramas, <margin>In the *Ion*.</margin> rhapsodies, or their other imitations, but even used a loud voice, <margin>C</margin> and sometimes uniform, sometimes varied and changed—just as Aristotle writes was once done in tragedy to increase the magnitude of grief and calamity. It is sufficiently clear, therefore, that the exercise of shouting was in use during the times of our ancestors by actors, and they had teachers called *phonasci* <note>Greek term for voice coaches or trainers</note>, just as the art of vocal training was named *phonascia* by Theophrastus. But as to where these exercises were performed and why they were established, I will bring forth what I have read in approved authors. Regarding the place, it is certain that both the Greeks and Romans had a place constructed in the image of a theater (according to Pausanias), into which poems were brought before they were performed in the theater, and from which musical contests were watched; this was called an *odeion* <note>original Greek: ὠδεῖον</note> by the Greeks and an *odeum* by the Latins themselves. I believe the aforementioned vocal exercises and contests were accustomed to be carried out in this place, since Suetonius Tranquillus writes that Nero established a musical contest, and Domitian built an *odeum* where, besides singers who accompanied themselves on the lyre, lyre-players and harp-singers might compete. Although elsewhere too—and especially in the *exedrae* <note>recessed seating areas</note> of the gymnasia, in which we have heard philosophers and rhetoricians were accustomed to dispute—I suspect the ancients competed in shouting and exercised themselves. We read that some, to shape and refine their voices, were accustomed to shout, read, and sing in hollow places, while others did so near the shores of the sea, as is told of Demosthenes. Plutarch, in his *Lives of the Ten Orators*, is the authority who states that because Demosthenes's tongue faltered due to a weakness of breath, he paid the actor Neoptolemus ten thousand drachmas to teach him how to utter long periods of verses in a single breath. Furthermore, the purpose for which the ancients brought such exercises into use was manifold, as we can understand from Plato, Aristotle, and Plutarch: for they were exercised in shouting either so that in choruses, or in the contests of the Sophists and others established for this purpose, they might overcome the *antistrophous* <note>original Greek: τοὺς ἀντιστρόφους; referring here to vocal adversaries or responding singers</note> or opponents, or so that in the scene and theater everyone might perform their duty with praise. However, whether the exercise of shouting was applied to both theatrical and medical use at the same time, I do not know for certain. But I have observed that Cornelius Celsus recommended loud reading among the exercises that benefit a weak stomach; similarly, Coelius Aurelianus, an ancient physician among the Latins, approved the vocal exercise called *anaphonesis* <note>Greek term for medical shouting or vocal exercise</note> by the Greeks for headaches, as well as for the loss of voice and other diseases, noting that the same exercise should be administered with a teacher's guidance...

I am led to believe that **Astrandum** <note>This likely refers to a specific authority or a mis-transcription of "Adstruere" (to affirm/build); the context suggests the author is affirming a historical point.</note> advised that in that age, vocal exercise held a place in the gymnastics of physicians, and that the gymnasts themselves were skilled in the methods, rhythms, and rules of exercising the voice. This occurred once it had been proven through many experiments that properly initiated vocal exercise was most effective—not only for preserving the voice and curing certain diseases, but also (as **Plutarch** says) for protecting good health and the strength of the body. This is because it exercises the chest and the vocal instruments beautifully, excites the natural heat, and implants internal force and firm, genuine vigor into the most vital and principal parts of the body. For these reasons, perhaps, **Galen** reports that the famous **Thessalus**—who lived in the age of Nero and was held in great esteem (as **Pliny** writes), even calling himself the <term>iatronicem</term> <note>original Latin/Greek: iatronicem, meaning "Conqueror of Physicians"</note>—also employed this exercise for curing malignant ulcers.

The method by which this kind of exercise was performed is recorded by **Coelius Aurelianus** in the chapter on madness: the beginnings were delivered in a gentle voice, the narration and demonstrations were extended and louder, and then the epilogue was delivered in a lowered and indulgent tone. The method indicated by **Antyllus**, however, was that after the bowels had been emptied, the person was first gently rubbed, especially the lower parts, and the face was either moistened or washed with a sponge. Then they began to speak, at first gradually and with moderate intervals; sometimes they walked first, and afterward proceeded to <term>vociferation</term> <note>loud shouting or declamation used as a medical exercise</note>. In this, those unskilled in formal teaching would say whatever they remembered—things that seemed clear and possessed many changes of smoothness and roughness. If, however, they knew verses, they would recite iambics; the third place was given to Elegies, and the fourth to musical measures and rhythms. In all of these, it was judged more excellent to recite from memory than to read. Furthermore, as **Plutarch** advised, one should use moderate rather than overly agitated shouting or quarrelsome cries.

In the book *On Preserving Health*.
</margin>

In the first stage of shouting, they would draw out the voice by making the deepest sounds possible, then raising it to the highest pitches. Then, after remaining at the high pitch for a short time, they would turn back in reverse, gradually diminishing the voice until they returned to the deepest tone from which they had begun. In this manner, the entire vocal exercise was completed, taking into account the person's strength, eagerness, habit, and finally other factors about which **Plutarch** discussed at length in the book he titled *On Preserving Health*. They performed all these things while reclining, sitting, or standing; for this reason, **Socrates** judged that large spaces were by no means necessary for this kind of exercise. To this belongs...

# BOOK [III] #

**D** Also relevant is the account related by Pliny in Book 34, Chapter 18: that the Emperor Nero demonstrated a method for nourishing the voice by placing a lead plate <note>original: "lamina"; singers often used lead plates on their chests to compress the torso and improve breath control</note> upon his chest and singing songs loudly while lying beneath it. And since we have stated that in this kind of exercise, rhythm and melody held the fourth place, someone might rightly ask us by what reasoning we believe this was done—given that Plato, in several places, made music distinct from and almost the opposite of gymnastics, on the grounds that one concerns the soul and the other the body. To this, I judge the answer to be that music, insofar as it is composed of rhythms, melodies, and harmonies, is entirely separated from gymnastics; this is because in that form, it seeks only the solace and delight of the mind and is suited to shaping human character in a certain way. For this reason, Plato and Aristotle decreed that music should be learned by boys in the best-governed republics. 

**E** However, insofar as music uses the voice itself—admitting sometimes low, sometimes high, and sometimes middle tones, which are not produced without some physical effort—it becomes clear that it holds a place in gymnastics. The reason assigned for this is that all music is full of organized vocal movements which, according to Aristotle’s opinion, <margin>Problems, section 19, Problem 38.</margin> both increase and preserve our nature and strength. For this reason, no one should deny that music, just like the vocalization of gymnastics, is considered a certain exercise by physicians. This was often testified to by the physician Caelius Aurelianus, <margin>Book on Chronic Diseases, Chapter 5; and Book 2, Chapters 6 and 13.</margin> <note>A 5th-century Roman physician known for translating Greek medical texts into Latin.</note> especially when he prescribed—for curing madness, catarrh, or loss of voice—sometimes a vocal exercise composed by a music instructor, sometimes <term>anaphonesis</term> <note>A specific ancient medical exercise involving loud shouting or chanting to strengthen the internal organs.</note> under the guidance of a teacher while maintaining a rhythmic order, and sometimes the same under the mastery of an <term>alipta</term> <note>original: "aliptae"; a trainer who anointed athletes and supervised physical conditioning.</note> or a supervising musician.

**F** To these, I believe that groaning should also be counted among the gymnastics of the voice; for beyond the shouts and wails which they almost always carry with them, they can also draw out tears and thus empty the "excrements" <note>In ancient medicine, "excrements" referred to any waste fluids or humors the body needed to expel, such as phlegm.</note> of the head, much like many other exercises. And for this reason, Aristotle <margin>Politics, Book 7, final chapter.</margin> rightly wished to disapprove of those who by law forbid children from crying. Indeed, he wrote as follows: *“Those who forbid the straining and crying of children in their laws do not do so rightly. For these contribute to growth, since they become a kind of gymnastics for the bodies; for the holding of the breath produces strength in those who labor, which is also what happens to children when they are strained while crying.”* <note>original Greek: "τὰς δὲ διατάσεις τῶν παίδων... διατεινομένοις." This passage argues that the physical exertion of crying is a natural form of exercise that helps develop a child's lungs and strength.</note> That is to say: the straining and crying of children, which some forbid in their laws, is not rightly prohibited, for these activities contribute to their growth...

Whether laughter is a "tickling of the midriff" <note>original: "titillatio praecordiorum"; referring to the diaphragm</note>—as Aristotle believed—or, as found in
