If all those things which were used in ancient times and were, so to speak, common knowledge, had either been handed down to us by hand—as Galen relates regarding the art of anatomy—or had not perished after being committed to writing by authors, men would surely have escaped many of the labors they undergo daily in bringing to light obscure and antiquated matters, without any loss. But since some things have become obsolete through the length and harshness of time, others have been corrupted by difficult obscurity, others have failed due to the death of writers, and still others have never recovered their proper luster through a certain common negligence of the ages, it has happened that men are daily forced to renew the obsolete, reform the corrupted, rebuild the abolished, and finally restore splendor to things neglected and defiled. In such great obscurity, they are sometimes forced to wander far from the truth, as if dreaming. Among these, since I too have undertaken a similar task—striving to bring back to light the <term>gymnastic art</term><note>The ancient Greek and Roman system of physical education and medical exercise</note>, once held in great value but now completely obscured and dead—I seem to myself worthy of all the greater excuse, as so few (or almost no) writers on Gymnastics survive.

# BOOK THREE #

...from whom my purpose might be guided, not to mention the many types of exercises which, because they have fallen out of use in our times and the ancients' method of performing them is no longer maintained, we must guess at how they were done or what they were like, rather than affirm anything with certainty. This is what happens regarding the *Cricilasia* and the *trochus* <note>The *trochus* was an iron hoop or wheel used for exercise, often driven by a rod.</note>. For although Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical writer and personal physician to the Emperor Julian.</note> seems to have explained the method and form of *krikēlasia*—which in Latin means "hoop-driving"—based on the writings of Antyllus, the matter itself is so shrouded in darkness that it is very difficult for any learned person to distinguish the exact form and conditions of such an exercise. But lest anyone justly mark us with the crime of thick ignorance, rashness, fear, or arrogance, I will bring forward the Greek words of Oribasius himself, copied from a Vatican codex, as read in the 6th book of his *Medical Collections* addressed to Julian.

<margin>Chapter 26.</margin>
> The hoop should have a diameter smaller than the height of the person, so that its height reaches as far as the chest. It should be driven not in a straight line, but in a winding path. The driver <note>The "driver" (elater) was the rod used to push the hoop.</note> should be made of iron with a wooden handle. Some people thought the thin rings attached to the wheel were unnecessary, but this is not the case; rather, the noise they make creates a sense of relaxation and delight for the mind. <note>original Greek: Ἐλλάσσονα δὲ χέτω ὁ κρίκος... καὶ ἡδονὴν τῇ ψυχῇ</note>

> That is: Let the hoop have a diameter smaller than the man's height, so that its height reaches up to the breasts, and let it be driven not lengthwise, but crosswise; let the driver be iron with a wooden handle. Some have thought the thin rings placed around the wheel were superfluous: but this is not the case at all; rather, the sound produced by them generates relaxation and pleasure for the mind.

From these words it is clearly evident that in this exercise, men were accustomed to drive a large hoop—to the circumference of which small rings were fixed—using a specific iron rod with a handle, pushing it sideways. From this practice, Marcus Cicero <note>The famous Roman orator and statesman.</note> drew a metaphor in his 9th letter of the 2nd book to Atticus, where he wrote: "Believe me, it happened quite charmingly, and this wheel of state <note>original: "orbis hic in repub."; Cicero uses the hoop as a metaphor for a political cycle or shift.</note> has turned with less noise than I expected." But since it is not used in this age, we can certainly guess at it, but it is not possible to fully know its form and conditions. As for the fact that it was a Greek wheel, about which Horace wrote in the 3rd book of his *Odes*:

-> *Or if you bid him play with the Greek hoop,* <-
<note>original Latin: "Seu Graeco iubeas trocho"; Horace is contrasting traditional Roman virtues with the "softness" of Greek sports.</note>

this may indeed be so; but for this reason, nothing more certain will be established, since that is equally unknown to us. Similarly, someone might perhaps imagine in their mind what the *petaurum* <note>A specialized acrobatic device, sometimes resembling a see-saw or a high-swinging balance beam.</note> was; yet they will very easily see that the matter is otherwise once they realize it was a wooden machine by which men were tossed into the air by certain wheels...

<margin>A</margin> Or, beyond the force of the name indicating it, this was attested both by Lucilius <note>Gaius Lucilius, a Roman satirist of the 2nd century BCE.</note> when he said, "Just as the stage-mechanics <note>original: "mechanici," referring here to acrobats or stagehands who operated performance machinery.</note> when they leaped from the high *Petaurum*," <note>original: "petaurum," an ancient acrobatic apparatus, likely a springboard or a type of flying trapeze.</note> and also by Juvenal <note>A Roman poet known for his *Satires*, active in the late 1st and early 2nd centuries CE.</note> in Satire 14 with this verse:
> *Or do bodies tossed from the petaurum delight the mind more,*
> *Or those who are accustomed to descend a straight rope?*
->& Martial, <note>Marcus Valerius Martialis, a Roman poet famous for his Epigrams.</note> Book 11.<-
> *Than the passing wheel so often struck by the petaurum,*
from which it is clear that this delightful type of exercise is in no way similar to hoop-rolling <note>original: "Cricilasiae."</note>. However, I believe that very similar to the *petaurum* is that tossing motion which today is performed among many girls and boys by a board <note>Latin "affere" is likely a misspelling of "assere" (a plank or board).</note> suspended from the ceilings by four ropes; there, with the boys or girls sitting, they are tossed as if through the air. I think this type was signified by the ancients under the name of <term>oscellæ</term> <note>original: "oscellarum." Originally "little mouths" or small masks hung in trees to swing in the wind, the term came to refer to the act of swinging itself.</note>. And perhaps it is this which <margin>B</margin> Avicenna <note>The Latinized name of Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian physician whose *Canon of Medicine* was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> mentions in the first book of the fourth volume, treatise 2, chapter 13, where, for the purpose of checking sweat, he recommends that the patient be placed upon an instrument on which children or youths are accustomed to be shaken in the air. For indeed, Aelius Stilo <note>A prominent Roman grammarian and teacher of Cicero.</note> says in the works of Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian who preserved much older linguistic knowledge.</note> that they are properly called "petaurists" in Greek because they "fly toward the air" <term>πρὸς ἀέρα</term> <note>original Greek: "pros aera."</note> or "fly toward the breezes" <term>πρὸς αὔρας πέτονται</term> <note>original Greek: "pros auras petontai."</note>, or because they fly into the air or the breezes. That this kind of exercise was also used in gymnastic games among the Thracians, Egyptians, and other peoples can be seen by anyone from history. This is no less indicated by the coins of the Emperors Augustus and Tiberius, in which the game of *oscellæ* <note>the swing</note> is represented in this manner.

**A** Although this exercise <note>Referring to the "petaurum" discussed on the previous page.</note> may differ in method from today's swings <note>original: "oscellis."</note>, it is nonetheless easily seen not to differ in substance; players in the air were seen to be tossed about in the same way as those who practice similar movements now. > *The wheel must be brought in; you give us a useful gift,* <margin>book 14.</margin>
> *This hoop shall be for boys, but for me it will be a song.* &

For in the *trochus* there was first a circle, and in the circle a ring, which brought pleasure to the spectators with its sound; and there was also a driver with a handle, called a "key" <note>original: "clavis."</note> by Propertius <note>A Roman elegiac poet of the 1st century BCE.</note> when he said,

> *And the hooked key of the turned hoop rattles.* <margin>book 3.</margin>

All of these features Antyllus <note>An influential Greek physician of the 2nd century CE.</note> described most aptly in his discussion of hoop-rolling, except that Antyllus states thin rings were placed *around* the circle (not just one ring), and furthermore, he made hoop-rolling an exercise for men. Martial, however, indicated that the *trochus* was a game for children. Led by these last two reasons, I have come to the opinion that the exercise of hoop-rolling was in some way different from the *trochus* of the Romans. Because of this, however, I hardly dare to affirm exactly what the *trochus* was, although I hold for certain it was that kind of <term>top</term> <note>original: "turbinis."</note> which boys make rotate in a circle by releasing it from a leather strap tied to a stick, and then eagerly drive it with lashes once it is spinning—which the Greeks call a <term>bembix</term> <note>original: βέμβικα.</note>, as seen in this ancient Epigram:

> *But the boys, having swift tops under their sticks,*

And Virgil described this most aptly in these verses: <margin>Aeneid, Book 7.</margin>

> *As sometimes a top flying under the twisted lash,*
> *Which boys, intent on the game, drive in a great circle*
> *Around empty courtyards; driven by the thong,*
> *It is carried in curved paths; the ignorant crowd stands amazed,*
> *And the youthful band marvels at the spinning boxwood.*

->*Blows give courage,*<- <note>original: "Dant animos plagae." A Latin proverb implying that the strike of the rod keeps the hoop or top in motion.</note>

It is not at all a spinning top, as some have wished, nor is it that exercise performed today on tables covered with cloth using wooden balls, which is called *truchus*. That modern game bears very little resemblance to the <term>trochus</term> <note>A metal hoop rolled with a rod.</note> of the ancients. First, the hoop was played in public gymnasiums or other open spaces. Second, it had a ring or rings that made a clattering noise, so that people walking along the road might hear the sound and take care to stay far from the path of the oncoming hoop. Finally, it was cast from bronze and had a hooked key, all of which—neither separately nor together—are found in our spinning tops or "truchus," as our own senses teach us. Thus, we ought rightly to believe that the ancient hoop was far different from these, and in my opinion, it is best represented by this figure:

<margin>E</margin>

This was all the more true because the entire city was essentially divided into four parts, with some favoring one faction and some another. "By Hera, Ischomachus, you please me by doing these things; for at the same time to utilize preparations for health and strength, and exercises for war, and care for wealth, all these things seem to me to be good." <note>original: "τως γὲ μοι ταῦτα ποιεῖς..." This is a quote from Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*, where Socrates praises Ischomachus for balancing physical fitness, military readiness, and business.</note> That is to say: *By Juno, O Ischomachus, by acting thus you please me, since at one and the same time you devote effort to acquiring health and strength, and you also exercise for war, and keep watch over the accumulation of riches—all of which clearly seem worthy of admiration to me.* From these conversations of both Ischomachus and Socrates, a very clear argument is drawn that the ancients used horse riding to prepare for military disciplines. 

But as to whether physicians and physical trainers used riding to recover or maintain health, as well as to produce an excellent physical condition, the testimony of **Galen** alone should suffice, in addition to the speech of **Socrates** just cited. Galen writes that among other gymnastic exercises, riding holds a position by no means the lowest, since it exercises not only the body but even the senses. This is supported by the approval of **Antyllus**, **Aetius**, and finally **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian physician (980–1037 AD) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard text in Europe for centuries.</note>, who categorized riding on both horses and camels among the suitable exercises. Indeed, **Suetonius** recorded that **Germanicus**, the nephew of the Emperor **Tiberius**, was cured of a disfiguring thinness of the legs by horse riding, which had been ordered by his physicians. 

By this example, we ought to be persuaded to believe that riding was always highly regarded by physicians as most useful—though among them it mattered greatly whether one was carried by a mule or a horse, and whether the animals were <term>amblers</term> <note>original: "gradarijs," horses that move with a smooth, rhythmic pace</note>, or <term>Asturconians</term> <note>original: "asturconibus," a small, hardy breed of horse from the Asturias region of Spain, prized for their comfortable gait</note>, or <term>trotters</term> <note>original: "succussatarijs," horses that move with a jolting, high-stepping motion</note>, or racing horses. We shall explain the different effects of all of these in their proper place.

### THIRD BOOK ###

<header>T H I R D</header>

As an ancient commentator on Aratus <note>Aratus was a Greek poet famous for the *Phaenomena*, a work on stars and weather signs.</note> testifies, the first who joined horses to chariots was Erichthonius <note>A legendary early ruler of Athens, often said to have been born from the earth and raised by the goddess Athena; he is credited with inventing the four-horse chariot to hide his serpent-like feet.</note>, whom Manilius writes was placed among the stars in the first book of his *Astronomica* for this reason. Furthermore, the form and manner of chariots were diverse. For Pliny <margin>Book 16, ch. 42 & 53.</margin> approves of fir wood as suitable material for making chariots, but for the wheel axles, he recommends Holm-oak, ash, and elm. From this, it is gathered that the ancients fashioned chariots from these types of wood, which in those earlier ages were constructed with only two wheels. The Phrygians added another two wheels, according to Pliny. <margin>Book 7, ch. 56.</margin> The most ancient author Hippocrates <margin>Book on Airs, Waters, and Places.</margin> recorded that the Scythians later even constructed chariots with six wheels. These wheels were adorned with tin in the time of Homer, but in later ages, we read in Plautus’s *Aulularia* that not only the wheels but entire vehicles were decorated with ivory, just as in Pliny’s time <margin>Book 34, ch. 17.</margin> entire carriages and vehicles were seen distinguished with gold and silver. It seems likely they were covered with various other materials, but mostly with skins, as Plutarch left written in his *Roman Questions*: just as they were sometimes drawn by horses, sometimes by mules, sometimes by oxen, and occasionally it is read they were commonly drawn by men in military cloaks <note>original: "uiri sagis." The *sagum* was a cloak associated with Roman soldiers; this suggests a display of power or humiliation where soldiers pulled the vehicle.</note>. Furthermore, they record that Heliogabalus <margin>Lampridius in the Life of Heliogabalus.</margin> <note>A Roman emperor (reigned 218–222 AD) notorious for his eccentric and often scandalous behavior.</note> joined not only various and monstrous animals to chariots, but even naked women, and was carried by them. Moreover, this mode of transport in chariots was once held in the greatest luxury among women in Rome; and it reached such excess at one time that the Romans were forced to forbid them from using them by a decree of the Senate. On account of this matter, when the women, moved by anger, conspired among themselves so that none of them would conceive or give birth, and thus they might take revenge on the men, Plutarch committed to writing that the Romans changed their minds and permitted them to use chariots again. Afterward, Marcus Aurelius Antoninus the philosopher, consulting the modesty of matrons, forbade them again from sitting in them or being carried by horses through the cities. No less is this same transport valued among the physical trainers <term>gymnasts</term>: for whether you look at the games and sacred contests, or search the books of physicians, it will appear common in all of them. Who, I ask, does not know that the chariot race was introduced into the Olympic games in the ninety-ninth Olympiad? Who is ignorant of the <term>synorides</term> <note>A two-horse chariot team.</note>, to which Plato most elegantly compared our souls in the *Phaedrus*, or that the <term>bigae</term> <note>Two-horse chariots.</note> and <term>quadrigae</term> <note>Four-horse chariots.</note> types of chariots frequently competed in public sacred rites? This pursuit was later so cultivated and increased among the Romans that few or almost no public spectacles were produced without honorable prizes being proposed for chariot races. B O O K

...it is recorded that the victor was accustomed to drink wormwood <note>Wormwood (absinthium) is a bitter herb used in antiquity for its medicinal properties, particularly for digestion and liver health.</note> as a prize, as the ancients considered it a great honor for health to be given as a reward. I do not dare to affirm anything for certain as to whether the ancients used chariot riding for the sake of acquiring military discipline. <margin>In the *Education of Cyrus* <note>A reference to Xenophon’s semi-fictional biography of the Persian king Cyrus the Great.</note>.</margin> However, I believe that since the custom of fighting from chariots in war lasted from the time of Homer until the time of Xenophon, and even into later centuries, the ancients practiced riding in chariots just as they trained in horsemanship, so that they might become more fit for waging war. This was done so that when they had to fight, they would not be overcome like men who were untrained and lacked experience in the various ways of driving a chariot.

Furthermore, the "gymnastic" physicians <note>Physicians who focused on the medical benefits of physical activity.</note> clearly testified that similar carriage riding was adopted both for preserving the health of the sound and for curing certain illnesses. These included Galen, Antyllus, <margin>Oribasius, Book 6, Chapter 25.</margin> Herodotus, and Avicenna. They not only wanted this to be categorized among the true gymnastic exercises, but even celebrated it as being especially beneficial for those with fevers (a benefit attributed to very few other exercises). <margin>Galen, *On Preserving Health*, Book 2, Chapter 11.</margin> Galen seems to have established two types of this: one in which people sat while being carried, and another in which they lay down. Both of these were rarely performed within the city, but very frequently on the roads and outside the city. <margin>In *Roman Questions*.</margin> For this reason, Plutarch wrote that the Romans were forced to prohibit the use of vehicles on the day of the Festival of the Seven Hills <note>The *Septimontium*, a festival celebrating the seven original hills of Rome.</note>, so that the city and the celebration would not be abandoned by people traveling out for exercise.

Herodotus seems to have indicated whether the healthy and the sick were exercised in the same vehicles; we read in his work that those with fevers were usually carried in hand-drawn chariots as well as in two-horse chariots. These patients would initially move for thirty stadia <note>A *stadium* was an ancient Greek measurement of roughly 600 feet (185 meters). Thirty stadia is about 3.5 miles.</note> and then double that distance. Others would start at thirty or forty stadia and proceed until they reached a distance twice as large. It is likely that healthy people used all kinds of chariots, both covered and open, without distinction. Though, perhaps we can believe that rulers traveled in covered rather than open ones. The historian Cassius Dio relates that when the Emperor Claudius was in good health—though he had a trembling head and hands and a stumbling tongue—he was the first of all Romans to be carried in a vehicle covered on all sides. Similarly, Pliny the Younger testifies in the seventh book of his letters that he used such a vehicle due to a weakness of his eyes, writing thus to his friend Cornutus:

> I obey you, most distinguished colleague, and I am caring for the weakness of my eyes as you command. For I arrived here enclosed on all sides in a covered vehicle, as if I were in my own bedroom. <note>original: "Pareo collega clarissime, & infirmitati oculorum, ut iubes, consulo. Nam & huc tecto uehiculo undiq. occlusus, quasi in cubiculo perueni."</note>

From all these things, then, anyone can recognize that such exercise is no less than the others...

<margin>Galen, *On the Preservation of Health*, Book 2, chapter 11.</margin>
...[transport] was approved by the gymnastic masters; indeed, Galen writes that they—and not the chariot-drivers—rightly understood the capacities and conditions of all the movements resulting from this form of carrying. It is as if this exercise, like others, had its own specific officials (namely the drivers), yet was ultimately subject to the general master of the whole art <note>The "gymnastes" or director of the gymnasium, who oversaw the medical application of exercise.</note>, who would diligently prescribe the manner, measure, quality, and time to be observed in such exercise. The ancients had many types of chariots or vehicles, such as the **Wagon**, the **War-chariot**, the **Four-wheeled Carriage**, the **Covered Cart**, the **Two-wheeled Gig**, the **Horse-drawn Carriage**, the **Coach**, the **Two-wheeled State Carriage**, the **Sacred Procession Chariot**, the **Light Gig**, the **Scythed Chariot**, the **Traveling Carriage**, the **Ladies' Carriage**, and the **Mule-litter**. <note>original Latin terms: Plaustrum, Esseda, Petoritum, Arcirna (Arcera), Birotum, Cantherinum, Carruca, Carpentum, Thensa, Cisium, Covinus, Rheda, Pilentum, Burdones. These varied by wheel count, suspension, and ceremonial use.</note> All of these were similar in that they were driven on wheels; however, they differed in form, material, size, and other ways. But there is no reason for us to speak of these individually, since the method of being carried was nearly the same for all, **B** and therefore physicians have grouped them all under the single category of the **Chariot**.

-> *On being carried in the Litter and the Chair.* Chapter XI. <-

<margin>C</margin>
There are those who believe that the **Litter** <term>Lectica; a portable couch or bed carried by poles</term> and the **Chair** <term>Sella; a sedan chair</term> were invented for the convenience of those who were prevented from walking by old age or illness, or for the sake of the luxuries which men have always sought, rather than for any other reason. This is perhaps not without reason; since no more probable cause appears for why the ancients devised such instruments than that those unable to ride horses or go on foot desired some means by which they could leave the house, wander through cities, and make journeys as comfortably as possible. Unless we say that Emperors, Kings, and Princes—in order not to be harmed during their journeys by the sun, wind, rain, storms, and the like—invented litters and chairs designed to be covered and uncovered on all sides. Later, other wealthy people adopted them for the sake of luxury, pleasure, or convenience; and finally, physicians and gymnastic masters adapted them for the use of the people entrusted to their care. However it may be, it is certain that the physicians and gymnasts I just mentioned used them to exercise the bodies of the sick frequently, and more rarely the healthy. Regarding the form of both the litter and the chair, nothing is held so certain that one might not doubt it; yet it is likely that a cushion and a spread bed were inside, so that those being carried could either lie down or sit as they pleased. Whether in other respects it was different from ours, or rather similar, I believe it was not very different, except that ours are almost always carried by mules or horses, while those of the ancients were for the most part carried by slaves...

<margin>Martial, Book 2.</margin>
<margin>Martial, Book 6; Tertullian, Book 1, *To His Wife*.</margin>
From these sources, anyone can clearly understand that a litter was almost always carried by six slaves. (Martial writes that Cappadocians were used for this purpose, while Tertullian mentions Germans). If anyone ever wished to increase the number of bearers, it was immediately noticed, as Martial indicated when he called a certain Philippus "insane." This was because Philippus’s litter was carried through the city by eight slaves as a vain display of wealth:

> *The "sane" Philippus is carried in an Eight-bearer,* <note>original: Octaphoro.</note>
> *But if you believe him sane, Avitus, then you are the mad one.*

Since the litter of the ancients was designed in this way, it was not only truly comfortable, but when closed, it even served to induce sleep, as Juvenal testifies with these words:

> *For a litter with closed windows brings on sleep.*

<margin>Juvenal, Satire 3.</margin>
Indeed, its use was so frequent that there were "stations" <note>original: "castra lecticariorum" (camps of the litter-bearers).</note> for the bearers who were assigned solely to carrying litters, or even to assisting matrons into and out of them (as mentioned by legal experts). These stations were located in several places where they were governed by their own laws and conducted other business typical of military-style camps. However, I believe that all freedmen <note>Former slaves who had been granted their liberty.</note> were forbidden from being carried through the city in a litter, based on the authority of Suetonius. He writes that the Emperor Claudius granted the right to be carried in a litter and to provide public spectacles to his freedman Harpocras as a special privilege. Furthermore, Antyllus—or rather his interpreter—records that there were two types of **sedan chairs** <note>original: "sella."</note>; one in which they sat, which was either covered or left open...

# B O O K   T H R E E

<margin>Book 1 on Chronic Diseases, chapter 1.</margin>
**A** ...was carried, and by some, such as Caelius Aurelianus <note>A 5th-century Roman physician known for his translations of Greek medical works.</note>, it was called a "carrying chair" <note>original: *portatoria sella*</note> and a "conveyance" <note>original: *fertorium*</note>; the other was a type in which they lay down. We can still see the first type in our own day, as those suffering from gout, the wealthy, and other princes too devoted to luxuries are carried in them daily. I believe the name of the "curule chair" <note>original: *sellae curulis*—the ivory chair used by high-ranking Roman magistrates.</note>, in which one only sat, originated from the fact that men holding magistracies were once accustomed to be carried in them. As for the second type, in which they lay down, we do not have it today, as far as I know, unless we say that our modern litter <note>original: *lectica*</note> takes its place, and that for the ancients the same object—the litter—signified a seat suitable for either lying or sitting. Aetius of Amida <note>A 6th-century Byzantine royal physician.</note> clearly seems to have subscribed to this opinion, for among the various forms of <margin>Book 8, chapter 6.</margin> **gestations** <term>gestations: a form of "passive exercise" where the patient is moved by external means, such as being carried in a chair or litter.</term>, he omitted specific chairs and mentioned only two types of litters: namely, the one in which they sat while being carried, and the one in which they lay down. Therefore, both the litter and the chair were instruments in which the wealthy, the elderly, **B** and those who could not walk were carried by slaves through cities and on journeys; these were also used not infrequently by "gymnastic physicians" <note>Physicians who specialized in exercise and physical therapy.</note> to exercise both the healthy and the sick for the sake of their health. For Galen <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note> relates that Antiochus the physician, who was already eighty years old and most diligent in his way of living, was accustomed to be carried sometimes in a chair and sometimes <margin>Book 6, *On Protecting Health*, chapter 4.</margin> in a carriage whenever he wished to travel a longer distance. Similarly, Pliny the Younger <margin>Book of Epistles, 5.</margin> relates that his uncle <note>Pliny the Elder, the famous natural historian.</note> was accustomed to be carried in a chair in Rome, so that the harshness of the weather would not steal any time from his studies. From this it can be judged that the elderly used gestations in chairs both for exercising themselves and for attending to private business, just as it is observed that physicians employed them for the faint and weak. In these cases, according to Herodotus <note>Likely referring to Herodotus the Physician (1st century AD), rather than the historian.</note>, a specific method was observed: such gestations were to be extended no less than five **stadia** <term>stadia: an ancient Greek unit of distance; five stadia is roughly 925 meters or half a mile.</term>, and no more than double that distance, and the same was observed the following day. **C** On the third day, however, they added five stadia each day until they reached thirty stadia. And lest anyone perhaps suspect that the chair and the litter were the same thing, we can cite Martial <note>A Roman poet famous for his witty epigrams.</note> above all others, in whose writing it is in no way obscure that <margin>Oribasius, in the place cited.</margin> they were different, when he says:

> *Shall I follow the litter and the chair? Nor do I refuse to bear* <margin>Book 10.</margin>
> *The struggles through the mud, but rather to go first,*

This is similarly confirmed by these words of Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage.</note> in his book *On the Cloak*:
"They have now also rejected the litters and chairs themselves, which were ,,

# B O O K

### On motion through hanging beds and cradles, and on the small couch. Chapter XII.

<margin>Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler.</note>, Book 6; Collections, Book 3, chapter 6.</margin>
Perhaps someone will wonder why I wish to include the motion performed in cradles and hanging beds—two things which I find the Greeks grouped under the single term for "bed" <note>original: κλίνης (*klines*)</note>—among the various gymnastic exercises. This is because, in our own time, cradles are used only for soothing children, and there are very few people for whom physicians would order hanging beds to be prepared. However, such a person will cease to wonder if they choose to carefully read Galen, the physician Herodotus <note>A physician of the Pneumatic school, not the famous historian.</note>, Aetius, and Avicenna. Since these authors numbered such motions among the other exercises for the human body, I do not see why I should pass them over in silence. Indeed, I do not deny that cradles were devised for infants rather than adults, but I believe that such motion can sometimes provide no small help to men, both for soothing pains and for inducing sleep. This was excellently written by Antyllus and Aetius, in whose works a bed having "movable supports near the corner feet" signifies, in my opinion, nothing other than cradles themselves. Celsus <note>A 1st-century Roman encyclopedist known for 'De Medicina'.</note> also understood these when he said: "If even that is not possible, a small rope should certainly be placed under one foot of the bed, and the bed should thus be pushed back and forth." And even if the translator of Oribasius preferred to translate the name for "bed" <note>original: κλίνης (*klines*)</note> as "litter," I believe those people are entirely mistaken who think these have no use in medical gymnastics. Similar to these is that exercise for children while they are carried in the arms of their nurses, which is wonderfully approved for their health both by physicians and by <margin>Republic, Book 7.</margin> Plato. Almost the same reasoning applies to hanging beds as to hanging baths <note>original: *balneorum pensilium*; these could refer to swinging baths or, more technically, the suspended floor heating systems of Roman baths.</note>. Since Pliny records that all these were frequently used by <margin>Book 26, chapter 3.</margin> Asclepiades of Prusa <note>A popular Greek physician in Rome who preferred pleasant treatments like massage and swinging over harsh medicines.</note> so that, by catering to the pleasures and delights of the sick, he might gain influence among men, it seems reasonable to conclude that just as they brought incredible glory and reputation to their inventor, they also brought much utility and delight to those using them. From there, it followed that later physicians approved of similar motion for exercising people. However, few or none (to my knowledge) have handed down the specific design of such instruments or the manner of using them, which would certainly suggest to us that their frequent use existed at some time—unless we believe that the ancient writers neglected to write about such things because they were common knowledge and obvious to everyone. Since in our times these things are ignored by most, it is worth the effort—

<summary>The author argues for the inclusion of cradles and swinging beds in the study of medical gymnastics, citing ancient authorities like Galen, Celsus, and Plato to show that these "passive" movements were once vital therapeutic tools for both children and adults.</summary>

# B O O K  T H I R D

<margin>A</margin>
I hope that I shall do something worthwhile if I briefly bring my own thoughts on this matter into the open. Regarding the **hanging beds**, which Pliny records were first devised by Asclepiades <note>A Greek physician who practiced in Rome and promoted exercise and diet over harsh medicines.</note>, I believe they were certain small beds
<margin>Book 26, ch. 3.</margin>
constructed sometimes of wood, sometimes of bronze, and sometimes of silver (Pliny wrote that our ancestors even possessed silver beds). These
<margin>Book 33, ch. 1.</margin>
were fastened at the four corners by ropes to the ceiling beams of the bedrooms, so that, being lifted slightly off the ground, they seemed to hang, as it were, in the air. Similarly, **hanging baths** were first invented by Sergius Orata <note>A Roman businessman and engineer famous for his innovations in luxury living and hydraulic engineering.</note>, according to Pliny. These were not built upon roofs or in vaulted rooms, as some have claimed; rather, I believe they were nothing other than
<margin>Book 9, ch. 53.</margin>
tubs—whether made of marble, bronze, or wood—suspended from the ceiling beams in imitation of the hanging beds, so that by the slightest push of the hand they could be moved, sometimes gently and sometimes more vigorously. Seneca, writing to Lucilius,
<margin>B</margin>
made this clear to us in these words: "The suspension of baths was invented: so that nothing might be lacking for luxury" <note>original: "Balnearum ſuſpenſura inuenta eſt: ne quid ad lautitiam deeſſet."</note>. Physicians, therefore, prescribed that people be exercised by these motions, primarily striving for this one goal: to provide movement without any labor or fatigue. Furthermore, they took care that this exercise should not lack a certain pleasantness. Indeed, great pleasure was found in the beds, but the greatest in the baths; for besides that most sweet motion, they added the delight of water, which touched every limb of the body with a very soft and seductive tickling. For if hanging baths were understood to be those built upon roofs, I do not see how that greater pleasure—devised for various reasons according to Seneca and Pliny—could be found in them more than in others. Regarding the hanging bed, Herodotus <note>The physician Herodotus, a practitioner of the Pneumatic school.</note> said that one should be carried in it for as long as it would take to travel
<margin>C</margin>
forty stadia <note>Approximately 4.6 miles or 7.4 kilometers.</note> in a sedan chair. However, I more willingly agree with another opinion of the same author: namely, that the duration of such an exercise cannot easily be defined by a number. I feel this way not only about these exercises, but about all others, because of the varied and diverse conditions of the sick; all those even moderately skilled in the medical art proclaim with one voice that the same treatments cannot suit everyone in the same way. I find that the ancients had another instrument similar to the hanging bed, which the Greeks called a *skimpodion* <note>original: σκιμπόδιον; a small, low couch or pallet.</note> and the Latins called by the same name, *scimpodium*. Although they never hung this from a ceiling, it was nevertheless either a small bed or something constructed in the form of a hanging bed. Men as well as women were carried upon it through cities and along the roads, as the historian Dio demonstrates. He writes that at first Augustus and Tiberius were sometimes accustomed to be carried in *scimpodia*, the same kind in which women were carried in his own time.

->Gymnastics.<-

<margin>10. Method of Healing.</margin>
Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> meant nothing else when, prescribing the method of entering baths for those with hectic fever, he committed these words to writing: <note>original: "ἀῤῥωσοῦντα βούλομαι κομίζεσθαι μὲν ἐπὶ τοῦ σκίμποδος εἰς τὸ βαλανεῖον."</note> "I want the sick man to be carried on a *scimpodium* to the bath." Nor did the rhetorician Libanius mean anything else in the book about his own life when he said: "When I am at home, I lie in bed; but when I am in the school, I lie on a *scimpodium*." The same was also understood by Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, author of "Attic Nights."</note>, where he writes that he found Cornelius Fronto, who was suffering severely in his feet, reclining on a "Grecian *scimpodium*." It is clear, therefore, that hanging beds, hanging baths, and *scimpodia* were used by our ancestors not only for luxury and pleasure, but were also employed by gymnastic physicians to exercise the bodies of the sick. Furthermore, as to what kind of instrument that "snatching machine" and the "long-rope" mentioned by Caelius Aurelianus <note>A 5th-century Roman physician known for his translations of Greek medical works into Latin.</note> might have been, and what the "rebounding Italian bolt" mentioned by the same author was—both of which were used for carrying people—is not yet fully clear to me, as I have found no mention of them by any other author until now. Unless, as we said above, it was a <term>petaurum</term> <note>A sort of springboard or balancing pole used by acrobats.</note>, or rather, the text of Caelius is corrupted.

# BOOK THREE #

## On Navigation and Fishing. Chapter XIII. ##

<sig>M ij</sig>

Among the varieties of passive transport <note>original Latin: *gestatio*, a form of exercise where the patient is carried or moved by an external force rather than by their own exertion</note> which have existed for exercising the body, Antyllus also included navigation. He was followed in this by Aetius, and after him, Avicenna clearly demonstrates that it was considered an exercise. In my judgment, both of them took this idea not so much from experience as from an ancient opinion of the divine Hippocrates, who said that navigation <margin>Aphorisms, Book 4, 14.</margin> both moves and disturbs the body. However, Avicenna categorized navigation among the mild exercises, whereas Hippocrates asserts that it disturbs the body greatly—an observation that seems to argue for a vigorous rather than a gentle motion. 

In this exercise of navigation, I find two types especially used in gymnastics, though not very commonly: the medical and the military. Physicians used it either to maintain the health of those who were well or to restore health to the sick. For the healthy, they utilized navigation because (as Aristotle wrote) the sea, due to its gentle <margin>Problems, Part 1, 54.</margin> breezes, brings about remarkable healthiness; hence, those who sail always have better color than those living in marshes. 

Regarding the sick, it is naturally suited to dry out putrid and harmful humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which needed to be balanced for health.</note>, both through the vomiting it very frequently produces (especially in those unaccustomed to it) and through the dry winds and vapors. For this reason, Avicenna said that navigation <margin>Book 3, Doctrine 1, 2.</margin> greatly benefits leprosy, dropsy, apoplexy, coldness of the stomach, and also flatulence. Pliny the Elder, moreover, testified that it brings relief to those with consumption <term>consumption: historically called "phthisis," a wasting disease usually identified with tuberculosis</term> and those coughing up blood, citing the example of Annaeus Gallio, who was cured in this way after his consulship. He likewise believed that those afflicted by such conditions sought out Egypt not for the land itself, but for the long duration of the sea voyage. Similarly, his nephew, Pliny the Younger, records that he sent his <margin>Letters, Book 5.</margin> freedman Zosimus there when he was spitting up blood, and that he returned restored to health. 

Nevertheless, that author falsely inscribed with the name of Pliny in the first book of *On Medicine* felt that for the consumptive, it is more useful to stay in the forests <margin>Chapter 6.</margin> where pitch is produced than to sail on the sea or visit coastal regions. This was also passed down by the physician Marcellus. For Galen, in the ninth book of *On Simple Medicines*, when speaking of Samian earth, mentions that many with ulcerated lungs traveled from Rome to Libya for this reason and lived for several years without symptoms, but later the disease recurred when they did not live with the same care. The method observed by the sick while sailing is described by Herodotus <note>The author refers to Herodotus the Physician, a practitioner of the Pneumatic school, not the famous historian.</note> as starting with sixty stadia <term>stadium: an ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters or 600 feet</term> and ending with double that amount. Furthermore, there were many differences in navigation, since some...

...on the sea, while others took place on rivers; some in large ships, others in small ones; some were powered by oars, others by towing, and others by the wind—be it violent or more gentle. Regarding navigation on rivers, it has been handed down by Plutarch <margin>In the book *On Natural Causes*</margin> that it produces less nausea than the sea, because both the smell and the fear arising from the sight of the sea disturb the bodies of those setting out and thus provoke vomiting, a thing which occurs very little on rivers. Conversely, Coelius Aurelianus <note>A 5th-century physician known for his translations of Greek medical works into Latin.</note> preferred long voyages across the seas for chronic headaches, because (as he himself says) river or harbor voyages, as well as those on ponds, are judged unsuitable. This is because they chill the head by moistening it with earthy exhalations, whereas sea voyages secretly and gradually open the body, "burning" it—so to speak—due to its salty quality, and restoring its condition through a certain transformation.

This, then, was the use of navigation among the gymnastic physicians, which we have said was likewise embraced by those devoted to war. Indeed, those <term>Naumachiae</term> <note>From the Greek *naumachia*, meaning "naval combat"; these were massive, staged naval battles for public entertainment and military training.</note> which were performed by the Romans in the circus or in some man-made basin near the Tiber designated for such exercise, were, according to some, primarily instituted to delight the people. Such were those which Lampridius records as being sometimes exhibited by the most impure Heliogabalus <note>A Roman emperor notorious for his eccentricity and decadence.</note> in <term>euripi</term> <note>Channels or ornamental canals.</note> filled with wine. However, it also seems probable to me that these displays served a great purpose: that the soldiers might be exercised in them to acquire discipline for naval battles. I am led to this opinion chiefly by the fact that the Romans, as Polybius reports, exercised their soldiers in naval discipline during the first Punic War when they were about to declare war against the Carthaginians by sea.

Similarly, Suetonius writes that Augustus, when he was about to fight against Pompey, kept his soldiers in naval exercise for a whole winter in the Julian Harbor near Baiae, which he himself had built. From this it can be clear that the Romans always gave effort to exercising their troops as much by sea as by land, and instituted the *naumachiae* for the sake of this study. They not only had the "Naumachian Bridge"—so named for that reason—which Pliny writes Tiberius rebuilt from larch wood cut in Raetia after it had been burned, but even a specific location, the remains of which still exist today. At the time of a *naumachia*, they would fill this place with so much water that it seemed like a sort of sea, just as Martial most elegantly demonstrated when he described a naval battle produced by the Emperor Domitian in this poem: <margin>Book 26, chapter 3.</margin>

We must consider their opinions weak for two reasons: first, because neither of them explained what good fishing brings, as if they did not particularly approve of this kind of exercise but were rather following a common way of speaking; <margin>Book 6, *On the Composition of Medicines*, section 38; *Problems*, Part 2.</margin> second, because Galen himself said that the physical condition of fishermen is "hard and dry." Regarding this dryness, Aristotle previously wrote that sea-fishermen are endowed with red hair <note>Aristotle and other ancient writers often associated red hair with a "burnt" or excessively dry temperament caused by sun and salt spray.</note>. Hence, I do not see how physicians, who strive to acquire a "good habit" <note>original: *habitum*; a healthy physical constitution or "fitness."</note> of the body through exercises, would wish to make it hard and dry through fishing; especially since almost all fishing is conducted under the sun and often in places filled with bad air—with the single exception of sea fishing. Thus, all these things force us to believe that physicians held the labor of fishing in low esteem. Nevertheless, there was no lack of Emperors who occasionally fished for the sake of exercise, as was written of Caesar Augustus by Suetonius, and of Alexander Severus by Lampridius, of whom he writes: "His way of living was this: first, if the opportunity allowed—that is, if he had not slept with his wife—in the morning hours in his shrine <note>original: *larario*; a private domestic chapel.</note>, in which..."

### *On Swimming.* ### Chapter XIV.

<margin>
Section 27. Problem 5 and 2. Rhetoric, chapter 4.
</margin>
The regard for swimming among the ancients was always great and almost incredible, and its use flourished through so many centuries that children were taught the art of swimming no less than the first elements of reading and writing. During that era, no greater mark of ignorance could be branded upon a person than to say they knew "neither letters nor how to swim" <note>original: *nec litteras, nec natare*. This was a common Greek proverb used to describe a completely uneducated person.</note>. As a result, later generations immediately adopted this as a proverb against the dull-witted and the utterly sluggish, and this habit of speaking still remains today; for even if the skill of swimming does not receive the same honors it was granted in past centuries, at least it lies neither entirely neglected nor useless. 

In my judgment, the primary reason our ancestors valued the knowledge of swimming so highly was this: in those early times, in any republic, brave men were honored above all others (as Aristotle writes), as if the safety of the cities and the expansion of the empire depended on them alone. For this reason, everyone—or at least the majority of the nobles and even the common people—devoted themselves from their very cradles to the acquisition of strength and fortitude. Therefore, so that men might better escape dangers or fear them less by trusting in the art of swimming—whether in naval battles, which were then fought more frequently, or in crossing shallows and rivers—they extolled the mastery of swimming. Indeed, soldiers were often forced to enter the water and were drowned because they did not know how to swim, as Xenophon records happened to the army of Cyrus <margin>On the expedition of Cyrus the Younger</margin>. By this same reasoning, the ancient Romans (as Vegetius writes <margin>Book 1 on military matters, chapter 10</margin>), whom so many wars and continuous dangers had taught military discipline, chose the Field of Mars <note>The *Campus Martius*, a public area in ancient Rome used for military training and exercise.</note> near the Tiber, so that in the former they might engage in weapons practice, and in the latter they might wash away sweat and dust, and at the same time

...at the same time they might learn to swim thoroughly; so that by these arguments, and by the authority of Vegetius <note>Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus was a Roman writer of the 4th century known for his treatise on military matters, *De Re Militari*.</note>, it is easy to judge that military gymnastics did not lack the exercise of swimming. Furthermore, in later times, swimming is found to have been used not only for the reasons mentioned, but Antyllus <note>A Greek physician of the 2nd century AD famous for his surgical techniques.</note> left it recorded that it was approved by gymnastic doctors for the preservation of health and the cure of several ailments. Galen seems to have felt the same in his first book *To Glaucon*, where he allows those suffering from a tertian fever <note>A fever that recurs every third day, typically associated with malaria.</note> to be anointed, to enter the bath, to be moistened there, and, if they wish, even to swim. Indeed, that swimming was held as a form of exercise is persuaded by the very nature of it—beyond the authority of Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler and physician to Emperor Julian.</note>, who treated it among other exercises and distinguished it from simple washing <margin>Book 7 of the Collections</margin> (about which he later wrote most extensively in his tenth book). This is because in this kind of motion the entire body is notably both moved and exerted, such that Aristotle once <margin>23rd section of Problems, Problem 3.</margin> did not consider it inept to compare it to running; and Galen wrote that the boys <margin>Book 4, On the Affected Parts</margin> of his time were accustomed to engage in **athletic games** <note>original: γυμναστικὰς παιδιὰς</note> in the waters. 

How such an exercise was performed was passed over in silence by almost everyone as if it were a most common thing <margin>Oribasius, book 6, chapter 27.</margin>, with the single exception of Antyllus. He maintained that those about to swim should first be moderately anointed and their bodies pre-heated with rubbing, and then they ought to cast themselves immediately into the water—as if everyone swimming for the sake of health observed these rules. Regarding the place where the exercise of swimming was performed, I have observed among the authors that it was sometimes done in the gymnasiums themselves or private baths, and sometimes outdoors. 

In the gymnasiums, they swam in two ways: either in a pool <note>The Latin term *piscina* literally means "fish pond," but came to refer to swimming pools.</note>, which we demonstrated above was located in the cold room <term>frigidarium: the cooling-off room in a Roman bath complex</term> (even though among Varro and other authors of the Latin language, *piscinis* are believed to properly signify places dedicated to feeding and fattening fish); or in those large basins <note>The author uses *labris*, referring to large, often stone, tubs or basins.</note> which are still seen in Rome. That they swam in pools which were built in the cold room of the baths—which Seneca records were sometimes surrounded by Thasian stone <note>A high-quality white marble from the Greek island of Thasos.</note>—is most clearly shown by Caecilius Pliny. In the <margin>Letters 7 and 13, book 2.</margin> second book of his Letters, describing his villa with great precision, he writes thus about his baths: "From there, the cold room of the bath is spacious and expansive, in the opposite walls of which two immersion basins <note>original: baptisteria. In this context, these are plunging pools or tubs, not religious fonts.</note> are curved as if projected outward, abundantly large enough if you consider swimming in the nearest part; nearby is the anointing room, the heating system <note>original: hypocastum [hypocaustum], the Roman underfloor heating system.</note>, and the furnace room <note>original: propnigeum, the area where the bath fires were tended.</note>; soon there are two rooms of the bath, more elegant than sumptuous." But he explains this more clearly in book 5, where, describing his Tuscan estate, he includes these details among others: "Then the large and cheerful undressing room <note>original: apodyterium.</note> of the bath leads to the cold room, in which there is a large immersion basin, should you wish to swim more broadly or in warmer water." From all of which it is clear enough,

Unless we wish to say that Martial was speaking instead of the public pool, which we can understand existed in Rome from many sources—and especially from the fragment of the "Regions" <note>The *Notitia Dignitatum* or similar Roman topographical lists that categorized the city's districts.</note> found under the Capitoline portico. Whatever swimming was performed outside of the gymnasia or private baths was done sometimes in very wide springs, sometimes in lakes, sometimes in rivers, and sometimes in the sea itself.

->**On Hunting. Chapter XV.**<-

<margin>In the book *On Exercise with the Small Ball*.</margin>
There exists a most excellent opinion of Galen <note>The influential 2nd-century Roman physician.</note> that, out of all physical exercises, that one undoubtedly appears most useful which is able not only to tire the body but also to delight the mind. For this reason, those should be considered most wise who invented hunting as a form of bodily exercise; in it, through a wonderful method, labor is so tempered by pleasure and a certain desire for praise that it cannot easily be judged whether the movement of the body or the mind is greater. Added to this is the fact that nature herself, which produced all animals for the sake of man, seems to prescribe and approve of hunting (as Aristotle wrote), since in this activity man seeks to acquire his rightful possessions, and a spectacle is presented that is unstained by any crime, but rather increases both the strength of the body and the vigor of the mind.

From this, everyone can see how prudently those physicians acted who so highly valued hunting for exercising the body and keeping it strong and healthy. Indeed, those ancient fathers of medicine—Chiron, Machaon, Podalirius, and Aesculapius <note>Chiron was a centaur and teacher of heroes; Aesculapius was the god of medicine, and Machaon and Podalirius were his sons, the surgeons of the Greek army at Troy.</note>—burned with such zeal for it (as Xenophon <note>A Greek historian and student of Socrates who wrote a famous treatise on hunting.</note> reports) that they thought no less labor should be spent on it daily than on the arts in which they so greatly excelled. ### B O O K  T H R E E

...are found most abundantly in the exercise of hunting, and especially in that kind which is not occupied with the deception of birds, but is laboriously engaged in capturing land animals without trickery—the kind we wish our present discussion to be primarily understood as addressing. <margin>D</margin> And lest I seem to put forward this opinion too boldly without the testimony of illustrious authors, I shall endeavor to follow the path already begun and demonstrate how every form of gymnastics has utilized the exercise of hunting. 

For Plato most richly testified that hunting was thought to provide the greatest help in attaining military courage. After he had distinguished the discipline of hunting into three species in the *Theaetetus* <note>A Socratic dialogue concerning the nature of knowledge.</note> and in the seventh book of the *Laws*—namely, the hunting of aquatic, winged, and land animals—and having rejected the other two for the education of youth, he concludes thus regarding the hunting of land animals at the end of the seventh book of the *Laws*: 

<note>original Greek: πεζῶν δὴ μόνον θήρευσίς τε, καὶ ἄγρα λοιπὴ τοῖς παρ' ἡμῖν ἀθληταῖς, ὧν ἡ μὲν τ' εὑδόντ' αὖ, καὶ μέρη νυκτερεῖα κληθεῖσα, ἀργῶν ἀνδρῶν. οὐκ ἀξία ἐπαίνε, οὐδ' ἡ τ' διαπαύματα πόνων ἔχουσα ἀρκυσίτε, καὶ πάγαις, ἀλλ' ὁ φιλοπόνου ψυχῆς νίκη χειρουμένων τὴν ἄγριον τῶν θηρίων ῥώμην, μόνη δὴ πᾶσι λοιπὴ καὶ ἀρίστη τῶν τετραπόδων, ἵπποις, καὶ κυσί, καὶ τοῖς ἑαυτῶν θήρᾳ σώμασιν, ὧν ἁπάντ' κρατοῦσι δρόμοις, καὶ πληγαῖς καὶ βολαῖς αὐτόχειρες θηρεύοντες ὅσοις ἀνδρείας θείας ἐπιμελές.</note> 

That is: "Therefore, only the hunting or capture of land animals remains for our athletes. Of these, the kind that pursues sleeping animals (known by the specific name 'night hunting') is suited to lazy men and deserves no praise; <margin>E</margin> nor does that kind which, by using nets and snares, allows for intervals of rest and does not attempt to overcome the strength of wild beasts through the victory of a hardworking soul. Hence, he leaves only that as the best form, in which men hunt four-footed animals with horses, dogs, and their own bodies. They surpass all others who, caring for the possession of 'divine courage,' devote their efforts to hunting with their own hands by running, striking, and throwing." 

From these words it clearly appears how much Plato believed hunting contributes to military practitioners in acquiring what he calls "divine military courage." We have indicated above how he includes these practitioners under the name of <term>athletes</term> <note>original Greek: ἀθλητῶν (athlētōn); here used to mean those who train for excellence, not just competitors in games.</note>. <margin>F</margin> Xenophon seems to have explained this point even more clearly than Plato; in his *Cyropaedia* <note>The Education of Cyrus, a semi-fictional biography of Cyrus the Great, often used as a manual on leadership and education.</note> he left it written as follows regarding Cyrus: 

<note>original Greek: τῆς πολεμικῆς δ' ἕνεκα ἀσκήσεως ἐπὶ θήραν ἐξῆγεν, ὥσπερ ἀσκεῖν ταῦτα ᾤετο χρῆναι, ταύτην ἡγούμενος καὶ ὅλως ἀρίστην ἄσκησιν πολεμικῶν εἶναι, καὶ ἱππικῆς δὲ ἀληθεστάτην.</note> 

That is: "For the sake of military training, he led them out to the hunt, as he thought they ought to practice these things, considering this to be both the best of all military exercises and the truest form of horsemanship."

### F O U R T H [BOOK]

...[of training] and the most true equestrian [discipline]. In this passage, no one fails to see how clearly he judged hunting to be the most conducive of all activities to military exercise. For this reason, he later exhorts young men in his book *On Hunting* <note>Referring to Xenophon’s *Cynegeticus*.</note> to take up this exercise for two primary reasons: first, because it provides good health to their bodies; and second, because it prepares them exceptionally well for war, turning them into vigorous soldiers fit for handling all other affairs. 

But Aristotle did not merely wish the study of hunting to be conducive to military <margin>Politics, book 1, chapter 5.</margin> exercise; indeed, he explicitly made it a part of that very discipline. Thus, no further doubt remains that hunting should be said to have held a place among the other exercises serving military <term>gymnastics</term> <note>In this context, gymnastics refers to the broad category of physical training and athletic discipline, not just modern acrobatics.</note>. Moreover, the fact that the profession of athletics did not lack this kind of exercise is demonstrated by the hunts frequently presented in the amphitheatres by the Emperors and celebrated in a wonderful manner by Latin writers. Although these [spectacles] appear to have been very different from our own style of hunting, they nevertheless bore its likeness; specifically, when the <term>bestiarii</term> <note>Fighters in Roman arenas who specialized in battling wild animals.</note> and others condemned to death contended against wild beasts right up until the death of one or the other (as Suetonius reports), in the same way that hunters are accustomed to fight against less monstrous beasts. 

Regarding the "medical gymnastics"—that is, the fact that doctors approved of hunting for obtaining and maintaining health and a good bodily condition—I believe this is clear to everyone. For, in addition to the opinion of Xenophon <margin>2. *On the Preservation of Health*. In the book *On the Exercise of the Small Ball*.</margin> already cited, we have the authority of Galen. He placed hunting among the exercises serving the health of the body, and in his work on the <term>game of the small ball</term> <note>Referring to Galen's treatise *De parvae pilae exercitio*, which praises ball games for being accessible to everyone.</note>, he judged hunting inferior to that game only because it requires greater equipment and is therefore not convenient for craftsmen or those entangled in civic business. Furthermore, Pliny the Younger suggests that he preserved a healthy body through hunting, <margin>Book 5, *Letters*.</margin> and besides the arguments of others, the single testimony of the most learned Arab physician, Rhazes, may suffice. In his writings, one reads that it happened during a certain plague that, while almost everyone else perished, the hunters alone <margin>In the 30th [book] of the *Continens*, treatise 13, chapter 3.</margin> escaped unharmed because of the excellent health they had gained through constant exercise. 

We should not, moreover, pass over in silence the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, by whom Dionysius of Syracuse was once received for dinner. He remarked that he found no pleasure in the food set before him; to which the cook immediately replied that this happened because he had not labored in the hunt or in the race. Therefore, he lacked the thirst and hunger which served as the seasoning for the Lacedaemonians' feasts. Thus, we should in no way be surprised if we read that Mithridates <note>Mithridates VI of Pontus, a famous enemy of Rome known for his physical endurance and study of medicine.</note>, whom we know to have been so devoted to health and life, gave himself so greedily to the work of hunting that for seven years he used the roof of neither city nor countryside. Therefore, it can now be manifest to anyone how much [benefit] in exercising for health—

### BOOK III.

...health <note>Original: *valetudine*. The sentence completes from the previous page.</note> of their bodies, hunting was highly esteemed among the ancients. Since there were many types of it—some conducted with nets, others with snares, birdlime, and fowling; others with carnivorous and raptorial birds, others with dogs, and arrows, whether plain or poisoned; which Pliny records <margin>Book 25, chapter 5.</margin> that Gaulish hunters were accustomed to dip in <term>hellebore</term> <note>A plant used in antiquity for medicinal and poisonous purposes; here, it was believed to tenderize the meat of the prey.</note>, because, once the wound was cut away, the meat was found to be more tender—others were carried out with weapons, sometimes against flying creatures and sometimes against land beasts. I believe those hunts were considered more suitable in which men, whether traveling or running on foot or carried on horses, pursued wild animals with dogs and weapons; surely no one would deny that these activities both exercise the body more, sharpen all the senses, and bring greater pleasure to the mind. 

For regarding that hunting which is practiced in these times with <term>hawks</term> <note>Original: *accipitribus*.</note> and <term>goshawks</term> <note>Original: *asturibus*.</note> against birds, I cannot affirm whether the ancient physicians recommended it. For although Aristotle <margin>Book 7 of *The History of Animals*, chapter 36.</margin> recorded that in that part of Thrace which was once called <term>Cedropolis</term> <note>A legendary city in Thrace mentioned by ancient naturalists where humans and hawks supposedly hunted in cooperation.</note>, men were accustomed to fowl in the marshes in partnership with hawks; nevertheless, that kind of hunting seems very different from ours. In that instance, the men themselves used sticks held in their hands to stir the reeds and bushes, so that when the birds were flushed out by the noise and took flight, the hawks pursued them from above. Struck with fear of the hawks, the birds would dive back to the ground, where they were struck with clubs and captured by the hunters, and portions of the catch were then distributed to the hawks. Our hunting, however, is performed with hawks and goshawks that have been specifically trained. Julius Firmicus implies that the ancients were ignorant of this method and that it was invented in the age of the Emperor Constantine; just as they were also ignorant of that hunting which is practiced with dogs trained with a certain skill, and with nets, against quails, partridges, and pheasants. But enough of these matters.

# THE ART OF GYMNASTICS
## BOOK FOUR

->*Chapter 1. On the method of procedure and the use of exercise.*<-

<margin>B</margin> Since we have now made clear, as far as is permitted, the origin of gymnastics, its types, and the sub-types <note>Original: *specierum (ut sic dicam) species*.</note> handed down and practiced by the ancients, it remains to complete the design of our treatise. To do this, we must first provide the universal or common rules for all exercises. By following these, everyone may not only recognize individual exercises but also understand them. Next, we must move on to the particular and more specific details, so that we may easily distinguish what is beneficial and what is harmful in each specific exercise—allowing us to embrace what we have learned to be good and avoid what is bad. Indeed, it would have been a nearly pointless labor and a vain study to investigate exercises so celebrated among the ancients unless those who choose to read these writings of ours—and use them for the benefit of their health—had a clear and thorough understanding of the utility and advantages for which the ancient <term>gymnasts</term> <note>In this context, professional trainers who also understood the medical effects of movement.</note> established them and brought them into the daily practice of physicians.

And in this task, I believe I must labor all the more because <margin>C</margin> Galen <note>A Greek physician and philosopher (c. 129–216 AD) whose works dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note>, following the views of Hippocrates and Plato, cries out that in all arts—but especially in medicine—universal methods are of little help unless they are joined by the treatment of particulars and the observation of individuals. By these means, things discovered through a general method are more certainly confirmed, and their similarities and differences are properly distinguished—for it is from these, as Plato wrote in the *Phaedrus*, that all human deception takes its start. 

Therefore, walking this path praised by ancient philosophers and physicians, we shall take our beginning for everything to be discussed from the very nature of exercise itself. Since we define exercise as a "certain movement of the body," and since certain differences necessarily follow every movement—namely, intensity <note>Original: *vehementia*.</note>, relaxation, speed, slowness, and the like—and furthermore, in every kind of local motion, the body that is to be moved, the place where it must move, the time in which it is moved, and the measure and manner of the motion itself are required by necessity...

The author argues that general rules must be balanced with individual observation, citing Galen and Plato to justify the need for specific medical guidelines for exercise.</summary>

L I B E R

...may follow, and having refuted the opinions of those who have judged exercise poorly, we will first declare those differences that result from exercise. Second, we will demonstrate which bodies are fit for exercise and which are unfit. Third, we will describe what kind of place is necessary for those who strive to either strengthen or preserve their health to devote their efforts to exercise. Fourth, we will discuss what time is considered opportune for exercising bodies; for just as all bodies do not tolerate every type of exercise, similarly, not every place nor every time is suited to everyone.

But, because this treatise would remain incomplete unless a measure of exercise were prescribed, I will therefore add fifth how much one ought to exercise. I will also add sixth the manner in which exercise should be approached, and thus, descending to examine the qualities of particular exercises, I will endeavor to leave nothing out that can rightfully be desired in this matter, and which was established by **Hippocrates** <note>The Greek "Father of Medicine," active in the 5th century BC.</note> or **Polybus** <note>Hippocrates' son-in-law, often credited with writing some works in the Hippocratic Corpus.</note> as necessary knowledge for handling labors <note>Original: *laboribus*, a term often used by ancient doctors to mean physical exertion or exercise.</note> or exercises.

1. On diet.

But before I begin this task, I judge that I must first say this: all these things we are about to hand down in this fourth volume are of such great moment in the entire business of exercise that, if they are either ignored or neglected, exercises bring about harm rather than any benefits. Indeed, as has been brilliantly written by **Galen**, innumerable exercises, when administered opportunely and prudently, are designed to correct and utterly erase errors—both those made by nature in the temperament of the body, and those committed by men in their way of living.

Such is said to have happened to **Marcus Tullius Cicero** <note>The famous Roman orator and statesman.</note>, whom **Plutarch** <note>The Greek biographer and philosopher.</note> writes was afflicted with poor stomach health, but so strengthened the habit of his body through opportune and measured exercises that he rendered himself robust for many great struggles.

Conversely, if these same exercises are done rashly and without regard for opportunity, they not only corrupt and sometimes utterly destroy the best constitutions granted by nature, but also secretly induce many and most savage types of diseases. Thus, it happens that those who could lead a healthy life and require no medicines through moderate and opportune exercise are instead tortured by almost perpetual weakness due to negligence in exercising, or they find themselves in need of constant medication.

# B O O K   F O U R T H

### Refutation of the opinion of those who condemned exercise in healthy people, and on the necessity and benefit of exercising. Chapter II.

<margin>Galen, *On the Preservation of Health*, book 2, chapter 11.</margin>
If, therefore, such and so great benefits of exercise exist, those who have not blushed to spread perverse and entirely harmful opinions regarding the exercising of bodies must be greatly refuted. For **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire (129–c. 216 AD), whose works dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> writes that these critics were divided into three sects in ancient times: some who completely abolished all exercises as being harmful rather than useful to health; others who wanted no one to be forbidden from exercising; and others who, walking a middle path, indicated that only those accustomed to it should exercise, while denying exercise to the unaccustomed. I consider it worthwhile to both recount and refute the decrees of all these groups, lest by remaining silent we seem to criticize them without cause, or if they are left unrefuted, they might appeal to some and be accepted as if they were conducive to health.

Therefore **Erasistratus** <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–250 BC) known for his descriptions of the heart and brain; he often challenged traditional medical views.</note>, the successor of **Praxagoras** and **Chrysippus** in medicine, as well as **Asclepiades of Prusa** <note>A popular Greek physician in Rome (c. 124–40 BC) who rejected the "humoral" theory in favor of a theory involving atoms and pores.</note>, a physician of great authority, believed—among other absurd opinions they held regarding remedies—that the use of medicines and bloodletting should almost be abolished for the sick. For the healthy, they established that physical exercises contribute nothing to good health, and they were led by several reasons to assert this latter point.

The first reason was that health is situated in the <term>just temperament</term> <note>The idea of a perfect "tuning" or balance of bodily qualities.</note> of all the <term>humors</term> <note>The four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient doctors believed must remain balanced for a person to be healthy.</note>. Indeed, the humors are produced and kept in moderation through the moderate intake and <term>concoction</term> <note>The ancient medical term for digestion, which was viewed as a process of "cooking" food within the body using internal heat.</note> of food. Any concoction is better perfected by rest, as sleep indicates, and is hindered and not infrequently corrupted by movement such as exercise; hence, the harmony of the humors itself is necessarily depraved, and thus health itself is destroyed.

The second reason was that all exercise has <term>labor</term> <note>original: *laborem*; in this context, it refers to the physical toil or strain of exertion.</note> annexed to it. Just as labor appears in some way an enemy to our nature, so too does it take away the delight and sweetness of which a healthy person should never be deprived; and thus it hinders rather than profits health.

The third reason was that present health is preserved by the same means through which lost health is recovered. Since lost health is restored through rest and not through exercise, it follows that it is also preserved through rest and not through any movement.

The fourth reason was that heat is increased too much by exercise, and consequently the <term>native moisture</term> <note>original: *humidum natiuum*; the essential biological fluid or "oil" that ancient physicians believed fueled the body's internal fire and determined lifespan.</note> is exhausted. No one doubts that these two things—excessive heat and the drying of moisture—corrupt rather than preserve health, since health consists in moderate heat and in a proportionate amount of native moisture.

<summary>This page begins a historical refutation of ancient medical schools, such as those of Erasistratus and Asclepiades, who argued that exercise was unnecessary or even harmful to the balance of the body's humors and internal heat.</summary>
<keywords>Galen, Erasistratus, Asclepiades of Prusa, humors, concoction, native moisture, digestion vs. exercise, ancient medical sects</keywords>
