<page-num>192</page-num>
<header>BOOK</header>

<margin>D</margin>
...[as if health] consists entirely in **moisture**. They added further that many people held in prisons for a long time lead a healthy life despite being unable to find any opportunity for exercise; from this, it would appear that health can exist without such activity. Induced by so many reasons, those physicians both believed that bodily exercises in no way contribute to health and attempted to persuade others of the same. However, everyone will clearly confess that they have strayed vehemently from the truth if they are willing to consider thoroughly both the necessity and the nature or utility of exercise. 

For since small particles <note>original: "corpuscula." In the medical theories of Asclepiades, these were tiny atoms that flowed through "pores" in the body; health depended on their smooth movement.</note> continually flow out from our bodies—which, if they were not restored, would very easily cause the loss of life—we always have a need for food as long as we live, so that the departing parts may be regenerated. However, no matter how appropriate and blameless the food chosen may be, it is never so perfectly converted into the substance of our limbs that useless waste <note>original: "excrementa." In this context, it refers to any metabolic byproduct the body needs to expel, including sweat and vapor, not just feces.</note> does not remain. Unless these were continually pushed outward, it would not be difficult for them to accumulate over a period of time to the point that they would suffocate the **natural heat** <note>The internal fire or vital warmth believed to be the source of life and digestion in ancient physiology.</note>. 

Sagacious nature, foreseeing this, prepared many passages and ways for purging these wastes. Since these passages are undoubtedly insufficient for emptying out everything, we require exercise so that these materials, worn down by movement, may be separated from us—some through sweat, others through sensible and insensible exhalations. Otherwise, if such waste products are retained through leisure and sluggishness, there is a danger that innumerable types of fatal diseases may be generated. And for that reason, **Socrates** spoke excellently in **Plato's** *Theaetetus* when he said that the condition of the body is destroyed by leisure and rest, but preserved by exercise and movement. 

<margin>E</margin>
<margin>Epidemics, Book 6, Section 4.</margin>
He had perhaps learned this from that oracle of **Hippocrates**, where, in briefly explaining the method for leading a healthy life, he wrote: <note>original: "ἄσκησις ὑγίης, ἀκορίη τροφῆς, ἀκονίη πόνων" (askēsis hygiēs, akoriē trophēs, akoniē ponōn)</note> **"Exercise is health, moderation in food, and unwearied toil."** This means that the preservation of health is found in avoiding a satiety of food and keeping bodily exercises in frequent use. Added to this is the fact that the natural heat, once unburdened of the weight of waste through exercise, is made more robust; the limbs acquire greater firmness, and all the powers of the body become more ready and stronger in performing their proper operations. 

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>On Regimen, Book 1.</margin>
Thus, **Hippocrates** (or perhaps **Polybus** <note>A student and son-in-law of Hippocrates, often credited with writing some works in the Hippocratic Corpus.</note>) rightly said: <note>original: "ἄνθρωπος ἐσθίων οὐ δύναται ὑγιαίνειν, ἢν μὴ πονέῃ" (anthrōpos esthiōn ou dynatai hygiainein, ēn mē poneē)</note> **"A person who eats cannot be healthy unless he toils."** But lest we seem to refute **Erasistratus** and **Asclepiades** without cause, we will weigh the nature of their arguments. First, we concede that health is situated in the balance of the humors <note>The four vital fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance was thought to determine health.</note>, and that this balance is preserved by the best production and **concoction** <note>The "cooking" or digestion of food by the body's natural heat.</note> of juices; nevertheless, we maintain that digestion itself is produced both by rest and by exercise at the proper time,

**A** But exercise, when applied moderately, is of no small help. For as we were saying just now, the **natural heat** <note>The "internal fire" believed by ancient physicians to drive digestion and life; it was thought that waste could "smother" this fire if not expelled.</note> is rendered stronger and more stirred up when it is relieved of the burden of superfluities through exercise. Once excited in this way, it prepares better **concoctions** <term>concoctio: the process of "cooking" or digesting food in the stomach via internal heat</term>; therefore, I do not see why timely exercises would not provide the best concoction of juices and, at the same time, contribute greatly to the preservation of health. While those critics claimed that untimely movement corrupts digestion—and we certainly agree with them—if they asserted that *timely* movement (which the ancient physicians defined as exercise) produces the same ill effect, then their dogmas are clearly seen by anyone to be based on open falsehood. This is even more certain because deeper sleep comes to those who have exercised, and during such sleep, better digestions are completed. Thus, Galen spoke with good reason in the first book of *On Aliments*, saying that even poor foods do not greatly harm those devoted to 

**B** exercise; for it is to these people that deep sleep comes as a result of their labors, and such sleep is followed by the best digestions. Furthermore, as for their second reason—where they asserted that exercise carries with it an element of toil, and therefore removes the pleasure associated with health and health itself—we partly confirm this and partly deny it. We certainly do not deny that exercise, which we have defined as a vigorous movement that alters the breath, will be somewhat laborious and, at the time it is performed, will lack enjoyment. However, we say that health can sometimes remain despite some discomfort, provided that the discomfort does not exceed moderation nor last for a long time. Such is the discomfort associated with exercise: it is momentary, not immoderate, and indeed is the preparation for a greater and longer-lasting delight—namely, because it frees the body from superfluities, and every natural evacuation, according to Aristotle's opinion, <margin>Problems, section 5</margin> 

**C** brings delight. To the third reason, by which even the philosopher Porphyry was led to condemn the use of meat for the sake of health, <margin>*On Abstinence from Animal Food*, Book 2.</margin> we respond that it is entirely false that current health is preserved by the same means through which absent health is recovered. For as Celsus and Pliny testify, even Asclepiades and Erasistratus <margin>Celsus, Book 1, in the preface; Pliny, Book 26, chapter 1.</margin> used to cure many ailments through a fast of three or four days; yet even a fool would affirm that such fasting is most harmful to the preservation of health. Furthermore, Hippocrates and his followers proved through infinite experiments that medicines recover health if they are applied at the right time; yet these same men openly declared that healthy people are not only not helped by medicines, but that their health is primarily damaged by them. From this, it is clear enough that the proposition they assumed wanders far from the truth. Lest my speech become too long, I will not bring forward into the open everything that would serve to refute it.

I would wish to bring a middle ground. Their fourth reason was that heat is increased by **D** exercises and, because of this, exceeds its proper limit—that is, moderation—and consequently the **innate moisture** <term>innate moisture: the vital fluid believed to act as the "fuel" for the body's internal heat</term>, upon which the entire state of health depends, is exhausted. However, it will easily be proven that this is by no means true if one considers exercise administered properly, just as the ancient physicians decreed. Although such exercise may increase the **natural heat** <note>The internal fire that drives metabolism and life</note> and drain off superfluous humors, if it is applied in the manner we shall demonstrate below, it is so far from consuming the innate moisture or undermining health in any way that it actually preserves it. It does this by dissipating external humors and scraping away the superfluities that could disturb or infect that very moisture; at the same time, it makes the moisture vivid with heat and makes the flesh and other members <margin>Commentary 3 on *On the Articulations*, aphorism 1.</margin> firmer and purer. Because of this, Galen most elegantly compared the flesh **E** of those who use exercise to "cheeses already exactly curdled" <note>original Greek: τυροῖς ἀκριβῶς ἤδη πεπηγόσι</note>, and the flesh of those who do not use it to "cheeses still undergoing curdling" <note>original Greek: τυροῖς ἔτι πηγνυμένοις</note>. 

Furthermore, regarding what they added last—that those shut up in prisons live a healthy life without any exercise—if they mean without "exercise" properly defined (which we defined as a vigorous motion), they speak the truth, and we also agree. But if they speak of "exercise" as it is commonly understood, as was their opinion, we say that those shut up in prison used either **friction** <note>therapeutic rubbing or massage</note> or some other motion. Otherwise, if they ceased entirely from all movement, it is impossible for them to live healthy for a long time, since we see many people every day grow sick and even perish in prisons for that very reason. Whence Averroes, intending to prove the depravity <margin>6 *Colliget*, chapter 2.</margin> arising from the deprivation of exercise, took his argument from prisoners; namely, those who (as he said) have **sallow faces** <note>original Latin: *facies cauticas*; likely referring to a burnt or unhealthy, yellowish complexion</note>, **F** impure color, and all their bodily functions impaired. He said this happens no more to humans than to other animals that stay hidden, or to birds kept in cages. If any are found who live healthily in prisons without any exercise, they are extremely rare, and formed with such a strong bodily constitution that they can stoutly resist all harms. 

Nor should it be thought that Hippocrates in any way contradicts our opinion when, describing that pestilential constitution of the air in Thasos and recounting the wicked diseases born in it, he said: "These things happened to the adolescents, the young men, those in their prime, and of these, especially those frequenting the wrestling schools and gymnasiums." <note>original Greek: Ἐγίνετο δὲ ταῦτα μειρακίοισι, νέοισιν, ἀκμάζουσι, καὶ τούτων τοῖσι περὶ παλαίστρων, καὶ γυμνάσια πλείστοισι.</note> <margin>1 *Epidemics*, commentary 3, aphorism 11.</margin> That is, these things happened to adolescents, young men, those in the flower of their age, and especially to those who were being exercised in the **palaestras** <term>palaestra: a Greek wrestling school</term> and gymnasiums—

Having refuted the false opinion of those who asserted that bodily exercise contributes nothing to health, let us now move to refute those who judged that exercises should be enjoined upon everyone without any distinction. Reason itself and the authority of Galen persuade us that these people held a better opinion than the previous group, yet they were still mistaken. For these men, noting that Hippocrates had uttered this indefinite proposition—"Labors should precede food" <note>original: 'Labores cibum praecedant'</note>—claimed that the Old Man <note>A traditional respectful title for Hippocrates</note> had commanded that all people should exercise themselves before taking a meal. Furthermore, they strove to confirm their opinion with other reasons. The first of these was that all humans are naturally inclined toward exercise, just as children seem to attest as soon as they are brought into the light of day. They argued that inclinations granted to everyone by nature ought to be put into use by everyone, and should by no means be rendered void—all the more so when it is manifest in many cases that nature bestows those inclinations for some excellent good. For example, no one denies that in the greater part of humanity, the inclination toward exercise, when put into use, provides that most excellent good: health. Another reason that moved these men to hold a similar opinion was that if all humans necessarily generate **excrements** <term>excrements: 'excrementa', referring not just to feces but to all metabolic waste products and superfluous humors</term> which must be continually expelled—lest, increased and accumulated by their own force, they spoil the **natural color** <note>original: 'natiuum colorem'; the vital heat and healthy complexion of the body</note>...

Persuaded by these reasons, they preached that exercises should be enjoined upon all people everywhere, at least before food; but they themselves are caught clearly hallucinating. For that authority of Hippocrates, which they thought favored them, by no means suggests (as Galen rightly perceived) that it is beneficial for all men to exercise; rather, the author was there discussing the order of exercise and food. He wanted to imply that for those for whom it is expedient to exercise, the exercise ought to precede the meal. The first reason by which they supported their opinion, although true and confirmed by Plato and Galen, nevertheless helps their argument very little. For men are indeed naturally inclined toward simple movement, and there is no one—provided they lead a healthy life—who remains numb in perpetual idleness and never moves. But no reason dictates, nor would anyone of sound mind pronounce, that these same people are inclined to those **violent movements** which we call "exercises" when they are governed by certain rules. From this, it appears that by reason of natural inclination, by no means should everyone be judged fit for exercise. To the second reason—which certainly does not lack much probability—we respond that the waste products continuously collected in our bodies must necessarily be removed; however, that this evacuation is performed solely by "exercises" in the proper sense of the word is false...

**A** is entirely false: since baths, massage, <term>insensible transpiration <gloss>the release of bodily vapors through the skin without visible sweating</gloss></term>, and <term>gestations <gloss>passive movements, such as being carried in a litter or riding in a carriage</gloss></term> without any violent motion can very well satisfy such an evacuation of waste. **B** Nevertheless, we confess the conclusion to be false; for it does not follow that "the weakest must exercise, therefore everyone else must." Indeed, those who are immoderately hot and dry, even if they are not weak, do not require exercise for the reasons stated before. This is because it is not their strength that prohibits exercise, but rather a bodily <term>intemperance <gloss>an imbalance of the four primary qualities: heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</gloss></term>, which, when increased by exercise, indicates that such movement is entirely harmful. He concludes, therefore, that by no means do all men require "exercises" properly so called, and those who asserted this have <note>original: "toto caelo aberraſſe"; literally "wandered by the whole width of heaven," a Latin idiom meaning to be completely mistaken</note> missed the mark entirely. We do admit, however, that exercise in the common sense—which encompasses even the smallest movements of the body—cannot be denied to any healthy person.

**C** This is because nothing is found to be as destructive and fatal to the health of both humans and <term>brutes <gloss>animals</gloss></term> as the cessation of all movement or total idleness. ->*Those who maintained that only those accustomed to it should exercise are refuted.*<-

### Chapter IV.

The false opinion of those who judged that only the accustomed ought to be exercised, and the unaccustomed should not be exercised at all, remains to be condemned. Although their sentiment presents a certain appearance of truth and deserves to be preferred over the other two views by right, it is nonetheless not entirely free from error, as it seems to attribute too much to custom <note>original: *assuetudo*; the concept that repetitive habit becomes "second nature"</note> and places it, as it were, above the conditions of nature. However, lest we be thought to unjustly refute their views, we shall set forth both the reasons that led them to this opinion and the errors they committed, so that the truth may more easily shine forth to a fair judge.

These men, then, having read in the prince of physicians, Hippocrates <margin>2nd Book of Aphorisms, 49. 50.</margin>, that those who are accustomed to bear their usual labors, even if they are weak and old, bear them more easily than those who are unaccustomed, even if they are strong and young; and that things which have been customary for a long time, even if they are of a poorer quality, cause less trouble than unaccustomed things, assertively pronounced that no one unaccustomed to exercises and labors should be committed to them, otherwise they would be greatly harmed. They argued that only those accustomed should exercise—namely, those whom experience demonstrates to have stronger exercised parts and who can therefore resist labors without harm. 

To this they added further reasons: first, that all those who become accustomed to anything largely choose a custom that suits their nature; for having experienced things that harm them, they reject those, and cling to those that help. Hence, those accustomed to exercises ought to be kept in them as something familiar to them; but those who have contracted a habit of resting should by no means be removed from it, as if they have learned by experience that they are harmed by exercise and find benefit in rest. 

Second, that according to the views of philosophers and physicians, custom passes into nature, and therefore those who change their custom are harmed no differently than those who try to pervert nature and strive against its impulses. 

Third, that if those accustomed to rest have lived healthily for a long time in that way, it is likely they will complete the rest of their life's course healthy in that same state of rest; on the contrary, it is to be feared that they might incur various illnesses if they change. Since it seems necessary that those changing to a contrary way of life, and other subsequent factors, are changed into a contrary state of health. Led by reasons of this kind, therefore, they constantly affirmed that custom ought not to be changed, and thus those accustomed to exercise should be exercised, and those accustomed to rest should remain in rest.

**A** [who are] accustomed to them. But, as I said, although these followers pursued a less blameworthy opinion, they were not themselves free from errors. This is because Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> judged that in all matters one must transition to unaccustomed things, lest we be forced to descend to them later and suffer more grievous harms. This is especially necessary when the things we are accustomed to are excessively destructive—such as a complete cessation of exercise. Therefore, the cited authority of Hippocrates ought to be understood in this sense: he wished (as we are also compelled to agree, whether we like it or not) that accustomed things disturb the body less than unusual ones. However, he did not, because of this, forbid transitioning to unusual things at times, especially when our habits are very bad and the unaccustomed things are much better. Thus, to the first reason, we respond that the assumption is false when understood universally. For just as many people adopt a habit that suits their nature,

**B** so too do many others persist in bad habits that are enemies to their own nature—either enticed by the sweetness of it, or through negligence, or because they are distracted by other studies, or because they are too dull to perceive themselves being harmed. This is exactly what those who are both accustomed and addicted to rest do; they are steeped in the pleasure of quiet and have grown used to it without sensing the offense it causes. It is not that they chose rest because it was truly suitable for them, but rather they chose what we have already proven is an enemy to all mankind. To the second reason, we say that nature and habit <note>original: *consuetudinem*; the "second nature" formed by repetitive behavior</note> indeed differ very little; yet it does not follow from this that habit should never be changed. Indeed, if physicians strive with every skill to correct "wicked natures"—that is, natural <term>intemperies</term> <note>A medical term for an imbalance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.</note>—and to change them for the better so that they may generate health and a good condition in the body, then I do not see why the worst habits cannot likewise be changed by them into 

**C** more honorable and healthy ones. This is especially true because things contracted through habit are more easily cast off than those handed down by nature from the very beginning of our birth. Added to this is the fact that the habit of being idle is dangerous because (as Celsus used to say)
<margin>Book 1, Chapter 3.</margin>
the necessity of labor can suddenly fall upon us. Hippocrates meant to imply this when he said that unaccustomed things disturb the body *less*, not that they do not disturb it at all. Nor should one be praised or approved for having spent a healthy life for a long time in such habits. ...they conceive bad habits within, which they do not perceive for some time, until the wicked <term>humors</term> <note>the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to govern health and temperament</note>, nourished by leisure and increased beyond measure, bring about incurable and most troublesome ailments. For this reason, all who desire a healthy life must strive so that, though raised in bad habits, they do not allow themselves to be deceived by pleasure and ignorance of the harm. Rather, they should strive to withdraw from such habits as soon as possible—yet gradually, and as Hippocrates said, *by gradual approach* <note>original: *ἐν προσαγωγῆς*</note>—holding it as certain that destructive habits ought to be exchanged, even with some discomfort, rather than persisting in them with delight. Let these words suffice for the refutation of those who think wrongly about exercise. Now is the time to show which bodies are suited for exercise, and at what time and in what place; but before we undertake this, we shall briefly run through the different kinds of exercises, as we promised above and as the order of this treatise requires.

->*On the Differences of Exercises. Chapter V.*<-

<margin>
Galen, *On the Preservation of Health*, Book 3, chapters 2, 11, 12.

Whoever among the ancients attempted to study the faculty of exercise and pass it down in writing, they established three primary differences among them: one they called *preparatory exercise* <note>original: *παρασκευαστικὸν γυμνάσιον*</note>, the second *restorative* <note>original: *ἀποθεραπευτικὸν*</note>, and the third simply "exercise." Preparatory or preliminary exercise, according to Galen’s interpretation, was a certain movement moderate in measure but more vigorous and faster in quality. It was performed not only through bodily movement but also through rubbings, oilings, and other similar means. It was used most often after <term>sexual intercourse</term> <note>original: *uenerem*; referring to Venus, the goddess of love and the physical act</note> to treat the body’s porosity or to tighten its looseness, although they also used it sometimes before other heavier exercises. Galen writes that this was characteristic of athletes, so that a transition would not be made from excessive rest to great movement—as if from one extreme to its opposite—without an intermediate state.

It was performed sometimes by rubbings, sometimes by walking, and by other such movements, which served to soften bodies dried out by excessive labor, and to loosen the passages of the body after heavier exercise, after sleepless nights, or after bouts of sorrow; and therefore this movement [is called] by Galen the final...

...is found named as a part of exercise, because almost always after great exertions, they employed this [specific movement] so that they would not pass over immediately to the opposite state of rest; for, on account of its slowness and the frequent rest periods interspersed within it, it held a middle ground between vigorous exercise and complete rest. Furthermore, one reads that "simple exercise" among the medical gymnasts <note>Physicians who specialized in the therapeutic use of physical activity</note> had many distinctions. Some were taken from external factors, others from the methods of use, and others from both the quantity and the qualities of the motion itself. Those taken from external factors were mostly named after the location, such as when the exercise was performed under the open sky, or under a roof, or in "mixed shade" (which the Greeks call *hyposymmige* <note>original: ὑποσύμμιγῆ; a dappled or partial shade</note>). Likewise, distinctions were made when the place was hot, or cold, or of a middle temperature; and furthermore, whether it was plainly dry, or humid, or tempered in a middle way. The differences taken from

<margin>B</margin>
the methods of use were of this sort: the motion was either continuous or intermittent. If continuous, it was either equal or unequal; if intermittent, it was done either in a certain order or without order. Furthermore, it was done either without dust or with dust—and that sometimes in great amounts, sometimes moderate. Similarly, it was performed either without oil or with oil, and with that oil being sometimes a little, sometimes a lot. Moreover, the differences found to be taken from the quantities of the motion itself are such that exercises either lasted for a long time (and were called "many" or "great"), or for a short time, or a moderate time (and were called "few" or "moderate"). There were also differences taken from the quantities of motion regarding the driving force: for if the force was great, it was called a "great exercise"; if small, a "small" one; if moderate, a "moderate" one. Furthermore, I find the differences taken from the qualities by Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the influential 2nd-century Greek physician</note> to be

Another was neither vehement, strong, relaxed, nor languid, but was the middle of all these, and was called **middle** and **moderate**, such as moderate horse-riding and moderate walking.

Of the simple ones, some were performed under the open sky; others under a roof; others in mixed shade; others in a cold place, others in a hot one, others in a moist one, others in a dry one, others in the middle of these. Furthermore, it was either perpetual and constant—and either equal or unequal—or intermittent, and either disordered or ordered; or with much dust, or little, or without dust; or with a little oil, or much, or without oil; or much, or less, or moderate; or swift, quick, and sharp, or tardy and slow, or moderate; or great, and either vehement and robust, or strong; or small, and either relaxed, or languid and weak, or middle.

There remain now two doubts to be resolved arising from our words. To the first doubt it is easily answered: exercise, as commonly accepted by us, was divided into so many differences, but Galen defined not this, but rather "exercise properly so-called" as being a vehement movement; and therefore our opinion in no way seems to conflict with his. # BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> ...although a vigorous movement always arises from itself, it is nevertheless called sometimes small, sometimes large, sometimes weak, and sometimes robust, when compared either to another movement or even to itself. For games with a large ball and wrestling are properly termed "exercises"; yet if these are performed by the same person at one time more slackly and at another more intensely, they will be called "large and intense" in the latter case, and "small and slack" in the former. Similarly, these same exercises will be large and vehement for a young man who is not particularly strong if they are done laboriously, but in a robust athlete, by comparison, they will appear small and slack. To solve the second doubt, we say that the specific character of things is mostly bestowed by their goals <note>Latin: "finibus," referring to the Aristotelian concept of the 'final cause' or purpose</note>, and therefore the same things obtain different characters and different names according to the various ends for which they are performed. For if someone contemplates the temperaments of human bodies solely for the sake of knowing, he will be called a scholar and a natural philosopher; but if he observes them for the sake of either preserving or correcting them, he will be worthy of the name of both craftsman and physician. Plainly the same must be said of digging: if its goal is the cultivation of the earth and the gathering of fruit, it must undoubtedly be called "work" and "labor"; but if the goal exists merely to exercise the body for health, it certainly ought to be called "exercise." This is how we understood it when we listed digging among other exercises. And what we have said of digging, we wish to be understood also of similar things that appear to be manual labor. For that famous Pittacus, King of the Mitylenaeans, used to grind at a mill, <margin>B</margin> "using it as a vigorous exercise," as Clement of Alexandria says. Indeed, our Galen reports of himself <margin>On the Preservation of Health, book 2, chapter 8</margin> that he was once caught in the fields in winter while he was splitting wood, pounding barley in a mortar, and husking it, doing these and other things solely for the sake of exercising his body—tasks which peasants are accustomed to perform as daily labor.

### *On the types of bodies, diseases, and health. Chapter VI.*

After we have argued against those who hold poor opinions regarding exercises, and demonstrated that neither should all human bodies be exercised, nor should exercise be forbidden to everyone: it is now right to teach which bodies it is appropriate to exercise. For three types of bodies are handed down by physicians: the sick, the neutral, and the healthy. Although many species and differences have been made of these, we, who intend otherwise, will accept only these three species of bodies: namely, those which enjoy present health and have their functions unimpaired, although <margin>E</margin> otherwise they may seem neither perfectly healthy nor tempered in every respect; those which are weak, and either already lie bedridden or have their functions so perceptibly offended that they are in no way able to perform the works of the healthy; and those which, placed as if in the middle between both of these, are called "valetudinary" <note>original: "valetudinaria" — referring to those in a state of delicate or fluctuating health, neither fully sick nor fully well.</note> by the authors of medicine, and which appear to our senses as neither utterly sick nor entirely healthy. These things being thus established, a third matter worthy of notice follows: that there also exist three types of diseases. The first is placed in "intemperance" <note>original: "intemperie" — a lack of proper balance between the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, the second in bad formation, and the third in the "dissolution of continuity" <note>original: "continuitatis solutione" — a physical break in the body, such as a wound, fracture, or ulcer.</note>. Disease in intemperance arises when the whole body (under the name of "body" I understand the humors, the spirits, and the solid members) or some part of it either becomes immoderately hot, or cold, or moist, or dry; or simultaneously cold and dry, or cold <margin>F</margin> and moist, or hot and moist, or hot and dry. For in all these is contained that whole type of disease which physicians have called intemperance. They are found to have called this sometimes "simple" and sometimes "with an influx of humors." Under the name of "simple," they understand that which by its own nature disturbs the body without the company of another affliction; but under the name of "intemperance with influx," they suggest nothing else but an intemperance which—both of itself and together with an affliction arising from the humors, such as an inflammation or some tumor—harms the operations of the body and removes the state of health. Disease in "depraved formation" is generated whenever the body, or a part of the body, lacks its proper shape, or its proper size, or its correct number, or its convenient position. Disease in the "dissolution of continuity" is effected when some part, or some [member] of the body...

FOURTH BOOK

<margin>A</margin>
A limb of the body, made as one by nature, suffers division, whether such division originates from within or from without. In just as many ways, health—the opposite of disease—is established; it surely maintains its own essence and consistency through a proper balance of temperaments, through optimal formation, and through the unity of its parts. For it is sufficient to have discussed each of these in a general outline <note>original: "τύπῳ" (typō) - meaning a general sketch or model</note> and in a universal sense. Those who read these words, if they desire to have a more exquisite knowledge of these matters, may scrutinize the books of the physicians. They ought not to require a more diligent treatment from us, as we are devoted to other studies and cannot wander too far beyond our proposed limits. But now, we are compelled to examine which bodies, based on what has been said, are suitable for exercise.

### *Whether it is proper for sick bodies to be exercised in any way. Chapter VII.*

<margin>B</margin>
It has been doubted since the most ancient times whether—just as healthy and robust bodies receive no small advantage from exercises for increasing, confirming, and preserving their health—sick bodies might also be able to be exercised in some way, so that it might be permitted to use them both to alleviate the troubles of illnesses and to recover health. Among those who asserted that the infirm ought to be exercised, Petronas stood first, then Prodicus (or Herodicus), who used to kill those suffering from fevers with running and wrestling; both were vehemently condemned by Hippocrates for such a dogma. In later ages, Asclepiades imitated Petronas; in order to catch the favor of men, he not only indulged the languid with various exercises looking toward pleasure rather than health, but even (as Celsus most elegantly wrote) subscribed to the luxury of the bedridden. Thus, it was not without great reason that Pliny later proclaimed that Asclepiades had mastered a "pleasant" method of curing. Those who preferred to cling to a similar opinion besides these said that Aesculapius <note>The Greco-Roman god of medicine</note> was so named from the phrase: "because he gently exercised the sick" <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ ἀσκεῖν ἠπίως τοὺς νοσοῦντας" (para to askein ēpiōs tous nosountas)</note>, whereas previously he was called "Gentle" <note>original: "ἠπίως" (ēpiōs)</note>. On the other side, there were those who asserted that no sick person should be exercised, but all ought to be kept in quiet. Between these, Galen, Herodotus, Antyllus, Aetius, and Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician of the Islamic Golden Age</note> held a middle ground. Just as they did not wish for exercises to be removed from all sick people absolutely, so it did not please them that everyone should be exercised by every kind of movement. Instead, they commanded that great distinction and care must be taken in choosing both the sick patients themselves and the types of exercises; so that what a diseased body...

<margin>D</margin> It must be thoroughly understood what exercise and what rest the body requires so that it does not suffer any disturbances or agitations. Therefore, according to those authorities, bodies suffering from an immoderate hot imbalance are not suited to any exercises, whether vigorous or mild; this is because the heat, which ought to be diminished, instead receives an increase from them. This is just as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> relates regarding Primigenes, who suffered from an extreme degree of heat; he was greatly harmed not only by vigorous exercises but even by short walks taken in the portico before his bath. For this reason, Asclepiades of Prusa <note>A Greek physician who practiced in Rome and favored "passive" movement over harsh drugs.</note> is rightly to be condemned; as Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, author of the Roman medical encyclopaedia 'De Medicina'.</note> reports, he used "gestations" <note><term>gestationes</term>: a form of passive exercise where the patient is carried in a litter, carriage, or boat.</note> during burning fevers. In other fevers and diseases, while removing medicines and emetics, he tortured the sick like an executioner during the first days with hunger, thirst, sleeplessness, and bright light; yet on other days, he exercised them with walks, gestations, baths, and hanging beds.

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> Dry bodies <note>referring to the "dry" temperament in humoral theory, often associated with thinness or dehydration</note> should be exercised either not at all or with very minimal and gentle movements, since they always possess weak strength in addition to the specific affliction of their disease. Cold bodies are not as easily harmed by exercise, nor are moist ones. Indeed, cold and moist bodies sustain exercise best of all; this is because the motion acts as a kind of remedy by drying and heating, provided it is not applied beyond measure. All these things should be understood to apply only to those patients who have an imbalance <note>original: "intemperatum," referring to a humoral imbalance</note> throughout their entire body. For if someone suffers an imbalance in only one part or limb, or in several, and a way can be found to exercise the healthy parts without harming the sick ones, exercise will undoubtedly be more suitable for that patient; by strengthening the good condition of the healthy parts, it provides a consequent aid even to the weak ones.

<margin>B</margin> Gathering our thoughts, therefore, we say that no body suffering from any kind of imbalance enjoys great and violent exercise; but some are found for whom small and very moderate exercises occasionally bring help. What those exercises are, and which ones suit which diseases and bodies, we shall declare in the following books, where we will describe the particular powers of individual exercises more fully. Regarding bodies that are diseased due to poor formation <note>physical deformity or malformation</note>, a similar path of determination should be followed, provided those conditions did not arise from the principles of birth, but emerged recently and by chance (so to speak). For these conditions—whether they have a distorted overall figure, as in <term>leucophlegmatia</term> <note>a type of dropsy or edema causing pale, swollen skin</note>, or some specific part deformed—receive benefit from exercises, provided other hindering ailments are not present.

<margin>C</margin> Indeed, exercise is able to straighten what is twisted, smooth what is rough, reduce what is swollen, raise what is depressed, empty what is overfilled, fill what is emptied, and open what is obstructed. Furthermore, exercises are often accustomed to removing diseases caused by "quantity" <note>excessive mass or weight</note>. There is nothing that more effectively reduces an increased universal body mass than violent and fast exercises performed while fasting. Hippocrates, and after him Galen, said that these draw away flesh and juices <note>humors</note>.

<margin>D</margin>
...may acquire: indeed, Galen boasts that he cured many who were wasted away both in their entire bodies and in their legs; just as we have mentioned elsewhere that Germanicus <note>The Roman general and nephew of Tiberius, known for his weak legs.</note> was freed from the thinness of his legs through the benefit of horse-riding. Furthermore, bodies afflicted by a disease of number <note>A classical medical category referring to an excess or deficiency of parts, such as extra fingers or missing limbs.</note>—whether it be superfluous or lacking—do not inherently refuse exercise, especially when a similar disease is not innate. An example is found in kidney stones <term>lapillis renum: small stones or calculi in the kidneys</term>, which, through the shaking of vigorous movement, descend from the narrow passages of the kidneys to the wider ones, and finally to the bladder itself, thereby removing great distress from the patients.

However, bodies suffering from a disease of position <note>Dislocations or organs out of place.</note>, provided it is not from birth, admit almost no kind of exercise. This is because when limbs have lost their proper place and position, they must not only be restored to their proper seat, but after being restored, they must be kept from every kind of movement until they are perfectly strengthened and have recovered their former condition. Otherwise, if they <margin>E</margin> were moved, they would be affected by greater harm. Thus it follows that those seized by this infirmity, for the most part, ought not to exercise.

Let these remarks suffice concerning the second kind of disease, namely bodies suffering from bad formation. There remain bodies afflicted by the third kind of disease, known as the breach of continuity <term>solutio continuitatis: a physical break in the body's tissues, such as a wound, fracture, or ulcer</term>. This breach usually occurs in the skin, the flesh, the bones, the nerves, or similar parts, sometimes alone and sometimes associated with fevers. Where the body has any such breach associated with fever, it must in no way be exercised; for if exercises are rarely suitable for those with a fever alone, how much less will they be suitable when disturbed by other diseases?

But if the breach of continuity is present without fever, and it is in a noble part <note>Vital organs essential for life.</note> especially necessary for life—such as the brain, the stomach, the liver, and the like—without a doubt any exercises are extremely harmful. They would greatly distract the spirits <note>The "vital spirits" believed to flow through the body to sustain life.</note> necessary for the affected part and agitate all the humors <margin>F</margin> at a time when they ought to be steady and quiet, lest the disease grow more severe due to their influx.

If other, less noble members suffer a division of continuity, the sick may be moderately exercised, provided the affliction is not significant and the laboring part itself is not exercised. There are some seized by this ailment who perceive no small utility from moderate and even vigorous exercises, such as those suffering from the itch <term>scabiosi: those afflicted with scabies or similar skin irritations</term>. Since their skin is torn by false and sharp humors, vigorous movement causes those humors to be evacuated both through sweat and through hidden perspiration; once these are evacuated, they are freed from the disease. For this reason, there is need for sharp judgment and diligent observation in all these matters, so that it may be best understood in which cases...

It highlights that exercise can cure skin diseases by sweating out harmful humors.</summary>

### On exercising the bodies of the convalescent and the elderly.
### Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring intricate floral and vine patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
ALTHOUGH among physicians (as we have said above) "neutral" bodies are placed between the sick and the healthy, and these are divided into many different types, they pertain little to our current discussion. In their place, we shall establish the "convalescent" <note>original: "valetudinaria"</note>, by which we wish to include both all those
<margin>B</margin> who have recently escaped from illness and bedrest and have not yet perfectly recovered their former condition, as well as most elderly people. Indeed, Galen <margin>See *On the Preservation of Health*, chapter 11; and *The Art of Medicine*, last chapter.</margin> taught that the elderly should be cared for in the same manner as the convalescent; and not without reason, since old age, according to Aristotle <margin>See *On the Generation of Animals*, book 4, chapter 4.</margin>, is a kind of natural disease. Hence, those who are burdened by age cannot endure the same regimen of living that the healthy tolerate. Therefore, for those convalescents who have just escaped from illness, among the other remedies suited to them for full health, the primary one is bodily exercise. By this, their limbs are strengthened, the remnants of the humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which ancient medicine believed governed health.</note> are emptied, internal heat is aroused, and finally, the entire habit of the body is restored. However, every effort must be made so that, at the beginning, the movements are gentle, brief, slow, and relaxed. Subsequently, as the strength grows more robust, the magnitude and duration
<margin>C</margin> of the exercise should be similarly increased. Finally, that principle of "gradual progression" <note>original Greek: ἐκ προσαγωγῆς (ek prosagoges)</note> so often repeated by Hippocrates must always be kept in mind, lest by an improper transition from one extreme to the other, greater errors be committed, and instead of a restoration of strength, a greater weakness or prostration should follow. Accordingly, Averroes <margin>6th book of the *Colliget*, chapter 6.</margin> deserves to be condemned, for he too freely advised that diseased bodies should be exercised daily until the onset of sweat and the elevation of breath. For such vehement exercise is so far from providing any benefit worth mentioning to the convalescent or the "diseased" (as he calls them), that it rather further prostrates their still-feeble strength and almost extinguishes—or at least significantly dulls—the innate heat that is barely reviving after the illness. Indeed, in those recovering, the blood is good but scanty (as Galen writes), and along with it the vital and animal spirits; the solid parts themselves are drier <margin>In *The Art of Medicine*, last chapter.</margin>...

Therefore, to correct an indisposition of this kind, whatever provides good and safe nourishment is necessary; and besides these, moderate movements, such as riding in carriages or gentle walks; not violent movements, which, just as they make solid parts that are already parched even drier, so too do they diminish heat and consume what weak strength remains. However, the elderly, whose age accumulates a great abundance of waste products <note>original: "excrementorum," referring to metabolic byproducts or "humors" rather than just modern excrement</note> due to a lack of heat, greatly benefit from exercises, both to purge these types of refuse and also to preserve and—like a gentle breeze—to rouse or kindle the heat, which otherwise would be in danger of being extinguished by excessive sluggishness.

<margin>E</margin>
Nevertheless, in prescribing exercises for the elderly, four things must be observed: strength, the condition of the body, habit, and the particular ailments which usually plague the bodies of the aged. By reason of their strength, which the elderly always possess in a weaker state, they must especially beware of sharp, violent, and numerous exercises which dry out, thin, and weaken the body; they should instead follow milder ones, such as being carried <note>gestation: a passive exercise like being carried in a litter or boat</note> and walking just short of fatigue.

<margin>1. Rhetoric, chapter 5.</margin>
For Prodicus <note>A Greek philosopher and contemporary of Socrates</note>, who was most studious of health and for that reason (on the authority of Aristotle) refused all those things which others enjoy with pleasure, when his age was already becoming heavy (as Plato reports in the *Phaedrus*), used to go from Athens to the walls of Megara and return home from there. This measure of exercise could by no means be suited to all elderly men, since Plato himself says that he caused trouble both for himself and for others by his excessive zeal for exercising.

<margin>F</margin>
Likewise, Antiochus the physician, being more than eighty years old, used to walk on foot almost every day, as Galen writes, from his home to the forum—a distance of three stades <note>about 600 yards</note>—and meanwhile to visit his patients. But if it was necessary for him to go further, he used a chair or a carriage. To these accounts, Pliny the Younger <note>original: "Plinius secundus"</note> relates that Spurinna, a man most provident in his way of living, who reached his seventy-seventh year with the vigor of his ears and eyes intact, as well as an agile and vivid body, most constantly observed this rule: that in the morning he stayed in bed; at the second hour he dressed and walked three miles; soon he would read or converse, then sit down; then he would climb into a carriage, and having thus completed seven miles, he would walk one mile again, sit again, or return to his chamber or his pen; when the hour of the bath was announced, which was the ninth hour in winter and the eighth in summer, he would walk naked in the sun if there was no wind; then he would move with a ball <note>pila: a common Roman ball game used for exercise</note> vigorously and for a long time; after a while, having washed, he would recline for a meal.

<margin>A</margin>And he should delay his food for a little while. Because of the condition of the entire body, the exercises of the elderly ought to be determined in this manner: just as a body in its best state—as in youth—is most fit for the most strenuous labors, so in old age it is suited only to moderate ones. Those elderly men who have either thick legs or a broad chest, or legs that are thinner than is proper, or whose body has a small or very narrow thorax <note>The chest cavity</note>, or who are bow-legged or knock-kneed, or departing from the middle-ground in any other way, are rendered unfit for all those exercises which might offend the faulty limbs more than help them—such as shouting for the chest, walking for the legs, and similar activities. Now, indeed, habit claims for itself the greatest role in choosing the type of exercise, since Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician of antiquity</note> said that those who are accustomed to bearing labors, even if they are weak or <margin>B</margin> elderly, bear their accustomed tasks more easily than those who are unaccustomed, strong, and young. For just as accustomed things tire those who practice them the least—indeed, they even delight them—likewise, unaccustomed things bring both distress and exhaustion. All elderly people, therefore, ought to be exercised in their accustomed labors, but with their intensity reduced; because, if senile bodies have diminished vigor, heat, strength, and everything else in comparison to youth, it is consistent with reason that they require lesser exercises as well. Finally, the specific ailments of senile bodies will indicate the types of exercises that are by no means suitable for them. For those who are easily seized by vertigo, the falling sickness <note>original: "comitiali morbo" - epilepsy</note>, severe ophthalmia <note>Inflammation of the eye</note>, or weakness of hearing, must avoid exercises that affect the head. Similarly, in all other conditions, not only the elderly but people of every age ought to conduct themselves so that they diligently abstain from those exercises which are naturally suited to strain and disturb the suffering parts. Thus, it must be decided regarding the exercising of the sickly and the senile.

...that body endowed with perfect health, which was established as a measure and rule for all others, can be described by the mind rather than actually found in any region; even though Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), a Greek physician whose writings dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> recorded that many bodies of balanced temperament are found in their own regions. **A** [Young men] are afflicted by strong convulsions and various ruptures of the flesh and veins more immediately and severely than the elderly. This is because they possess robust and dry bodies, with dense, strong flesh that adheres tenaciously to the bones, over which the surrounding skin is stretched very tight. All these qualities are less present in the elderly, and for that reason, they are more rarely seized by evils of this kind. Regarding the universal habit of the body, I deem it should be determined thus: that the fat and obese enjoy more prosperous health the more they exercise, as Aristotle used to say that fat is melted away by movement. Indeed, even if the exercises are vigorous and intense, they will do no harm at all. For Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> maintained that the walks of corpulent people ought to be swift; furthermore, Galen <note>A prominent Roman physician whose work shaped Western medicine for centuries.</note> testifies that among the other remedies he administered to thin down a certain obese man forty years of age, he employed fast running.

**B** On the contrary, he demands that slender people be kept in almost complete rest. Just as the corpulent and the thick-set have contrary constitutions arising from contrary origins, so they seem to require contrary things for their health; otherwise, they are greatly harmed. Thus, if there are some slender people for whom exercise is judged beneficial, they undoubtedly have need of only a little, and that very relaxed. Whence the most wise Hippocrates, with the highest reason, ordered that slender people about to make a journey should walk with slow steps. Similarly, the *Magones* <note>Likely referring to ancient trainers or slave-dealers who prepared people for sale.</note> and physicians, wishing to fatten such people, would beat them with rods so that the flesh might be raised up and nourishment drawn toward it. However, those who exist between the fat and the slender—either the *well-fleshed* <note>original: εὐσάρκοι (eusarkoi)</note>, or "square-built," or those declining only slightly toward one side or the other—perceive a notable benefit if they exercise moderately or even vigorously, provided it is not immoderate. This is because their [innate] heat is better preserved and daily superfluities <note>Waste products or "humors" believed to cause disease if they accumulate.</note> are exhausted.

**C** Regarding the particular condition of the limbs, the same must be said: namely, that thick parts should be exercised more, and thin parts less, unless their thinness proceeds from a defect or an obstruction in the distribution of nourishment. In that case, both exercise is appropriate and that kind of ointment devised by physicians even for plucking out hairs, called a *Dropax* <note>A pitch-plaster used for hair removal or to stimulate blood flow to a limb.</note>, of which Martial <note>A Roman poet known for his Epigrams.</note> speaks in Book 3:

Those who are thin should be kept from exercise, lest they be further dried out, or a greater distress be added to their existing distress. On the other hand, those who eat much ought to exercise much, since Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> used to say that a man who eats cannot live healthily unless he works. For in such people, much heat is needed so that they may digest much; and as Galenus <note>Galen of Pergamon, a prominent Roman physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> said in <margin>2, On the Preservation of Health</margin> much heat is easily supplied by exercise. Furthermore, those who eat much generate a great abundance of waste products, which, unless diminished by great and frequent labors, lead the body into wicked dispositions. Similarly, those who sleep much and deeply also require many exercises, since in them the "perspirations" <note>The process of releasing vapors or fluids through the skin, thought to maintain balance.</note> are held back, and thus the abundance of blood leaves the external parts and goes into the interior, <margin>5. On the History of Animals, ch. 19</margin> so that if a knife were applied, it would not be able to flow out as easily, just as Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher whose biological works were foundational to medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note> writes. Because of this, all sleepy people become discolored; hence it is necessary for them to be exercised sufficiently, <margin>E</margin> so that an opening may be made for the perspirations, and the blood may be recalled to preserve and nourish the exterior parts. Finally, regarding the reasoning of the "temperament" <note>The balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, I believe judgment concerning exercises should be rendered thus: that those who are dry should be exercised either not at all, or quite slowly and with the least amount of labor. For no one of sound mind would doubt that exercises—which are known to be drying by their very nature—if applied to dry bodies, would increase the imbalance. Those who are hot, and especially those endowed with a sharp and biting heat, require moderate exercises, lest they grow hot beyond what is right from the motion; <margin>4. Aphorisms 13; 6. Epidemics, section 4; Aphorism 15; 6. Problems, part 1.</margin> and for them, as Galen writes, the motions made in performing necessary actions alone are sufficient. Hence Aristotle, asking why some grow fat by sitting while others grow thin, says it happens because some are cold, others hot, some full of waste products, and others not. Those who are hot grow fat by sitting, since their heat is sufficient for the digestion of food without motion; <margin>F</margin> likewise those who are not full of waste. But those who abound in waste and are of a cold temperament grow thin by sitting, because from rest their heat becomes, as it were, sluggish, and for that reason digests less; likewise, the waste products are not expelled, but rather increase. <margin>6. Epidemics, section 4.</margin> Hippocrates spoke of hot natures in this way when he said: *In a hot nature, cooling, the drinking of water, and rest are appropriate* <note>original: "Εν θέρμῳ φύσει ψύξις, ποτὸν ὕδωρ, ἐλλινύειν"</note>; and similarly when he wrote: *those whom thirst seizes, for them both food and labors must be diminished* <note>original: "ὁκόσες δὲ δίψαι λαμβάνουσι, τετέοι σιτῶν τε σιτίων, καὶ τῶν ταλαιπωριῶν ἀφαιρέειν"</note>, namely, that labor and food must be reduced for those whom thirst plagues on account of heat. From this it is simultaneously made clear that cold bodies ought to be exercised vehemently and much. <margin>5. Problems, part 9.</margin> Furthermore, whether moist bodies perceive benefit from exercises might not undeservedly be doubted, because Aristotle writes—

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> It has been left in writing <note>referring to Aristotle</note> that moist bodies are suffocated by labor, because the moisture is converted into vapors by the heat of movement; these vapors, soon becoming copious and burning, suffocate the innate heat. However, reason seems to persuade us otherwise, demonstrating that moist bodies abound in waste products <term>excrementis: in this context, metabolic byproducts or "superfluous humors" rather than modern waste</term>, and therefore vigorous labors are suitable for them, both to consume the exuberant moisture and to remove the abundance of superfluities. For this reason, as Peter of Abano <note>original: "Petrus Apponensis," a 13th-century physician and philosopher</note> notes, one must understand Aristotle's opinion to apply to those in whom four conditions concur: that they are moist and hot, and that the moisture is plentiful, easily evaporated, and located around the lung. For if such people labor and exercise much, there is a danger that the moisture, converted into vapors by the sharp intrinsic heat, might occupy the region of the lung and heart and induce suffocation.

<margin>B</margin> Those who possess a moist bodily temperament apart from these specific conditions receive no harm, but rather excellent benefit from exercises and labors. For this reason, among women—who are generally endowed with a moist temperament—those who work and exercise longer and more vigorously lead a healthier and less troublesome life. Likewise, among those nations and in those places where women are accustomed to labor, they give birth more easily, as Aristotle writes; nor do they carry the womb with difficulty, since labor consumes those remnants <note>recrementa: bodily residues</note> which increase in idle and sedentary women.

<margin>4. On the Generation of Animals, chapter 6</margin> Truly, whatever bodies are simultaneously hot and dry should by no means be exercised. Those that are hot and moist admit exercise, but let it be moderate, not vehement or rapid. Cold and dry bodies should be exercised by reason of their coldness, but by reason of their dryness they require movements that are neither fast nor vigorous, but moderate and rather 

<margin>C</margin> slow. Cold and moist bodies are helped most of all by vehement and swift exercises, as these consume the superfluous moisture and excite and increase the innate heat. Thus, the determination regarding the exercising of bodies in general is established.

<page-num>216</page-num>

are born or nourished, they are affected by diverse and wonderful conditions. <margin>D</margin> For this reason, the ancient physicians are worthy of the highest praise, as they commanded with all diligence that the qualities of locations must be considered in almost every operation of their art. For there exist places and regions in which, if those things are done which are performed successfully in others, they result in nearly the opposite end. This is something that, above all others, those people must also greatly observe who wish to exercise their own bodies or the bodies of others for the sake of protecting health <note>original: "sanitatis tuendae"</note> or acquiring a good physical habit. Unless they apply their minds strongly to choosing suitable places, they frequently incur non-negligible damages and affections that should not be ignored, even while they believe they are helping.

Therefore, regarding the choice of a place for exercising, three things especially occur that are worthy of great consideration. The first is that it should be breathed upon by the best winds and sheltered from the wicked ones. Hence, places situated toward the north and the east, from which more healthful breezes blow, are to be continuously preferred over western and southern ones. <margin>E</margin> For the former neither boil with immoderate heat, nor contract mold from cold and moisture, nor are they infected by pernicious vapors brought in by the blasts. The latter, however, besides the intense heat and cold which are induced at one time or another, mostly suffer very unhealthful respirations by reason of the winds. 

But if places can be obtained which enjoy a tranquility of winds and which are entirely temperate—such as Galen reports his own homeland and that of Hippocrates <note>Hippocrates of Cos and Galen of Pergamon, the two pillars of ancient Greek medicine.</note> to have been—without a doubt these will surpass all others. <margin>Galen, *On the Preservation of Health*, book 2, chapter 7.</margin> Otherwise, the greatest care must be taken that the winds do not at least blow most violently there; for the bodies of those exercising, being opened by motion and heat, very easily admit the incursions of the winds to the interior parts, and thus afterwards conceive pernicious ailments with great danger. 

And for this reason, derived from the winds and the best situation of the sky, I think it happened that some built winter baths <note>original: "thermas"</note> and others summer ones. <margin>F</margin> For Vopiscus <note>Flavius Vopiscus, one of the purported authors of the *Augustan History*.</note> is the authority that the Emperor Aurelian built winter baths in the Transtiberine region <note>The Trastevere district in Rome, across the Tiber river.</note>, which, being exposed to the south, were tempered by the rays of the sun and were therefore very well suited for winter exercises. Julius Capitolinus writes that Gordian the Younger built summer baths, which, being placed between the Caelian Hill and the Esquiline, offered a certain pleasant shade and most welcome shadows to those exercising themselves. 

The second thing to be considered in the selection of a place is that it be open, not enclosed, and not dark; since where the air exists more freely and is less compressed, bodies exercised in it are rendered more agile and vivid than if they were exercised in thick, dense, and enclosed air. And from this it is...

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> It is for this reason that (as we stated in Book 2) among the places intended for walking, Vitruvius <note>Roman architect, 1st century BCE</note> and Cornelius Celsus <note>Roman medical encyclopedist</note> recommended the *hypethron* <term>hypethron: an open-air space or courtyard uncovered by a roof</term> more than the portico or the *hypogeum* <term>hypogeum: an underground chamber or vaulted cellar</term>. Similarly, Phaedrus, in Plato’s dialogue inscribed with his name, follows the opinion of the physician Acumenus—who is also celebrated by Xenophon <margin>Book on the Memorable Deeds of Socrates</margin>—and preferred a walk taken outside the city to one performed within the city walls. He used these words: <note>original Greek: "τῷ δ’ ἐμῷ καὶ σῷ πειθόμενος, Ἀκουμενῷ κ[αὶ] τὰς ὁδὸς ποιοῦμαι τοὺς περιπάτους φασὶ γὰρ ἀκοπωτέρας τῶν ἐν τοῖς δρόμοις εἶναι"</note> "Obeying your companion and mine, Acumenus, I take my walks along the roads; for he said that these are less tiring than those taken in the race-courses." Since I promised above that I would say more regarding this passage of Plato, a suitable opportunity to fulfill that promise now presents itself—all the more so because Marsilio Ficino <note>Famous Renaissance humanist and translator of Plato</note>, otherwise a most learned man, committed a shameful double error while believing Phaedrus’s meaning to be that "walking is easier than running."

<margin>B</margin> He erred first because he either did not understand the literal Greek text or changed it unnecessarily; for in place of "those [walks] in the race-courses," he translated it as if the text had read "than running." Secondly, he did not notice that he attributed a nearly ridiculous sentiment to Phaedrus and Acumenus: for who, I ask, is so dull and ignorant as not to know that walking is easier than running? Therefore, Janus Cornarius <note>German humanist and physician</note>, who recently produced a Latin translation of Plato, interpreted that sentiment better when he had Phaedrus saying that walks taken on the roads are healthier than those taken in the race-courses. Regarding how this is to be understood, I have found various opinions among learned men. Some have thought that among the ancient Greeks, the *dromoi* <term>dromoi: literally 'courses' or 'tracks'</term> were level streets within the cities, but somewhat rough due to the paving stones and short in length, named so because of the frequency of people walking through them; 

<margin>C</margin> just as today, among many peoples, the most frequented city streets are called "courses" <note>likely referring to the Italian 'Corso'</note>. This opinion seems to be supported by Hippocrates in the 5th book of *Epidemics*, where he mentions a certain man who lived near the "course" in these words: <note>original Greek: "ὁ παρὰ τὸν δρόμον οἰκέων, τῆς νυκτὸς αἷμα ἐμέσας"</note> "A certain man living near the course vomited blood during the night." These scholars say that *hodoi* <term>hodoi: roads or ways</term> referred to any roads outside the city, built without artifice and paved by no laws, but uneven, not at all level, and finally, such as are found made by nature or by chance. They argue Acumenus approved of walking on the roads more than in the "courses" because, according to Celsus and even the older Aristotle (who perhaps followed Acumenus in this), <margin>Book 1, Ch. 2. 5. Problems 1. 37.</margin> <note>original Greek: "τῶν περιπάτων οἱ κ[ατὰ] τὰς ὁδὸς ἀκοπώτεροί εἰσιν οἱ ἀνώμαλοι τῶν εὐθειῶν"</note> "Among walks, those on uneven roads are less tiring than those on straight ones."

# BOOK

Of walks, those are less fatiguing which are done on <margin>D</margin> uneven paths rather than straight ones; for those walking through flat and level places always strain the same limbs, whereas those walking through uneven terrain distribute the labor more across the whole body, and for that reason are less exhausted. Thus, walks taken along roads, being naturally uneven, are easier for the same reason than those taken in "courses" <note>original: *cursibus*; referring to the level, prepared tracks of a gymnasium</note> which are level. Others have said that <term>the courses</term> <note>original: *τοὺς δρόμους* (tous dromous)</note> were specific places of short length dedicated to walking, similar to those which the ancients used to build in the wrestling school <note>original: *palaestra*</note> for the convenience of walking, which *<term>Vitruvius</term>* <note>Roman architect, 1st century BCE</note> records were called <term>running-galleries</term> <note>original: *ἐπιδρομίδας* (epidromidas); covered walks or colonnades</note>. *<term>Eupolis</term>* <note>Athenian comic poet</note> made very famous mention of these in *<term>Laertius</term>*'s life of *<term>Plato</term>*: <term>in the shaded courses of the god Academus</term> <note>original: *ἐν εὐσκίοις δρόμοισι Ἀκαδήμου θεοῦ*; referring to the Academy in Athens</note>, that is, in the shaded walkways of the god Academus. However, the "roads" were those which I indicated a little earlier according to the opinion of the aforementioned authors. For this reason, *<term>Acumenus</term>* <note>A physician and friend of Socrates</note> was right to believe that walks on roads are less tiring than in the courses. Indeed, <margin>E</margin> <margin>Section on Problems, 1</margin> *<term>Aristotle</term>* left it in writing that those who go along short paths and are forced to turn back again and again are more fatigued than those who walk along long roads and never turn back; for the former, now resting, now moving, are disturbed by the uneven motion, which clearly happens less to the latter.

I have always thought that these last authors understood the matter better than the others, not only because a walk performed on roads is more desirable than in the courses—both for the reasons stated and because of the freer and purer air which flows more frequently in open roads than in short, enclosed places—but also because it is more likely that *<term>Plato</term>* understood "course" in this way in the *Phaedrus*. This is especially true since at the beginning of the *Theaetetus* he seems to use a similar word with exactly the same meaning in these words: <term>For just now some of his companions were being anointed in the outer course, and he himself as well; but now they seem to me to be coming here after having anointed themselves</term> <note>original: *ἄρτι γὰρ ἐν τῷ ἔξω δρόμῳ ἤλειφοντο...*</note>. <margin>F</margin> *<term>Antyllus</term>* <note>A famous Greek surgeon and physician</note> in the works of *<term>Oribasius</term>* seems to have suggested the same thing.

And so much for the explanation of *<term>Plato's</term>* passage. A third thing must be considered regarding the choice of locations by those who devote effort to physical exercises for the sake of preserving health and attaining an excellent condition of the body: every care must be taken so that no taint can spread from neighboring regions to the place of exercise. Such a taint, infecting the air, would soon undermine the exercised bodies, which, like a sponge, are ready to receive anything. For such places are usually near marshes, stagnant pools, caves, lakes, pits <note>original: *syros*; underground granaries or pits</note>, and the like, which one must always avoid with diligent and great care. For the same reason...

# BOOK FOUR

**A** ...and locations facing the sea toward the south or west should be avoided because, according to Vitruvius <margin>Book 1, chapter 4</margin> <note>Vitruvius was a famous Roman architect and engineer whose work "On Architecture" influenced the Renaissance deeply.</note>, the southern sky grows warm in the summer as the sun rises and burns at midday; consequently, no one can exercise there without great discomfort. If those most magnificent and countless porticos <note>covered walkways supported by columns</note> built for strolling and other exercises were still standing—as we mentioned above—and if those vast gymnasiums magnificently constructed by our ancestors for this purpose were still available, surely no more suitable place could be found that would better suffice for almost every kind of exercise. But, since we can now scarcely behold even their ruins, effort must be made for each person to choose a location according to the conditions already explained, always keeping in mind that although there are many exercises that seem to require narrow and enclosed spaces, even in those, **B** a careful selection must be made. If they cannot possess all the ideal qualities, they should at least have some of them, and the better ones among those we have proposed. For this reason, Galen <margin>On the Preservation of Health, Book 2, chapter 17</margin> <note>Galen was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire; his theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> most wisely advised that the house in which men are to exercise should be chosen to be warm in winter, cool in summer, or always temperate. If this is not possible, care should be taken that it does not become hotter or colder on that particular day than the general air of the whole city. Aetius of Amida <margin>Book 3, chapter 7</margin> <note>A 6th-century Byzantine Greek physician and medical compiler.</note> seems to have embraced all these aforementioned conditions in a single word when he wrote that "gestation" <note>term: gestation; here meaning passive exercise like being carried in a litter or carriage</note>, sailing, and finally every kind of exercise ought to take place in a healthy location and in pure air. Other conditions of locations could similarly be pointed out, namely the unevenness of the site, level ground, and the like; but because these have been partly explained and are partly unnecessary, and most are included under those already mentioned, I shall bring this discussion of location to an **C** end and proceed to the explanation of time. First, however, I will note that men are sometimes forced to exercise in a place struck by the sun; these men must take great care never to sit or rest there. Indeed, Aristotle <margin>Section 38, Problem 16</margin> left it in writing that those exercising under the sun are burned more while they sit than while they move. This is because when they are in motion, they stir the air and are, as it were, fanned by a breeze; but when they sit, because the air remains motionless, they experience the sharper force of the sun.

BOOK ON THE PROPER TIME FOR EXERCISE. Chapter XI.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' containing a landscape scene with classical architecture, including a prominent tower or column and an arched building in the background.</image-desc>

**D**uo—There are two types of natural time, so named by the authors of medicine, without the observation of which not only matters pertaining to health, but indeed all human actions and operations are carried out poorly and unsuccessfully. One is universal, under which spring, summer, autumn, and winter are included; the other is particular, which encompasses the hours of individual days separately. I have called these "natural" to distinguish them from "accidental" or "contingent" times, which do not occur in such a perpetual and firm order as the former. For southerly, northerly, or boreal weather—being excessively cold, hot, dry, cloudy, clear, bright, or foggy—are accidental differences occurring inordinately and by chance. Regarding these, when exercising the body, it must be briefly established in this manner: namely, that those specific atmospheric conditions should be avoided in which the winds blow most vehemently, especially when they are at their worst—the southerly and northerly winds being the most frequent—by which bodies, thinned <note>original: "rarefacta," meaning the pores are opened or the flesh made less dense</note> and weakened by movement, are greatly harmed. Similarly, times that are too cold, too hot, or too dry must also be shunned. For excessive cold, when it cannot be overcome by the heat of those exercising, affects them more powerfully;

<margin>
6. Particular
Problems, 6.
</margin>
because, according to Aristotle <note>The author refers to Aristotle’s *Problems*, a collection of questions on natural phenomena</note>, fat consumed by labor cannot preserve heat and warmth. Furthermore, bodies are made more porous and loosened by movement, and the passages <term>meatus: the pores or channels of the body</term> are opened through sweating, which allows the cold to penetrate the internal parts with greater force. Added to this is the fact that those exercising are continually changing and moving the air around them; and therefore, as Aristotle said, those running in winter

Problems, 12.
