This is because the air surrounding our bodies when we stand, once it has been warmed, causes no further distress; however, when we run, one cold patch of air after another continually meets us, and thus it happens that we shiver more. Likewise, those who exercise in extreme cold are more violently struck by the chill. Moreover, excessive heat forbids exercise, as does immoderate dryness, since the former immoderately dissolves the innate heat and the entire body, while the latter dries out the fluids <term>humiditates: the "moistures" or humors of the body</term> more than is proper. Likewise, a clear and bright time should be chosen for exercises, while cloudy, dark, and thick weather should be avoided; for when the air is thus corrupted, it easily enters the open passages of the body even without exercise, and carrying humors <note>The four vital fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note> with it, it attaches them to the limbs not without harm, and consequently—not without reason—renders the bodies heavier and the mind thereafter...

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> [The heavy air] thereafter weighs one down: a phenomenon never observed in clear weather; rather, it is evident that by clear skies, bodies are assisted toward movement, the spirits—being by their own nature friends to light—are strengthened, and the mind is refreshed. This is what I believe Hippocrates meant when he said, <margin>Book on Airs, Waters, and Places</margin> <note>original Greek: ἅμα ταῖς ὥραισιν μεταβάλλονται αἱ κοιλίαι, καὶ τὰ πνεύματα</note> "the bellies and the spirits change along with the seasons," meaning that the internal organs and the vital spirits are altered by the conditions of the weather. Furthermore, concerning the natural types of times for exercising, I find various rules determined by the ancients. First, as far as the universal season is concerned, Aristotle—following the opinion <margin>Section 2, Problems 21, 33, and 41</margin> of all the ancient authors—judged that human bodies ought to be exercised in the summer rather than in the winter (understanding "winter," as Peter of Abano <note>A 13th-century physician and philosopher</note> judged, to include autumn, winter, and spring). And he was moved to believe this for the reason that in summer, the natural heat—being sluggish and weak—less effectively digests food and raw <margin>B</margin> humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to control health</term>. Whence more waste products are generated, and for that reason, the native heat must be more greatly excited by exercise so that it may digest more properly; likewise, sweat must be drawn out by movement so that those wastes may be emptied, lest they be retained within and contract rot. In winter, however, because the native heat is stronger and consequently better at finishing off food and undigested humors, very few wastes are generated. Thus, it is less necessary for them to be drawn out, nor is exercise suitable, as it brings little benefit while carrying a great danger: namely, that the winter air, filled with dampness, might glide into the bodies opened up by movement and greatly harm them. On the other hand, that most ancient author Hippocrates (or perhaps Polybus) wished men to be advised of three things regarding exercise: <margin>On Diet, Book 3</margin> that they should avoid fatigue at all times; that they should exercise the body with morning walks; and that <margin>C</margin> in winter and cold weather they should exercise more and for longer, yet stopping before they feel fatigue or [excessive] heat. Following Hippocrates, Soranus of Ephesus, Paul of Aegina, and <margin>In the Introduction to Medicine, ch. 5; Book 1, ch. 53</margin> many other physicians preferred that one should exercise less in summer and autumn, and more in winter and spring. They judged that in summer and autumn, bodies are already sufficiently dried out and parched by the surrounding air and should not be further withered by movement; nor should the heat, which is otherwise sluggish and feeble, be further blunted or diminished. However, Galen—the great authority on many matters which physicians follow—seems to have judged that <margin>On the Preservation of Health, Book 2, ch. 7</margin> just as balanced bodies require exercise in a balanced season (namely, spring), in a similar fashion, cold bodies should be exercised in the heat, hot bodies in the cold, moist in the dry, and dry in the moist. It is as if this rule should always be observed: that for bodies declining toward some imbalance, the time and place [of exercise should be adjusted accordingly].

<summary>This page debates the ideal seasons for physical exercise, contrasting Aristotle's view that summer exercise is necessary to aid weak digestion with Hippocrates' and Galen's views that winter exercise is better for maintaining heat and balance.</summary>

# BOOK II.

<margin>Book 9, penultimate letter to Fuscus</margin>
...contrary things should be chosen in exercising. <margin>D</margin> Nor do I think I should overlook in this place what *Pliny* the Younger writes concerning the exercise he was accustomed to perform during the summer. When asked by *Fuscus* how he dispensed his day in Tuscany during the summer, he replied in this manner regarding his exercises:

> "When it is the fourth or fifth hour <note>roughly 10:00 or 11:00 AM</note>—for there is no fixed or measured time—as the day invites, I betake myself to the terrace or the covered portico; I meditate on the rest of my work and dictate it. I then enter my carriage. There I continue the same study as when walking or lying down. My concentration endures, refreshed by the very change of activity. I sleep again for a short while, then walk, and soon read aloud a Greek or Latin oration clearly and with intent, not so much for the sake of my voice as for my stomach <note>Pliny believed the physical act of declaiming aided digestion</note>; yet the voice is likewise strengthened by it. I walk again, am anointed with oil, exercise, and bathe. And a little later: Sometimes some things in this order are changed. For if I have lain down or walked for a long time, after sleep and reading I am carried not in a carriage, but—because it is shorter <margin>E</margin> and swifter—on horseback; sometimes I hunt."

Furthermore, in describing the particular time for exercise, *Aristotle* sometimes commended <margin>Plutarch in the book on Preserving Health</margin> that motion (as *Plutarch* also attributes to him) which occurs after taking food, on the grounds that the heat increased by the motion might then more easily digest the recently ingested food. <margin>B</margin> However, the contrary of this occurs: when heat is withdrawn by motion from the stomach to the entire circumference of the body, it not only fails to aid digestion, but actually hinders it, and hurries raw and undigested juices into the veins. Therefore, <margin>Cited place</margin> if *Aristotle* held this opinion, he is caught in a manifest error, all the more because *Hippocrates*, *Galenus*, and finally all approved physicians have pronounced with one voice that exercise must always be performed before food. <margin>Book on Good and Bad Juices</margin> "For just as," *Galen* used to say, "exercise before eating is the greatest thing for health, so is all movement after food most harmful." <note>original Greek: ὥσπερ γὰρ μέγιστόν ἐστι εἰς τὴν ὑγίειαν τὸ πρὸ τοῦ σιτεῖσθαι γυμνάσιον, οὕτω καὶ βλαβερώτατον ἐπὶ σιτίοις ἡ πᾶσα κίνησις</note> <margin>F</margin> That is, just as exercise performed before food is most conducive to health, so any movement after food is most destructive. For when exercise precedes food, a double and equally remarkable utility follows: first, that the innate heat <term>innate heat: the vital warmth believed by ancient doctors to drive digestion and life</term> is excited, increased, and beautifully prepared for future digestion; second, that it best distributes the useful juices throughout the entire body as they are intended, and provides an easier exit for excrements. If these are otherwise retained, they are accustomed to produce obstructions and many other diseases by stifling the innate heat. Conversely, if anyone approaches exercises after food, not only are innumerable raw humors stuffed into the constitution of the entire body, but even the universal cooking <note>the process of digestion was viewed as a form of internal "cooking" or concoction</note> of the juices is hindered. *Theophrastus* testified that this happens in all things, where those things which are being cooked are hindered by motion...

The author aligns with Galen and Hippocrates, arguing that exercise must precede eating to properly prime the body's "innate heat" for digestion.</summary>

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>

...wrote in this manner: *since even things being boiled are spoiled if they are moved at the wrong time.* <note>original: "ἐπεὶ καὶ τὰ ἑψόμενα κωλύεται, μὴ ἐν καιρῷ κινεύμενα"</note> For this reason, **Erasistratus** <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician</note> and **Diocles** <note>A 4th-century BC Greek physician</note> are to be greatly condemned; deceived by false reasoning, they prescribed walks after meals as exercise for those coughing up blood, for consumptives, and for many other invalids. However, I believe these warnings should be understood as referring to more violent movement, because **Avicenna** <note>The Persian "Prince of Physicians," Ibn Sina</note> teaches that a tiny amount of movement after food settles it better in the stomach, especially when one is about to sleep soon. It is also consistent to believe that **Aristotle** meant this when he wrote that a walk after dinner prevents food from floating to the mouth of the stomach. Nevertheless, I judge that three things must be observed in this matter: the first is that no one should attempt exercise unless they have first expelled excrements through the nose, mouth, bowels, and bladder, since **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> and **Avicenna**

<margin>
B
Galen, *On the Preservation of Health*, book 2, chapter 2.
Avicenna, book 1, fen 1, doctrine 2, chapter 3.
</margin>
proclaim that exercise is not safe unless the body is emptied; and in addition to this, yesterday's food must be perfectly digested. For if anyone approaches exercise too early or too late, they will either be filled with raw humors and various wastes, or they will increase the production of pale bile. Moreover, it will be known that the food is already digested both from eructations <note>belching</note> and from the urine; for as long as the urine is whiter, it shows that one must abstain from movement, but when it has turned from white to more yellow, it indicates that the time for exercising is now at hand. The second thing to be observed is that labor or exercise should not be undertaken with an immoderately empty and clearly hungry stomach. For in this way it will happen that the food later ingested—not yet settled or digested by the "raving" stomach and consequently by the very famished limbs—is seized too greedily, and therefore countless "crudities" <note>undigested matter</note> and obstructions arise. Understanding this well, **Hippocrates** <note>The "Father of Medicine"</note> said: *where there is hunger, one must not labor,*

<margin>
C
Hippocrates, *Aphorisms*, section 2, aph. 16.
Avicenna, book 1, fen 3, tract 2, chapter 3.
Hippocrates, *Epidemics*, book 6, section 3.
Galen, *Commentary on Epidemics 6*, section 3, aph. 2.

that is, when hungry, one must not work. The third thing to be observed is that food should not be taken immediately after exercise, but a moderate delay should be interposed until the heat subsides and the agitation of the body appears settled. **Pliny the Younger** is the authority that the elder **Spurinna** <note>A Roman official known for his disciplined lifestyle</note> always observed this most diligently in preserving his health; and Galen writes that this was confirmed both by Erasistratus and by other more ancient physicians. However, fat people who strive to become thinner are to be excepted; **Hippocrates** (or perhaps **Polybus**) advised them to take food while still panting from exercise in the book *On a Healthy Diet*. **Aristotle** also judged that this should not be done [by others] because immediately after exercise the body is still being purged of labor and is not yet at rest, and furthermore, the stirred-up wastes are overflowing; hence hunger does not arise then, nor can the heat be free for cooking <note>digesting</note> the food. For this reason, those who have exercised should even less frequently wash immediately with cold water, or drink wine or cold water.

# BOOK

<margin>D</margin>

For this reason, athletes avoided it entirely after their workouts, if we believe Galen <note>Galen was a prominent Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,300 years.</note>. Regarding the specific hour of the day in which healthy men—with whom almost this entire treatise is concerned—ought to devote themselves to bodily exercises for the sake of their health, I find it decreed in the works of Galen and Avicenna <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian physician and philosopher, author of The Canon of Medicine.</note> that in the Spring, the midday hour should be chosen, when the state of the air is more temperate. In the Summer, the morning hour is best, so that the heat of the day may be avoided as much as possible. Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" in Ancient Greece.</note> seems to have simply recommended this hour for walking,

and we read in Plutarch that Alexander, King of the Macedonians, always loved it. He used to say, having rejected professional chefs, that he brought much better ones along with him: namely, a morning walk to season his lunch, and a light lunch to season his dinner. In Autumn and Winter, the evening hour is best, unless either food taken in the morning or something else forbids it. For since in these seasons the air is colder in the morning, and the other short parts of the day are consumed in necessary business—and furthermore, even a small amount of food taken in the morning cannot be digested until the evening—that hour alone was approved by the ancients as fit for exercise. Hence the Emperor Marcus Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius, the Stoic Emperor.</note>, who was most diligent regarding everyone's health, used to enter the wrestling school <note>term: palaestra (a public place in ancient Greece or Rome for training in wrestling and athletics)</note> on the shortest days at sunset, as Galen reports. (I believe he exercised there with the ball, running, and boxing, since Capitolinus writes that these kinds of exercises pleased him exceedingly and that he excelled in them.) On the longest days, however, he entered at the ninth or at most the tenth hour. Martial seems to testify that this hour, along with the eighth, was common to almost all men for exercising their bodies, where he writes to Euphemus regarding how the hours of the day were distributed in Rome:

Because the body is strengthened by the preceding sleep, it is ultimately more free from any impediments; furthermore, there is less danger that the food from outside has not been properly digested. On the contrary, in the evening—when food has not yet achieved <term>concoction</term><note>The archaic term for digestion, likened to a "cooking" process in the stomach.</note> and the body is more overflowing and burdened with superfluities—everyone sees that one ought to rest rather than exercise. I believe Avicenna noticed this as well when he said: *In winter, it would be reasonable for exercise to be delayed almost until evening, but other prohibitive factors forbid this.* Therefore, in our times, healthy people should almost always undertake exercise in the morning before eating. No author will be found who recommends exercise after a meal, provided they are consulting wisely; if they do so, it will be recognized that they do it not for the sake of health or acquiring a good constitution, but rather for the sake of curing some particular ailment. <margin>E</margin> There is also another matter to be greatly considered in this place: the ancients, both Romans and many others, always divided days and nights separately into twelve hours. Some were called the "greatest" hours of the day (as in summer), others the "smallest" (as in winter), <margin>
Book on the Knowledge and Cure of Every Soul's Affections, Chapter 5.
</margin> and others "equinoctial." Galen writes that this number was chosen by them as the most useful of all because it contains a half, a double, a fourth, a sixth, and a twelfth—which no other number after it seems to contain until one reaches twenty-four. Therefore, lest anyone—thinking the hours of the ancients' day were the same as the Italian hours and many others of our own times—should have cause for error in exercise or other matters, they must keep in mind this division of hours used by the ancients. In this way, they will be able to judge customs correctly and easily adapt ancient practices to new ones.

->Chapter XII. How much exercise should be performed.<-

<note>Decorative historiated initial 'E' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or physician, surrounded by ornamental scrolling and architectural elements.</note>

Among those things which lead many to believe the art of physicians is conjectural and almost uncertain, the principal reason has always been thought to be the *measure* of all remedies to be applied. Some of the ancients at times valued this so highly that, as if dejected by the hope of ever knowing it, they refused to practice medicine. For this reason, both professors of medicine and those who strive to preserve health by the help of exercise have need of every care and diligence to know the measure and quantity of their actions, without which incredible errors <insert>occur</insert>.

<margin>Pliny, Book 29, chapter 1.</margin>
Such errors are commonly committed, and for the most part (to use the words of Pliny) <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author.</note> ignorance turns out to be fatal. Since we profess to hand down the entire art of exercise, we shall now endeavor to show how much each individual ought to be exercised. And lest our discourse wander too far while explaining individual details, the entire treatment of the quantity of exercises will consist of these points: What the common limit of exercise ought to be; how much the strong, the weak, the elderly, men, and boys should exercise; how much in winter, summer, spring, and autumn; how much those living temperately, and those of a moist, hot, cold, or dry temperament; how much the sickly; and how much those unaccustomed to it. For once these things are known, one could rightly desire nothing more as far as the present chapter is concerned.

But before I approach the matter, I consider it should be noted that this discourse will not be concerning sick bodies; both because they require few exercises, and because the types and measures of exercises vary according to the varieties of diseases; and therefore they cannot be defined by a fixed rule.

<margin>C</margin>
The common limit of exercises, therefore, which <margin>Galen, *On Affected Parts*, book 5, ch. 5; *On the Method of Healing*, book 6, ch. 11; *On the Preservation of Health*, book 1, sentence 13; book 2, ch. 3; *Commentary on Hippocrates' Epidemics*, book 6, commentary 2.</margin> Galen, Oribasius, Avicenna, and Aetius <note>These are the primary authorities of ancient and medieval medicine: Galen (Greek), Oribasius (Byzantine), Avicenna (Persian/Islamic), and Aetius (Byzantine).</note> have taught following Hippocrates, is twofold. One is specifically when a vapor mixed for a little while with sweat is felt, the veins swell, and the breathing is altered. For since two things are required from exercise—the strength of the limbs and the increase of heat which may digest the juices <note>The "humors" or fluids of the body.</note>, distribute the digested juices to nourish the limbs, and finally dissipate useless waste—unless the exercise is of such a degree and reaches a similar limit, all those things can be obtained neither well nor perfectly.

The other limit is that each person should exercise for as long as a florid color is produced in his face and body; and as long as he performs his movements sharply, steadily, and gracefully, and perceives no weariness worth mentioning. But if the heat begins to vanish, or the mass of the body appears a little more contracted, or weariness now looms: one must stop immediately. This is lest, if one proceeds further, the body becomes thinner than is right; the good juices are exhausted along with the bad; and finally the natural heat is rendered weaker. Thus, instead of acquiring strength, the forces of the body would rather be destroyed.

<margin>C</margin>
Similarly, when the alacrity, steadiness, or grace of the movements is seen to slacken or collapse in any way: one must certainly stop at once. Likewise, if any change in the quality or quantity of the sweat occurs; for it is proper that the sweat be produced more copiously and more fervently as the movements become more vehement. Therefore, when it is rendered either less or colder: know then that the body is being exhausted, chilled, and dried out more than is right. And accordingly, it is fitting to attend diligently to the body being exercised so that, when any of the aforementioned signs appears...

# BOOK

As soon as [the body] begins to produce [sweat], the exercise should immediately be stopped. <margin>D</margin> And these are certain common limits which the great majority of those exercising themselves ought to maintain. Afterward, particular limits follow, for which I wish it to be decreed that the strong can be exercised longer than others (unless something else stands in the way), even if their strength should flag for a little while; for indeed, their strength can very easily be restored. The weak, certainly, ought to be exercised very little; otherwise, if their strength suffers even the slightest bit, it is repaired only with difficulty and over a long time. Therefore, it will be enough for them to warm up without reaching the beginning of sweat. 

The elderly, while they exercise, ought to avoid sweat with every care; for being naturally dry and parched, they would thus contract an even greater dryness. Furthermore, although we have already said that exercises accustomed in youth are suitable in old age, it must be known in this place that the elderly must always be exercised less than they were accustomed to as youths. They must entirely avoid the sensation of fatigue, <margin>E</margin> and the limit of their exercise should be set at the arousal of hunger—just as we read that Socrates, when already an old man, was accustomed to exercise until he became hungry. 

Men—under which category are included all those existing between adolescence and old age—require moderate exercises. For they are either harmed if they are exercised more than is right, or they reap very little fruit if they are exercised less, or in either case, they contract some disordered habit of body. Therefore, the common limit already explained will be wonderfully suited to all of them. 

Boys, from their first until their third seven-year period of age <note>roughly ages 7 to 21</note>, can properly withstand many labors. Therefore, it is permitted for them to grow warm, to pant, to sweat, and to be tired for a little while without penalty. For abounding in many waste products <note>original: "excrementis," referring to bodily fluids or humors needing expulsion</note> due to the imprudence of their way of living, they are helped by sweats and many labors; moreover, being endowed with strong powers, they are not at all harmed by light fatigue. <margin>F</margin> Nevertheless, it is never fitting for boys to exceed moderation in labor, and all the less so the closer they are to their first seven-year period. Indeed, by the untimely hardship of exercise, the growth of a boy's body—which is prepared by nature for maximum increase—is inhibited. <margin>Galen, On the Preservation of Health, book 1, chapter 10; Aristotle, Politics, book 7, chapter 4.</margin> On this account, Galen condemned several physical trainers <term>paedotribas: Greek term for those who trained youth in gymnastics</term> of his time because they exercised boys more than was fair. Similarly, Aristotle judged that the Spartans <note>original: "Laconas"</note> should be disapproved of, who by excessive labors and exercises rendered boys wild—as he also did those nations who, desiring to produce the physique of athletes in boys through labors, deformed their bodies and impeded their growth. For among those who won at the Olympic Games, only two or three have existed who achieved victory both as adolescents and as men, because through violent and excessive...

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>In the book *On Good and Bad Juices* <note>original: "In lib. de cibis bon. & ma. suc." referring to Galen's treatise on the humors produced by food.</note></margin>
**A** In children, the exercises applied to them took away their strength and power along with the growth of the body. Therefore, children can be exercised a great deal, but not immoderately. In winter, one should exercise much, yet short of sweating—lest the cold do more harm—and only until the entire body grows warm. In spring, more exercise is needed, even unto sweating. In autumn, less; and least of all in summer; for at that time (whatever Aristotle may have said), it is not expedient for anyone to sweat, grow hot, or become fatigued, as everyone is already sufficiently exhausted and weakened by the surrounding air. Those who lead a temperate life, even if they abound in few superfluities <note>waste products or excess humors</note> and therefore seem to require less exercise according to Galen’s opinion, must nevertheless exercise moderately themselves. This prevents the limbs from becoming sluggish through idleness or the internal heat from becoming dormant, which would cause them to lose their proper and natural condition; it also ensures that the waste products necessarily generated even in those living temperately are not retained.

<margin>Book 1, *On the Properties of Foodstuffs*</margin>
**B** Those who are incontinent <note>lacking self-control in diet or lifestyle</note>, however, just as they aggregate many waste products and many superfluous humors, so they have need of much exercise and labor. These activities consume those humors and wastes and, by inducing deep sleep, more successfully aid digestion. Indeed, Galen feels that ditch-diggers and reapers are very little harmed by a poor way of living for this reason: because they are cast into deep sleep by their labors, they digest even the worst foods well and reduce them to a better nature. Therefore, provided that a mountain of raw humors lurking in the periphery of the body, or a weakness of strength (which usually accompanies these), or something else does not prohibit it, the more and the longer these people exercise, the more they will benefit themselves—whether they only grow warm, or sweat, or even become lightly fatigued.

**C** Moist bodies <note>referring to the "wet" temperament</note> require much exercise, so that the excessive moisture may be dried out by the frequency of movement; hence, these can be exercised until a copious sweat flows out without a loss of strength. Dry bodies should be exercised less, and should never wait for heat or sweat during exercise. It is expedient for cold bodies to be exercised until the person perceives themselves to be warmed through. Hot bodies, however, are to be exercised sparingly; one should never expect sweat, intense heat, or a significant change in breath in them. Furthermore, hot and dry bodies enjoy little or no exercise, lest both the heat and the dryness be increased at the same time. Cold and dry bodies, by reason of their coldness, have need of exercise up to the point of manifest warming; however, on account of their dryness, they must be very careful to avoid sweating. It is fitting for hot and moist bodies to use moderate exercise, since too little does not diminish the superfluous moisture, while too much melts it down and heats it excessively, and from there—

For this reason, it is necessary for such bodies to avoid any violent alteration of the breath and excessive heating. Furthermore, those with cold and moist temperaments should be exercised only to the point that they breathe deeply, grow warm, and even sweat a little. In short, bodies of this kind require the most exercise of all; for in this way, the waste-like moisture with which they are filled is emptied, the natural heat is awakened, and all digestions are most beautifully perfected. Finally, no one is ignorant of the fact that convalescents <term>valetudinarios: those recovering from illness</term>, who are just rising from their sickness, ought to use very little exercise. Since their strengths are extremely weak, their heat feeble, and their limbs dried out, they cannot help but suffer the greatest harm if they are agitated by much exercise. Therefore, these individuals should be exercised only until the breath changes, until heat arrives, or until any sign of fatigue appears. However, as they are restored, as their strength grows, and as they begin to feel better, they ought to increase their exercises.

Lastly, regarding those who are unaccustomed to exercise: since we have already shown that such a bad habit must be set aside, they ought first to be purged of the humors and superfluities arising from sluggishness, according to the counsel of Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note>. Otherwise, there is an imminent danger that they may be immediately attacked by the destructive diseases of the fluxes. Next, they should be exercised very sparingly for several days; afterwards, the amount of exercise is to be gradually increased until that limit is reached which experience teaches is sufficient for the unaccustomed and warms them without any distress. Always observe this (as we have also demonstrated above): immoderate exercise harms everyone. Indeed, it robs children of their growth and melts away their limbs; in men, it produces unequal distempers and sometimes a fever, <margin>Galen, *On the Causes of Symptoms*, Book 3</margin> just as Galen relates concerning a man forced to exercise immoderately in his book *On Pre-initiating Causes*. In the elderly, it produces incurable weariness and dryness; and finally, in everyone, it always causes some good quality to flow away.

Let these be the signs of immoderate exercise: when the joints are felt to have become too hot; when the whole body appears dry and uneven; when a sensation of a certain ulcerous pain arises during movement; when labor is set aside by force and not by will; and when paleness succeeds sweat, as is seen in athletes <margin>Problem 5, section 38</margin> who [exercise] immoderately...

->On the Method of Exercising. Chapter XIII.<-

<margin>B</margin>
In addition to the place, time, and quantity—which we have demonstrated must be observed with the greatest care in performing exercises—there is also the *method*. This carries such weight in these matters, as in the correct performance of most other things, that unless it is applied, all other efforts are rendered superfluous, and the way lies wide open to almost infinite errors. For this reason, it is highly relevant to the completion of this treatise that we explain in a brief discourse the method which the ancients maintained in exercising their bodies, and which everyone in our own times who is eager for health can and should use with profit. The method, therefore, which we read the ancients used for health, was that which Oribasius of Pergamon (physician to the Emperor Julian), Aetius of Amida, and Avicenna (the most learned of the Arabs) brought to light. <margin>Oribasius, Collection to Julian, Book 6, ch. 15; Aetius, Book 1, series 3, ch. 2; Avicenna, Book 1, fen 3, ch. 3.</margin>

<margin>C</margin>
For when men and youths were to be exercised, once a perfect digestion appeared through the urine <note>Physicians of this era judged the completion of digestion by the color and consistency of urine</note> and they had emptied the bowels of waste, the majority stripped themselves. Soon they were rubbed moderately until a blooming color settled on the surface of the skin, and the flexibility of the limbs and agility for every movement were convincing. Having been rubbed, they were anointed with sweet oil; so that it might better penetrate every limb, it was applied with the hands pressing and smoothing from all sides. After the anointing, those who wished to be exercised in wrestling or the *pancratium* <note>A grueling ancient Greek sport combining boxing and wrestling</note> were sprinkled with dust. Others descended immediately into exercise, according as one seemed more useful or more pleasing than another to each person. When the exercise was finished, they rested a little; then, with *strigils* <note>Curved metal scrapers used to remove sweat and oil</note> or somewhat rough cloths, they scraped the scrapings from the body. Once this was done, they were sometimes rubbed again with the friction called *apotherapeutike* <note>original: ἀποθεραπευτικὴ; a restorative or "after-care" massage intended to soothe the body after exertion</note>, and similarly anointed, sometimes in the sun, sometimes by a fire, as Cornelius Celsus <note>A 1st-century Roman medical encyclopedist</note> testifies. <margin>Celsus, Book 1, ch. 2.</margin> And so, almost always, they entered the bath—

**D** ...in a chamber as high, bright, and spacious as possible; only then, having rarely dressed themselves <note>The author implies they remained lightly clad or nude during the process</note>, did they approach to take their food. And this was the entire method which, whether in public gymnasiums <term>gymnasia: ancient Greek and Roman centers for physical training and education</term> or in private places, the greater part of free men—and those who solemnly devoted themselves to caring for their health and acquiring a good physical habit—frequently employed. Nor should anyone wonder how free men were occupied every day with so many cares for the body, since many authors, and especially Columella in the thirty-sixth chapter of his book <note>original: "Columella trigesimo sexto lib. cap." referring to the Roman writer on agriculture</note>, have committed to memory that all men, not to mention the more distinguished ones, were accustomed to be rubbed down daily. Concerning this custom and method of rubbing, we shall, if it please God, at some time add a treatise to this work.

**E** Furthermore, it is likely that many others existed who were hindered either by public or private business; or detained by the necessary labors of various arts; or compelled by some reason of health not to exercise in this manner at all. Instead, having dismissed the formal rubbings <term>frictionibus: therapeutic massages or skin-rubbing</term> and anointings <term>unctionibus: the application of oils</term>, they embraced whatever exercises they could. Likewise, many were found who, for some of the aforementioned reasons, had no leisure at all to devote to exercise; <margin>Book 1, On Good and Bad Juices of Foods</margin> for all of whom Galen <note>A famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose theories dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> teaches that there is need for a more exact diet and healthy medicines.

But truly, since in our age those gymnasiums built by the ancients for the convenience of exercising have ceased to be in use, and we have neither gymnasts nor physical trainers <term>paedotribas: specialists in gymnastics and physical education</term>, nor oilers <term>aliptas: servants who anointed wrestlers</term> and re-anointers <term>reunctores</term>, from whom we might seek the methods and conveniences of rubbing, anointing, and finally exercising in whatever way you wish, it will suffice for those who, hindered by some necessary occasion, have no leisure to exercise themselves freely, that they should rather be exercised in whatever way they can, than to live always in total rest. However, let them observe this one thing: that they do not, immediately after food, too anxiously undertake those exercises which they wish to do for the sake of health, **F** but at least allow some hours to pass between, so that the least possible harm may follow from it.

Furthermore, those who are their own masters and can freely devote greater leisure to the care of their own bodies ought to observe all these things diligently: first, they should strive to accurately cleanse the body of feces and urine, as well as mucus and spit, comb the head, and wash the hands and face, lest the excrements lurking in various cavities of the body and in its very circumference, being stirred up by motion, cause offense by their vapors; or, being sometimes stuffed into narrow passages or melted by the heat of exercise, produce obstructions and various fluxes <note>In ancient medicine, "fluxes" were the harmful flow of bodily fluids or "humors"</note>. Second, they should cover the body with those garments which cannot add labor to the exercise itself, and which meanwhile protect them from winds, if there be any, or from cold; or even if the heat is pressing, can in no way increase or foster the fervor; for unless garments...

# BOOK FOUR

<margin>A</margin> If clothing is not prudently adapted for those exercising, besides the notable hindrance they usually present to those laboring in motion, they also cause one to sweat without the proper measure of movement and to endure other inconveniences. Indeed, if sweat occurs in such a way—produced while heavily clothed but without sufficient movement—it is worse than sweat emanating from labor, as <margin>Aristotle, *Problems*, section 2, problems 30 and 38; and section 3, problem 3.</margin> Aristotle <note>original: "Aristoteles disputat"</note> argues. The proof of this is that those sweating in this manner become more discolored; since the moisture has spread through the surface of the body and, becoming heated, cannot be cooled by the external air, it easily contracts a paleness. At the same time, the perspiration of the body, from which a pleasant warmth usually emanates, is inhibited by the garments. Third, it must be observed that everyone should begin to exercise slackly and gently, then gradually increase the intensity until reaching the limit that seems appropriate for them. Then, one should endeavor to slacken that vehemence again step by step, until one feels, taught by experience, that they have exercised enough.

<margin>B</margin> For to begin suddenly with intense exercises was judged by Galen <note>Claudius Galenus, the influential Roman physician</note> to be highly pernicious, not only for weak bodies but even for robust ones. Fourth, those who <margin>In the commentary on falling sickness (epilepsy).</margin> sweat during exercise must take care that, once the exercise is finished, they strip off the garments soaked with sweat and put on dry ones. This should be done, if possible, in a warm or temperate place, or at least one that is neither cold nor swept by winds. For if those damp clothes are kept on, it is easy for the sweat to be absorbed again by the flesh (which has been relaxed by the heat), and thus the passages <term>meatus</term> <note>The pores or channels of the body through which fluids and vapors pass.</note> of the body are obstructed again. Furthermore, wet cloths soon grow cold and induce shivering, foul odors, and other troubles, and from this, fevers are sometimes known to arise. Fifth, it must be observed that (as we also warned above) one should not give oneself to rest or take food immediately after exercise. Instead, one should engage in some gentle and very relaxed

<margin>C</margin> motion, and abstain from taking food until that disturbance and "fluctuation" of the body caused by the heat of exercise has entirely ceased, and a certain tranquility and relief has followed. Therefore, the whole method and order of exercising shall be: first, to cleanse the body of any superfluities <note>Waste products or excrement.</note>, comb the head, wash the hands and face, clothe oneself appropriately, begin with slow and relaxed movements, proceed to faster and more vehement ones, then gradually slacken again, strip off the sweat-soaked garments, move gently at the end, and take food only when the agitation of the exercise has settled. Let these points suffice regarding the universal theory and method of exercises. It remains now to describe the particular natures and effects of individual exercises, which we shall endeavor to fulfill as fully as possible in the following books.

# THE FIFTH BOOK OF THE ART OF GYMNASTICS

### *Chapter 1: On the order of things to be done, and on several matters worth knowing.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring a figure amidst scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
Just as no fruit could be expected from the knowledge of particular exercises unless a correct and universal method—which we have handed down sufficiently in the previous book (unless I am mistaken)—were perfectly possessed; so indeed would that method turn out to be fruitless and almost vain, unless <margin>E</margin> this treatment of almost all particular exercises, which we are about to undertake, were connected to it. Indeed, that knowledge might seem uncertain and deceptive by which an exercise, understood in a general way, is thought to help. But if it is known what kind of exercise it is, what harm it might cause, or what benefit it is fit to provide, it is certain that nothing further remains that ought to rightly satisfy the mind of one desiring the science of any exercises whatsoever. And therefore, lest the treatment of gymnastics begun by us be left imperfect, we shall pursue in the following sections the individual effects of the exercises already described; and we shall endeavor to state these both from the proven testimonies of the experience of ancient authors, and from the inspected nature of the thing itself, which <margin>Galen, Method of Medicine, Book 12</margin> Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his "Method of Medicine" was a foundational text for Renaissance doctors.</note> wrote was the true way of finding the conditions of things. And lest the entire discourse to follow wander without order, we have resolved to declare the matter in such a way that first the benefits flowing into the human body from each species of exercise, and then the <margin>F</margin> disadvantages, shall be explained one by one. For no one is ignorant of the fact that what is proven by experience to happen with many medicines—namely, that if they benefit some part of the body or some condition, they harm others—likewise happens in exercises. Furthermore, in explaining the utilities and harms, we shall take our beginning from the upper members and, for the most part, conclude with the last and lowest members in series, having first described those things which do not seem to regard any particular member of the body. Once these things have been so treated, I hope that I shall achieve at least two things: first, that these matters will settle in the minds of whoever reads them with greater ease and firmer knowledge; and second, that once a constant selection of exercises is made by those eager for health, either no errors or as few as possible will be committed, and thus finally many of those ruinous diseases will be avoided,

# BOOK FIVE

<margin>A</margin> ...will be [harmed], those whom laziness, avoidance of labor, and ignorance of exercise render not insignificant, and whom the untimely use of exercise is accustomed to continually produce. For all know that it is so arranged by nature that those things which are observed to be remarkably beneficial when applied to our bodies, often bring great detriment if they are applied either in no way, or in a distorted order, and altogether unseasonably. Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> judged that this almost always happens in the exercises themselves, <margin>In the book *On Good and Bad Juices*</margin> where he left it written that those who exercise before meals and at the opportune time have no need for an exquisite dietary regimen; indeed, they sometimes correct the defects committed by Nature in their health. Quite to the contrary, those who approach exercises neither before meals in any way, nor with order and time preserved, stand in need of both a more accurate diet and constant medications, and moreover, they corrupt their native health.

<margin>B</margin> Since, therefore, it is my purpose to join to the aforementioned things those which remain for completing the whole of gymnastics in such an order, I lead myself to preface this before all else: that in the preceding sections we placed the gymnastic faculty not in the curative, but in the preservative part of medicine. And yet, one may clearly understand from the books of Cornelius Celsus <note>A Roman encyclopedist known for *De Medicina*.</note> (who followed Asclepiades in many things), as well as the Methodist Caelius Aurelianus and Aretaeus, that all the sects of ancient physicians—and especially the Methodists, whose leaders were Asclepiades, Themison, and Soranus—greatly commended certain exercises in curing almost all long-term diseases. <margin>On Chronic [Diseases]</margin> Galen, and those who followed Galen in the Dogmatic sect, confirmed this for the most part.

But lest anyone think that either I or all of them have erred, I wish our opinions to be received in this way: <margin>C</margin> that the gymnastic art is principally concerned with the preservation of health, and consequently with the curative part. For you will find no exercise, of whatever kind it may be, that cannot be administered in healthy bodies without harm; yet, with a few exceptions—namely walking, being carried <note>gestatione: being moved by a litter or carriage</note>, sailing, and the like—scarcely one or another is found that can be granted to the sick with impunity. Indeed, those which are applied are commended as remedies rather than as exercises, since in the healthy all exercises are done solely to protect good health and induce the best habit of body; but in the sick, the same are administered so that they may cooperate like other medications in expelling disease. Therefore, when we bring into the open the custom of the ancients in using certain exercises for various diseases, there is no reason for anyone to be seized by wonder or to rebuke us, as if—

# BOOK

<margin>D</margin> Since we have determined that gymnastics serves solely for the preservation of health, and because we, keeping the nature of the matter itself before our eyes, have decided to define it in this way, we find that the ancients—moved at times by constant experience and at others by the conditions of diseases—seemed to hold slightly different views, yet in truth, they did not depart from our own opinion. Furthermore, I consider another point in this place to be highly worthy of consideration: although the custom of the ancients in many exercises differed from that which is in use today among almost everyone—such as ball games, wrestling, the discus, combat, and similar activities—nevertheless, since our custom departs little from the ancient one, differing only in certain accidental features and not in the nature of the thing itself, we can attribute almost the same effects to our exercises as they did to theirs. We need only observe one or two things: that the ancients were accustomed to employ ointments <note>original: "unctiones"</note> and powders in many exercises, which no one today, or very few, do. <margin>E</margin> And this is of great importance in varying the qualities of both, since Hippocrates, speaking of these matters, wrote <margin>In Book 2 of *On Regimen*, near the end.</margin> that exercises performed in powder and oil undergo great differences. For powder is cold, while oil is warm; hence it arises that in winter, oil increases the body more by preventing the cold from taking anything away from the body. In summer, however, by creating an excess of heat, it melts the flesh, since the body is heated by the season, the oil, and the labor alike. Conversely, powder increases the body more in summer by moderating the heat of the air and the body, while in winter it induces cold and chill. Furthermore, the greater part of men then were sated with food only once in the evening, whereas our people take food twice, which likewise matters not a little in varying the conditions of the exercises. Therefore, whoever wishes to pass a fair judgment on the exercises of our time must exactly weigh what the ointments and the single daily meal imply, and by removing all of that from our practices, consider the remaining effects to be the same or only slightly different. <margin>F</margin>

**A**ccording to Galen <note>Galen was a prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, there was a reason why athletes—who sought to prevent sweating by increasing the density of their bodies and consequently preserve their strength—used preparatory exercises before all other training. Many men likewise employed this practice after sexual intercourse to correct the looseness of the body generated by venereal motion. I speak here of midday intercourse, since the looseness arising from nighttime activity is sufficiently cured by sleep. For this reason, I am accustomed to greatly praise Soclarus, who, in the works of Plutarch, disputes most gravely against the physician Epicurus, arguing that intercourse ought to be practiced at night for this very purpose. Similarly, I have been accustomed to prefer the opinion of Paul <note>Likely Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical encyclopedist.</note> over the views of Galen and Aetius; for Paul believed, contrary to their decrees, that the opportune time for lying together is after food in the evening before sleep comes on, so that the weariness contracted from the act may be immediately relieved by falling asleep.

<margin>3. On Preserving Health, chapter 2.</margin>

**B**y Galen’s tradition, "apotherapeutic" exercise <note>From the Greek *apotherapeia*, meaning a "recovery" or "cooling down" routine intended to relieve fatigue.</note>—accepted both as a part of exercise and as a specific type—softens bodies that have been dried out by immoderate labors and purges excrements by relaxing the passages of the body. Hence, it was rightfully applied most often after more vehement exercises, after periods of wakefulness, or after sorrows, by which the passages of the body are closed and strength is significantly depressed. It was also recommended for those accustomed to the labors of the wrestling school <term>palaestra<gloss>a Greek wrestling school or gymnasium</gloss></term> who were forced to give them up due to the business of life. The differences in exercise, simply understood, which are derived from external factors, produce those effects which the conditions of the places themselves are able to produce. Therefore, those who exercise in hot places are more "burnt up"; those in damp places contract humidity, and so on for each condition. For bodies thinned out by exercise are very easily disposed to absorb whatever qualities of the air and location are present.

<margin>5. part, problem 1 and 12.</margin>

**C**oncerning the differences derived from the modes of use, it must be decided in this manner: that perpetual exercises—that is, those that are continuous and uniform—cause more fatigue than unequal ones. The reason is the same as that brought forward by Aristotle in his *Problems*: namely, that the limbs are broken down by much motion, and that motion which is single, continuous, and uniform constitutes "much" motion. However, unequal motion does not cause as much weariness because rest is born from change, and labor distributed among all parts is felt less by each individual part. By the same logic, interrupted and regulated motion produces less exhaustion, since the interruption brings rest, and rest induces less weariness. Exercises performed with oil not only mitigate present fatigue but also prevent future weariness, ward off dryness, and generate a greater readiness for movement. For this reason, Pollio, at ninety years of age, maintained his lifespan with oil...

<margin>A</margin> Even if we had decided to pass over these matters, I nevertheless believe it has been explained here not without use, since it has already been demonstrated quite often that universal treatments of such things are of great importance for acquiring a complete understanding of them. ### On the Effects of Dancing. Chapter III.

<margin>B</margin> Whoever wishes to accurately contemplate the types of dances used among the ancients will know that they did not lack temporal order, reason, proportion, and musical harmony. Therefore, one might judge that our modern dances—the *ballismos* <note>original: "βαλλισμὸς" - a rhythmic leaping or tossing movement</note> and the gesticulating movements which both women and men practice today for pleasure and delight—are not entirely dissimilar to them. Nevertheless, anyone can see this difference between the dances of the ancients and our own: just as those ancient dances sometimes served health, ours are either never or rarely performed with the goal of aiding the preservation of well-being. Indeed, they are mostly practiced after dinner and at night amidst drinking parties, when it would be better to attend to rest and sleep. Hence, if dancing is administered opportunely—just as our ancestors did, and just as <margin>C</margin> <margin>Book 4, Ch. 11</margin> we demonstrated above that all exercises ought to be performed—we can by no means deny that it produces many benefits. For anyone can understand that *Cubistica* <note>original: "Cubisticam" - a form of acrobatic dancing or tumbling, often involving headstands.</note>, which we said was the first species of dance, strengthens the arms and likewise the legs, which are certainly the parts most vigorously moved. Therefore, those who desire to have robust arms and a body flexible in every part should use this exercise frequently. However, because the head is necessarily heavily filled with blood while one tumbles onto it and bends it toward the ground, and secondly, because all the internal organs are shaken and the intestines moved from their places, and finally because the back and joints (which are violently moved during the flexions) suffer greatly, it is reasonable to avoid this exercise if one has a weak head, infirm viscera, or feeble loins and joints, whether by nature or by some accident. Regarding the third species of dance (for we shall treat the second in the following chapter...

<margin>D</margin> Regarding that which we have called the true art of dance <note>original: "orchestica"</note>, there were many types among the ancients. Since it is well established that almost all of these have been abolished today, or at least are no longer in use, it would be superfluous to review the effects of each one individually. Therefore, it will suffice to note those qualities in which it is likely that all those ancient forms agreed, and in which our own modern practice also agrees. For <term>cheironomia</term> <note>Greek: χειρονομίαν; the art of rhythmic hand gestures</note>, or the gesticulation of the hands, was held by Hippocrates (or perhaps Polybus) to thin the humors and draw the flesh upward. <margin>2. On Diet. Book 1. On Chronic Diseases, ch. 1.</margin> Similarly, Aretaeus recommended it for chronic headaches when the ailment is gradually resolving, as well as for those suffering from vertigo, epilepsy, and abdominal disorders. Finally, Dancing, which warms the entire body through movement, is very well suited for warding off stiffness and even certain tremors; it stands as a useful remedy particularly when the stomach labors in digestion or accumulates raw humors. <margin>E</margin> Furthermore, it strengthens and firms up failing hips, weak legs, and unsteady feet to such a degree that few things can be found that provide similar assistance. Nor does this kind of exercise yield to any other in the expelling of small stones from the kidneys or the bladder. However, Hippocrates left a testament that it is wonderfully harmful to pregnant women; <margin>In the book On the Nature of the Child.</margin> he advised a singing woman—who wished to cast off the fetus of her womb to avoid scandal—that she should jump and dance, promising that the conception would be destroyed by that dancing, as indeed happened afterward. Truly, whoever has a weak head and is liable to dizzy spells is undoubtedly harmed by those circuits, turns, and continuous movements. Similarly, those whose eyes water or who have dull vision are injured; for it happens to someone in these dances just as it does in rapid rotations, in which the eyes often suffer such damage that they see nothing at all, and sometimes the person falls. <margin>F</margin> It is appropriate for those who have sluggish or overheated kidneys, or those suffering for any reason from a flow of seed—called <term>gonorrhea</term> <note>Greek: γονορροίαν; here referring to a general discharge or weakness</note> by the Greeks—to abstain from dancing; otherwise, their conditions grow more raw and painful from the heating motion. And let all these things I have said be understood as referring to that species of dance which the ancients performed without weapons. But if anyone desires to learn the conditions of the "Armed Dance," as they called it, he may determine the matter truly and briefly in this way: namely, that all the effects produced by the former, whether good or bad, are produced by this one as well, except that the armed dance exercises the limbs more vehemently and causes them to heat up and sweat more. For this reason, Galen <margin>On the Preservation of Health</margin> placed it in no low rank among the "vehement" exercises, provided that one is covered in heavy armor while moving swiftly.

# BOOK FIVE
## On the effects of ball games. Chapter IV.

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>Chapters 4 & 5</margin>
In the second book, we judged extensively that many types of ball games existed in antiquity among both the Latins and the Greeks. For this reason, it is of no value in this section—where we have proposed only to explain the qualities of the exercises—to repeat the same things. I only wish this to be noticed: even if our modern types of ball games do not correspond in every respect to the types used by the ancients, they are nevertheless for the most part very similar. Therefore, we shall strive to relate their benefits and harms individually, so that by making a comparison of our games with theirs, it can be understood at once what they contribute and how they might be harmful. But so that this treatment does not become confused, we shall follow the same order we used above: first the Greek games, then the Latin ones.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Avicenna, Book 1, fen 3, doctrine 2, chapter 2.</margin>
Indeed, Avicenna <note>A Persian physician (980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note> held that all types of these exercises agree in the fact that they are "vigorous." Furthermore, this common benefit is perceived from all games of this kind: those who exercise themselves in them, or in any one of them, are rendered more ready for movement, and their vital actions are strengthened. Specifically, however, Galen and Paul <note>Referring to Galen of Pergamon and Paul of Aegina, influential ancient medical writers.</margin>
<margin>Galen, On Preserving Health, Book 1, chapter 18.</margin>
place the exercise of the small ball among the "swift" exercises, falling short of violence and extreme strength; for this reason, it thins out thick bodies, just as it was said similar exercises do. Therefore, one finds written by Lucilius in the works of Nonius:
<margin>»</margin>
> When with zeal in the gymnasium I had dried out my body with the double ball. <note>original: "Cum studio in gymnasio duplici corpus siccassem pila." Lucilius was a Roman satirist; "drying the body" refers to reducing excess humors or fat.</note>
<margin>»</margin>
<margin>»</margin>
<margin>Oribasius, Book 6, collection, chapter 32.</margin>
Now, the first species of the small ball of the Greeks, according to the opinion of Antyllus <note>A Greek surgeon of the 2nd century AD.</note>, renders the flesh solid and offers great utility to the arms, the back, and the protruding ribs; and since the legs labor greatly in that exercise, they profit not a little in acquiring strength.

<margin>C</margin>
The second species of small ball exercise was once considered the most excellent, as it provides a healthy body, ready for movement joined with strength; it steadies the gaze and does not "fill the head" <note>A medical term meaning it does not cause congestion or headaches.</note>. The third species, however, helps the eyes and the arms; it brings benefit to the spine on account of the bending that occurs while running, and it strengthens the legs in a wonderful way due to the running involved. Furthermore, I judge that all those things which Galen embraced in a few words in his short book dedicated to them apply to all these species of small ball: namely, that they produce virtue of the mind, and by exercising all parts of the body proportionately, they bring about good health and a harmony of the limbs. The first species of the large ball, according to Antyllus, strengthens the whole body; and since it cooperates vehemently in drawing matter <note>Referring to the "downward" movement of bodily fluids or waste.</note> downwards, it brings no small help to the head especially, and to all the upper parts. I believe Alexander of Tralles <note>A 6th-century Greek physician</note> was speaking of this when, in the treatment of priapism <note>A persistent and painful erection</note>, he recommended the exercise of the sphere <note>ball-playing</note>, so that the matter might be drawn away in a different direction and the flatulent spirit <note>The "pneuma" or gases believed to cause the condition</note> might be dispersed. The second species, which is performed with a ball larger than is right and is thrown with both hands because of its size, strengthens the arms; however, it inflicts too harsh a blow, and for that reason, it is not only useless for the sick or those recovering, but even affects those in good health with immoderate exhaustion. The empty ball <note>likely a bladder filled with air</note>, which we have made the third type, exercises just as much as the "motory" ball in which one runs; nevertheless, it is not very easy nor suitable, and therefore <margin>D</margin> <margin>Book 9, last chapter</margin> Oribasius <note>Personal physician to Emperor Julian</note> advised that it should be omitted, following the opinion of Antyllus. Aretaeus judged that the exercise of the ball, both large and small, was harmful to those suffering from vertigo, since the turnings and strain of the head and eyes bring on dizziness. <margin>Book 9, last chapter</margin> Paullus <note>Paul of Aegina</note> numbered the exercise of the *corycus* <note>A punching bag filled with grain or sand</note> among the "swift" exercises; since we have said that these thin out thicker bodies, <margin>E</margin> <margin>Book 5 on Chronic Diseases, last chapter</margin> Caelius Aurelianus, with the highest reasoning, approved of this exercise—which he writes is called *corycomachia* <note>original: "corycomachiam"; literally "bag-fighting"</note> by the Greeks—for reducing obesity <note>original: "polysarchiam"</note>. In this, I believe he followed <margin>Book 1 on Diet</margin> Hippocrates, who taught that *corycomachia* and *chironomia* <note>A form of shadow-boxing or rhythmic hand movement</note> provide the same benefits as wrestling. Antyllus judged that this type of exercise makes the body muscular and brings strength, and furthermore is suited to the whole body; moreover, because of the blows it inflicts, it is suitable for all the internal organs. Aretaeus likewise praised "bag-throwing" <note>original: "κορυκοβολίας" (korykobolias)</note> in cases of elephantiasis. However, if one considers the blows usually dealt to the chest by the *corycus*, he will easily perceive that those troubled by a weak chest are endangered by such exercise, and it can sometimes happen that vessels in the thorax are ruptured. And that is as much as can be said regarding the qualities of the ball games of the Greeks.

For this reason, I think Caelius Aurelianus spoke of this ball game <margin>Book 1 on Chronic Diseases, chapter 4</margin> when he ordered the shoulders to be exercised by the play of the sphere in epileptics. When it is sent forth by the fists, however, a greater utility comes to the hands; yet both help the internal organs, and contribute wonderfully to extruding stones from the kidneys and bladder, and they strengthen weak hips and legs. The "trigonal" ball <note>original: *pila trigonalis*; a ball game played by three people standing in a triangle</note>, which we have proved was small and corresponds to the third species described by Antyllus, produces exactly the same effects as that one. Indeed, watery eyes and those infected with inflammation are further aggravated by any movement, even the slightest; whereas rest restores and helps them, just as it does for those with indigestion. For we have said that no exercise should be undertaken unless the digestion of food has been completed. From this it follows that the game of ball is in no way suitable for those whose stomachs are still unwell from raw and undigested food—as perhaps Virgil was (being otherwise of a weak stomach) at the time when Horace wrote of him. But if there are those whose bellies and stomachs are filled with wind <note>gas</note> and are troubled by pains due to cold, the exercise of the ball is so far from causing them any harm that, by warming them and remarkably dispersing the wind, it offers no small benefit. <margin>Book 4, Chronic Diseases, Chapter 7.</margin> On this matter, Caelius Aurelianus is to be praised, who especially recommended the game of ball among other exercises for curing colic. <margin>C</margin><margin>Book 1, Chapter 2.</margin> Cornelius Celsus <note>Roman medical writer</note> likewise handed down that it is beneficial for those with weak stomachs for a similar reason.

The "Paganica" ball <note>a feather-stuffed ball used in the countryside</note>, on account of its breadth and hardness, was not without some difficulty, and therefore it was more suitable for peasants and hardy bodies than for city-dwellers. Today, it should not be permitted for the infirm, the elderly, or children to be exercised by movement of this kind. The "Harpastum" <note>a strenuous "snatch-ball" game</note>, which has been shown to agree with the *harpaston* of the Greeks, ought to be numbered among the swift and violent exercises. Because of this, it is able to thin the body, empty out waste products, increase heat, and produce strength. It especially strengthens the arms and shoulders; indeed, while the players struggle against one another, mutually forbidding the one stationed in the middle from catching the ball, the labor is greatest and most violent. <margin>Galen, On the Small Ball, Chapter 2.</margin> It is mixed with many twistings of the neck and many wrestling-style grapples, so much so that the head and neck are exercised by the neck-turnings, while the sides, chest, and belly are exercised by the lifting and lowering of the face, and by...

<margin>D</margin>They are fatigued by pushing, resisting, and other wrestling-like grips, by which exercises the loins and legs are also stretched in no small measure. ### *On the advantages and disadvantages of wrestling. Chapter V.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'L' featuring floral patterns and scrolled foliage within a square frame.</image-desc>

<margin>E</margin>Wrestling, which was almost always held in great use and esteem by the ancients—even if it was not, as we have said, greatly approved for health by physicians, and is today neglected by nobles and practiced almost solely by peasants in the manner it was by athletes among the Ancients—is nevertheless still used by some for maintaining health and preparing strength. Perhaps many others will imitate them if, as we have done thus far, we set forth for them the advantages and also the disadvantages observed by authors through long experience and natural reason. For Galen and Avicenna <note>Galen (2nd century) and Avicenna (11th century) were the primary authorities on medicine in the Renaissance</note>, above all others, have left it well-attested that wrestling is a vehement and great exercise. From this, it can be certain to anyone that the same results proceed from this as we have already declared to come from similar exercises. It must be added that wrestling can be performed in four ways, now as in ancient times: sometimes on the floor—a type we previously mentioned was called "rolling" <term>pancratium</term> <note>a no-holds-barred combat sport</note> by Plutarch <margin>F</margin> <margin>Book 2, ch. 8.</margin>—and other times with the body upright; and in both cases, sometimes vehemently and sometimes gently. Nor should it be overlooked in this place that among Latin writers, wrestling is usually, or at least sometimes, understood under the name of the <term>palaestra</term> <note>the Greek wrestling school or the art of wrestling itself</note>, just as the Greeks almost continually accept that very thing by the name of <term>pales</term> <note>original: "πάλης"</note>. Wrestling which is performed <margin>1 on diet.</margin> vehemently and with an upright body, according to Hippocrates <margin>In the place cited.</margin>, provides more labor to the external parts of the body, warms the flesh, strengthens it, and increases it. Indeed, in the opinion of Antyllus <note>An important Greek physician of the 2nd century AD</note>, it renders the breath firm and strong, and likewise makes the body solid and muscular; it also strengthens the nerves and finally corroborates all natural actions. <margin>A</margin>
<margin>2. Problem 7.</margin>
Wrestling moves sweat more effectively after a period of rest, as **Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristoteles"</note> believes, when the moisture collected during repose is suddenly drawn out by exercise; however, if the activity is continuous, the heat of the sun alone can dry out the body. It is particularly beneficial for the head; **Caelius Aurelianus** <note>A 5th-century Roman physician known for his translations of Greek medical works</note> praises wrestling performed under the guidance of a master for chronic head pain, as it sharpens the senses. For this reason, perhaps, <margin>Book 1, Chronic Diseases, ch. 1; Book 2, ch. 8.</margin> **Theodorus Priscianus** prescribes it for curing those suffering from <term>melancholy</term> <note>A condition then believed to be caused by an excess of black bile, resulting in despondency</note>, and it aids the stomach when oppressed by "cold" diseases. Regarding this, <margin>Book 3, Chronic Diseases, ch. 5.</margin> the same **Caelius** recorded that the <term>palaestra</term> <note>The Greek wrestling school or the exercise itself</note>, by agitating the body, is of great use; likewise, it brings great relief to cold bellies and the genital organs if they are troubled by humors or gas, since it warms nearly the entire body through those great exertions and movements. For this reason, **Oribasius** wrote that the palaestra or wrestling cures dropsy <note>edema or swelling</note>, and **Theodorus Priscianus** wrote that it extinguishes <term>satyriasis</term> <note>excessive sexual desire, then treated as a medical imbalance</note>. <margin>Book 6, ch. 28; Book 2 to Timothy, ch. 21.</margin>
<margin>B</margin>
However, exercise of this kind, due to its intensity, is hostile to all those suffering from fever; thus **Hippocrates** rightly and sharply rebuked **Prodicus** for killing feverish patients with wrestling. <margin>6th Epidemics, commentary 3, aphorism 32; 1st On Diet.</margin> **Hippocrates** advised that those of a "moist" nature should by no means exercise by wrestling; he moved by this somewhat obscure reasoning: lest the hollow passages, having been made more cavernous, be filled up. It is greatly harmful to the throat and neck; for these parts, when squeezed or wrenched more than is fair during grappling, receive damage. **Galen** wrote that such an event happened to **Commodus**, the son of the Emperor **Marcus [Aurelius]**, <margin>Book on Prognosis to Posthumus.</margin> recounting that while he was still a boy, he suffered an inflammation of the mouth from wrestling. **Josephus**, at the end of the first book of the *Antiquities of the Jews*, is the authority for the story that **Jacob**, while wrestling, injured his broad nerve <note>The sciatic nerve; a reference to the biblical struggle with the angel</note>, and for that reason, both he and the Jewish people thereafter abstained from eating that nerve. <margin>4th On the Method of Healing in Acute Diseases; In 6th Epidemics, commentary 3, aphorism 6; In the book on Diseases of the Kidneys.</margin> Furthermore, it is entirely foreign to the chest, <margin>C</margin> where there is great danger of either a ruptured vessel or the interruption of breath due to constrictions. Hence **Galen** did not say without reason that wrestlers run the risk of being suffocated; he also wished that such exercise be avoided by those with poorly affected kidneys and loins, although **Rufus of Ephesus**—who flourished in medicine at Rome under **Trajan** alongside **Crito**—did not at all forbid the palaestra to those recovering from kidney disease. **Celsus** wished it to be avoided in cases of internal ulcers, lest the healing ulcers be aggravated by wrestling, running, or any other means. Moreover, since the legs are frequently bent significantly during wrestling, it must be believed to be harmful to those afflicted with weakness of the legs. But all these things should be understood as referring to "upright" wrestling performed vehemently. That which is performed more moderately and calmly, on the other hand, according to **Antyllus**, generates much flesh. From this it follows that for those who are beginning to recover from illnesses, it is more suitable than the more intense form, and least—

[The exercise of wrestling] brings strength and fortitude even in the face of great danger; it benefits the head and the chest, and strengthens the nerves. I believe Plutarch was speaking of this when he wrote <margin>In his Life [of Lycurgus].</margin> that Lycurgus exercised the bodies of young women with running, wrestling, and the throwing of discs and javelins, so that—just as the root of a sprout germinates better when it takes a strong hold in harsh soil—these women might robustly endure childbirth and fight against its pains both honorably and easily. Furthermore, the wrestling that is performed upon a floor, if we believe Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler and personal physician to Emperor Julian.</note>, aids the afflicted midriff and intestines; <margin>In the place cited.</margin> it makes weak loins and infirm knees stronger, but it is less suitable for the head. Rolling in the wrestling-school <note>original: "palaestra"</note>, since it is counted by Galen among the "swift exercises," will be suited for thinning the body, just as it was commended by Caelius for reducing excessive fleshiness <note>original: "polysarchia" (obesity)</note>, and by Aetius—if done in the dust—for curing dropsy <note>An old term for edema or swelling caused by fluid retention.</note>. For Hippocrates, in the second book of *On Regimen*, is the authority that it cools the body by exhausting the humors. But according to Galen's opinion, it must be avoided with great care by those <margin>Book 5 of *On Preserving Health*, chapter 3.</margin> who suffer from dizziness for slight reasons, the "falling sickness" <note>original: "comitiales morbi" (epilepsy)</note>, severe inflammation of the eyes, or earaches. In a similar way, it should be avoided by those prone to tonsillitis and quinsy <note>A complication of tonsillitis involving an abscess in the throat.</note>, and those in whom "fluxions" <note>The movement of harmful bodily fluids or "humors."</note> readily fall upon the uvula <note>original: "columellam"</note>, the gums, the teeth, or finally any of those parts located around the neck or the whole head.

Thus far concerning wrestling. Regarding this, a doubt might arise for many: why Galen—who understood the gymnastic art <term>Gymnastics: In the ancient sense, this refers to the whole system of physical education and medical exercise.</term> better than all others—not only recommended wrestling to almost no one for any purpose, but rather condemned it as being of little use or entirely harmful? For in some places he said that the vessels of the chest are ruptured in wrestlers; in others that the legs are twisted, or they are suffocated; and elsewhere that wrestling is held in hatred by a well-ordered republic. But such doubts may be resolved in this way: <margin>To Thrasybulus, chapter 41.</margin> that in the opinion of Galen himself, the true wrestling-school <note>palaestra</note> without wrestling (through which only a tiny part of medical gymnastics exists) is less useful to man than all other exercises. Indeed, according to him, it is better to throw the javelin, run, ride, jump, hunt, sail, or dig, than to be exercised by wrestling. And just as wrestling is more closely related to and serves the "athletic" art <note>Professional competition for prizes, which Galen often distinguished from healthy exercise.</note>, so too it recedes further from the "medical" art. Hence it is no wonder if Galen did not wish to explain the powers of that exercise which he believed held the smallest benefit in medicine. We, however, have deemed it necessary to explain those things handed down by other authors—not so that I might place Galen’s authority behind the others (either those before him, whom he wrote had poor views on exercise, or those after him), but to demonstrate that if any benefits are to be expected from wrestling, they will be those indicated by these authors, and no others. For concerning this, I find it written in Hippocrates <margin>Book on Healthy Regimen.</margin> that those who use exercises should, in winter, run...
