<margin>A</margin> They ought to wrestle; in the summer, however, they should wrestle only a little and run not at all, but rather walk extensively, following the wind and the cool air. ### On the properties of boxing, the pancratium, and the weighted gauntlets. Chapter VII.

<note>The pancratium was an ancient Greek combat sport combining boxing and wrestling; the caestus was a leather hand-wrap, often weighted with metal, used by boxers.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative initial Q with a woodcut illustration of a figure seated in a landscape, within a circular frame.</image-desc>ALTHOUGH among the various exercises aimed at health, boxing <note>original: "pugilatus"</note> seems to claim the smallest share for itself, and appears to be a demonstration of the profession of athletes rather than of free-born men: nevertheless, if we accurately contemplate the parts of the body that are agitated by such motion, we will not immediately judge it to be performed without some benefit. For both the arms <margin>B</margin> and the hands are so strengthened and solidified by the help of this exercise in some individuals, that they do not hesitate to strike stones and wood with their fists and break them, to the great admiration of onlookers. Certainly, no one would deny that such people are in excellent health and enjoy a firm constitution in those parts. Therefore, for whoever desires to be strengthened in the arms, hands, and fingers, and to use them robustly, I do not see what more suitable exercise they ought to seek. This is even more true because, although in ancient times boxing was always practiced by those standing upright, it can nevertheless sometimes be performed—out of urgent necessity—by those lying down or sitting, no less than by those standing and moving. But it differs significantly whether it is performed upright or otherwise: since in those who are upright and moving, the upper parts of the body primarily feel the benefit of the exercise, yet the lower parts are not entirely deprived of it; this is not the case for <margin>C</margin> those lying or sitting, whose lower parts remain entirely idle. Boxing is harmful to the head. I cannot wonder enough why Aretaeus <note>A Greek physician of the 1st century AD</note> approved of it for those suffering from vertigo; it is harmful to the ears and the chest, which, being quite delicate, are greatly offended by those blows and the striking of fists. Similarly, all those whose teeth are weak and loose ought to beware of these strikes. Regarding the exercise of the hands, it has been handed down to memory by Aristotle <margin>2. prob. 5.</margin> <note>Referring to Aristotle's "Problems," Section 2, Problem 5</note> that sweat flows more from those exercising the hands if the other parts of the body maintain a similar state: because in that exercise the breath <note>original: "spiritus"</note> is held, and the parts under the armpits near the heart are rubbed. Since heat increases from this friction, the moisture is easily summoned out from the body by the help of both that heat and the friction which opens the pores. Indeed, I believe the physician Philagrius was speaking of all these exercises in the works of Aetius <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine physician</note> when he stated that exercise...

### On the Nature of Running. Chapter VII.

<margin>Galen, On Preserving Health, Book 6, chapter 10.</margin>
<margin>B</margin> JUST AS we have shown that boxing, a private exercise of the hands, had few uses among physicians, so it shall be demonstrated that running—in which almost the feet alone are exercised—has proven to be of the greatest utility, and has therefore been more frequently commended by physicians and <term>gymnastai</term> <note>ancient athletic trainers who specialized in the medical effects of exercise</note>. For since it is placed by Galen among those exercises which are swift without strength or violence, we cannot deny that it thins the body and reduces the flesh and the <term>juices</term> <note>the bodily humors or fluids</note>. This is what that most ancient author Hippocrates, as well as Galen, asserted based on the opinion of trainers and doctors. <margin>Commentary on Hippocrates' Epidemics, Book 6, commentary 3, aphorism 2.</margin> There is, however, a manifold distinction in the performance of running: one type can be done more swiftly and vehemently, another more slackly and calmly. For this reason, its effects must necessarily vary, just as the modes of running also vary: some are in a straight line, others oblique; some forward, others backward; some in a circle; some with naked bodies, others covered; <margin>C</margin> some over flat ground, others over uneven or mountainous paths. It was prudently handed down by Hippocrates and Galen that any kind of running brings harm to those with fevers. I perceive that Galen—who wrote that no one cures the sick with running—was speaking only of the more vehement sort; for even in his book *On the Exercise of the Small Ball*, he rightly disapproved of running as being unhealthy, thinning the overall habit of the body more than is right, and possessing nothing of manly exercise. <margin>Commentary on Epidemics 6, commentary 3, Aphorisms 31 and 2.</margin> Antyllus <note>a famous Greek surgeon and physician</note> likewise spoke of this kind of running when he called vehement running an "exercise." Otherwise, he would have held an opinion repugnant to Galen. Therefore, vehement running is almost always more harmful than useful for defending health; and if it brings any help, it undoubtedly contributes to the removal of flesh and immoderate fat, as Caelius Aurelianus <note>a 5th-century physician</note> proved. **A** If they suffer from an ulcer, or have recently suffered from one, Rufus of Ephesus <note>A famous Greek physician from the 1st century AD</note> believed they receive no small harm from running. Beyond these cases, it is well known among everyone that such exercise greatly aids the feet and legs, which are the primary parts in action. Therefore, since running brings so many benefits, it cannot be held to be without some disadvantages (which is the common nature of all remedies). For the great philosopher Aristotle proved that it is primarily laborious; comparing a runner to a walker, he tries to persuade us that the runner labors more because, being lifted and suspended, he sustains his whole body above himself, whereas the walker is supported by each part in turn as it steps, resting as if leaning against a wall. Regarding this, I consider that it should not be passed over in silence what Aristotle left written for us: namely, that those who run at a rapid pace are most especially seized by convulsions if someone should stand in their way while running. This is because those parts are most powerfully convulsed which we are violently pulling and moving in an opposite direction. Hence, if someone stands in the way of a man running and violently propelling his limbs forward, it happens that those parts which are still stretching and rushing forward are twisted back in the opposite direction. This certainly happens more to those who run while clothed and those who sleep too much; for being, as it were, bound and almost strangled, they flourish less in color than others who refresh themselves with moderate sleep. Hippocrates—or perhaps Polybus—believed in the second book *On Diet* that running, generally speaking, is more useful in winter than in summer. Conversely, Oribasius <note>Personal physician to Emperor Julian</note> felt it was suitable in both winter and midsummer. His <margin>C</margin> opinion will perhaps be judged truer if one agrees with Aristotle that sweat should be procured more in summer and less in winter. # BOOK FIVE

<margin>A</margin> ...abrupt and excessively violent twists are extremely harmful. Jumps performed high into the air, while beneficial to the hips, bring detriment to the chest; those performed toward lower ground cleanse the head of superfluous fluids <note>original: "superfluiditatibus"</note> by diverting them to the lower parts and strengthen the legs. However, they shake all the internal organs quite violently. For this reason, those who suffer from hernias (or what are otherwise called ruptures) or who have legs swollen with varicose veins, ought to avoid such exercises with the greatest care according to the opinion of Paul <note>likely Paul of Aegina, a 7th-century medical authority</note>; so too should all those with gout, and those who, for any slight cause, are troubled by "distillations" <note>an old medical term for the downward flow of harmful humors</note> to the feet and by all kinds of swellings. <margin>Book 3, chapter 5.</margin> These, then, are the effects of jumping. Galen demonstrated that when purging or bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note> is necessary, but cannot be administered due to age or some other impediment, jumping can substitute for them and empty out the redundant humors. Nevertheless, I have later found among various medical authors—and most notably <margin>B</margin> <margin>6th Commentary on the Epidemics, 3rd Aphorism, 2.</margin> in Rufus of Ephesus—that this same jumping is harmful to those who easily suffer from the passing of blood in the urine or a flux, or those who incur weakness and heat in the kidneys, as well as those who either have or <margin>Book on the Diseases of the Kidneys.</margin> recently had an ulcer in them. Indeed, it is even written in Aetius that in healthy kidneys, the veins are sometimes ruptured by a powerful jump. I wish all these points to be understood as referring to jumping performed simply. For those who strive to jump with their hands full of stone, lead, or some other weight, differ from others in this: as Aristotle and Theophrastus used to say, those who swing an empty hand create more labor for the arm, <margin>5th Part, Problem 8; in the book "On Movement."</margin> while these [with weights] create less. This is because the arm is almost convulsed by an empty swing since it has nothing to lean upon; but in a swing performed with small weights grasped in the hand, no such convulsion occurs, <margin>C</margin> since the jumper holds in his hands that which he leans upon, as it were, to prevent exhaustion. This is not unlike runners, who run faster while shaking their hands back and forth than they do with hands stretched out and idle; for in this way they support themselves, and by leaning on that spreading and unfolding of the hands, they move more vehemently, more firmly, and consequently more swiftly. <margin>Aristotle, Book on the Progression of Animals.</margin>

# BOOK [VI]

<margin>D</margin>
This exercise is suitable for warming the body, and especially the back, which seems to be most engaged when swinging the dumbbells; furthermore, it builds muscle. Galenus <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note> recorded that the upper parts of the body are specifically exercised by it. For this reason, even before him, Aretaeus <note>Aretaeus of Cappadocia, a Greek physician of the 1st century AD known for his descriptions of diseases.</note> approved the use of this kind of exercise for chronic headaches that are gradually subsiding, as well as for those suffering from abdominal complaints and vertigo. However, Oribasius, on the authority of Antyllus, writes that it exercises the shoulders and is suited for a stomach troubled by "flux" <note>An excess of bodily fluids or indigestion.</note>, or one that is weak and in which food turns sour or is digested with great effort. 

<margin>Book 3, *Chronic Diseases*, chapter 2.</margin>
Caelius Aurelianus praises it for arthritics <note>Those suffering from joint pain or gout.</note>, suggesting that first, wax should be given to be softened in the hands, or bundles should be held which the wrestlers call *halteres* <term>halteres: ancient stone or metal weights used in jumping and strength training</term>. Then, first waxen or wooden ones with a small amount of lead enclosed should be offered to be moved, and later heavier ones according to the degree of progress. 

<margin>6. *On the Preservation of Health*, chapter 14. E</margin>
Galen advised a certain man—who reported that he felt a stinging, excessively hot seed <note>Semen.</note> during ejaculation, which was felt not only by himself but also by the women with whom he had relations—that among other remedies, he should exercise with the dumbbells. 

<margin>Book 9, last chapter.</margin>
Following him later, Alexander Trallianus <note>A 6th-century Byzantine physician.</note> recommended this kind of exercise in treating priapism, because he noticed that it was conducive not only to dulling and weakening the seed, but also to drawing the matter in the opposite direction and dispersing sluggish spirits through the breath. 

<margin>*On the Composition of Medicines according to Kind*, chapter 2.</margin>
Similarly, Galen approved of exercise performed with dumbbells in the treatment of leg ulcers, unless something else prevents it, because it prevents harmful humors from flowing down to the lower parts. 

<margin>8. *Commentary on Hippocrates' Aphorisms*, 3. aph. 2.</margin>
He also judged that it could take the place of purging or bloodletting <note>original: "phlebotomia"</note> when these are required but the age or the will of the patient does not permit them.

<margin>F</margin>
But truly, no one would affirm that such exercise is suitable for either the head or the chest; the former is shaken too much and unevenly, while for the latter, there is an imminent danger that the vessels might be weakened in some way by the great force used by the arms. # BOOK FIVE

<margin>A</margin>
<margin>5. Eliac.</margin>
I deem it appropriate to add to all this that, although in this day and age that specific shape of the ancient jumping-weights <note>original: "halterum"</note> described by Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer</note> is no longer in use, other objects are used in their place. Some use small masses of lead or iron, while others use bricks or stones that are nearly spherical and heavy. The shape itself matters little in terms of varying the effects or preventing the same benefits from being found in our modern practice as in that of the ancients. This is especially true because those who exercise today by throwing stones or metal masses move and twist their arms, back, and all upper parts of the body in the same way as the ancient practitioners of the jumping-weights did. For this reason alone, all the effects we have explained above should also be expected in our own exercises.

## *On the effects of the discus and throwing. Chapter X.*

<margin>B</margin>
Regarding the discus, although I find very little mention made of it among the approved authors of medicine—and perhaps for that reason this section might demand to be skipped—nevertheless, Galen <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> has recorded that the throwing of the discus was not only an exercise that existed among the ancients and was commonly performed in the gymnasia, but it also held a significant place among the "vehement" <note>intense or vigorous</note> exercises. Furthermore, since it is still used today among many nations for the purpose of exercising the body, I did not want to pass over it entirely with "dry feet" <note>a Latin idiom meaning to pass over something without getting involved or touching upon it</note>. Therefore, it should first be known that this exercise, provided no errors are made in other respects, warms the body appropriately. Consequently, it is perfectly suited for cold constitutions and for those to whom fast-paced exercises are denied.

<margin>C</margin>
It also moderately strengthens those who are weak or infirm in their lower limbs. Since great and vehement efforts are required to throw the discus a long distance, the intensity of the movement and the tension of the muscles cause the joints to become more solid and purged of waste products <note>original: "excrementis," referring to metabolic byproducts or "bad humors" in Galenic medicine</note>. By virtue of this purging effect, Galen sometimes advised <margin>In the 6th book on Epidemics, commentary 3, aphorism 2</margin> that if a purging or bloodletting <note>term: phlebotomia (the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood)</note> were required, but could not be performed due to certain impediments, exercise performed with the discus should be admitted in their place. This would surely provide what was desired from bloodletting and medicinal purging. Specifically, however, this exercise is fit to strengthen the arms, the loins, and finally the entire back, which are the parts most agitated of all during the act. It is also recommended by Aretaeus <note>A Greek physician of the 1st century AD</note> for those suffering from vertigo. However, it must be greatly avoided by all those who have poorly affected kidneys or chests; for those—

<margin>E</margin>
I feel that this should by no means be shrouded in silence: namely, that the ancients, not without mystery, placed Aesculapius and Apollo—both authors of medicine and both masters of health—over the art of throwing as patron gods. Surely, by this sentiment they were hinting that this kind of exercise brings strenuous aid to the preservation of good health and the acquisition of a good physical condition. After we have established several species of this exercise—some taken from the variety of javelins or arrows, others accepted from the bows or catapults <term>balistae: ancient missile launchers, here referring to crossbows or similar mechanical bows</term> by which they are sent—I affirm that all possess plainly the same faculty. However, I would wish those who exercise in throwing what are called "iron poles" to be warned to apply great care; for experience has found that the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> is frequently ruptured and the intestines descend into the scrotum, and consequently hernias are generated in such exercises. 

<margin>F</margin>
And since the greatest force and an intense retention of breath are employed in the release, I think this kind of throwing is harmful to a constricted and weak chest. Nor should that be ignored which Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator</note> recorded in his memory: that Philoctetes <note>a hero of the Trojan War famous for his archery</note>, while he was tormented by unbearable pains, nevertheless prolonged his life by fowling <note>hunting birds</note> performed by the shooting of arrows.

# BOOK FIVE
## On the qualities of walking. Chapter XI.

<margin>A</margin>
There is no kind of exercise that those who devote themselves to health must more greatly seek out and understand, nor is there any practiced more frequently by almost all people at every time, than walking. No one will deny this, for there is no one—whether child, adult, or elder—who does not believe walking to be not only the most excellent exercise, but indeed the only one. Yet, few are found who, either through reason or long experience, have perfectly observed which parts of the body it benefits and which it harms. I believe this has happened partly because of the various types of walking, and partly due to the carelessness of later generations, who have conducted themselves more negligently and listlessly in these matters, as in

<margin>B</margin>
so many other ancient traditions. Therefore, I hope I shall be doing something worthwhile if, by reviewing the principal types of walking, I subsequently demonstrate what good or ill each one is capable of producing. But before all else, I desire two things to be considered by everyone. First, that one often finds among the Greek and Latin medical authors that "walkings" and "exercises" are prescribed at the same time, as if the former were separate from the latter and not truly exercises. I wish to interpret their opinions in this way: whenever they separate the two, they use the name "exercises" to signify those activities properly so-called <note>The author distinguishes between "proper" vigorous exercise (like wrestling or gymnastics) and "common" exercise like walking</note>, whereas walkings deserve to be called exercises only in a general and not a strict sense. The second point is that Galen <note>Claudius Galenus (129–c. 216 AD), the most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note>, and those who followed his teaching, handed down two principal types of walking:

<margin>C</margin>
one called "apotherapeutic" <term>apotherapeutic: from the Greek 'apotherapia', referring to a soothing post-exercise routine intended to eliminate fatigue</term> by physicians, which is usually employed after the labors of other exercises have been set aside (about which it is not our current purpose to speak much); the other is called by the simple name of "walking," which our ancestors used—and we may use—as a certain aid, either in afflicted bodies to restore health, or in healthy ones to preserve and increase it. Our entire discussion shall be concerning this latter type. Galen assigned no specific classification to it, as he did for other exercises, because since it has so many diverse types, it seems impossible to encompass them all under a single definition. Walkings are therefore divided by the motion itself, from which (so to speak) their essence exists; by the place in which they are performed; and by the time. By motion, because some are fast, some slow, some vigorous, some gentle, some long, some short, and some

It is doubly beneficial, and in short, for all those in whom it is necessary either for something to flow down from the upper parts to the lower, or to expel those things which are carried downward toward the lower parts. However, for all those suffering from fever, walking of this kind is harmful; for, as <margin>Commentary 3 on Epidemics 6, Aphorism 3.</margin> Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire.</note> believes, it increases heat and consequently increases the fevers. In cases of headache, Caelius <margin>Chronic Diseases, Book 1, chapter 1; Chapter 4.</margin> Aurelianus approved of the patient being exercised by walking—first slowly, then after a while more vigorously, and a little more upright with the legs extended. He also approved of light walking for epileptics, namely that which can draw down the humors from the highest to the lowest parts without shaking the head, gently dissipating and thinning them, and warming the general habit of the body without harm. <margin>D</margin> Caelius and Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a 1st-century Roman encyclopedist</note> suggested that walking is suitable for those with chronic conditions, especially when performed on soft straw or leveled ground. For those troubled by **gout** <note>original: "podagra"</note> and joint afflictions—as written by Trallianus—ought to be moved **moderately and without great fatigue** <note>original: "μετρίως, & ἄνευ κόπω πολλῷ"</note>, primarily before and not after meals. For exhaustion is most harmful to these patients, as it heats and inflames the joints more than is right; the joints then attract and seize other matter from distant parts of the body, providing a constant cause for further "fluxes" <note>The flowing of harmful humors to a specific site</note>. According to the opinion of Antyllus, much walking helps those who have an afflicted head or chest, those whose lower body parts are not being nourished, or those who require more vigorous motion in their exercises. However, it is of little benefit to those who do not bathe after exercise, those who need to walk after eating so that food descends to the bottom of the stomach, and those who feel a heaviness in the body.

<margin>E</margin> A long and straight walk causes less distress than a short one and benefits the head. <margin>Oribasius in the same place, book 1, ch. 4. Book 3, ch. 33. Celsus, book 3, chronic diseases, 7.</margin> Thus, Caelius and Cornelius Celsus rightly judged it useful for treating **epileptics**. However, it excessively draws out moisture and dries the body; for this reason, Themison <note>Founder of the Methodic school of medicine</note> is deservedly criticized for advising those suffering from wasting diseases <note>original: "atrophia"</note> to complete a walk of twelve stadia <note>Approx. 1.4 miles</note>. A long and brisk walk is vigorously helpful for suppressing hiccups according to the opinion of Aetius. A short walk, however, is more tiring because (as Aristotle used to say) the constant change arising from the motion and rest during the turns causes labor; likewise, it weakens the head due to those continuous reversals. For this reason, it is condemned for epileptics by the same Caelius, and not without cause. On these grounds, circular walking is also rightly disapproved of, as it makes the head dizzy and greatly harms the eyes.

<margin>Problem 38. F</margin> For Cassius, an ancient physician, in his small book of *Problems* written in the Greek language, investigated the cause of why movements made in a straight path do not generate dizziness, but only circular ones do. He says this happens because straight movements do not hinder the dispersal of matter, whereas circular ones do not allow it to occur because the air, struck more violently, prevents it. Furthermore, the matters inside are agitated just as they are outside; when they are carried around and are unable to exit, they produce a dizzying motion in the head. For just as all those with jaundice <note>original: "icterici"</note> perceive external tastes as bitter, and those suffering from "suffusions" in the eyes <note>likely cataracts</note> judge all colors to be red, similarly in circular motions, when the humors in the eyes are driven in a circle, all external things seem to be carried around, and thus the dizzying passion arises. ### Again on the Qualities of Walking. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' within a square frame, showing a landscape with foliage and a small figure.</image-desc>

<margin>B</margin>Among the types of walking categorized by location are those performed in the mountains, practiced either by ascending or descending. If done by ascending, the entire body is certainly fatigued; for according to Galen <margin>Galen, On the Preservation of Health, Book 2, Chapter 9</margin>, in this kind of motion, all the remaining members of the body are lifted and supported like a burden by those instruments of motion that move first. Aristotle writes <margin>Aristotle, Problems, Part 2, Problem 38</margin> that walking up steep inclines, even if the movements are slower, provokes more sweat than walking down slopes, and also causes shortness of breath. This is because, just as it is natural for every heavy thing to be carried downward, so it is against nature to be carried upward. Thus, the nature of the heat that propels our bodies, while it labors not at all on a decline, struggles under a heavy burden on an incline; it grows hotter more sharply due to such motion, moves the sweat, and halts the breath—especially since the various bending of the body can contribute to the loss of the direct rhythm of breathing.

<margin>C</margin>For this reason, according to the opinion of Antyllus <note>A famous Greek physician of the 2nd century AD</note>, such walking is beneficial for a chest that takes in little breath, especially before a meal, and it sometimes takes the place of more strenuous exercises. We read of Demosthenes that he was accustomed to walk while ascending and to recite orations during the walk, so that he might become used to the sustained exertion of breath required by orators in speaking. Truly, however, this same exercise is very harmful to weak knees; because, as Aristotle said, while we ascend, we do not merely throw the body upward and move the stretching of the body and knees, but the knees themselves—which are born to be bent forward according to nature—are bent backward as if against nature, and for that reason, they ache and labor greatly. On the other hand, walking on a decline, which is performed by descending, draws more from the head to the lower parts; but it harms weak thighs in no small measure, which, in the opinion of the same Aristotle... <margin>Aristotle, Problems, Part 5</margin>

# BOOK

**On** the contrary, these movements are performed against the natural inclination of the body, and as it were, the legs sustain the entire weight of the body while moving <margin>D</margin> and are therefore greatly fatigued. Walks that are carried out both by ascending and descending are approved by *Cornelius Celsus* <note>A Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work 'De Medicina'</note> <margin>Book 1, chapter 2</margin> because the entire body is moved by a certain variety of motion; unless, however, the body is exceedingly weak. But those walks which take place on flat and level paths, according to the opinion of *Aristotle*, affect the body with more labor because of the uniformity (so to speak) of the motion they maintain. Yet, because of the similarity they hold to nature, they finish the labors more quickly; furthermore, they are better suited for balancing the spirit and the body equally than those done on uneven ground. 

However, strolls taken through unequal paths not only fatigue one less, but are even useful to those who are quickly exhausted by walking. *Antyllus* <note>A famous Greek surgeon of the 2nd century AD</note> understood this when he wrote that walks performed on open roads are done with less effort <margin>E</margin> than those we undertake in places specifically dedicated to strolling <note>referring to formal walkways or gymnasia</note>. *Acumenus* the physician, in *Plato's* *Phaedrus*, intended to suggest this same thing <margin>Oribasius, in the place cited</margin> where he preferred walking on roads to walking in racing circuits, about which we have disputed more extensively above. Nor did *Ischomachus* in the works of *Xenophon* <margin>In the Oeconomicus</margin> mean anything else when he preferred the walk in which he followed a servant with a horse into the field over a walk performed in the *xysti* <term>xystis: covered porticos or galleries used by Greek athletes for exercise</term>. 

In distinguishing these, however, it matters greatly whether they are carried out in meadows, in rough places, or in sandy ones. For if they are done in meadows, they are undoubtedly the most pleasant; they do not strain the senses at all, nor do they cause agitation. Yet *Antyllus* is the authority for the fact that they "fill the head" <note>likely referring to causing congestion or heaviness in the head</note> both because of the sweetness of the scent and because of the moisture inherent in them. Walks made in rough places also fill the head. 

When, however, they are performed in sand, and especially deep sand (which is a type of the most vigorous <margin>F</margin> exercise), they possess great efficacy for strengthening and corroborating all parts of the body. For this reason, *Augustus* <margin>In the Life of Augustus, chapter 80</margin>—while he did not have good health in his hip, thigh, and left leg, and indeed often limped in that part—was strengthened by this kind of strolling. For I believe the passage in *Suetonius* <note>Roman historian</note> ought to be interpreted in this way, where he records that Augustus used the remedy of "sands and reeds." I judge the sands were used both to dry out the humors <note>original: "fluxiones," referring to the flow of bodily fluids in ancient medicine</note> and to strengthen the hip, while the reeds were for support and to prevent limping. *Cato* taught how this ought to be done in his book *On Agriculture*, chapter 160. 

Immediately following this, for drawing matter down from the upper to the lower parts and for dissipating it, these exercises are most powerful. Therefore, *Erasistratus* <note>A Greek anatomist and royal physician</note> is perhaps wrongly criticized by *Caelius* <margin>Book 2, Chronic Diseases, chapter 1</margin> for advising that paralytics should be exercised by strolling in sandy places. Walks performed under a portico...

Walking in enclosed spaces, such as caves and similar locations, is not particularly approved of by Celsus <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a 1st-century Roman medical writer.</note> or by others. This is because such places do not enjoy free air, but rather air that is immoderate, tainted, thick, and prone to filling the entire body with impurities. An exception is made, however, if the porticos or covered areas are located in the upper stories of a house and have floored levels; in such cases, Antyllus <note>A famous Greek surgeon of the 2nd century AD.</note> prefers these walks above all others because they are free from the vapors that flow out of the earth and possess a purer air. Just as we see moisture sucked from the earth by the air through mists, the prince of architects <note>Referring to Vitruvius.</note> advised that very large and ornate open-air and roofless buildings for walking should be placed within cities so that troublesome humors might be drawn out of the bodies by the air. **B** In almost all cases, however, it will be beneficial to walk under those shadows which Aretaeus approved for epileptics and those suffering from vertigo: namely, under myrtle or laurel trees, or among sharp and sweet-smelling herbs like calamint, pennyroyal, thyme, and mint—especially those that are wild and grow spontaneously. If a plenty of these is lacking, one may walk among those produced by human cultivation. There is also no small difference regarding the sky: when it is serene, walking lightens the body, draws out vapors through breath, thins the humors, and prepares one for good respiration and ease of movement. But when the sky is covered with clouds, it brings heaviness, does not draw out vapors, and eventually fills the head. Regarding walks to be taken in winter, summer, or other times, we spoke in the fourth book, where we defined the time suited for exercises.

# SIXTH BOOK ON THE ART OF GYMNASTICS

### *On the effects produced by standing upright. Chapter 1.*

<margin>B</margin>
Since we have abundantly demonstrated in the previous sections that those who remain upright on their feet are indeed exercising, it would be utterly ridiculous to bring this matter back into dispute any further. Therefore, I shall declare in how many ways this exercise may be varied, and what effects each variation produces.
For that this exercise specifically affects the parts of the back, Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd, a prominent 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and physician.</note>—by no means the least among the Arabs—
<margin>6th Collection, chapter 2.</margin>
stated clearly enough. Those, therefore, who have been allotted a weak back by nature or by accident, ought to avoid this kind of exercise with the greatest care; namely because (as we have said quite often) it produces a greater fatigue than walking itself. Rufus of Ephesus <note>A Greek physician of the 1st century AD known for his anatomical studies.</note>
<margin>Book on the parts of the kidneys.</margin>
judged that those in whom inflammation or ulcers have arisen in the kidneys must take great care not to stand. They also ought to shun this kind of exercise who are troubled by the labor of a hernia, or in whom varicose veins <term>varices: permanently dilated and twisted veins</term> are expanding in the legs or the scrotum, or if ulcers have arisen in the lower parts, or are arising from any cause whatsoever. Even if the authority of physicians did not confirm this opinion, reason itself would persuade us it is true; for it shows that in those who are standing, heavy humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) whose balance determined health.</note> rush downward without difficulty.
<margin>C</margin>
These humors then generate, nourish, and increase now hernias, now varicose veins, now ulcers. Indeed, even the poet Juvenal recognized that varicose veins are generated this way;
<margin>Satire 6.</margin>
when he mocked a certain woman asking Janus about the future victory of a friend, he wished to signify that because of the persistent petitions of women, the soothsayer <term>haruspex: a priest in ancient Rome who practiced divination</term>—if he had served them all by standing (for thus each soothsayer asked God on behalf of others)—would suffer no small labor, saying: *The soothsayer will become varicose.* <note>original: "Varicosus fiet haruspex."</note> We all know also that Marius <note>Gaius Marius, the Roman general and statesman.</note> was a man of great labor;
<margin>Plutarch in his Life [of Marius].</margin>
on account of which, if anyone should say that the varicose veins with which he was afflicted in both legs arose because of excessive labors in standing, I would think that person would be making very little error. But truly, even in this exercise, not a few diversities are found: because time, place, and posture seem to create various "species," as it were. From time, two species are born: when one is exercised by standing either before food or after food, and either for a short time or a long time. Whatever is under the sun increases bile, and consequently, it is greatly opposed to those whose natural heat is sharp <note>original: "mordax," meaning stinging or caustic</note>, as has been written by Galen. By making the spirit <note>The "pneuma" or vital force believed to circulate in the body</note> thicker or denser, it exacerbates asthma and orthopnea <term>orthopnea: a form of severe shortness of breath where one can only breathe comfortably while standing or sitting upright</term>. Furthermore, if sun-exposure is applied without anointing the body with oil, it produces the same effects in other respects, except that it dries out the body more—as if that fatty layer were scorched—and subsequently stains the entire surface with a greater blackness. By thickening the flesh like a kind of cautery <note>a branding iron or heat-treatment</note>, it causes the waste products to evaporate less through "insensible transpiration" <note>the invisible breathing of the skin</note>. For this reason, I believe such sun-exposure was praised by Aetius for reducing polysarchia <term>polysarchia: an early medical term for obesity or "much flesh"</term>.
<margin>Aetius, Book 1, series 3, chapter 32.</margin>
However, I think two things here are worthy of notice. First, that when physicians approved of staying under the sun, I believe they wanted the heads to be protected with cloths. This is because, beyond the authority of Caelius, both reason and experience demonstrate that uncovered heads are greatly harmed if exposed to the sun. Specifically, when overheated, they attract vapors to themselves from the entire circuit of the body, and thus generate an entire "Iliad of evils" <note>a classical idiom meaning a vast series of troubles</note>, and especially catarrhs <note>excessive buildup of mucus or drainage</term>.
<margin>E</margin>
One should not suspect this to happen when the heads are covered because, as Aristotle wrote, clothed bodies are heated less by the sun than naked ones, since they are struck less by its rays.
<margin>Aristotle, Section 1, Problem 9; On the Causes of Disease.</margin>
And I believe this whole point was indicated by Galen when he said that those who remain naked under the sun heat their whole body, but those who are clothed heat only the head. For we demonstrated in the third book that our ancestors almost never used to cover their heads; let us not wonder then that Galen, while writing of those clothed under the sun, said they grew very hot in the head alone.

The second thing worthy of notice is that, just as experience proves that those sitting or standing under the sun grow more violently hot—or rather are scorched—than those walking or running, they likewise receive the other aforementioned effects, both good and bad, more easily.
<margin>F</margin>
And let all these things said by us be understood as referring to those standing on flat and whole feet. For standing propped up on the heels not only induces labor and annoyance, but is also believed to provide no benefit worth mentioning. Similarly, it has been found that those who try to stand on the tips of their toes, besides the fatigue that follows immediately, afflict those parts with very troublesome calluses, especially when one does so frequently. Indeed, they seem sometimes to receive only this one advantage: that they are able to see further than many others. For this reason, a "scout" <note>original: "speculator"</note> or *skops* <note>original: "σκώψ" — a type of owl or a person mimicking one to see better</note> was depicted by the ancients with the face of a man standing on his toes and moving the top of his hand to his eyebrows in the shape of a sunshade, as Aeschylus mentions in *Theoros* <note>A lost satyr play by the Greek playwright Aeschylus</note>.

### On the effects of fighting. Chapter 11.

<margin>A</margin>
Of the types of FIGHTING which served our ancestors for the sake of health—and which likewise retain the capacity to serve in our own times—some are performed with mock weapons that neither cut nor pierce against a person, others against a column or a post, and others against a shadow. Furthermore, all of these can be performed either by combatants who are not armed at all, or by those who are armed. Galen classified armed combat against a person or a column among the "great" <note>meaning intense or vigorous</note> exercises. <margin>Commentary 1 on Epidemics 6; Aphorism 6; Collection 6, chapter 2.</margin> Following him, Averroes—by no means the least among the Arabs—said that a contest carried out with swords was among the swift and powerful exercises. I believe all these points should be understood as referring to those who contend without heavy armor, since Galen clearly classified fighting in armor as being simultaneously an exercise and a functional labor. Similarly, Galen judged that fighting against a shadow (which the Greeks call *skiamachein* <note>original: σκιαμαχεῖν; literally "shadow-fighting"</note>) <margin>On Preserving Health, Book 2, chapters 8 & 10; and Book 1, fen 3, doctrine 2, chapter 2.</margin> was a swift exercise without great strength, as Avicenna and Paul <note>likely Paul of Aegina</note> after him also seemed to believe. Since this is the case, the fighting of unarmed men—whether conducted against other men or against a column—primarily warms the body to a great degree, draws out waste products, induces sweats, and reduces excessive flesh. Consequently, it is employed by Caelius in treating "polysarchia" <note>original: polyfarchia; a medical term for obesity or excessive fleshiness</note>. <margin>Chronic Diseases, Book 1, last chapter.</margin> Furthermore, it strengthens the arms and shoulders and exercises the legs and feet in a wonderful manner; however, it significantly weakens heads that are already frail or prone to vertigo. Galen also instructed those suffering in their kidneys to avoid this kind of exercise. Moreover, *skiamachia* <note>original: σκιαμαχία</note>, or shadow-fighting, <margin>Commentary 1 on Epidemics 6, aphorism 5; On Preserving Health, Book 2, chapter 10; Collection 6 in Oribasius, chapter 29.</margin> thins the body and draws away flesh and fluids, which we showed above to be consistent with swift exercises. According to Galen, it is specifically an exercise for the arms and hands. Furthermore, if we believe Antyllus, it is effective for soothing the sensation of fatigue, for firming up the humors, and for correcting weakness and trembling of the nerves. It is also useful for ailments that tend to plague the chest; it benefits the kidneys and the colon, and draws matter down to the lower parts—especially in those who imitate boxers with their feet, and who do not only fight the shadow with their hands, but also with their legs, sometimes as if leaping, and sometimes as if striking with their heels. Fighting performed against a post is similarly effective for all these same things; it differs from shadow-fighting only in this: striking a post brings greater force to the arms than striking the air. One must not ignore, however, that a fight entered into against a human opponent provides more exercise and force...

And to exert a greater force upon the bodies than that: since, as was very beautifully indicated by Alexander <margin>D</margin> <margin>Book 1, Problem 120</margin> <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle</note>, if an athlete resists his antagonist, he increases the opponent's strength; but if he yields and does not struggle back, he dissolves the other's force. Now, that fight which is carried out between the armed bodies of the combatants must be placed among the "vehement" <note>intense or high-intensity</note> exercises. Since these ought to produce robust and powerful bodies, Nicias—in that dialogue of Plato entitled *Laches*—rightly and deservedly said that <term>fighting in arms</term> <note>original: "τὸ ἐν ὅπλοις μάχεσθαι"</note>, or armed combat, renders bodies more robust than almost any other kind of exercise, and produces no less labor than any other. <margin>In the place cited.</margin> Regarding this exercise, it is also found recorded by Antyllus <note>An influential Greek physician of the 2nd century AD</note> that the body is rendered more fit for movement and for taking on flesh <note>building muscle/mass</note> by it; nevertheless, its specific and greatest promise is that it generates firmness of the body and "long respiration" <note>stamina or endurance</note>, since those who devote themselves to such fights can endure every other expulsion of the breath. However, this kind of fighting makes the flesh loose and soft, and is also quite harmful to the head, especially when it is covered by a helmet more than is right, as the head suffers no small amount when pressed by its weight. 

I do not wish it to be ignored here: <term>armed combat</term> <note>original: "ὁπλομαχία" (hoplomachia)</note>, or the exercise of armed fighting, should not deceive anyone into thinking it is the same as "armed wrestling," called <term>hoplite-wrestling</term> <note>original: "ὁπλιτοπάλη" (hoplitopale)</note> by Aeschylus. For the latter, as a species of wrestling, in no way used weapons in the hands, but rather the contestants were simply armed over their whole bodies, and thus armed they wrestled one another. I judge <margin>E</margin> that the "armed rolling" or "swift agitation" which Galen placed among the number of vehement exercises <margin>On Preserving Health, Book 2, Chapter 10</margin> was a certain species of this wrestling. 

Whether Coelius Aurelianus <note>A 5th-century Roman physician</note> understood this specific type of armed fighting when, in treating <term>obesity</term> <note>original: "polyfarchia" (polysarcia)</note>, after approving many other kinds of exercises, he said: <margin>F</margin> "Then *hoplomachia*, that is, a feigned clashing of arms," leaves no doubt in my mind, as is clear from the above. For even if the Greek name seems to signify this very thing, nevertheless, both the explanation of the name brought forward by him and the demonstrated use provide manifest proof that he was speaking of that fight which is practiced with the body stripped of armor, which was praised by us for reducing flesh; whereas Antyllus judged that this latter [armored] kind rather increases the flesh, though making it soft and loose. 

Regarding gladiatorial combat, this does not seem to be the place to require any discussion, because since it was conducted in ancient times with cutting and piercing weapons, it usually ended either in lethal wounds or in the death of one of the fighters, or even both. For this is the practice which today is carried out among many Christian nations under the name of the **Duel**, sometimes resulting in the great slaughter of citizens. I have always believed this practice was devised by Satan—the greatest enemy of mankind—in both ancient and modern times for the destruction of souls. Those who have treated the subject of the duel until now have falsely tried to prove it is the same as the "single combat" <note>original: *monomachiam*</note> of the ancients; however, it more closely resembles the gladiatorial combat of our own time. Besides the many points I declared in my fourth book, this is further evidenced by the fact that duelists fight with the same weapons and for nearly the same purpose as the gladiators of old. There is only one difference: the gladiators were led to the contest sometimes for the sake of empty glory, sometimes in hope of rewards, but almost always by some form of compulsion—being either condemned to punishment or purchased and trained for the task. These modern men, however, act of their own free will, driven by no one except the enticing lure of a vain and false defense of "honor." For this reason, they should be considered less worthy of excuse, as they rush headlong into their own destruction by choice. If only men would finally come to their senses and see that what almost no Barbarian tribes do is even less becoming of Christians! If they did, many cities currently shaken by savage internal dissensions would be restored to a better state, and the souls and bodies of many would be better cared for. But lest our discourse wander too far from the purpose, it will suffice if I add what Celsus, Scribonius, Largus, Pliny, Aretaeus, and many others report: namely, that it was believed by the Ancients that drinking the blood of a slaughtered gladiator helped those with epilepsy <note>original: *epilepticos*</note>. I wanted to mention this more to expose their wild superstition than because I think any faith should be placed in the remedy.

It is established among Galen, Aetius, Paulus, and Avicenna <margin>D</margin> that this held a place among the "swift exercises without strength." Consequently, it possesses the power to heat the body, thin the frame, and draw away flesh and humors, as Hippocrates seemed to aptly suggest. In his writings, we read that *acrochirismus* thins the body and draws the flesh upward; however, according to Galen, the hands and arms are specifically exercised in this practice. From this, it follows that it is suitable for those who intend to strengthen these parts, just as it is very harmful to those whose <term>chiragra</term> <note>Gout of the hand</note> or other disease is accustomed to infesting the hands and arms. Who can believe that Celsus was speaking of this when he approved of "exercises performed with the hands" for those troubled by a dry cough?

Furthermore, <term>ecplethristare</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκπλεθρίζειν; a running exercise performed within the space of a 'plethron' (approx. 100 feet), involving rapid turns</note> is reckoned by Galen among the swift exercises without strength or violence. <margin>In the cited place.</margin> Avicenna, however, says it is among the more vigorous ones, unless we wish to say he is speaking in comparison to weak movements, as appears from his words; <margin>E</margin> otherwise, he would have written things clearly repugnant to the truth itself and to Galen, from whom he received all these things. This exercise is, therefore, primarily useful for all those things which swift movements benefit: but it particularly exercises the legs and feet. It also fatigues the chest not a little, and I believe it is very harmful to the chest when it is already in some way afflicted, just as I believe it vehemently harms those with poorly affected heads. For because of those constant reversals and "circular" paths, such people can very easily fall into either dizzy spells or apoplectic conditions.

In the same rank of exercises is <term>pytilissare</term> <note>original Greek: πιτυλίζειν; a rhythmic movement of the arms, often mimicking rowing or rapid swinging</note> or *pytilisma*, as Politian preferred. Although this is numbered by Galen and Avicenna among the swift movements without violence, in my opinion <margin>F</margin> it is not entirely lacking in some vehemence. This is because that stance upon the tips of the feet, as well as the swift agitation of the hands—now forward, now backward—cannot be performed at all without the tension of the muscles, and therefore without some force or strength. Hence, I do not hesitate to affirm that bodies grow vehemently hot in undergoing this kind of exercise. Additionally, this motion significantly exercises the arms. But it greatly weakens those who are infirm in the head; it also renders the feet liable to contracting <term>podagra</term> <note>Gout of the foot</note>. I truly believe its peculiar use existed for when, after a long illness or numbness of the arms, they intended to accustom them to making movements in every direction and to free them from torpor.

# BOOK SIX

<margin>A</margin> I did not wish to entirely overlook these matters, as they contribute much to our understanding: "For if someone orders another to pull and twist him violently, while he himself—standing firm not only with his hands, but also with his legs and spine—resists being bent, he will certainly be vigorously exercised. This is the very kind of training that Milo <note>Milo of Croton, a legendary 6th-century BCE wrestler famous for his incredible strength.</note> is said to have practiced, allowing anyone who wished to try and wrench him or move him from his spot. This will cause no small amount of heat in the body and will generate significant strength in the limbs." <margin>Book 5, Chronic Diseases, last chapter.</margin> For I believe Caelius Aurelianus <note>A 5th-century Roman physician and translator of Greek medical works.</note> was speaking of a similar exercise when he recommended that those suffering from <term>polyarchia</term> <note>original: "polyarchia"; a medical term for an excess of humors or "plethora" in the body.</note> should be exercised by the labors of others—that is, by those wrestling or training with them in what the Greeks call <term>haterocopia</term> <note>A form of wrestling or physical struggle involving the hands and neck.</note> or <term>trachelismus</term> <note>A wrestling maneuver involving gripping or twisting the neck.</note>. Nevertheless, such exercise is most to be feared by those who are not particularly strong in the chest, back, or head. In the same way, if someone (as Milo used to do) allows another to try and pull or move him from his place, <margin>B</margin> he will be able to greatly strengthen his legs. Likewise, he will exercise his hands most effectively and acquire strength in them if he offers his clenched fist to be opened by someone, or holds a pomegranate or something similar in his hands to be taken away. However, this is least suitable for those prone to <term>arthritis</term> or <term>chiragra</term> <note>Gout of the hand.</note>. Furthermore, one both exercises and firms the strength of the body parts if, having grasped another around the middle—or being grasped himself—with hands and fingers joined like a comb <note>Interlocking the fingers.</note>, he either orders the one he is holding to break free, or he himself breaks free from the one holding him. The only danger here is that the internal organs might be weakened by the great straining exerted while seeking to break the hold. So too, if someone approaches another from the side while the latter leans toward him, and grasping his flanks with his hands, lifts him like a weight, extending and pulling him back in turn—and even more so if, while carrying him, he uses the straining and counter-straining of his own body. <margin>C</margin> In this way, he will strengthen the entire spine, though it will be harmful to those with weak loins and kidneys. Equally, those who lean against each other's chests and push back with great effort, and those who hang from the neck and pull downward, are indeed vehemently exercised and consequently gain strength for the whole body; but they undergo the risk that some vessels in the chest might be ruptured, or that the head or neck might be injured. Therefore, although all these things were held among the other exercises by the ancients, they were nonetheless not in such frequent use, especially among the nobility and those who pursued health with a certain degree of pleasantness. In this present age, there are still those who use them, and provided that moderation is applied, I do not wish to discourage them entirely.

## *On the properties of breath-holding. Chapter IV.*

<margin>Chapter 6.</margin>
Since we have abundantly demonstrated in the third book that the holding of the **breath** <note>original: "spiritus," referring here to the pneuma or vital breath</note> is a certain type of exercise, there is no need to repeat that further. I will merely add this: it is not easily determined in which category it should be placed, except that by observing that in this kind of exercise the muscles of the abdomen and the chest are powerfully strained, and immediately thereafter
<margin>2nd part, Problem 2, on diet</margin>
heat is increased in the internal parts—as Aristotle and Galen have recorded—we can judge that it does not occur without intensity. For this reason, it was rightly said by Hippocrates that the holding of the breath can open up the passages, thin the skin, and even
<margin>On the preservation of health, chapter 2.</margin>
push moisture out from under the skin. Similarly, it was written by Galen and
<margin>In the book on the Art of Medicine, ch. 87. Book 1, section 3, doctrine 2, ch. 2.</margin>
by Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> that the retention of the breath warms, strengthens, and cleanses the respiratory organs, and also makes narrow cavities wider. Indeed, it is clearly evident that restrained breath is able to purge the chest; for in the act of retention itself, the breath is driven from all sides and forced to retreat into the narrow passages. If it is pushed and propelled further, it even passes through them entirely, carrying away some of the waste matter <note>original: "excrementi," referring to bodily byproducts or phlegm</note> which has been thinned by the agitation. This happens in much the same way as we see craftsmen clean out the narrow holes of their instruments with a more forceful blast of breath. For as much as the breath is driven further by force, some things are pushed by it and others are pulled; those things encountered in front are pushed forward, while those positioned at the sides are drawn along, both being forced by the very impetus of the motion. Furthermore, that the cavities become wider from retained breath is proven by this: since the chest is located in the middle of the body, surely when it is filled with air by a great inhalation, and then the topmost opening of the larynx is closed by the action of the epiglottis <note>original: "ligulae," the little tongue or valve</note>, and the muscles press upon the whole chest, it is necessary for the compressed air to be driven everywhere into all the passages of the body. Thus thrust in, it dilates them on every side—sometimes the lower ones when it is driven there, sometimes the upper ones. Thus, through the retention of the breath, the cavities of the body are enlarged, the parts of the chest are cleansed, and these as well as other internal parts
<margin>In the Symposium; 2nd part, Problems; book on medicinal faculties; and book 2 on the causes of symptoms.</margin>
conceive heat. By virtue of this heat, cold ailments and especially "inflations" <note>flatulence or trapped wind</note> are removed. It was not without reason that Plato, speaking through the character of Eryximachus the physician, and also Aristotle, recorded that held breath frees one from hiccups. Following their decrees, Galen taught that not only hiccups, but even a cough arising from a cold instrument...

A <column-break/> [Diocles] left a record stating that [the coldness] contracted from an imbalance of respiration is extinguished [by breath-holding]: because when the heat in the chest is increased by such restraint, the compressed spirit <note>The "spirit" or *pneuma* was believed to be a vital force carried in the breath and arteries.</note> penetrates any narrow passages, and thus everything is equalized and returns to its former temperament. Hence it follows that we should generally come to the opinion that such exercise is suitable for all those who possess respiratory organs that are chilled, weak, or otherwise beset by waste products, and those who have any expulsions of the body that are either slow or corrupted. Just as it is clear that yawning and stretching dissolve this kind of spirit-retention by means of warm wind dissipating it, so Hippocrates rightly said in the 2nd and 6th books of *Epidemics* that a long breath is the remedy for frequent yawning. Celsus approved of exercising with the breath held for a paralysis <note>term: *resolutione* - a loss of function or loosening, often translated as paralysis or palsy</note> of the tongue, as did Aetius for every paralysis of the vocal instrument.

Similarly, midwives testify to this, as they instruct women in labor to hold their breath to make the expulsion of the birth easier and faster.

# BOOK

<margin>D</margin>
<margin>Book 1, Chapter 4</margin>
I hold it as a certainty that Diocles <note>Diocles of Carystus, a 4th-century BC Greek physician</note> was entirely mistaken when he claimed that holding the breath <note>original: "spiritum retentum"</note> provides a safeguard in treating epilepsy. In this, I praise Coelius <note>Coelius Aurelianus, a 5th-century AD physician of the Methodist school</note> who, in his treatment of the same condition, maintained that holding the breath must be avoided, since an imminent and certain danger exists that the blood will then rush back to the head and further exacerbate the disease. In cases of coughing up blood <note>original: "sanguinis reiectione"</note>, I find that such exercise was also condemned by the Methodists <note>A school of ancient medical thought that focused on "tension" and "relaxation" of the body's pores</note>, and I am compelled to agree with them. This is because the weak and relaxed vessels are very easily broken—and once broken, reopened—both by the heat generated in the chest cavity and by the inflation and stretching of the vessels. Furthermore, those who suffer from hernias or ruptures, or those who have possessed thin and fragile membranes <note>original: "peritonaeum"</note> and intestines from birth, should by no means exercise by holding their breath.
<margin>Coelius, Book 2, Chapter 23</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
This is because these parts are violently strained during that action, and consequently, unless they are robust, they are torn apart without much effort. Children can provide the clearest evidence of this; if they sometimes hold their breath longer than is proper while crying or in some other way, their peritoneum or scrotum is immediately ruptured. Subsequently, the descending intestines or trapped gases <note>original: "flatus"</note> produce hernias that are scarcely curable. This similarly tends to happen frequently to trumpeters and singers while they attempt to hold their breath too much, and especially when they wish to "plant the foot" <note>original: "πόδα ἐρεῖν" (poda erein). A technical term for a forceful vocal or physical stance</note> (as Galen says in the second book of *On the Movement of Muscles* at the end, and in his commentary on the *Epidemics*, Book 6, commentary 4, text 24; a subject we have dealt with in our *Various Readings* and will say more about soon when we release that book again, revised and enlarged), or when they wish to make a proclamation. A single rule will protect against dangers of this kind: if such retention of breath is performed moderately, or rather below a moderate level, when it must be done. Otherwise, it is impossible to prevent the aforementioned inconveniences from following.
<margin>F</margin>

However, desiring to provide a fuller knowledge of this entire matter, we shall divide vocal exercises into six types, just as we have done for the most part in the preceding sections: namely shouting, song, reading, speech, laughter, and weeping. # BOOK SIX

A little remains that can be added to our knowledge of this particular exercise. Therefore, regarding loud shouting <note>original: "vociferationibus"</note>, whatever sparks of insight were recorded by Antyllus, Plutarch, Paul <note>Paul of Aegina</note>, Aetius, and Avicenna, the first condition is that it excellently exercises the chest and the vocal instruments. Averroes used to say that the lungs are specifically benefited by the exercise of the voice. Furthermore, it increases natural heat, cleanses, strengthens, and thins [the humours], and it renders the solid parts of the body robust, pure, and minimally liable to injury. Avicenna added that this exercise beautifies the complexion; for because the heat receives an increase, it arises from there; because the breath, by constant motion—both inhaled and exhaled—is struck together and rubbed, and thus from that collision and attrition, heat is excited. Truly, this kind of exercise cleanses: both because it makes the flesh thinner and more manageable, and because from the motion of the vocal instruments, internal moisture
<margin>Oribasius book 6, ch. 8; book on the preservation of health book 1, ch. 29; book 3, ch. 5; book 1, f. 3 d. 2 ch. 2. 6 collections ch. 2.</margin>
B is consumed, which is most evidently shown by the thick vapor coming forth from the mouths of those shouting, and the superfluities of older humours adhering to every passage, which are excreted not only in the aforementioned shoutings, but also in many other ways. Now indeed, the heat is strengthened and thinned because the vessels are wiped clean, and many humours—such as spit, mucus, and phlegm <note>original: "pituitae"</note>—are consumed; just as these previously obscured, weakened, and thickened the heat, so once they are drawn out, they leave the heat purer and stronger, and from this, greater strength and greater resistance to suffering subsequently grows in the solid parts. If, therefore, these things are so, it is consistent with reason that for those who have internal parts occupied by moisture, and who have the entire constitution of the body chilled, shouting exists as a noble defense. Just as for these aforementioned reasons, we know it was commended by Antyllus, Caelius Aurelianus, and Aetius for those with stomach ailments, those vomiting, those belching acid, those digesting with difficulty, those loathing food,
C those suffering from atrophy <note>wasting of the body</note>, the listless, the cachectic <note>severely malnourished/weak</note>, the dropsical <note>suffering from edema/swelling</note>, the asthmatic, the orthopneic <note>those who can only breathe while upright</note>, the consumptive <note>original: "phthisicis"</note>, those vexed by long-term pain of the chest or diaphragm, those having ruptured abscesses in the chest, pregnant women obsessed with pica <note>cravings for non-food items</note>, or according to Alexander, even those in labor
<margin>Alexander [of Aphrodisias] Problem 87.</margin>
to bring forth the birth more easily, and finally for those with quartan fevers, the phlegmatic, and almost all convalescents. Thus Galen, in book 8 of *On the Affected Parts*, chapter 4, commends to those suffering in the stomach: ointments, exercises, and shoutings applied by a skilled practitioner. <margin>D.</margin>
Aetius believed that this same practice <note>vociferation, or loud shouting/singing as exercise</note> was beneficial for a poor bodily habit, which is called *cachexia* <note>original: καχεξία; a state of ill health or malnutrition</note> by the Greeks. Indeed, if the voice is poorly affected either by disease or by its own nature, it is corrected by such exercise according to the opinion of Antyllus. Since the voice suffers partly because of excessive and long speech, partly because of the magnitude of shouting, and partly because of silence—as if it had forgotten its own functions—it follows that in all these cases mentioned, the use of vociferation is useful. It breaks up the effects of long speech and heals the harm contracted from the magnitude of shouting by a calm and quiet reduction; it also counters high-pitched sharpness by interspersing deeper sounds. Furthermore, the labor that arises from silence, although it is not a labor of the voice proper, nevertheless bears a certain proportion to vocal labor. Therefore, vociferation is also useful for this, as it exercises the voice, just as if the vocal instruments were exhausted and the whole body did not maintain its tone or was besieged by weariness.
<margin>E</margin>

<margin>On Diet, Chapter 7.</margin>

This is not suitable for afflictions of the head, as it possesses some faculty for filling the head <note>likely referring to "congestion" or "plethora"</note> as well as the instruments of the senses contained in the head.

This, besides making the head full and more heavy, as
<margin>F</margin>

For this reason, Caelius disapproved of shouting for the bodies of epileptics, as it violently shakes the suffering parts; and Pliny the Younger rightly complained that his freedman Zosimus, while studying to restore his voice, again coughed up blood from a reopened vein. Therefore, it must not be ignored in this place—as almost all authors have observed—that vociferations should be used neither rashly nor without consultation, especially by those who begin this exercise without being accustomed to it. For no one ought to use them when an abundance of wicked and corrupt humors is present; indeed, the voice must not be exercised if great and evident...

# BOOK SIX

<margin>A</margin> If the stomach is troubled by indigestion or raw humors, one must take care that the forced intake and expulsion of breath—which becomes stronger and faster as the voice increases in volume and frequency—does not cause corrupt vapors to be distributed more widely throughout the body. For this reason, Aretaeus <note>Aretaeus of Cappadocia, a Greek physician of the 1st century AD</note> urged that the voice be exercised gently, and that one should emit sound using deep tones. This is because sharp, high-pitched voices cause tension in the head, palpitations in the temples, throbbing in the brain, swelling of the eyes, and ringing in the ears. Conversely, a moderately projected voice is beneficial to the head. One must also beware of using the voice after eating, as the voice is greatly corrupted then. Hence Aristotle used to say <margin>Section on Problems 11, Problem 22</margin> that actors, choruses, and others of that kind approach their vocal exercises with an empty mouth <note>i.e., on an empty stomach</note>. Otherwise, the breath—made hot by both the ingested food and the shouting—ulcerates the windpipe <term>aspera arteria</term> <note>literally "rough artery," the historical term for the trachea</note> as it exits, and thus the voice is ruined. Finally, one must avoid, according to Plutarch's advice, <margin>Book on Preserving Health</margin> <margin>B</margin> straining the voice too sharply if one is conscious of being overfull, or of immoderate lust, or of exhaustion, lest it irritate the throat; nor should one engage in overly agitated shouting or quarrelsome cries. Indeed, those unequal tensions and impulses of the breath tend to induce ruptures and convulsions.

After shouting comes singing, which differs from the former in that it consists of a certain harmony and is not performed with such a strained voice. Because of this, it can provide pleasure beyond all else, a quality which shouting lacks. For it was written by Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisiensis</note> <margin>Book 1, Problem 76</margin> that those carrying heavy loads feel the burden less if they sing, because the mind, soothed by the melodies and the sweetness of the rhythms, is distracted from the weight and thus suffers less distress. This same reasoning explains why the Ancients used flutes and sound for those in mourning or otherwise laboring <margin>Section 19, Problem 1</margin> (which Aristotle also acknowledged). <margin>C</margin> It was also customary for people to gather and engage in various conversations with those who were either grieving the death of their kin or troubled by disease; for when the mind transfers itself to the word, it feels the adversity less. Understanding this, the ancients devised various entertainments of the stage for themselves, so that the mind, taken up by these various comforts, might be separated from its anguish.

Regarding singing, or shouting performed with harmony, Antyllus, Aetius, and Paullus <margin>In the place cited</margin> wrote that it provides no help to health. But I find that it was sometimes employed in diseases: for Caelius Aurelianus <margin>Book 1 on Chronic Diseases, Chapter 5</margin> wrote that vocal exercise arranged by a musical instructor is beneficial for the insane during the decline of their illness. Furthermore, Aulus Gellius reports <margin>Book 4, Chapter 13</margin> that he found in the writings of Theophrastus and Democritus that the melodies of flutes and songs could cure the diseases of both vipers and men.

Even the brother of Philistion, in the 22nd book of *On Remedies*, confessed this to be true. Some have handed down the tradition that this kind of remedy was devised by Pythagoras; however, Soranus—whose three books *On Acute Diseases* were translated into Latin by Caelius Aurelianus—bitingly criticized Asclepiades (who claimed to cure those suffering from frenzy <note>original: "phreniticos" — likely referring to delirium or inflammation of the brain</note> with song). Soranus aptly enough said that those who believed the strength of a disease could be shut out by melodies and chanting were tossed about by the vanity of their own minds. If, therefore, singing contributes little to the preservation of health, but the sound of deeper tones is useful, those eager for health ought to devote their efforts to shouting <note>original: "vociferationi" — loud vocal exercise or declamation</note> rather than to singing. This is because, in shouting, a great deal of air is drawn in,
<margin>E</margin>
distending the chest, and it opens or dilates the belly and the passages disseminated throughout the entire body. In singing, however, only a certain pure and futile delight is found, which is more apt to soften robust bodies than to preserve or strengthen them. For this reason,

By the benefit of these baths, the peritoneum, the scrotum, and the sacs of the testes were moistened; thus softened, they were more safely stretched and did not easily tear. In our times, however, it is by no means easily permitted to use remedies of this kind; for this reason, it is necessary to observe greater moderation in shouting or singing.

#### Chapter VI.

We can consume food without harm <note>The author suggests that moderate vocal exercise aids digestion</note>, a point which Plutarch <insert>D</insert> also did not disapprove of. Speaking on this subject, Aristotle left it in his writings that ignorant and melancholic men <note>In the theory of the four humors, "melancholic" refers to an excess of black bile, often linked to depression or sluggishness</note> are seized by sleep as soon as they begin to read, because they are unable to fix their intellect; for that reason, thick and cold vapors are stirred up which, by chilling the brain, induce sleep. Conversely, men of outstanding intelligence do not sleep at all while they read, because as they strengthen their intellect, their internal heat is increased, and thus they emerge alert rather than drowsy. After shouting, singing, and reading comes speech, or conversation, which is itself an exercise of the voice; however <insert>E</insert> it yields to all the aforementioned in both intensity and strength, and therefore deserves to be numbered among the weak exercises. For it is primarily suited to those who are excessively inclined toward sleep, and those whose senses are sluggish or as if oppressed, whether due to a melancholic humor or phlegm. Such people are purged by speech, and their minds are so awakened that their senses are soon easily liberated from the body. Furthermore, that phlegm is consumed by speech is indicated by the spittle flowing abundantly from the speaker's mouth; since these fluids come partly from the head, partly from the stomach, and partly from the chest, it demonstrates that all these members enjoy the benefit of speech.
