# BOOK SIX

<margin>A</margin>
Plutarch’s little book on talkativeness <note>original: "loquacitate"</note>, and Galen’s work on the diagnosis and cure of the soul’s diseases, can suffice for those desiring to know these things. Thus far we have discussed the exercises of the articulated voice. Besides these, however, there are two exercises which, although they seem to belong very little to the voice itself and are for the most part passed over by authors, nevertheless are not lacking in the power to exercise certain parts of the body: and these are laughter and weeping. For we cannot at all deny that laughter—while it agitates the internal parts and especially the face through the widening of the mouth or the tickling of the midriff—significantly warms those parts. This is all the more true because the redness blooming in the faces of those laughing stands as a very clear proof of sharp heat. And for that reason, some have believed that Homer called laughter <term>unquenchable laughter</term> <note>original Greek: "γέλωτα ἄσβεστον"</note>, just as grammarians have taught that the word for <term>laughter</term> <note>original Greek: "γέλως"</note> is derived from <term>warmth</term> <note>original Greek: "ἕλη"</note>, a word which signifies heat.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, Problems, section 11, problems 13, 15, & 35; section 35, problem 8.</margin>
Laughter will therefore be beneficial primarily to those whose heads and chests are cold: to those suffering from melancholy, to those losing their senses due to a cold imbalance <note>term: "intemperie" - a medical lack of balance between the four humors</note> of the brain, to the stunned, and to those who have fallen into fevers or other ailments on account of grief and sadness. I believe Caelius Aurelianus was speaking of laughter when, in the treatment of <term>atrophy</term> <note>wasting of the body</note>, he recommended a relaxation of the mind called <term>diffusion</term> <note>original Greek: "διάχυσιν" - a spreading out or relaxation of spirits</note> after food; and when he similarly ordered the same to be applied in cases of headache, lest the head be overfilled by mental strain. For in all these cases, since a cold imbalance dominates, laughter rightly provides aid, doubtless because it moves much air in the chest and emits a warmer breath, as was written by Aristotle. For this reason, Aristotle judged that those laughing produce a deeper voice than those weeping. This benefit is all the more to be hoped for if those wishing to exercise themselves with laughter

### On the Qualities of Hoop-Rolling, the Wheel, and Mall-Ball. Chapter VII.

<margin>B</margin>
<margin>Oribasius, Collection 6, chapter 16.</margin>
Although the exercise of *Cricilasia* <note>original: "Cricilasiae"; an ancient Greek exercise involving rolling a small hoop with a rod</note> is not in use among any nations (that I know of), and its form and manner among the ancients have not yet been fully discovered by me, I nevertheless do not wish to omit its properties as described by Oribasius <note>Personal physician to the Emperor Julian</note>. This is so that if perhaps another person knows how to practice *Cricilasia* itself, or something similar, they will not be ignorant of its powers. It is recorded by Antyllus <note>A famous Greek surgeon of antiquity</note> that it held a place among the "great" or vigorous exercises. He also said <margin>Oribasius in the place cited</margin> that *Cricilasia* softens tense bodies and, through both the revolutions and the variety of body postures, prepares parts that cannot be set in place so that they may be easily bent and stabilized. It strengthens and relaxes weak nerves <note>In this context, "nerves" often refers to tendons or ligaments</note>, excites heat, and recalls the intelligence—which has wandered from its path and is agitated by black bile <note>Melancholy or depression</note>—back to its proper state. Likewise, it is not sufficiently clear to me what the *Trochus* <note>A larger hoop or wheel</note> of the ancients was, unless we say it was either the same as what is called our "wheel," or slightly different from it. All affirm that this should undoubtedly be placed among the slow and relaxed exercises. 
<margin>C</margin>
Since it is performed with rods driving balls into an iron circle, and is practiced sometimes by standing and sometimes by walking, it seems primarily suited to convalescents and those who, held back by weakness of strength or some other impediment, cannot undergo greater exercises. In the second place, it is suited to the elderly and others who grow too hot from greater labors; it will also be more appropriate in summer. Specifically, the sight is exercised in this, as well as the arms and legs. It cannot be denied that all these parts, working gently and without any violence in such motion, acquire strength. Just as experience daily proves in many cases, it stimulates the bowels, thrusts humors down to the lowest parts, and assists in digesting the juices of the stomach and the whole body. However, those who are subject to dizziness in the head, and those who are accustomed to be troubled by gout, or by ulcers and tumors of the legs, ought to abstain from this exercise.

# BOOK SIX

<margin>A</margin> ...they intend to complete [digestion], distribute useful juices throughout the entire body, and empty out superfluity <note>excess bodily fluids or waste</note> as much through sweat as through secret evaporation <note>insensible perspiration through the skin</note>. However, no one even moderately skilled in the medical art is ignorant of the fact that this exercise is not at all suited to the sickly and the weak, whose strength is destroyed by the slightest cause; even less so to those whose heads are poorly affected or in some way feeble. For those who are not very strong in the back, and those who have hot kidneys and sharp <note>acidic or burning</note> urine, are greatly harmed by such movements, just as this exercise is harmful where the lower parts are prone to inflammation or other tumors. In summary, those who enjoy good health can exercise with the **mallet-ball** <term>pilamalleo: an ancestor of golf or croquet played with a wooden mallet and ball</term> to maintain it and to produce an excellent physical condition; but those who are occupied by illness in any way ought to abstain entirely. And it is always worthwhile to keep in <margin>B</margin> memory that the benefits we promise from exercises are found to be true only if that proportion of time, place, quantity, manner, and bodies is observed, which we showed to be necessary in Book 4. Otherwise, if it is neglected, it would be no wonder if irremediable evils succeed in the place of good things. I know for certain that this frequently happens in the proposed exercise, which, since it is performed by many mostly after lunch with no choice made for a healthy place or time, induces pernicious affections and depraved habits—not by its own fault, but by the carelessness of those exercising. Therefore, I warn everyone that, imitating as much as is granted the diligence observed by our Ancestors in exercising bodies, they should better consult their health and the strength of their limbs; they should not allow themselves, through their own errors, to lose both health and honor at the same time. As our **Galen** <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years</note> says, it is a <margin>5. On the Preservation of Health</margin> <margin>C</margin> great disgrace to those who, having been granted a healthy constitution of the body by nature, corrupt it and render it diseased through negligence of exercise and right living. And since we have said two things in this chapter—one, that the mallet-ball exercises the back, and the other, that it must be avoided by those whose backs are feeble—it should be known that Galen wished that in the elderly, weak parts should never be exercised, but in <margin>5. On the Preservation of Health, chapter 3</margin> others they always should be. I believe the reason which led him to say this was this: because the weakness of the elderly cannot be corrected, since it proceeds from a defect of the motor faculty, while that of others is repairable. Hence, when we advise that some weak parts should not be exercised at all, we always wish our words to be understood as referring to a confirmed and irremediable weakness, and not to a recent and curable one; lest we seem to depart in this opinion from the decrees of Galen, whom all physicians are bound to follow.

# BOOK SIX

<margin>A</margin> The foremost authority on pain of the hips—called <term>sciatica</term> <note>original: "ischiados"</note> by the Greeks—used to command his patients to ride horses, so that by the violence of the motion he might cause a greater disturbance of the parts. After him, the same was confirmed by Theodorus Priscianus and Pliny, whom I just cited. On the other hand, we have already mentioned that Hippocrates considered riding to be an enemy to the hips and the parent of such pains; following him, Caelius Aurelianus attacked the opinions of Themison <note>Themison of Laodicea, a physician who founded the Methodic school of medicine</note>, as if they were destroying the true cure for sciatic patients. For my part, when I observe that the hips become violently heated during this exercise and are weakened by the motion, I feel that the flowing humors easily settle there and thus excite painful conditions. I believe that already existing conditions, being as it were chronic, are made even more bitter and harder to resolve. For these same reasons, I think riding was rightly condemned by Celsus for those suffering from <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagricis," specifically gout of the feet</note>.

<margin>Nonius Marcellus.</margin>

# BOOK SIX

### Chapter IX: On the General Powers of Gestations.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'A' with scrolling floral motifs and a central mask-like face.</image-desc>
Before we begin our discourse on gestations <note>The term "gestation" here refers to passive exercise where the patient is moved by an external force, such as being carried in a litter, a boat, or a carriage</note>, we wish first to note for our readers that we are by no means ignorant of the fact that many have placed horse-riding among the types of gestation—among whom was Aetius of Amida <note>A 6th-century Byzantine Greek physician</note>; 
<margin>Book 3, ch. 6</margin>
but we have in no way wished to follow their opinion. This is partly because Cornelius Celsus <note>A Roman medical encyclopedist from the 1st century AD</note>, 
<margin>Book 2, ch. 15</margin>
an author both ancient and celebrated, when he enumerated the types of gestation, did not wish to say even a word about horse-riding, as if he judged it foreign to gestation—an opinion which many others held, as is 
<margin>B</margin> conjectured from Antyllus <note>A famous Greek surgeon of the 2nd century AD</note>. It is also because Galen expressly declared gestation and horse-riding to be different things in the second book of *On Preserving Health*, where he taught that some exercises are performed by ourselves, others are from without (such as gestations), and others are mixed, such as horse-riding. Furthermore, if gestation—as all authors define it—is a mixture of motion and rest, where many parts of the body appear not to move while the whole body is moved by being carried, this condition is far removed from horse-riding, in which almost all parts of the body are most clearly seen to be moved. But these points matter little, since even Antyllus and Aetius spoke of horse-riding separately. This "gestation," I say, which is separate from horse-riding and called <term>aiōran</term> <note>original: "αιώραν" — a Greek term for swinging or suspension, used medically for passive motion</note> by the Greeks, has many species, as we declared in the preceding sections. But first, those powers attributed to all things included under the universal name of gestation will be explained; finally, we shall pursue the particular effects assigned to each type. But first, I do not want it to be ignored that among authors, gestations and exercises are frequently named together as if they differ from one another; their opinions must always be interpreted as referring to "proper" exercises (which are more violent movements than gestations) and not to those commonly accepted. Therefore, according to the opinion of Antyllus, Aetius, 
<margin>C</margin>
<margin>In the places cited</margin>
and Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>, gestation is among the most gentle and weak exercises. For that reason, it is suited not only to the healthy and the sickly, but even to those with long-lasting and declining illnesses, and finally to those in whom the slow remnants of diseases remain and cannot be expelled otherwise. In some acute cases, it is approved by Aretaeus <note>A Greek physician of the 1st century AD</note> for those suffering from lethargy or kidney ailments.

Indeed, Celsus records that Asclepiades <note>A Greek physician who practiced in Rome and favored gentle treatments</note> even used gestation in the case of a fresh and violent fever—especially a burning one—to dispel it...

...had proven, which is certainly achieved with some danger; it is better that such impulses be sustained through rest. <margin>D</margin> For in both the healthy and the sickly, **gestation** <note>Latin: *gestatio*. A form of passive exercise where the patient is carried in a litter, carriage, or boat.</note>, since it does not produce weariness in the body—but rather moves it in a manner similar to great exercises—is able to increase natural heat, disperse a multitude of matter <note>Refers to the "humors" or bodily fluids thought to cause disease when in excess.</note>, firm up the habit of the body, rouse dull senses, dissolve sluggishness, calm bodily disturbances, and procure sleep for those tormented by wakefulness. Conversely, it can also prepare a return to consciousness and alertness for those who are lethargic and faint. For it procures sleep by digesting through breath the waste products that slip down from the head to the stomach, which are undoubtedly the primary causes of wakefulness; but it later induces alertness by recalling and strengthening the body's tone. And although Seneca <margin>E</margin> in his *Epistles*, Book VI, seems to make gestation more laborious than walking, his speech must be interpreted as referring only to one who, being stricken by ill health, is disturbed by almost everything. In which diseases it is pleasing to make a trial of gestation, Celsus <margin>cited in that place</margin> advised that it should be tested thus: if the tongue is not rough, if there is no swelling, no hardness, no pain in the internal organs, the head, or the diaphragm. He wished for a body in pain never to be carried at all, whether the pain is in the whole or in a part, except perhaps when only the nerves are painful; nor ever during a fresh fever, but rather during its remission. Nevertheless, setting aside many observations, it is found that gestations have been approved by authors for various afflictions. Caelius Aurelianus, in the books he titled *On Chronic Diseases*, recommended them for the "incubus" <note>A term for sleep apnea or night terrors; the author notes a historical outbreak in Rome.</note> (from which disease Symmachus, a follower of Hippocrates, reports that many at Rome once perished as if from a contagion); likewise for loss of voice, for those coughing blood <margin>F</margin> (in which cases Asclepiades condemned the practice), for asthma, for stomach ailments, for elephantiasis <note>A term used historically for various skin diseases, including leprosy.</note>, for colic, and for arthritis. Theodorus Priscianus also, and before him Aretaeus, wished for gestations to be employed in cases of melancholy, atrophy, spleen disorders, and also in pains of the stomach. It is read that Galen <margin>7th book of *The Method of Healing*</margin> sometimes used these same exercises for those who were greatly dried out and in need of restoration. Indeed, Celsus himself praised gestation for curing "sacred fire" <note>Latin: *sacro igne*. Likely referring to Erysipelas or shingles.</note>. Thus, we are able to demonstrate by these authorities that the conditions he laid down are not always necessary to observe. <margin>Book 2, *On the Cure of Chronic Diseases*, Chapter 7</margin> However, it must not be ignored that it matters greatly in what place one utilizes gestations. For this reason, Aretaeus, demonstrating exercises for those with abdominal disorders, preferred that which is performed among laurels, myrtles, and thyme.

### On the specific powers of being carried in a carriage, a litter, and a chair. Chapter X.

Having explained what has been handed down by authors concerning the benefits of being carried <note>original: "gestationum" — a term for passive exercise where the patient is moved by an external force</note> in general, it is now appropriate to descend to the specifics. First, we must recall that medical writers, when they mention the use of "gestation" for the healthy and the infirm without further qualification, intend it to be understood as any species of it; for almost no form is found that cannot be usefully applied to them. However, when they speak regarding the sick, they sometimes mean all forms (during the remission of diseases), and sometimes only the gentler types. Among our ancestors, there were many kinds of vehicles, the luxury <margin>B</margin> <margin>Pliny, Book 34, ch. 27.</margin> of which sometimes grew so great in Rome that, as Pliny reports, they did not shrink from making them of gold and silver. But this is outside our present purpose. For the vehicles used by physicians for the healthy or the sick were either driven by animals—namely mules or horses—or moved by men, and both were conducted either somewhat slowly or quickly. Although Celsus <margin>Book 2, ch. 15; On Preserving Health, ch. 11; On Preserving Health, Book 5.</margin> stated that being carried in a carriage is sharper <note>more vigorous</note> than the others, it nevertheless deserves to be numbered among the "weak" exercises according to Galen's opinion. Thus, it is least suitable of all for the healthy, unless they are otherwise prevented from exercising. It is more for the infirm and the elderly, just as we have heard that Antiochus and Caecilius Plinius exercised themselves; but it is especially for the sick, of whom Antyllus, speaking on the subject, said that being carried in a carriage has a certain power of dislodging and stirring up stable and permanent diseases. For this reason, Seneca writes in Epistle 56 that it was wonderfully beneficial to him for dispersing bile fixed in the throat and for thinning out the density of the breath; for <margin>C</margin> because he was frequently exercised even to the danger of his last breath by difficulty in breathing—or "sighing" <note>original: "suspirio" — likely referring to asthma</note> as he calls it—he used this kind of exercise against the disease. Aetius <margin>Book 3, ch. 6.</margin> teaches that this exercise is twofold: one milder, the other more vehement. Regarding the milder form, he left it written that it should be used in affections of the head and for those whose intestines labor with a flux <note>diarrhea or dysentery</note>. Whence Caelius Aurelianus <margin>Book 1, ch. 1.</margin> wisely judged that those vexed by headache ought to be carried along a long, straight road, lest a vertigo be induced in the patient by frequent turning. Likewise, not without reason, he wished the carriage moved by hands to be employed in curing madness and paralysis, although he later disapproved of the same in the treatment of epilepsy, because the motion of the wheels causes vertigo and darkness to the patient, which bears the image of the suffering itself. For although <margin>On Preserving Health, Book 5, ch. 3.</margin> Galen, Trallianus, and Aetius [recommend it], in cases of vertigo, epilepsy, severe inflammation of the eyes, or those seized by ear pain or deafness, as well as in hemi- <note>The text cuts off, likely referring to hemicrania (migraine) or hemiplegia</note>

Therefore, unless healthy men are urged by some of the aforementioned causes, I advise that they abstain from the litter. For, besides that shaking which is accustomed to trouble the heads of many, it also generates a certain numbness in bodies while almost all the limbs are kept from motion, so that it soon becomes difficult to accustom them to greater and more useful exercises. Truly, however, it does not seem to me that carriage in a litter should be deprived of this particular convenience: that healthy men can use it after meals, not for exercising their bodies, but for attending to necessary business, without the loss of movement or of comfort and cheering...

Furthermore, according to Aetius, those who are in the complete decline of fevers ought to be carried sitting in a litter. For the same reason, this applies to those who cannot undergo other exercises, who are entangled in some long-term but light disease, or who, while still weak, desire to restore their strength, and those who digest their food slowly. For this reason, Cornelius Celsus <note>A Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work *De Medicina*</note> quite prudently advised that where consumptives <note>original: *phthifici*, those suffering from tuberculosis</note> cannot travel by sea, their bodies should be moved by a litter; just as Alexander Trallianus wrote that such carryings made by ship and litter help those with dropsy more than anything else. In a chair—which the most eloquent Celsus preferred to call a <margin>Book 2, ch. 15</margin> bench <note>original: *scamnum*</note>—carrying was performed, and although it is frequently found confused with the litter among authors as if they were the same, I nevertheless think it stood apart from the litter in two ways. First, because a litter was capable of holding two people, as Suetonius implies when he writes that Nero was sometimes accustomed to be carried with his mother in a litter; which is never read (unless I am mistaken) concerning a chair. Second, because a litter was sometimes carried by six slaves, sometimes eight, and sometimes more. However, it seems likely that the chair, being shorter and capable of holding only one person, was carried by fewer people. Indeed, in our own times, there is no greater difference between the covered chair and the litter than that the former is usually carried by two servants and holds only one person, while the other is carried by beasts of burden and can contain two. Healthy people were carried in a chair for the sake of luxury and the display of majesty rather than for health; although <margin>Letters, Book 3</margin> Pliny’s nephew <note>Pliny the Younger</note> relates that Pliny was carried in one in Rome so that he might have leisure for his studies even while traveling. Celsus makes this carrying by chair, and likewise by litter, more vigorous than sailing in a harbor or on rivers. Antyllus <note>A prominent Greek surgeon of the 2nd century AD</note> held that patients ought to be carried under a roof. In another manner, it is useful for those lying down with fevers to be carried, especially those suffering from lethargy and those pressed by *cataphora* <note>A state of pathological sleep or semi-coma</note>. Therefore, in feverish patients who are reaching the point of recovery, or those whose remission is very long, or those held by long fevers even if they do not have great intervals of relief, this gestation is appropriate. It is clearly held in the books written by Caelius Aurelianus on chronic passions <note>diseases</note> that he similarly recommends this for many other conditions: namely for headaches, epilepsy (if the patient can be carried), mania, and paralysis. Thus, we also may safely exercise the sick with similar 
<margin>E</margin>
gestations when the situation demands it, provided that it is done when the disease is mature and already declining. Otherwise, if gestation is administered while the affliction is still increasing or beginning, more bitter and dangerous accidents follow. For just as motion can usefully dissipate concocted <note>digested or 'ripened'</note> humors and the remains of excrement, it is also naturally suited to increase heat and agitate spirits and humors that are not yet quieted or purged. For this reason, the greatest care must be taken that neither gestation nor any other exercise is administered during the growth of raw <note>undigested or acute</note> diseases, especially hot ones, but only in those that are mature, cold, or clearly observed to be declining.

Navigation on rivers is less harmful, surely because—on the authority of Plutarch—it is free from fears and does not provoke nausea in any way. Compared to the two aforementioned, maritime navigation <note>sea travel</note> is believed to be far superior, since dry and warm vapors are always drawn out from the sea; these secretly and gradually open up the bodies of those sailing, and also consume waste products by means of a salty property. They restore the constitution of men through a certain easy transformation. For this reason, this kind of exercise is approved by physicians in almost all moist and cold diseases: specifically by Celsus for every cough; by Caelius and Aretaeus for head pain, for epilepsy (if it can be borne), for the spitting of blood, for consumption <term>phthisis: a wasting disease, usually pulmonary tuberculosis</term>, and for jaundice; and for dropsy <term>hydrops: swelling caused by excess fluid</term> and a cold imbalance of the stomach, it is recommended by Trallianus.

# BOOK SIX

<margin>Oribasius <note>A 4th-century Greek medical compiler</note> book 6, chapter 23.</margin>
**A** It is recognized that sea travel is capable of provoking massive vomiting, and consequently of driving out every chronic disease. Therefore, Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> rightly said that this sailing is more effective for extinguishing the aforementioned ailments. Furthermore, that mixture of motion and rest with which it is endowed is, if anything else is, properly suited to nourish the body. Carriage in a ship which is performed on a calm sea does not (as Antyllus <note>A 2nd-century Greek surgeon</note> used to say) bring about a very great disturbance or jarring; from which it follows that it is generally suited to those for whom carriage in chariots is also appropriate—except that this has the added benefit of being performed in purified air, where the vapors are not humid, but dry and sharp. However, travel undertaken on a stormy sea agitates the mind and body more, and provokes vomiting more intensely; therefore, it should be avoided as much as possible by everyone, since it possesses the sharpest and most violent movements while the ship is driven by the wind, never ceasing, and thus most intense for the body.

**B** It must not be kept silent that for those suffering from kidney disease <term>nephriticis: people with kidney ailments or stones</term>, sea travel and the entire maritime life are commended by Aretaeus <note>A Greek physician of the 1st century AD</note> in these words: <note>original Greek: καὶ πλοῦς, καὶ ἡ ἐν θαλάσσῃ βιοτὴ, ἅπαντα τοῖσι ἐπὶ νεφρῶν ἔσιν ἄκεα</note> "Both sailing and a life spent at sea are entirely remedies for those with kidney disease."

### On the effects of swimming and fishing. Chapter XII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' depicting two figures in a landscape setting with trees.</image-desc>
<margin>book 5, chapter 14.</margin>
We have already sufficiently demonstrated that swimming existed among the exercises of the medical gymnasts, and was held in the highest esteem by the ancients above all else, because it liberated men from the greatest dangers (as Plato said in the *Gorgias*) and rendered them braver and more spirited for daring deeds. Therefore, it only remains to investigate its powers. For I find that this also had various distinctions: for swimming was done either in waters occurring naturally or in others;
<margin>C</margin>
and if in others, either in fresh waters or in maritime ones; if in fresh, either in rivers, or lakes, or ponds; and all these either in hot or in cold waters. Swimming in naturally occurring waters—all of which are hot, as the authority of Aristotle, reason, and experience demonstrate—was disapproved of by Antyllus on the grounds that it "fills the head" <note>likely referring to causing congestion or heaviness</note>; however, Caelius Aurelianus <note>A 5th-century Roman physician</note> believed it provided assistance in curing paralytics,
<margin>
24th part of the Problems.
book 6, chapter 27.
book 2, chapter 1.
and book 5, chapter 2.
</margin>
provided it was administered in such a way that inflated bladders were attached to the suffering parts to lessen the labor of swimming. Furthermore, the swimming which is performed in fresh waters is less effective for all those poorly affected than maritime swimming. For which reason it is mostly to be avoided: for if anyone stays in it too long, his nerves will be harmed both on account of the cold and on account of the humidity. Nevertheless, of the swimmings done in fresh waters, those in rivers bring less harm to healthy bodies, and are especially commended by Horace Flaccus <note>The Roman poet Horace</note> for inducing sleep, where he writes:

<margin>book 2, Satires.</margin>
->—thrice anointed<-

# BOOK
<sig>D</sig>
<sig>E</sig>
<sig>F</sig>

<margin>Horace, Satires 1.</margin>
5. ->Let those who have need of deep sleep swim across the Tiber.<- <note>original: "Trans nanto Tiberim, somno quibus est opus alto." A quote from Horace suggesting swimming as a cure for insomnia.</note> <sig>D</sig>
However, those swims undertaken in marshes and stagnant waters are most pernicious; for the putrid vapors, gliding into the passages of the body along with the moisture, contaminate not only the head but indeed the entire body. Lake swimming occupies a middle ground: these will be less unhealthy the larger and purer the lakes where they are performed appear to be. Swimming in the sea is employed by Aretaeus <note>A Greek physician of the 1st century AD known for his descriptions of diseases.</note> for chronic headaches. It is approved by Aetius, following the mind of Galen, for blockage of the nostrils and impairment of the sense of smell, if it is done regularly. By Celsus <note>A Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work 'De Medicina'.</note> and Antyllus, however, it is considered suitable for those with dropsy <note><term>dropsy</term>: an old term for edema or swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, those with the itch <note>likely scabies</note>, and those troubled by skin eruptions, as well as those suffering from elephantiasis <note>a disease causing extreme thickening of the skin and tissues</note>, and those whose legs or other parts of the body are afflicted by a "downward flow" of humors. It also benefits those who do not feel the nourishment from their food. And therefore, not without merit, Caelius Aurelianus left it written that sea swimming is of use for paralytics, just as Celsus noted it for those with stomach, liver, or spleen ailments, and those of a "bad habit" of body <note><term>cachectic</term>: a state of physical wasting and malnutrition</note>. <sig>E</sig> Nevertheless, I cannot help but be held in the greatest wonder as to how that author praised swimming in the open air for headaches and even for epilepsy; for Antyllus taught that not only sea swimming, but any kind of swimming whatever, harms the head. Reason itself seems to persuade us of the same, demonstrating that both the very position of the swimmers and the continuous exhalations emanating from the waters fill the head and affect it poorly. I think it should not be kept silent in this place what the great philosopher Aristotle left written in his *Problems*: namely, that it is easier to swim in the sea than in rivers. 
<margin>Section 23, Problem 12.</margin> This is because he who swims does so by diligently pushing against the water; moreover, we can push more firmly against that which is more "corpulent" <note>meaning denser or having more substance</note>. Since sea water is more corpulent, thicker, and stronger for resisting than river water, it sustains the swimmers pushing against it more effectively. <sig>F</sig> Furthermore, regarding any kind of swimming, it must be noted that few long-term diseases are found in which it is perfectly suitable; for that reason, swimming should be used very rarely, and only in summer, when it can make one lean, draw out vapors through the breath, strengthen, warm, thin the humors, and finally make a person less liable to injury. It was written by Pliny 
<margin>Book 31, Chapter 6.</margin> that the dislocated bodies of men and four-footed animals return most easily to their joints by swimming in any kind of water. Warm swimming is believed to soften hardened parts and warm those that are chilled. For this reason, it was commended by Caelius Aurelianus in treating those with arthritis, and by Aetius (following Galen) for those who have thickened skin. But no one would deny that the head is offended by it and the strength is in a certain way weakened; Caelius said it also lacks not another fault: namely, that it pours out the humors but does not resolve them. Cold swimming, by repelling the innate heat inward, makes it stronger and produces the best and quickest digestion of food...

# BOOK SIX

<margin>A</margin>
It provides a benefit: it dissipates overflowing humors <note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determined health.</note> and warms parts that have been chilled internally. For this reason, Aurelianus rightly praised it for those suffering from arthritis, moved by the same reasoning as Hippocrates, who said that cold water poured liberally over those afflicted with tetanus was a remedy. Similarly, Celsus recommended it for those suffering from the "royal disease" <note>original: "regio morbo"; likely referring to jaundice</note> in the summer, and Herodotus (as cited in Aetius) commended cold swimming to avoid the heat. However, experience shows that if one uses it too frequently, the nerves are damaged and deafness is sometimes contracted, which Agathinus (as cited in Oribasius) admitted. And let all these things we have said be understood as referring to those nations which practiced medical gymnastics but were not always exercising in the gymnasiums. Those practices, however, <margin>Chapter 14</margin> which we proved in Book 3 were customary in the gymnasiums themselves—whether performed in swimming pools or in very large basins—had two primary goals in our opinion: one, that by that gentle motion with which swimmers are agitated, the water might better permeate the bodies and thus the limbs might be more abundantly moistened; the other, that they might enjoy a greater pleasure in moving themselves. For indeed, water in motion, and especially that sweet touch of the baths, brings a singular delight.

<margin>B</margin>
Regarding the exercise of fishing, which we mentioned—following Plato's opinion—benefits neither the mind nor the body (and therefore he hoped that young men would not apply themselves to it), I will say only a few words. This is partly because it is almost entirely reduced to the category of sailing, so there is no need to repeat the same things, and partly because it is established that almost no physicians held it in use. The exception is Avicenna, <margin>7th book of Laws; in The Sophist; Book 3, Chapter 13</margin> who numbered it among the weak exercises when one is moved in a small fishing boat. For this reason, it is not to be believed that any fishing increases the innate heat, since Aristotle also <margin>Section 38, Problem 2</margin> wrote that sea fishermen are reddish in color because they are cold inside, while on the outside they are, as it were, scorched. For those who fish in the sea

<margin>C</margin>
have this particular advantage: that their bodies are greatly dried out, and therefore they are the least subject of all to corruption. Indeed, if any putrefaction lies hidden within, it is immediately sucked out and consumed. Thus, Galen wrote with great reason that the constitutions of fishermen are hard and dry, <margin>1. On Simple Medicines; 6. On the Composition of Medicines</margin> and their ulcers appear continuously dried out, just as if they had been salted. As for what Suetonius wrote—that Augustus was sometimes accustomed to fish with a hook— <margin>In the Life of Augustus, Chapter 83</margin> that was done by him more for the sake of relaxing the mind than for the sake of health.

->*On the conditions of hunting.* Chapter XIII.<-

<margin>Book 2, On the Exercise of the Small Ball.</margin>
Comparing the exercise of hunting to the game of the small ball, Galen seems to have placed only this distinction between them: that the latter requires modest equipment and is therefore an easy exercise for anyone, while the former requires many instruments and is not practiced by everyone, but only by the well-born and the wealthy.

# BOOK

<margin>D</margin>
...could be said. Although this might have been true perhaps in the time of Galen <note>Galen (129–c. 216 AD) was a prominent Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note>, and even in some types of hunting in our own times, it has nonetheless been found to be otherwise in the majority of cases. We frequently see peasants and poor men frequenting the practice of hunting with only one or two dogs, or very few tools. For this reason, hunting earns no less praise than the game of ball, nor should its qualities be explained by us in fewer words. For since Galen
<margin>On the Preservation of Health, Book 2, Chapter 8.</margin>
reckoned hunting among those things which he called "exercises and labors," and since its observed nature clearly shows that it is performed not without intensity, magnitude, and speed—inasmuch as many other exercises, namely running, walking, jumping, throwing, shouting, and others are necessarily required—it follows by reason that it is endowed with these powers: it vehemently
<margin>E</margin>
heats the bodies, dissipates waste products, reduces excess flesh and humors <note>In pre-modern medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determined health and temperament.</note>, produces deep sleep, and therefore greatly assists in digesting food or raw humors. Furthermore, as Xenophon <note>Greek philosopher and soldier, author of a famous treatise on hunting.</note> says, it sharpens hearing and sight, and at the same time delays old age. Because of these excellent qualities, we ought to consider as true that which Rhazes the Arab <note>Rhazes (c. 865–925 AD) was a Persian polymath and influential physician.</note>, a most serious author, recorded from the opinion of Galen: namely, that in a certain
<margin>
In the 3rd [book] of the Continens, tract 13, chapter 1.
Book on the Pulse, epilogue, commentary 115.
</margin>
plague it happened that almost everyone perished, and only the hunters, on account of their constant exercise, escaped unharmed. However, as is found attributed by physicians to vigorous exercises, the labor of hunting does not seem to lack the power to strike the head most forcefully if it is performed unseasonably, just as one reads in the fourth book of *On the Regimen of Acute Diseases* by that same author. As for the qualities of particular types of hunting, I shall speak of only two, as if in these alone consists the entire power of hunting pertaining to health or sickness: these are hunting on horseback and hunting on foot. For everyone knows that any hunting, whether it be practiced with dogs, nets, birds, bows, or other instruments, is carried out by men who either go on their own feet or sit upon horses. Those practicing equestrian hunting (if I may call it so), since they are moved sometimes by galloping horses and sometimes by walking ones, and are forced sometimes to shout and sometimes to be still, seem to work all parts of the body. Therefore, many have believed that by this exercise the chest, stomach, intestines, back, and legs are strengthened. I, however, command those to avoid it whose heads are easily affected, those who are in danger of bursting veins in the chest, those in whom stones accumulate in the kidneys, those with a weak peritoneum or any suspicion of a hernia, and finally those whose entire bodily constitution has acquired a heat more than moderate; since one may see many...

# BOOK SIX

A Although hunters are sometimes seized by illnesses similar to those caused by loud shouting or violent movement—which have occasionally led to their death—Martial wisely advised Priscus not to use a *Veredus* <note>original: "Veredus"; a fast-breeding light horse or hunter</note> (which was a swiftly running horse) while hunting, using these verses:
<margin>Book 12.</margin>

> *I warn you, Priscus, use the rushing hunter-horse sparingly,*
> *and do not go so violently against the hares.*
> *Often the hunter has become the prey himself, and having been*
> *thrown from his fierce horse, he falls, never to return.*
> *The field has its traps; though there be no ditch, nor mound,*
> *nor rocks, the flat ground is often deceptive.*
> *There will be no lack of those to provide such spectacles for you:*
> *but they fall with a gentler envy of fate.*
> *If spirited dangers delight you, courage is safer*
> *among the Tuscans; let us lie in wait for wild boars.*
> *How do those reckless reins help you? It is more often*
> *granted to them, Priscus, to break the rider than the hare.*

B Furthermore, hunting on foot contains almost the same advantages and disadvantages found in hunting on horseback, except that while the hunter pursues wild beasts by running and leaping through mountains, valleys, remote places, woods, and forest-pastures, he is certainly subjected to less danger than in mounted hunting. However, he is affected by greater labor, grows hotter, and strengthens his feet and legs more. Beyond these things, it restrains the impulses of lust, as they say Hippolytus <note>A figure from Greek mythology known for his chastity and devotion to the hunt</note> practiced this kind of hunting out of a zeal for virginity.
<margin>Seneca in the tragedies.</margin>
Hunting also excites the appetite, just as that famous cook replied to Dionysius when he was turning away from a feast: that he lacked the labor of the hunt which would have generated an appetite. Nevertheless, neither form of hunting, because it is quite strenuous, is found to be suited to the elderly or the weak,

C but only to those who have been blessed with robust strength in all parts of the body and who are in the best of health. Thus, it was not without the highest judgment that Cornelius Celsus said that a healthy and well-functioning man ought to sail at one time and hunt at another.
<margin>Book 1, chapter 1; Letters, book 5.</margin>
But if Pliny the Younger <note>original: "Plinius nepos"</note> seems to have once attributed his health to the hunting he performed in the countryside among the Tuscans, it must be judged either that he practiced it very moderately, or rather that he was so strong in his robust and healthy body that he was in no way harmed by the intensity of such great labor. Therefore, it will be necessary for all those desiring to enter into this exercise to diligently consider two things: first, whether they excel in bodily strength and enjoy unimpaired health; otherwise, it seems rightly doubtful whether they can avoid sustaining the gravest dangers. Second, whether they devote their efforts to hunting with a certain moderation and pleasantness, or rather without any discernment and by mere chance, as most often happens. For whoever [takes] some account of their own strength, the air, the time, the quantity, the place, and the manner...

# BOOK SIX

<margin>D</margin>
Those who wish to maintain some degree of health can certainly avoid many of the evils to which others—who exercise haphazardly—are subjected. This is all the more true because hunting has this particular characteristic, which no other exercise seems to possess in the same way: it often requires almost the entire day for itself. Consequently, hunters are either forced to take food while exercising and then undertake great labors immediately after eating—than which nothing can be more destructive to health—or they fast the whole day. Although this latter practice might perhaps be less harmful, it is still not entirely without its own dangers when done contrary to one's usual habit. Furthermore, they afterwards gorge themselves to such an extent due to hunger that they exhaust the stomach <note>original: "uentriculum"</note> in a marvelous way during digestion, and thus they undergo indigestion <note>original: "cruditates"; literally 'raw states' or undigested matter</note> and countless other evils.
